Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, Scaffold improves success rate by 11.1–17.2 absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse. We release the code and documents in the Github [repository](https://github.com/BokwaiHo/SCAFFOLD).

paper.title: How Order-Sensitive Are LLMs? OrderProbe for Deterministic Structural Reconstruction
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at semantic understanding, yet their ability to reconstruct internal structure from scrambled inputs remains underexplored. Sentence-level restoration is difficult to evaluate automatically because scrambled sentences often admit multiple valid reorderings. We introduce OrderProbe, a deterministic benchmark for structural reconstruction using fixed four-character expressions in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, which have a unique canonical order and thus support exact-match scoring. We further propose a diagnostic framework that evaluates models beyond recovery accuracy, including Semantic Accuracy, Logical Validity, Structural Consistency, Robustness, and Information Density. Experiments on twelve widely used LLMs show that structural reconstruction remains difficult even for frontier systems: zero-shot recovery frequently falls below 35%. We also observe a consistent gap between meaning-oriented generation and exact structural reconstruction, suggesting that structural robustness is not an automatic byproduct of semantic competence.

paper.title: EIBench: A Simulator-Based Benchmark and Turn-Credit RL for Emotion Management
paper.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) in large language models (LLMs) is often evaluated through static understanding tasks or single-response dialogue generation. However, emotion management is interactive. A good response should improve the user’s emotional and relational state over several turns. We introduce EIBench, a simulator-based benchmark for interactive emotion management. EIBench contains 2,222 scenarios, with 2,009 for training and 213 for held-out testing. The scenarios are organized by a 2×2 taxonomy covering Support, Defense, Repair, and Charm. We evaluate 15 open- and closed-source LLMs. Current models perform well on support and rapport-building scenes, but struggle with boundary maintenance under user pressure. To improve the EI ability of LLMs, we propose Centered Turn-Credit GRPO (CTC-GRPO), a GRPO extension that reuses the simulator’s per-turn state updates as dense turn-level feedback while preserving the final outcome reward. CTC-GRPO improves Qwen3-8B from -22.4 to +22.4 on EIBench and also improves on out-of-distribution evaluations including SAGE (+12.4) and EQBench3 (+20.9%). Our results show that simulator-tracked user states can support both evaluation and training for multi-turn emotion management.

paper.title: CoRe-MoE: Compact Reusable MoE for Continual Multimodal Instruction Tuning

author.affiliation: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Continual multimodal instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to acquire new task abilities sequentially while preserving previously learned knowledge. LoRA-MoE provides a promising solution by introducing expert-based capacity, but repeatedly learning and maintaining full LoRA experts leads to substantial parameter overhead. This raises a natural question: is full expert expansion necessary for every new task? To answer it, we analyze the SVD of task-specific LoRA updates and observe substantial overlap in their input- and output-side LoRA direction subspaces, with task-specific adaptation largely captured by lightweight coordinates over these subspaces. Motivated by this observation, we propose CoRe-MoE, a Compact Reusable MoE framework for parameter-efficient continual multimodal instruction tuning. CoRe-MoE extracts reusable input- and output-side direction bases from an initial expert bank, and for subsequent tasks trains only compact coordinate experts together with task-specific low-rank routers. Experiments on two representative MLLMs show that CoRe-MoE improves final average performance over the strongest competing baseline by up to 5.90 points, while using less than 1% of the trainable parameters required by sequential LoRA for later tasks.

paper.title: Modality Fault Lines: Structural Corruptions Reveal Fragile Omni-Modal Reasoning
paper.abstract: Omni-modal large language models are increasingly evaluated on clean text–vision–audio inputs, where every channel is present, synchronized, and readily interpretable. Such scores are often taken as evidence of robust cross-modal fusion, but clean evaluation cannot tell whether success depends on stable cross-modal structure or on cues sufficient only in intact inputs. To address this gap, we define a modality fault line: a boundary at which model behavior becomes unstable when a modality remains present and human-interpretable, but its internal evidence structure is perturbed. We introduce SCEval (Structure-Corruption Evaluation) a diagnostic evaluation protocol that keeps the question, answer space, and modality channels fixed while applying controlled structural corruptions to text, vision, and audio individually and jointly. Built from 273 human-verified tri-modal examples from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR, SCEval evaluates 15 proprietary and open-source omni-modal systems. The results show that structural corruption lowers clean accuracy, text–vision damage forms the most stable shared fault line, and multi-modal degradation is non-additive rather than a simple function of the number of corrupted modalities. Clean omni-modal accuracy therefore does not establish that a model will remain reliable when cross-modal evidence becomes structurally unreliable.

paper.title: Diagnosing Order Dependence in Vision-Language Task-Progress Judgment with Equal-State Supervision
paper.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to embodied task settings, yet it remains unclear whether their task-progress judgments are grounded in physical state comparison or in input-order shortcuts. We study a diagnostic two-frame setting: given two robot manipulation states and a task goal, the model must decide which state is closer to completion, or whether the two states are effectively equal. We observe a strong Forward-Backward Performance Gap: models often answer correctly in the natural forward order, but fail when the same two physical states are shown with their image slots swapped. This reversal is not intended to mimic the dominant deployment order of robot execution; rather, it is a counterfactual diagnostic for testing whether the selected physical state remains consistent under input-slot inversion. To reduce this order dependence, we introduce Equal-State supervision as a zero-point calibration signal, training models to output equal when no task-relevant progress difference is present instead of defaulting to a directional answer. From real manipulation videos, we construct the Embodied Causal-Temporal Reasoning (ECTR) dataset and propose Tri-Stage Weighted Alignment (TSWA), a staged fine-tuning procedure that strengthens spatial description, task-conditioned comparison, and answer calibration in sequence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, TSWA reduces GAP from 60.50% to 5.14% and raises overall accuracy from 44.66% to 80.19%. This comes with a small decrease in forward accuracy, but large gains in backward accuracy, equal-state recognition, and pairwise consistency, suggesting that TSWA replaces order-dependent correctness with more calibrated state comparison.

paper.title: RegioZH: Unveiling Comprehension Disparities across Regional Chinese Varieties in LLMs

author.affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design and A*STAR
Singapore University of Technology and Design

paper.abstract: Current evaluations often treat Chinese varieties as monolithic, obscuring failures for regional users. We introduce RegioZH, a 2,607-item multiple-choice benchmark for regional lexical reasoning across Mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. Built by region-specific annotators and expert-validated, it targets localized idioms, slang, code-mixing, politeness conventions, and sociocultural expressions. Zero-shot results on eleven LLMs show large disparities, including a 29.4-point average accuracy gap between Taiwan and Singapore. Persona and structured chain-of-thought prompts for five models yield selective gains, suggesting that some errors stem from retrieval or framing rather than only missing knowledge. Representation, attention, calibration, and surface-feature analyses show a dissociation between marker attention and semantic grounding, overconfident forced-choice errors, and localized lexical density as a consistent difficulty predictor. Qualitative analysis finds terminology misunderstandings, sociocultural inference gaps, and cross-regional semantic divergence. RegioZH demonstrates that apparent Chinese proficiency can mask uneven understanding across regional varieties, motivating intra-language robustness evaluation alongside multilingual generalization.

paper.title: Cascade: Hierarchical Recoverability Control for Large Language Model Unlearning

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or copyrighted knowledge while preserving general utility. Existing methods often leave residual knowledge in intermediate representations, which can still be recovered. To address this, we propose Cascade, a hierarchical recoverability control framework that minimizes the internal identifiability of target knowledge. Cascade combines three complementary controls: path-level routing to suppress privacy-associated activation routes, representation-level compression to reduce geometric separability, and decoding-level intervention to limit residual recovery. Experiments on TOFU, MUSE-News, and WMDP, including robustness tests with query reformulation and extraction-style prompts, show that Cascade effectively reduces recoverability while maintaining stable model utility.

paper.title: PeLA: Prompt-Enhanced Logit Adaptation for Personality-Trait Steering in LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in long-running user-facing applications where responses may need to maintain a consistent interaction style. Prompting is easy to reuse but often weak, while fine-tuning and representation interventions can be stronger but are typically model-specific. We present PeLA, Prompt-Enhanced Logit Adaptation, a parameter-efficient framework for Big Five personality-trait steering. PeLA keeps the base LLM frozen, uses a personality prompt to specify the desired trait direction, and applies a learned logit adapter during decoding. The adapter contributes a base-relative residual controlled by a token-position gate, refining the prompt-conditioned distribution only when intervention is useful. Because the control module operates in output-token space, it can be reused across models with identical tokenizer vocabularies and token-id order. On open-ended PersonalityBench questions, PeLA improves macro-average target-direction scores over a strong Personality Prompt baseline on Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, while cross-size experiments demonstrate tokenizer-compatible transfer within both the Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 families after validation-based scale calibration. PeLA narrows the gap to model-specific steering while preserving a frozen base model.

paper.title: Evidence Absence Is Not Evidence Insufficiency: Diagnosing NEI Construction Artifacts in Fact Verification
paper.abstract: Evidence absence is not evidence insufficiency, but fact verification benchmarks can make them observationally similar. The Not Enough Information (NEI) label is often operationalized through constructed evidence conditions, and that choice silently determines what a verifier learns. We introduce NEI-CAP, a construction-aware diagnostic protocol for insufficient-evidence evaluation. Each NEI example carries the construction family that produced it; NEI-CAP audits shortcut cues, validates hard cases through human adjudication, and tests whether competence transfers across constructions. We instantiate the protocol on SciFact, with FEVER and HoVer as bounded external controls. Across these settings, NEI competence does not transfer reliably: encoder verifiers and an instruction-tuned decoder trained on shortcut-prone constructions fail to recognize semantically related insufficient evidence, and mixed-construction training narrows but does not close the gap. Fixed-claim diagnostics further show that the evidence condition shifts confidence in the reference Support/Refute label, not only NEI recall, so an aggregate NEI score can hide which problem a model has actually solved. We therefore recommend reporting the construction family alongside the score, and distill the results into a checklist for benchmarks that carry an insufficient-evidence label.

paper.title: CoEffi: Enhance Efficient Code Generation via Dynamic Collaborative Decoding
paper.abstract: Code LLMs exhibit remarkable capabilities in automated code generation, but the generated code often suffers from low computational efficiency. Existing solutions have two limitations: (1) direct fine-tuning lacks transferability across model scales; (2) The efficiency optimization method for iterative generation-evaluation loops incurs high overhead. We propose CoEffi, which adopts inference-side intervention that directly operates on the decoding process without modifying base model parameters, enabling real-time efficiency improvement across different model scales while avoiding iterative reevaluation. CoEffi uses a small efficiency expert model for proposal and the base model to evaluate its acceptability, additionally introducing a region-aware dynamic acceptance threshold mechanism that maintains a sliding window to record historical acceptance rates and adjusts the dynamic threshold accordingly. We extensively evaluate CoEffi on four mainstream code LLM families and three efficiency benchmarks. Compared with vanilla instruction-tuned models, CoEffi improves average Beyond@1 by 9.12%–38.62% across the evaluated model families. It also improves Pass@1 on Mercury and ENAMEL, while EffiBench exhibits model-dependent correctness gains and regressions. A family specific trained expert can be reused across compatible base model scales within the same model family.

paper.title: A Cross-lingual Comparison of Human and Classification Model Entrainment Behavior in Code-switched Speech Settings
paper.abstract: Conversational entrainment is well-studied in monolingual and written contexts, but remains underexplored in spoken code-switching (CSW). We present a cross-lingual analysis of entrainment in Mandarin-English, Hindi-English, and Spanish-English dialogue, replicating and extending an established Spanish-English framework (Bhattacharya et al., 2024) to two new language pairs, and show that, while lexical entrainment generalizes across language pairs, entrainment over acoustic-prosodic and CSW style aspects exhibits context-specific variation. We build on these findings by asking whether classification models capture these human behavioral patterns. Using feature importance and ablation analyses, we find that classical and Transformer-based classifiers detect entrainment reasonably well but consistently prioritize features other than those most salient to human entraining behavior. Our approach introduces a human-grounded framework for evaluating model decision-making in multilingual stylistic contexts, and suggests challenges for developing conversational agents capable of producing naturalistic code-switched speech.

paper.title: KV Cache Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TraceKV and KProtect. TraceKV reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. KProtect uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, KProtect achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.

paper.title: Improving Information Extraction with Learned Queries

author.affiliation: Dartmouth College and Massachusetts Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: When information extraction fails, a natural instinct is to improve the model doing it: for example, by scaling it up or refining its reasoning. In this paper, we show that another part of the pipeline matters at least as much: the queries used to elicit this information. Across four clinical benchmarks and five LLMs, improving the question design alone raises performance by 18.6 F1-score points, i.e. more than using larger extraction models. To make such question design learnable, we introduce List of Questions (LoQ), which generates document-specific question sets, and FeedQ, a feedback-driven optimization method that iteratively refines questions against extraction outcomes. The resulting optimized questions can be used to train lightweight generators: with fine-tuning, 4B-parameter models match or outperform expert-derived baselines and substantially exceed the performance of much larger untuned models. We release a dataset of 12,820 optimized questions to support a broader shift in information extraction research toward treating question design as a first-class problem.

paper.title: Beyond Single Gold Labels: Human Variability and Conceptualisation in Chinese Classifier Use
paper.abstract: Chinese classifier prediction is often evaluated as a single-label classification problem, assuming one gold classifier for each context. We argue that this assumption overlooks the inherent variability and conceptual nature of classifier use. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying Chinese classifiers in humans and vision-language models across three tasks: Classifier Choice, Head Noun Completion, and Referring Expression Generation. Based on a human behavioural dataset, we evaluate models against human response distributions rather than single gold labels. Our results show that classifier use is shaped by noun specificity, animacy, and task setting, and that models differ from humans not only in classifier choice but also in classifier-mediated conceptualisation. Although explicitly encoding the behavioural patterns learned from the human experiments into prompts improves model alignment with human behaviour, especially for smaller models, its effect is uneven across tasks: it helps models better match dominant human preferences, but does not enable them to reproduce the full distribution of human variability or fully close the gap in natural generation settings.

paper.title: From Topical Relevance to Answerability: Entailment Distillation for Conversational Retrieval

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Southwest University of Finance and Economics
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Existing conversational retrievers commonly treat topical relevance as a proxy for answerability. However, a passage that closely matches the dialogue context is not necessarily the one that supports the correct answer. We identify this mismatch as a systematic answerability gap. To address this issue, we propose CLEAR, a framework that shifts conversational retrieval from topical relevance to answerability. The core of CLEAR is entailment distillation, which transfers answer-passage entailment supervision into a cross-encoder reranker so that the reranker discriminates answer-supporting passages from topical distractors at inference time, without requiring answers. CLEAR is complemented by a passage-centric abductive recall module that brings low-similarity yet answerable passages into the candidate pool by inferring answerable queries from passages with an LLM. Across TopiOCQA, QReCC, and out-of-domain TREC CAsT datasets, CLEAR consistently improves top-ranked precision over strong query-rewriting and dense-retrieval baselines, with the largest gains observed in conversations involving heavier topical noise. Moreover, applying our reranker on top of an LLM-driven query rewriter yields further gains.

paper.title: DualEval: Joint Model-Item Calibration for Unified LLM Evaluation

author.affiliation: LMArena and University of California, Los Angeles

paper.abstract: Current LLM evaluation relies on two complementary but often disconnected signals: static benchmarks with objective correctness labels and arena-style preference data that better reflect open-ended user interactions. We introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that represents models and evaluation items in a shared space, jointly estimating model ability together with item difficulty and sharpness. We apply DualEval across four domains: coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic everyday user queries. Our evaluation uses 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences for open-ended model responses. Empirically, our framework produces reliable and balanced model rankings, and its learned item-level profiles support downstream applications such as benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis. Overall, DualEval unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, producing model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.

paper.title: PaperGraph-Bench: Graph-Guided Benchmark Construction and Multi-Turn Evaluation for Scientific Paper Reading

author.affiliation: Wuhan University and Shanghai Innovation Institute

paper.abstract: Scientific-paper reading requires models to recover a paper’s core argument, connect claims to textual and multimodal evidence, and avoid unsupported inferences across dialogue turns. We introduce PaperGraph-Bench, a graph-guided benchmark that turns each paper into a paper-specific evaluation state graph with macro stages, evidence-grounded knowledge components (KCs), verified reasoning edges, multimodal assets, rubrics, and trajectory state. The graph drives macro coverage questions, challenge questions, reasoning threads, and bounded repair turns, while the evaluator tracks KC coverage, challenge failures, hallucination events, and repair outcomes. Experiments on a human-audited prototype with ten models show that coverage, robustness, hallucination type, and repair behavior reveal distinct paper-reading abilities. Our code and current dataset are available at https://github.com/furao0011/PaperGraphBench.

paper.title: Know When to Reflect: Entropy-Guided Adaptive Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Self-correction has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing LLM reasoning, yet recent studies reveal a troubling phenomenon: without external oracle feedback, iterative reflection often degrades rather than improves performance. Our analysis uncovers that toxic reflection, where correct answers deteriorate into incorrect ones, occurs at rates comparable to effective corrections. We identify the root cause as the shortsightedness of existing methods: models focus only on the previous output while neglecting the global reasoning state, rendering them unable to quantify uncertainty. To address this, we propose two complementary reflection signals — Reflecting Entropy for snapshot disagreement among reasoning trajectories and Belief Shift for inter-round belief revision — paired with a two-stage hierarchical controller that schedules reflection adaptively. We instantiate these ideas as REGAR (Reflecting Entropy-Guided Adaptive Reflection), a framework that maintains a pool of candidate reasoning trajectories and applies a single, uniform reflection primitive when correction is needed. Experiments on mathematical and commonsense reasoning demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines while reducing computational overhead, highlighting both effectiveness and efficiency.

paper.title: Take Only What You Need: Rank Minimization as an Implicit Forgetting Regularizer in Continual Learning
paper.abstract: The central tension in continual learning (CL) is the trade-off between plasticity (acquiring new knowledge) and stability (retaining prior knowledge). We study how a pre-trained backbone can be continually updated to absorb new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities, via capacity control: regulating the effective rank of each parameter update, a per-step quantity directly controllable inside a LoRA update. A controlled probe of LoRA rank and placement across modules and tasks reveals a consistent trade-off, with a moderate-rank sweet spot that varies by placement and task, leaving no universally optimal fixed rank; a formal bound shows forgetting grows with rank. Building on these findings, we propose Continual Dynamic Rank-Selective LoRA (CoDyRA), which jointly trains each LoRA update with rank minimization via sparsity-promoting regularization on per-component importance weights. The supervised objective drives plasticity; rank minimization regularizes forgetting. We show that rank minimization serves as an implicit forgetting regularizer in the CL regime, protecting general capability and prior-task knowledge simultaneously by controlling forgetting against the current model state. Across MTIL, X-TAIL, and TRACE (CLIP, LLaMA, Gemma), CoDyRA outperforms prior CL methods on new knowledge learning and forgetting, achieving a strong plasticity–stability balance. Project page: https://artificer-ai-lab.github.io/CoDyRA.

paper.title: The Illusion of \textit{What If}: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs
paper.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present \textbf{WhatIfBench}, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose \textbf{PRISM}, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.

paper.title: IterInject: Indirect Prompt Injection Against LLM Agents via Feedback-Guided Iterative Optimization
paper.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for complex tasks requiring planning, tool use, and interaction with external services. Their reliance on untrusted external content exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack agent behavior. Existing attacks rely on static payloads that cannot adapt to agent-specific defenses; even recent adaptive methods lack structured feedback to guide optimization. We introduce IterInject, a feedback-guided iterative framework that closes the loop between injection, diagnosis, and refinement: a rule-based diagnoser produces structured outcome labels with behavioral descriptions, and an LLM-based optimizer refines payloads conditioned on the full optimization history. A synthesis step generates new disguise seeds from failure patterns, enabling the strategy space to self-evolve. On AgentDojo and InjectAgent, IterInject substantially outperforms static baselines and existing adaptive methods across four victim models. Extension experiments on Claude Code, a production-grade coding agent with layered defenses, show that optimized payloads achieve full success on 5 of 9 targets; even those that resist full exploitation exhibit measurable improvement from iterative refinement. We further present a mechanistic analysis of IPI, identifying an attention-mediated threshold mechanism in mid-to-late layers; three causal interventions validate this finding and point to concrete defense directions.

paper.title: Typology-Aware Dual-Track: Detecting Hybrid AI Text Across Languages
paper.abstract: Existing generalist detectors, such as mDeBERTa based classifiers, struggle with fine-grained AI-text detection in multilingual settings, particularly when hybrid authorship and morphologically rich languages obscure machine-generated artifacts. We propose a typology-aware Smart Routing Late Fusion Framework for 4-class detection: Human-Written (HW), Machine-Generated (MG), Machine-Humanized (MH), and Human-Polished (HM). The framework consists of two complementary tracks. Branch A targets agglutinative languages, including Korean, Turkish, and Hungarian, using error focused hard-negative refinement and Dependency Distance Minimization(DDM) / Uniform Information Density(UID) based pairwise calibration to recover weak generative signals hidden by dense morphology. Branch B applies RADAR-inspired invariant learning to capture machine-originated artifacts that persist after adversarial rewriting in languages with clearer segmentation cues. Experiments across eight languages show that typology-aware routing improves detection in agglutinative languages while maintaining strong multilingual performance. Our results highlight the importance of modeling both linguistic typology and hybrid authorship for robust multilingual AI-text detection.

paper.title: LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: Students increasingly use LLMs as tutors for coursework and problem solving. Little is known about the level of assistance LLMs provide when students use them as tutors in authentic learning interactions. This matters because tutoring responses can differ substantially in how directly they help students complete a task. We operationalize this dimension as scaffolding level and develop a five-level scale, validated against human annotations, that characterizes responses according to the degree of direct assistance they provide. We apply the scale to 14,637 LLM responses from 203 students in a university AI course, where the model received no pedagogical instruction beyond a generic helpful-assistant system prompt. Responses are overwhelmingly concentrated at high levels of assistance, with more than 95% classified as either Explaining or Solving. Scaffolding level is systematically associated with students’ subsequent conversational behavior, but provides little additional predictive information about performance on three subsequent exams beyond prior achievement and dialogue behavior. These findings provide an empirical baseline for LLM assistance in tutoring interactions and a measurement framework for evaluating how alternative tutoring designs change that assistance.

paper.title: Style-Ruler: Inference-Only Stylized Translation via Unsupervised Extraction and Agentic Collaboration
paper.abstract: While Large Language Models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in general machine translation, they frequently struggle to adhere to complex stylistic nuances and lexical constraints strictly and often revert to a neutral style. The scarcity of style-specific parallel data hinders existing solutions, whereas standard prompting lacks rigorous verification mechanisms. To bridge this gap, we propose Style-Ruler, an inference-only agentic framework that operationalizes style via unsupervised extraction and neuro-symbolic verification. Style-Ruler orchestrates three specialized agents: (1) a Style-Reverse Analyst (SRA) that mines quantifiable linguistic constraints from monolingual reference texts via unsupervised extraction; (2) a Constraint-Adaptive Translator (CAT) that employs a Style-Chain-of-Thought mechanism to plan stylistic adherence before generation explicitly; and (3) a Sandbox-Augmented Auditor (SAA) that provides heterogeneous feedback through deterministic code execution. These components form a closed-loop refinement mechanism where symbolic logic guides neural generation. Extensive experiments on the GuoFeng Webnovel dataset and WMT24++ benchmark demonstrate the superiority of our approach. Style-Ruler achieves a CSR of 82.4% on stylized translation, surpassing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by over 50%, while improving BLEU scores by +1.0 on En\toZh.

paper.title: Diagnosing Subword Boundary Conflicts in Diffusion Language Models through Sentence Simplification
paper.abstract: Sentence simplification is a source-grounded rewriting task in which outputs often keep parts of the source while editing adjacent spans. Diffusion language models (DLMs) are well suited to this setting because masked denoising can fill rewritten spans using bidirectional context. However, parallel filling can create subword-boundary errors when incompatible subword fragments are committed together. We define these errors as Subword Boundary Conflicts (SBCs): malformed output words, such as Australianways, formed from incompatible fragments at subword boundaries. To measure them, we introduce a surface-form taxonomy and a detection pipeline based on candidate extraction, LLM-as-a-Judge filtering, and human verification. We evaluate Dream and LLaDA variants on ASSET and MED-EASi, with autoregressive and task-specific simplification baselines. We find that SBCs occur across DLMs but vary by model. Under standard unmasking, LLaDA variants remain at or below 2.80%, whereas Dream-7B-Instruct reaches 6.32% on ASSET and 9.03% on MED-EASi. Beyond model choice, decoding parallelism is a key driver. In the Dream unmasking setting at 128 denoising steps, increasing parallelism from 1 to 4 raises SBC rates from near zero to 25.63% on ASSET and 34.67% on MED-EASi. Further analyses show that SBCs occur under light-to-moderate edits, are not limited to rare words, and can often be repaired by local masked span regeneration. These findings establish SBCs as a word-form reliability target for robust diffusion-based text generation.

paper.title: RouteVerify: A Diagnostic Study of Tool-Augmented Chest X-ray Agents

author.affiliation: Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)

paper.abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents promise clinical control and interpretability, yet their specialized outputs are often invoked broadly and compressed into text. It remains unclear whether failures arise from this textual interface or low-fidelity upstream tools. We study this question through RouteVerify, a transparent diagnostic sandbox combining a lightweight linear router, compact evidence cards, and verifier-gated multimodal reinspection. On matched and held-out ChestAgentBench splits, RouteVerify improves answer accuracy by about seven points over naive always-call-tools execution while roughly halving token use. However, it remains about two points below a direct VLM-only baseline and uses nearly twice the tokens. Oracle probes clarify the bottleneck: replacing predicted evidence with benchmark-side gold explanations raises the same downstream text reasoner above 95 percent accuracy, or above 91 percent after removing explicit answer cues. Thus, text cards can express sufficient evidence on this benchmark; the dominant practical limitation is upstream tool quality. An external JSRT/SCR audit supports this diagnosis, revealing limited nodule-classification discrimination and structure-dependent segmentation quality. The remaining raw-versus-sanitized oracle gap also indicates sensitivity to human-authored cues. We present RouteVerify as an empirical boundary study of where current tool-augmented medical agents fail.

paper.title: ARIA: Affect-Responsive Interaction Alignment for Emotional Support Policies via Implicit Multimodal Affective Feedback
paper.abstract: Effective emotional-support dialogue requires more than fluent empathy: responses must adapt to the support seeker’s evolving state. Existing emotional-support systems are largely optimized at the response level and may therefore learn the form of supportive counseling without reliably adapting to client-side change. We introduce ARIA, Affect-Responsive Interaction Alignment, a client-centered alignment framework that constructs DPO preference pairs from the support seeker’s subsequent multimodal affective trajectories observed in human interactions. ARIA distills audio- and visual-derived valence trajectories into text-based predictors and uses cross-modal consensus and uncertainty-aware filtering to identify high-confidence preferences associated with delayed client-side valence improvement. Experiments show that ARIA improves process-oriented measures of client progress beyond surface compliance and produces support that is more timely and calibrated to the seeker’s evolving openness. Behavioral analyses further show a phase-sensitive shift from restrained pre-open support toward more active support after openness emerges. Human and counseling-expert evaluations provide evidence that ARIA’s responses are more timely, targeted, and supportive of the client’s own process.

paper.title: Learning Solvability Boundaries in LLMs: Improving Reasoning, Detecting Unsolvability, and Calibrating Refusal
paper.abstract: Reasoning alignment usually assumes each query has a determinate answer, rewarding models for reaching it and penalizing or ignoring failures. This assumption breaks on flawed queries with missing information or contradictory constraints, causing models to hallucinate invalid answers or over-refuse difficult valid tasks. We study this failure mode as solvability boundary learning: separating input-side answerability defects from model-side inability on well-posed tasks. To address this, we introduce UnsolvableQA, a verifier-backed multi-domain benchmark built with deterministic checks and audited math verification, and UnsolvableRL, an alignment framework that decouples reasoning, unsolvability detection, and capability-calibrated refusal. UnsolvableRL yields over 85% unsolvability detection on Qwen3-4B while improving solvable accuracy from 43.4% to 69.4%, with a +35.4-point solvable-accuracy gain on Llama3-8B. Diagnostic tuning further distinguishes missing-information defects from constraint conflicts and transfers to interactive clarification, improving Detail Recovery from 47.8% to 60.7% for Llama3-8B. Ablations reveal Capability Collapse: refusal penalties degrade detection without unsolvable data, but act as a rigor regularizer when such data are included.

paper.title: Decoupled Analysis-Judging: An Automated Creativity Evaluator Using LLMs in Complex Multi-step Creativity Tasks
paper.abstract: Automated evaluation of creativity tasks remains challenging for LLM-as-a-Judge, as LLM is susceptible to biases such as verbosity bias and leniency bias. Such limitations are particularly evident in Contextually-Grounded and Procedurally-Structured Tasks (CGPST), a complex multi-step creativity task where inter-step dependencies, highly subjectivity, and wide scoring ranges lead to more unstable and biased judgments. Existing approaches either rely on task-specific training or directly apply LLM-as-a-Judge, both of which struggle to ensure reliable evaluation under such complexity. To bridge these gaps, we propose **CreaEval**, an automated **crea**tivity **eval**uator for CGPST that decouples typical LLM-as-a-Judge into analysis and judging. Correspondingly, CreaEval involves two critical phases: **Memory-augmented Analysis**, a SoT-LLM converts multi-step responses into structured evaluation evidence, incorporating cross-step memory; and **Evidence-based Judging**, a Judge-LLM uses the extracted evidence for judging without accessing raw responses. Comprehensive experiments on CGPST show that CreaEval achieves an average human-LLM agreement of 0.64 (QWK) on CGPST, improving over the second-best baseline (supervised training) by 0.17. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CreaEval-0058/.

paper.title: IA-RAG: Interval-Algebra–Driven Temporal Reasoning for Dynamic Knowledge Retrieval

author.affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Harbin Engineering University

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has shown strong effectiveness in grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge. However, existing RAG and Graph RAG frameworks largely treat knowledge as static or associate time with coarse-grained timestamps or metadata, failing to capture rich temporal structures such as duration, overlap, and containment. We propose IA-RAG, a hierarchical temporal RAG framework that models knowledge as time intervals and performs retrieval under formal temporal constraints. IA-RAG represents facts as Interval Event Units (IEUs) and organizes them into a hierarchical Thematic Forest, where temporal dependencies are governed by Allen’s Interval Algebra. To handle incomplete or uncertain temporal boundaries, IA-RAG further introduces a Sub-graph Time Tightening mechanism that refines fuzzy intervals through logical constraints within connected event subgraphs. In addition, IA-RAG supports implicit temporal semantic retrieval through interval-algebra-guided traversal. Experiments on multiple temporal question answering benchmarks, including TimeQA, TempReason, and ComplexTR, demonstrate that IA-RAG achieves strong temporal retrieval and reasoning performance, particularly on complex compositional temporal reasoning tasks. Our code is released at https://github.com/xiaoAugenstern/IA-RAG.

paper.title: CHisAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Event Taxonomy Construction in Ancient Chinese Cultural Systems
paper.abstract: Due to the long temporal span and highly diverse expressions in historical documents, large language models (LLMs) still struggle with historical and cultural reasoning in Chinese history. Although taxonomic structures can effectively organize historical knowledge and facilitate knowledge-rich applications, existing historical taxonomies remain limited due to the high cost of manual construction. To address this limitation, we propose CHisAgent, a multi-agent LLM framework for automated historical taxonomy induction in ancient Chinese history. CHisAgent explicitly decomposes taxonomy construction into three role-specialized stages: a bottom-up Inducer that derives an initial hierarchy from raw historical corpora, a top-down Expander that introduces missing intermediate concepts using LLM world knowledge, and an evidence-guided Enricher that integrates external structured historical resources to ensure faithfulness. Extensive reference-free and reference-based evaluations show that the collaboration among these agents improves taxonomy coverage and hierarchical completeness, while further analysis suggests that the induced taxonomy facilitates cross-cultural alignment of historical concepts. Code and experimental data are available at https://github.com/tangxuemei1995/CHisAgent.

paper.title: Grounding Structure in Language: Enriching Symbolic Representations for Molecular Reasoning

author.affiliation: A*STAR Centre for Frontier AI Research (A*STAR CFAR) and Nanyang Technological University

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for scientific applications but struggle when domain knowledge is encoded in complex structures. Chemistry exemplifies this challenge: molecular structures encode rich relational data that dictates chemical meaning, yet standard formats like SMILES obscure this through arbitrary linearization. In this work, we systematically characterize which structural information lost during linearization most severely hampers LLM reasoning, decomposing the problem into IUPAC-grounded dimensions: substituent positions (locants), attachment points (anchoring), and modification constraints (valency). Our diagnostic reveals non-uniform failures across dimensions, with locant identification being especially challenging. We directly address the failures by grounding the linearized representations in structural context with each component targeting its corresponding diagnostic dimension. General-purpose LLMs with explicit grounding can outperform chemistry-specialized models on structure-aware molecule manipulation, suggesting structural context can compensate for domain-specific training. Moreover, we investigate a training-free inductive protocol that nearly doubles the accuracy of weaker models. These results point toward explicit structural grounding as a principled path to more reliable molecular reasoning across model scales.

paper.title: A Four-Stage Decomposition of Word-Problem Solving and Mechanistic Fragility in LLM Math Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large language models solve grade-school math word problems with high accuracy, yet a single irrelevant clause inserted into the problem can collapse it. We reconcile these observations with a mechanistic account. We show that the model’s internal computation decomposes into a four-stage sequential pipeline, Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation, each stage producing a distinct intermediate representation in an identifiable band of layers. Using the same scaffold to diagnose distractor-induced failure, we localize the corruption to a single stage, Operation Planning, implemented by a set of attention heads whose causal role we validate bidirectionally. In short, we provide a mechanistic interpretation of math word problem reasoning in LLMs, and their failure when distracted.

paper.title: ReimburseBench: Benchmarking LMMs as Full-Workflow Auditors for Financial Internal Control
paper.abstract: Expense reimbursement internal control is a high-stakes corporate finance task that combines multimodal, visually rich evidence (e.g., receipts and approval forms), firm-specific policy text, and multi-step compliance reasoning. No existing benchmark evaluates large multimodal models (LMMs) in this domain. We introduce ReimburseBench, the first benchmark targeting full-workflow multimodal audit reasoning in corporate internal control. It comprises 151 expert-constructed reimbursement workflows, each packaging an application, receipts and supporting documents, and a firm-specific policy, evaluated by a process-level rubric grounded in twelve auditing logic points. Benchmarking nine frontier and locally deployable systems, we find the strongest attains only 72.5%, and no model exceeds 47.7% on hard workflows. Beyond this aggregate score, risk-aware, process-level evaluation surfaces three structural findings: (i) a persistent gap between binary admissibility judgment and precise quantitative computation; (ii) a systematic lenient bias in monetary predictions that poses deployment risk; and (iii) a performance pattern consistent with compositional-generalization difficulties under realistic workflow load. We provide ReimburseBench as a testbed for advancing LMMs toward trustworthy financial systems. Data and code: https://github.com/ikerzhan/ReimburseBench.

paper.title: PersonaTree: Structured Lifecycle Memory for Person Understanding in LLM Agents

author.affiliation: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Persistent LLM agents require memory representations that make the formation of person understanding explicit across long term interaction. Existing agent memory methods emphasize information retention and retrieval, yet give limited account of how accumulated interaction evidence is abstracted into person understanding. We view this process as schema formation, where situated evidence is abstracted into reusable patterns and stable person level claims. We introduce PersonaTree, a structured lifecycle memory framework that realizes this view as a three level persona tree with explicit support paths from evidence to claims. PersonaTree maintains the tree through conservative writing, confidence guided consolidation, and query conditioned path retrieval, returning only the evidence depth required by each query. Across six person understanding and persistent memory benchmarks with three answer backbones, PersonaTree ranks first in 12 of 18 compact scores and reaches the top two in 16 settings. Ablations show that hierarchy improves abstract person understanding on KnowMe, while support path retrieval improves RealPref alignment under a comparable context budget.

paper.title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?

author.affiliation: Borealis AI and University of Alberta

paper.abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

paper.title: From AI Scientists to AI Scientific Communities: A Survey of Collective AutoResearch
paper.abstract: Scientific research is not merely a sequence of tasks to be automated, but a knowledge-production process in which claims must remain verifiable, criticizable, revisable, and accountable. Yet most AutoResearch systems remain single scaffolds that collapse generation, execution, interpretation, and review into one loop. This survey diagnoses three resulting epistemic limits of such architectures: collapsed skepticism, where a single scaffold produces not only errors but also the narratives that allow them to survive; unverified translation from discovery to application, where proposal generation outpaces independent verification; and invisible evidence trails, where final manuscripts hide the failed attempts and post-hoc decisions that produced them. To overcome these structural fragilities, we propose a shift from autonomous AI scientists to AI research communities, where specialized agents, shared memory, inspectable artifacts, and governance checkpoints distribute epistemic labor. We synthesize AutoResearch as a transition from metric-driven search loops to AI-scientist workflows, domain-mediated discovery, research infrastructure, and accountable human–AI co-evolution. Across these layers, we argue for a fundamental shift from productivity-centered evaluation to verifiability-centered evaluation.

paper.title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Peking University and Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn setting. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over that representation before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our main evaluation, twelve current LLMs achieve only 27.5%–51.0% aggregate pass rate on 490 scenarios. The failures show that current LLMs can remain fluent and cooperative while losing the global state of the conversation, exposing a gap between conversational helpfulness and robust requirement reconciliation.

paper.title: ProtSynGen: Knowledge Graph-Guided Open-Ended Data Synthesis for Protein LLMs
paper.abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) depends critically on the quality of their instruction-tuning data. For protein LLMs, existing instruction-tuning datasets are typically derived from structured protein annotations through template-based or label-guided generation. Although these datasets capture important biological facts, their construction paradigms often lead to two limitations: instruction homogenization and reasoning superficiality. The former refers to questions concentrating around repetitive forms and narrow topics; the latter to answers relying on shallow annotation lookup rather than evidence-rich biological reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose ProtSynGen, a knowledge graph-guided open-ended data synthesis framework for protein LLMs. ProtSynGen integrates structured protein databases with unstructured scientific literature into a protein-centric knowledge graph, and uses hierarchical graph sampling to guide LLMs in generating open-ended QAs across atomic, aggregated, and complex reasoning scenarios. Experiments show that ProtSynGen produces instruction-tuning data with broader topic coverage, richer reasoning depth, and stronger quality metrics than existing protein LLM instruction datasets. Models trained on ProtSynGen data further achieve superior performance on open-ended protein QA benchmarks, consistently outperforming baseline methods across atomic, aggregated, and complex reasoning scenarios.

paper.title: BanglaMemeX: Advancing Cultural Metaphoric Image Interpretation in Bangla with a Multimodal Explainable Dataset
paper.abstract: Vision Language Models have achieved strong performance on multimodal benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about culturally grounded and metaphor-rich content remains insufficiently studied. Internet memes present a challenging setting where meaning emerges from implicit interactions between image, overlaid text, sarcasm, and shared socio-cultural knowledge rather than literal visual recognition. This challenge is amplified in low-resource languages such as Bangla, where code-mixing, stylized scripts, and culturally specific symbolism introduce substantial distribution shift. In this work, we introduce **BanglaMemeX**, a culturally grounded multimodal benchmark comprising 3,000 Bangla memes annotated with multi-dimensional labels (humor, sarcasm, offensiveness, motivational intent, and overall sentiment) and human-written explanations that explicitly describe textual and visual metaphors. We systematically evaluate modern VLMs on both classification and explanation generation, revealing that current models struggle to interpret implicit cultural cues despite reasonable surface-level accuracy. Our results highlight the need for culturally-aware multimodal systems capable of grounded reasoning under linguistic and cultural distribution shift.

paper.title: SignFLIP: A Unified Model for Sign Language Translation and Generation via Stage-wise Alignment at Scale

author.affiliation: Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Sign language translation and generation share the goal of bidirectional alignment between text and sign representations. However, existing approaches either treat them as isolated tasks or are only verified on limited datasets, limiting effective modeling between modalities. In this paper, we propose SignFLIP, a unified LLM-centered framework for translation and generation. To enable bidirectional mapping between text and sign, SignFLIP adopts a symmetric architecture together with a stage-wise training strategy built on large-scale data. The shared sign–text representation is progressively refined: pre-alignment facilitates subsequent SLT, while the SLT-adapted representation further benefits SLG. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SignFLIP shows competitive performance compared with task-specific models on both translation and generation tasks, as well as strong transferability to sign language recognition.

paper.title: Title It Right: Faithful and Attractive Paper Title Generation via Pareto Dominance Alignment

author.affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Computer Network Information Center (CNIC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS)
Computer Network Information Center (CNIC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and Computer Network Information Center (CNIC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS)
Computer Network Information Center., Chinese Academy of Sciences
Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Generating academic paper titles requires balancing two key goals: faithfulness to the content and attractiveness to readers. Existing methods often treat title generation as a simple summarization task, producing accurate but unengaging titles. While multi-objective Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) offers a potential solution, our empirical analysis shows that combining conflicting objectives into a single reward is associated with substantial gradient interference during training. To address this problem, drawing inspiration from Pareto dominance in multi-objective optimization, we propose Multi-Objective Dominance Alignment (MODA), a data-centric training strategy tailored for academic title generation. MODA retains preference pairs with strict Pareto dominance, thereby reducing exposure to supervision with opposing reward directions. We implement MODA using dual reward models to independently score both dimensions. Across our experiments, this filtering strategy improves the observed balance between faithfulness and attractiveness, outperforms Human Author baselines, and approaches the performance of frontier models despite using an 8B backbone. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/realyoume/title_it_right.

paper.title: RecoverAgent: Intent-Preserving Recovery from Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-using LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents execute multi-step tasks by iteratively reasoning and interacting with external tools. However, they are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in tool outputs can divert benign user intents into unsafe actions or unintended goals. Existing defenses mainly prioritize reducing unsafe behaviors, while paying limited attention to preserving the original user intent. As a result, safety improvements may come at the cost of interrupting execution or distorting benign task goals. This reveals a key gap in current LLM-agent defenses: the trade-off between safety and intent preservation remains largely underexplored. We propose RecoverAgent, an intent-preserving recovery framework that enables agents to continue execution after detecting unsafe intermediate responses. Instead of terminating the task, RecoverAgent rewrites unsafe responses into safe and executable alternatives while maintaining alignment with the original user intent. Experiments on R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, and BadAgent demonstrate that RecoverAgent reduces attack success and harmful behaviors while substantially improving trajectory completion and intent fidelity compared to other defenses under IPI.

paper.title: Reinforcing Step-level Reasoning for Effective Self-Correction in LLMs
paper.abstract: Achieving effective self-correction, where models verify and correct their own mistakes, remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). In this work, we propose Self-Fix Step-DPO (SFS-DPO), a reinforcement learning based, two-stage framework for step-level self-verification and self-correction. The first stage strengthens step-level reasoning via step-level preference optimization, while the second stage explicitly trains models to self-verify and self-correct. We further introduce a teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, which incorporates explanatory rationales for error verification to provide stronger corrective signals. Comprehensive in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple LLMs demonstrate that SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform prior step-level training baselines. Our analysis further reveals improvements in self-correction frequency and effectiveness, highlighting the importance of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.

paper.title: OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Memory has become a standard substrate for self-evolving agents, yet retaining experience is not the same as learning how to evolve through it. Existing memory agents can store trajectories, retrieve reflections, or accumulate skills, but often lack the holistic competence to select useful experience, act on it, write reusable knowledge, and maintain a growing repository. We introduce OPD-Evolver, a slow-fast co-evolution framework that cultivates such an agent evolver through on-policy self-distillation. In the fast loop, OPD-Evolver interacts with a four-level memory hierarchy to read, use, write, and maintain experience for rapid test-time evolution. In the slow loop, outcome-calibrated memory attribution and privileged hindsight distill these four abilities into the deployable policy. Across multi-domain benchmarks, OPD-Evolver surpasses memory systems such as ReasoningBank by up to 11.5 points, and training-based methods such as Complementary RL by ~6.45 on average. Further analysis shows that OPD-Evolver internalizes high-value experience and memory management, enabling OPD-Evolver-9B to challenge giant counterparts such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Step-3.5-Flash, pointing beyond memory-augmented agents toward genuinely qualified agent evolvers.

paper.title: Clarify User Expertise: Towards Proactive Conversational Agents Tailoring Responses to User Proficiency
paper.abstract: In the context of information seeking, conversational agents are undergoing an evolution from reactive tools to proactive, personalized assistants. A critical aspect of this evolution is the ability to tailor strategic interactions to a user’s unique needs and expectations. Unlike existing studies that focus on proactively clarifying query ambiguities, we center on clarifying the user’s expertise in order to tailor responses for better user comprehension. We find that existing agents struggle to determine user expertise from queries alone, a limitation that prevents them from dynamically adapting their responses. To address this gap, we introduce PASSING to empower the agent to proactively clarify a user’s expertise through targeted inquiries. This is achieved by our What-to-ask and How-to-ask strategies, induced by LLM self-play. Our extensive experiments also show our superiority. We believe that PASSING represents a crucial step towards creating more human-centric conversational agents.

paper.title: Progress-SQL: Improving Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-SQL via Progressive Rewards
paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning has recently shown promise in improving large language models for Text-to-SQL generation, yet existing methods typically optimize one-shot rewards defined over a single SQL state. Such rewards provide limited guidance for iterative SQL correction and are insufficient to capture the improvement of multi-turn SQL refinement. In this paper, we propose Progress-SQL, a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework with progressive rewards for Text-to-SQL. Our approach introduces an Oracle-guided Diagnostic Tree (ODT), which abstracts SQL queries into clause-level structural profiles and produces diagnostic feedback for next-turn refinement. To provide dense and robust reward signals, we combine ODT-based structural alignment with lexical alignment and define a progressive reward that measures the improvement from the initial SQL to the final SQL. We further incorporate a progression latency reward that favors earlier correctness and an execution status reward that encourages recovery from the invalid SQL. Experiments on BIRD, Spider, and Spider robustness variants demonstrate that our method consistently improves Text-to-SQL performance across both primary and robustness evaluations.

paper.title: Dual-Group Exploration: Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly enhanced reasoning in Large Language Models. However, applying state-of-the-art RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to video-based Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains sub-optimal. We identify two key exploration bottlenecks: (1) Advantage Vanishing: generating multiple responses from invariant video contexts leads to near-uniform rewards, neutralizing learning signals after in-group standardization; (2) Visual Overfitting: standard RL lacks mechanisms to regularize sensitivity to visual perturbations under single-epoch training, causing policies to overfit to sparse temporal cues. To address these, we propose Dual-Group Exploration, a framework revitalizing learning signals at both input and output levels. At the input level, a Dual-Group Sampling strategy breaks visual determinism via complementary temporal sequences. At the output level, an Entropy-rated ELO Advantage captures inter-group quality variances. Concurrently, a Cross-Visual Counterfactual Weight establishes a Visual Consistency Region, safely driving exploration by enforcing reasoning consistency across varied views. Achieving state-of-the-art performance across six video reasoning benchmarks, our method demonstrates that consistency-guided exploration is beneficial for video understanding.

paper.title: TRONTOR: To RoPE or Not to RoPE for Long-Context Modeling
paper.abstract: While Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely used in large language models, its inductive biases can impair long-context reasoning and lead to attention sinks. In this work, we propose TRONTOR, a method that effectively combines RoPE and No Positional Encoding (NoPE) through a simple fine-tuning phase, bypassing the need for expensive pretraining modifications. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that mixing RoPE and NoPE at the attention-head level can enhance long-context capabilities, while static selection strategies fail to capture the varying complexity of inputs. Based on this observation, TRONTOR employs a lightweight context-aware routing method that dynamically switches each attention head between RoPE and NoPE at every token step. This router-only configuration provides an efficient operating point, yielding long-context performance gains with minimal inference overhead. For further gains, we extend TRONTOR to TRONTOR-Agg, which applies simple unweighted averaging over multiple RoPE bases within RoPE-active heads while avoiding learnable intra-head routing. Evaluated on the RULER benchmark using Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B) and Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B), TRONTOR improves long-context performance by mitigating attention sinks and dynamically reallocating attention toward relevant mid-context tokens.

paper.title: Demystifying Entropy Conflict: Why Reasoning Compression Stalls in Large Reasoning Models
paper.abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong problem-solving performance, but often generate excessively long chain-of-thought outputs, which substantially increase inference cost and limit practical deployment. Existing reasoning compression methods reduce length only partially and often suffer from unstable optimization or accuracy degradation. We trace this limitation to an underlying trajectory-level objective conflict: when the compression objective and the accuracy objective are optimized jointly, compression favors short-and-correct trajectories while accuracy optimization continues to preserve long-but-correct ones that remain useful on hard problems. This conflict creates opposing gradients on the same behaviors and can trap training in a local trade-off where further compression harms accuracy while accuracy recovery reintroduces verbose reasoning. At the model-decision level, we refer to the resulting failure mode as entropy conflict: the policy fails to fully collapse onto concise trajectories because accuracy-oriented updates keep restoring broader support over long-correct reasoning paths. To address this issue, we propose an entropy-guided training framework. Instead of forcing a mixed objective to follow an unstable path toward the final efficient-output set, we first contract the policy to a short-output set and then expand from this compact regime to recover accuracy and robustness. Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our method achieves performance comparable to the original model using only about 25% of its reasoning tokens.

paper.title: Write Policy Determines Source Retention in External FIFO Memory: A Delayed-Copy Diagnostic
paper.abstract: External hidden-state memories can extend Transformers beyond local attention windows, but the write policy deciding which states enter finite memory is often treated as an implementation detail. We study this factor with a controlled delayed-copy diagnostic using a windowed Transformer augmented with an external FIFO hidden-state memory. Under forced masking, query-to-source attention is blocked, removing this shortcut and making source retention directly testable. We define a capacity boundary as the minimum memory size needed to reach a fixed copy-accuracy threshold. We find that write policy changes this boundary predictably under constrained FIFO memory: an idealized source-only policy, which assumes that relevant states are identifiable at write time, yields an approximately delay-invariant boundary near the source length, whereas an unfiltered prefix-all policy induces a delay-dependent boundary that grows with written non-source content. Intermediate partial-prefix write policies produce intermediate boundaries, while source-pinned controls and memory diagnostics show that prefix-all degradation is dominated by FIFO eviction of source states rather than retrieval interference from retained non-source states alone. A symbolic key–value retrieval diagnostic shows the same qualitative trend. Within this controlled setting, our results highlight write policy as a central variable in evaluating finite FIFO external-memory Transformers.

paper.title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
paper.abstract: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS within a standard rejection sampling (RS) pipeline and derive a scaling form for it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, fit on low budgets, the form predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses at large budgets. Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol consistently outperforms plain RS across matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

paper.title: Efficient Language-to-Vision Feature Injection for Referring Single-Object Tracking

author.affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Referring single-object tracking enables language-grounded target initialization and subsequent tracking by jointly leveraging semantic cues and visual templates. The core difficulty is to use language differently across stages: it is indispensable for grounding but can induce semantic drift during tracking when overemphasized. Meanwhile, current methods often require costly vision-language alignment training. We present LVTrack, a pure transformer framework that introduces a mode-conditioned Gated Feature Injector to adaptively regulate textual guidance and alleviate semantic drift. Together with targeted adaptations, it directly harnesses a frozen vision-language pretrained model, greatly reducing training cost and preserving strong language understanding. To further improve temporal localization, LVTrack integrates hybrid relative-absolute positional encodings with a lightweight memory mechanism and optimizes autoregressive box prediction using a Gaussian-smoothed KL loss. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that LVTrack achieves strong performance.

paper.title: CreaMem: A Scene-Aware Memory Architecture for Personalized Agents

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Long-term memory is a core capability for personalized LLM agents. To support it, existing memory systems organize information using various criteria such as topic segments or summary hierarchies. However, we identify two major limitations in these designs. First, they lack scene awareness: memories from unrelated life scenes share the same retrieval space, which inflates the search space and introduces cross-scene interference. Second, they encode each memory from a single perspective, making it difficult to retrieve complementary views of the same event. In this paper, we propose the CreaMem architecture, which enables scene-aware memory organization by partitioning memory into several Life Scene Memories to reduce cross-scene interference at retrieval. Within each memory, entries are dual-coded from both episodic and trait-based perspectives. To go beyond the single perspective and achieve cross-memory synergy, we further devise a per-memory balanced sampling strategy at retrieval time. Extensive experiments on two long-term memory benchmarks show that CreaMem improves QA accuracy across all evaluation metrics, with particularly large gains on multi-hop reasoning performance, validating scene-aware partitioning and cross-memory synergy.

paper.title: ToolDF: Tool-Integrated Reasoning for Mixed-Authenticity Audio Deepfake Detection

author.affiliation: Korea University and Korea Electronics Technology Institute
National Forensic Service, Republic of Korea

paper.abstract: Audio deepfake detection is commonly formulated as clip-level binary classification of single-domain audio. However, real-world manipulated audio can exhibit mixed authenticity, where genuine and manipulated cues coexist across temporal transitions, overlapping sources, or both. This setting requires not only detecting manipulated audio but also localizing the components that provide evidence for the decision. We propose ToolDF, a tool-integrated reasoning framework for mixed-authenticity audio deepfake detection. ToolDF employs an audio large language model as an orchestrator trained with supervised tool-use trajectories. It adaptively analyzes the audio scene, selectively performs source separation, routes components to domain-specific experts, and aggregates their evidence into an interpretable verdict. We further introduce a mixed-authenticity ADD benchmark covering temporal transitions, acoustic overlaps, and hybrid mixtures. Experimental results show that ToolDF achieves the best overall performance on composite-type detection, achieving macro-F1 gains of 3.72 and 14.39 points over the strongest monolithic baseline and a fixed pipeline, respectively, while providing interpretable evidence localized to temporal regions and acoustic sources. Our source code and dataset are publicly available online at https://github.com/rlataewoo/tooldf.
