Grounded in these mechanistic findings, we propose Head Competition Steering (HCS), a mechanistically grounded inference-time strategy that explicitly leverages the competition between safety heads and continuation heads to suppress harmful generation, and further distill its behavioral signal into a student model via knowledge distillation, achieving inference-time safety improvements without additional computational overhead.

paper.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation

author.affiliation: Tianjin University and Kunming University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM’s generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.

paper.title: MemGovern: Enhancing Code Agents through Learning from Governed Human Experiences

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ByteDance Inc. and East China Normal University
Institute of Information Engineering，Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: While autonomous software engineering (SWE) agents are reshaping programming paradigms, they currently suffer from a “closed-world” limitation: they attempt to fix bugs from scratch or solely using information from the current repository, ignoring the immense historical human experience available on platforms like GitHub. Accessing this open-world experience is hindered by the unstructured and fragmented nature of real-world issue-tracking data. In this paper, we introduce MemGovern, a framework designed to govern and transform raw GitHub data into actionable experiential memory for agents. MemGovern employs experience governance to convert human experience into agent-friendly experience cards and introduces an agentic experience search strategy that enables logic-driven retrieval of human expertise. By producing 135K governed experience cards, MemGovern achieves a significant performance boost, improving resolution rates on the SWE-bench benchmark by 4.65%. As a plug-in approach, MemGovern provides a solution for agent-friendly memory infrastructure.

paper.title: TokenPilot: Cache-Efficient Context Management for LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Zhejiang University and ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center

paper.abstract: As LLM agents are deployed in long-horizon sessions, context accumulation drives up inference costs. Existing approaches utilize text pruning or dynamic memory eviction to minimize token footprints; however, their unconstrained sequence mutations alter layouts, introducing prefix mismatches and cache invalidation. This reveals a critical trade-off between text sparsity and prompt cache continuity. To address this, we present **TokenPilot**, a dual-granularity context management framework. Globally, *Ingestion-Aware Compaction* acts as a framework harness to stabilize prompt prefixes and eliminate open-world environmental noise at the ingestion gate. Locally, *Lifecycle-Aware Eviction* monitors the ongoing residual utility of context segments, enforcing a conservative batch-turn schedule to offload content segments only when task relevance expires. Experiments on ‘PinchBench‘ and ‘Claw-Eval‘ under both isolated and continuous modes demonstrate that TokenPilot reduces costs by **61%** and **56%** in isolated mode, and **61%** and **87%** in continuous mode, while maintaining competitive performance compared to prior systems.

paper.title: Romanized Arabic Across Dialects: Views, Usage Patterns, and Linguistic Variation

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Tunis Business School, University of Tunis

paper.abstract: Arabizi refers to Arabic written in Latin script. Although previous studies have shown that the prevalence and usage of Arabizi vary by factors such as region and age group, most NLP research on Arabic texts treats it as a temporary phenomenon resulting from limited technological support for the Arabic script. In this work, we engage with Arabic speakers to collect insights on their perceptions and usage of Arabizi. We further examine writing norms among speakers of different dialects, focusing on Algerian, Egyptian, Lebanese, Moroccan, and Tunisian Arabic. To this end, we release two resources. First, we perform a character-level alignment of Arabic words to study inter- and intra-dialectal variation across these five dialects, based on words transliterated by the surveyed participants (VARabiziLex), finding systematic intradialectal regularity and inter-dialectal variation. Second, to study Arabic speakers’ ability to identify this stylistic variation at the sentence-level, we build VARabiziCues, a manually curated parallel corpus of sentences written in Arabic script alongside multiple Arabizi transliterations, collected from speakers of the same five dialects. Our study presents the largest human-centered, cross-dialectal study of Arabizi’s perceptions and practices to date.

paper.title: HeTGB: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Heterophilic Text-Attributed Graphs

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunication

paper.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demon- strated success in modeling relational data pri- marily under the assumption of homophily. However, many real-world graphs exhibit het- erophily, where linked nodes belong to dif- ferent categories or possess diverse attributes, such as webpages, Wikipedia articles, social networks, and e-commerce platforms. Addi- tionally, nodes in many domains are associated with textual descriptions, forming heterophilic text-attributed graphs (TAGs). Despite their sig- nificance, heterophilic TAGs remain underex- plored due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks that jointly capture heterophilic structures and rich textual attributes. To address this gap, we introduce the Heterophilic Text-attributed Graph Benchmark (HeTGB), a novel bench- mark comprising five real-world heterophilic graph datasets from diverse domains, with nodes enriched by extensive textual descrip- tions. HeTGB enables systematic evaluation of GNNs, pre-trained language models (PLMs) and co-training methods on the node classifi- cation task. Through extensive benchmarking experiments, we showcase the utility of text attributes in heterophilic graphs, analyze the challenges posed by heterophilic TAGs and the limitations of existing models, and provide in- sights into the interplay between graph struc- tures and textual attributes.

paper.title: Alignment by Stereotyping: How LLMs Sacrifice Individual Distinctiveness for Cultural Adaptation

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed for personalized interaction, and demographic conditioning via user profiles is a widely adopted strategy for cultural adaptation. We ask whether this approach genuinely serves individual users or achieves accuracy by erasing individual distinctiveness. Studying seven models including frontier GPT-5.1 on the World Values Survey, we find that demographic profiles improve value alignment accuracy for most models, but at a systematic cost to individuality. That is, models pull responses toward demographic group centroids rather than preserving individual differences, a behavioral pattern we term alignment by stereotyping. Permutation tests (10,000 permutations, six demographic attributes, seven models) certify that top-performing models compress individuals far above the human baseline; within-family scaling amplifies this tradeoff while degrading intrinsic cultural understanding. Using a synthetic dialogue dataset validated on real human-chatbot conversations from PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024), we further show that distributing demographic signals across conversational turns partially suppresses prototype retrieval compared to compact demographic labels, a finding validated on real conversations via PRISM but requiring replication at larger scale.

paper.title: EM²Mem: Event-Centric Multimodal Memory for Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Zhejiang University and ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center

paper.abstract: Multimodal memory offers a scalable interface for long-video question answering, but existing methods often retrieve captions, frames, transcripts, summaries, or graph facts as isolated fragments. Although searchable, such fragments are not generation-ready: language models must reconstruct cross-modal and temporal alignments at inference time, when context is limited and attribution is difficult. We propose EM^2Mem, an event-centric multimodal memory framework that binds heterogeneous evidence to event anchors during memory construction. Each event-indexed memory cell aligns multimodal records, temporal context, graph-linked relations, semantic facts, and provenance, enabling compact evidence readout over grounded multimodal events rather than modality-specific fragments. Across three long-video QA benchmarks, EM^2Mem improves average accuracy over the strongest memory baseline by 2.0, 2.4, and 3.7 points, improves strict event-level Top-5 evidence recall by 7.0 points, and reduces per-query latency by 4.67\times and total inference tokens by 63.66%.

paper.title: AIMER: Calibration-Free Task-Agnostic MoE Expert Pruning

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Carnegie Mellon University
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models increase parameter capacity without proportional per-token computation, yet deployment still requires storing the full expert pool, making expert pruning important for reducing memory and serving overhead. Existing task-agnostic expert-pruning methods are typically calibration-dependent: they estimate expert importance from routing or activation statistics on a calibration set, making pruning decisions sensitive to calibration-data variation while introducing substantial preprocessing cost. We propose AIMER (Absolute mean over root mean square IMportance for Expert Ranking), a simple calibration-free criterion that identifies more distinct experts by capturing the concentration pattern of expert weights, making it well suited for task-agnostic expert pruning. Across 7B to 47B MoE language models with distinct architectures and 16 diverse benchmarks, AIMER consistently delivers stronger capability balance across diverse tasks than existing calibration-free methods. Surprisingly, AIMER also achieves better balance than strong calibration-based expert-pruning baselines calibrated on the widely used task-agnostic C4 corpus, while requiring only 0.22–2.06 seconds to score all experts.

paper.title: EMemBench: Interactive Benchmarking of Episodic Memory for VLM Agents

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University

paper.abstract: We introduce EMemBench, a programmatic benchmark generator for evaluating long-term episodic memory of agents through interactive games. Rather than using a fixed set of questions, EMemBench generates questions from environment-grounded trajectories, covering both text-only and visual game environments. Each template computes verifiable ground truth from underlying game signals, with controlled answerability and balanced coverage over memory skills: single/multi-hop recall, induction, temporal, spatial, logical, and adversarial. We evaluate memory agents with strong LMs/VLMs as backbones, using in-context prompting as baselines. Across 15 text games and multiple visual seeds, results are far from saturated: induction and spatial reasoning are persistent bottlenecks, especially in visual settings. Persistent memory yields clear gains for open backbones on text games, but improvements are less consistent for VLM agents, suggesting that visually grounded episodic memory remains an open challenge. A human study further contextualizes the difficulty and interpretability of EMemBench.

paper.title: LiST: Local-Simplex Test-Time LoRA Fusion

author.affiliation: Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
Hong Kong Research Center, Huawei Technologies Ltd.
Southern University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Task-specific LoRA adapters offer a modular way to specialize large language and vision-language models. However, existing adapter composition methods are mostly static and cannot adapt to individual test inputs. To address these issues, we propose LiST, a label-free test-time LoRA fusion framework that converts an existing LoRA bank into a target-conditioned local simplex and searches sample-specific fusion weights at inference time. LiST builds joint task representations from LoRA parameter anchors and prompt-level behavior vectors, retrieves neighboring adapters as a local search space, and performs branch-preserving fusion without updating the backbone or adapters. Candidate weights are selected by a prompt-level energy with prior, geometric, and stochastic-consistency constraints, and are deployed only when they pass a safe acceptance rule. Otherwise, LiST falls back to a target-conditioned prior. Experiments on multimodal and language benchmarks show that LiST outperforms static LoRA merging and conventional test-time adaptation baselines, while preserving task-specific adapter utility and improving robustness on unseen tasks.

paper.title: ChapterRL: Chapter-Aware Reward Framework for Novel Generation Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Multi-chapter novel generation requires models to balance two quality dimensions simultaneously: chapter-level reader engagement and global narrative rhythm. Existing approaches have mainly focused on planning, memory, and execution, while paying limited attention to the mismatch between training signals and reader experience. We propose **ChapterRL**, which reformulates multi-chapter generation as a reward design problem. Specifically, ChapterRL introduces two complementary reward signals. **Reading Depth Residual** (RDR) derives debiased chapter-level quality signals from reader continuation and completion behavior through genre–position stratified normalization. **Dynamic Rhythm Trajectory** (DRT) uses an arousal estimator to impose a threshold-gated penalty on systematic rhythm collapse in the later part of a story. The two signals correspond to chapter attractiveness and global narrative momentum, and are jointly integrated into reinforcement learning training. We evaluate the full ChapterRL policy on three automatic benchmarks and separately validate its RDR reward model on task-aligned narrative domains of the Chinese WritingPreferenceBench. Results show that ChapterRL improves chapter quality and rhythm stability over supervised fine-tuning and single-reward variants, while RDR exhibits strong narrative preference alignment as an efficient scalar reward model.Code is available at [ChapterRL](https://github.com/SorBetQ/ChapterRL).

paper.title: Activation-Space Anchored Access Control for Multi-Class Permission Reasoning in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed over knowledge bases for efficient knowledge retrieval and question answering. However, LLMs can inadvertently answer beyond a user’s permission scope, leaking sensitive content and complicating deployment under fine-grained access-control requirements. We identify a geometric regularity in intermediate activations: representations associated with different permission scopes exhibit consistent and distinguishable structure in activation space. Building on this observation, we propose Activation-Space Anchored Access Control (AAAC), a training-free framework for multi-class permission control. AAAC constructs a compact bank of permission-specific activation anchors from a small offline calibration set and requires no model fine-tuning. At inference time, the trusted permission metadata is used by the controller to steer query activations toward authorized anchors and away from unauthorized ones, thereby mitigating the risk of over-privileged generation. Across three LLM families, AAAC achieves permission violation rates of 0.005–0.009 and prompt-based attack success rates of 0.084–0.101, while maintaining competitive utility with 10.3%–25.2% inference overhead.

paper.title: Improving Low-resource Grammatical Error Correction Via Automatic Linguistic Neurons Probing and Optimizing

author.affiliation: Kunming University of Science and Technology
Kunming University of Science and Technology and Yunnan Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence
Kunming University of Science and Technology
Kunming University of Science and Technology
Yunnan Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Kunming University of Science and Technology
Kunmimg University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong language understanding and instruction-following abilities, making them promising backbones for grammatical error correction (GEC). However, prompt-only correction for low-resource languages still suffers from the over-correction challenge, since LLMs cannot fully understand their internal grammar. To address this issue, we propose an automatic linguistic neuron probing and optimizing approach to improve the low-resource GEC with only a few neuron activations. Concretely, we first utilize multiple low-resource GEC corpora to observe the changes in neurons, thus obtaining a linguistically specific probe matrix to ensure whether the neuron is activated. Then, we construct an extra weight matrix to determine the activation intensity of each neuron. Finally, we combine the probe matrix and the weight matrix to obtain an activation matrix, which is injected into selected model layers during inference to guide the frozen LLM toward more controllable GEC. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that our approach consistently improves GEC performance, indicating that lightweight sparse activation rescaling is extremely useful for low-resource grammatical knowledge understanding. Detailed analysis demonstrates that our approach can further provide interpretable neuron-level control without large-scale parameter fine-tuning.

paper.title: JudgePanel: A Compact Judge with Panel Deliberation via Adaptive Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: Amazon and University of Notre Dame

paper.abstract: The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation. However, single-model judges are limited by their inherent model biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that mitigate this through diverse deliberation are prohibitively expensive at inference time. To this end, we propose JudgePanel, which equips a compact Judge model with multi-agent Panel deliberation capability. Specifically, we first train on panel deliberation traces from an ensemble of strong evaluators, capturing structured patterns of discussion, disagreement, and resolution. To further improve judgment quality beyond SFT, we introduce AdaReward, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as different objectives saturate at different rates during RL training. For practical deployment, we further design a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains with few hundred labeled samples. As a result, (i) Novel: the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost; (ii) Effective Reliable: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and rapidly specializes to new domains with few hundred samples.

paper.title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
paper.abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts — especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes — to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each extracted fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.

paper.title: IRIS: Iterative Refinement of Internal States for Safer Language Models

author.affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Attack success rate (ASR) is insufficient for evaluating the safety of large language models (LLMs). Many defenses rely on surface-level refusal behavior, which can over-refuse benign-sensitive prompts and remain brittle: once the initial refusal boundary is bypassed, the model may still follow a harmful continuation trajectory. We analyze model activation spaces to examine the limits of static interventions, finding substantial overlap among useful, benign-sensitive, and harmful representations. This suggests that a single global intervention may suppress harmful outputs only by perturbing general utility. We propose IRIS, Iterative Refinement of Internal States, a routing-conditioned internal correction method. To address this, IRIS leaves low-risk states unaltered while routing high-risk states to a shared module for multi-step latent refinement. To make the refinement module learn behavior-level correction, we introduce model-owned base-source prefix recovery, which trains IRIS to recover from base-model failure prefixes toward safe continuations. Extensive evaluations on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B demonstrate that IRIS drastically reduces ASR from around 70% to around 10% and successfully defends against prefilling attacks. Furthermore, IRIS preserves general benchmark utility and maintains near-zero over-refusal rates.

paper.title: Probing Benchmark-Specific Regularities in Knowledge Gating via Lightweight Feature Analysis

author.affiliation: Minzu University of China and Minzu University of China
Minzu University of China and National Language Resource Monitoring & Research Center of Minority Languages

paper.abstract: We study whether knowledge-gating benchmarks support transferable retrieval decisions or expose benchmark-specific structural regularities that can be exploited without full semantic interpretation. Knowledge gating is the binary decision of whether a dialogue system should retrieve external knowledge at a given turn. We audit this question with a lightweight logistic-regression probe over ten dialogue-metadata features: position, length, and question-form cues. Despite using only metadata and surface signals, the probe reveals non-trivial in-domain signal and markedly different structural patterns across benchmark families. Cross-benchmark transfer provides the clearest evidence: transfer within the related DSTC9/DSTC11 family is near-lossless (Macro F1 0.81–0.84; ROC-AUC ≈ 0.90), whereas transfer across the KETOD–DSTC benchmark-family boundary has weak ranking quality (ROC-AUC 0.41–0.48) and poor detection of knowledge-needed turns (positive-class F1 ≤ 0.22 in one direction). Sentence embeddings and fine-tuned BERT show the same qualitative weakness in the DSTC→KETOD setting: MiniLM ranking is sub-chance (ROC-AUC 0.40–0.44), while BERT remains near chance (0.50–0.53) despite having the strongest KETOD in-domain positive F1. These results suggest that strong in-domain gating scores can partly reflect benchmark-specific regularities and should not, by themselves, be interpreted as evidence of transferable retrieval reasoning. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/zilongcheng582-cyber/RAGate-analysis.

paper.title: CrossAlpha: An Annual-Report Benchmark for Cross-Market Factor Research with LLM Agents

author.affiliation: CMU, Carnegie Mellon University and National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Cross-market factor research studies whether firm-level signals from one or more markets can predict returns in a target market, but existing public benchmarks do not support cross-market disclosure-to-return evaluation. Building such a benchmark is challenging because filings differ across languages and regulatory systems, disclosure-derived similarity can be biased by common reporting components, and cross-market signals must be evaluated under feasible trading-time alignment. We introduce CrossAlpha, a public annual-report benchmark for cross-market factor research. CrossAlpha addresses these challenges through three corresponding components: Disclosure Distillation, which standardises heterogeneous filings into ten-category English business descriptions; Residual Schema Graph Construction, which builds PCA-whitened cross-market firm-pair scores from schema-level disclosures; and Timing-Aligned Evaluation, which pairs the graph with 11 years of daily OHLCV data to construct forward-return labels under feasible cross-market execution protocols. CrossAlpha covers 3,587 firms and about 10,700 firm-year reports from the United States, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and Hong Kong, and releases about 19M directed firm-pair scores. In experiments, disclosure-derived cross-market peers outperform domestic text, industry-code, and return-correlation peers in the US-to-Japan setting (ICIR 0.39 versus 0.07–0.18), and cross-market sources beat the domestic text baseline in most target markets. CrossAlpha offers a publicly released, reusable, return-grounded benchmark for cross-market financial NLP.

paper.title: AEMAgent: Cognition-Inspired Active Memory Formation for Very-Long Video Understanding

author.affiliation: Nanjing University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Embodied AI and wearable assistants require agents to retrieve sparse evidence from continuous days-level videos. Existing memory-based methods typically follow a passive recording paradigm based on fixed-window captioning and periodic memory construction, which produces redundant memories and inefficient long-horizon reasoning. Inspired by human memory formation, we propose Active Explore Memory Agent (AEMAgent), which transforms passive recording into active memory formation by deciding when to remember, how to explore events, and when to reflect. These decisions are instantiated as a coherent pipeline: Surprise-guided Event Selection detects salient event changes for selective memory writing, Exploratory Episodic Memory Encoding enriches accepted events through self-questioning, Predictive-Coding-Guided Reflection updates knowledge from expectation-observation mismatches, and Semantic Memory Consolidation distills noisy episodic updates into compact long-term memory. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that AEMAgent achieves the best overall performance among all compared methods while maintaining lower storage overhead than strong full-memory baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of selective and efficient memory formation for scalable very-long video understanding.

paper.title: Talking to Itself While Coding: What Makes Comments Help Code Generation?
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate natural-language comments while writing code, and these comments become part of the context used to generate the code that follows. However, it remains unclear which properties of comments affect code-generation performance. We study this question through observational analyses and controlled interventions. On LiveCodeBench, neither comment frequency nor broad comment intent reliably predicts pass@1. We then prefill weaker recipient models with comment blocks written by stronger source models, allowing us to separate comment surface form from the solution content they convey. Comments from source solutions that pass the tests raise recipient pass@1 by 17.2% on average. In contrast, comments describing failed solutions provide no reliable gain, while comments written for a different problem reduce pass@1 by 20.8%. Finally, across a wide range of models and prompt variants, most recipient models show no significant recovery of the external-comment gain, and the best case recovers only 24%. These results show that comments help code generation not merely because they are comments, but because they can provide correct solution content that prompting cannot reliably elicit.

paper.title: Skill0.5: Joint Skill Internalization and Utilization for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Equipping large language models with explicit skills has emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling autonomous agents to solve complex tasks. Agent skills can be inherently divided into general skills for broad cognitive transfer and task-specific skills for dynamic execution. However, existing skill-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods typically force a rigid choice between full externalization, which incurs prohibitive context overhead, and full internalization, which risks overfitting and knowledge conflicts. To address this dilemma, we propose Skill0.5, a novel agentic RL framework that explicitly differentiates skill treatments by combining general skill internalization with task-specific skill utilization. Driven by a dynamic, difficulty-aware router, Skill0.5 streams tasks into distinct mastery tiers to apply tailored optimization strategies: it internalizes general skills via privileged distillation to build a cognitive foundation for hard tasks, while using diagnostic probing on easy tasks to penalize shortcuts and enforce specific skill utilization. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that Skill0.5 outperforms both memory-based and skill-based RL baselines, yielding performance improvements across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Skill0_5-1234/.

paper.title: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier

author.affiliation: University of Lorraine and ALE International

paper.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must learn anonymized geographic relations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing FFT with QLoRA ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition–retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves OOD performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at increasing cost to unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining.

paper.title: One prompt is not enough: Instruction Sensitivity Undermines Embedding Model Evaluation
paper.abstract: Instruction embedding models have become common among state-of-the-art models, however are evaluated using a single prompt per task. The single-point evaluation ignores a main problem of the instruction-based approach namely: sensitivity to the phrasing of the instruction. We present an empirical study of prompt sensitivity across 6 embedding models and 11 datasets. We show that reported scores misrepresent the distribution of scores over plausible prompts. The default prompt can both systematically understate or overstate performance. Furthermore, we show that the leaderboard ranking is not robust to prompt selection: a developer improve their rank by favorably selecting prompts, and under adversarial prompt selection any model can be promoted to first place. Our findings suggest that single-prompt evaluation is insufficient for instruction-tuned embedding models and that benchmarks should incorporate prompt robustness, either by evaluating over multiple prompts or by reporting sensitivity alongside point estimates.

paper.title: SkillMol: Skill-Conditioned Action Editing for Molecular Optimization

author.affiliation: Zhejiang University and Shanghai Innovation Institute
Tongji University and Shanghai Innovation Institute

paper.abstract: Existing LLM-based molecular optimization methods frame the task as molecule-to-molecule mapping, forcing models to implicitly learn structure-property relationships from paired SMILES alone. We argue this misses a key ingredient: task-level chemical knowledge that tells the model which structural motifs to prefer or avoid for a given property direction, before it ever looks at a specific molecule. We propose SkillMol, which constructs compact task skills – sets of recommended and discouraged structural motifs for each optimization objective – from domain knowledge, and pairs them with an atom-anchored action interface that decomposes editing into discrete, executable operations. Skills are used twice: as explicit training context so the model learns skill-conditioned edit actions, and as functional-group constraints during inference search. A deterministic RDKit executor applies the proposed graph edits. On the MoleculeSTM benchmark across 14 molecular editing tasks, SkillMol achieves 92.5% loose and 80.0% strict hit ratio on single-property tasks and 65.3% average across loose and strict multi-property columns, outperforming strong LLM baselines. Our code can be found at https://github.com/jiajunyu1999/SkillMol.

paper.title: Expected Contribution Matching: Optimal Value Merging for KV Cache Compression
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) use KV cache for efficient auto-regressive generation, but its linearly growing memory footprint bottlenecks long-context inference. Existing compression methods typically merge evicted information into retained tokens by additively combining both key and value vectors, despite their distinct roles in the attention mechanism. However, this uniform treatment overlooks the distinct roles of keys and values in attention: perturbations to keys are amplified through the Softmax exponential, whereas perturbations to values remain bounded and linear after Softmax. Based on this observation, we propose a differentiated strategy that evicts keys while merging values. Specifically, we formulate value merging as an MSE minimization problem and derive Expected Contribution Matching (ECM), a closed-form scheme that redistributes evicted values by their historical attention contributions. We further preserve semantic coherence by routing evicted information to semantically similar retained tokens via global semantic matching. Experiments on LongBench and LongBenchV2 demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which achieves consistent improvements over existing training-free merging-based and eviction-based approaches under the same cache budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lpzhan931/ECM.

paper.title: Enhancing Event Candidate Acquisition for Event Linking
paper.abstract: Event linking associates event mentions in text with entries in a knowledge base (KB), or identifies them as out-of-KB events. Although existing methods use different architectures, candidate event acquisition can still be weakened by short ambiguous mentions, noisy arguments, and evidence that is unevenly useful for retrieval. We present MACE, a Multi-Agent Candidate Event acquisition method that refines event structure before linking. MACE uses evidence-specialized LLM agents to acquire time, location, participant, and event-type evidence, exposes intermediate queries to candidate-event lookup tools, and lets a coordinator revise the evidence set before final candidate construction. Experiments on two event linking benchmarks show that adding MACE to different event linking models consistently improves accuracy. These results show that MACE improves event linking through better candidate event acquisition without modifying the event linking model.

paper.title: DeALOG: Decentralized Multi-Agents Log-Mediated Reasoning Framework
paper.abstract: Complex multi-hop question answering over text, tables, and images requires integrating heterogeneous evidence with inspectable reasoning. Single-LLM chain-of-thought is opaque, while planner–executor pipelines concentrate faults in a central plan, propagating early errors. We introduce DeALOG, a decentralized, central-planner-free multi-agent framework whose specialized agents, i.e., Table, Context, Visual, Summarizing, and Verification, coordinate only by reading and appending to a shared, typed natural-language log as persistent memory, with a lightweight scheduler rather than a planner. Rather than competing on raw accuracy, DeALOG targets what a central planner forfeits: robustness, since no single plan concentrates errors and evidence stays globally visible, and transparent, since the append-only log yields a provenance-anchored, human-readable reasoning trace. We position decentralized log-mediated coordination as a robustness-and-transparency primitive for multimodal reasoning

paper.title: Building Long-Term LLM Memory with Neo-Davidsonian Discourse Units
paper.abstract: Long-horizon conversational agents need persistent memory beyond a fixed context window, yet memory effectiveness depends on the units stored and retrieved. Existing systems either discard fine-grained details during compression, retrieve units that are too coarse or context-poor, or fragment discourse into entity-relation triples. We propose Neo-Davidsonian Discourse Units: enriched Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs) that each express one event or fact with normalized entities, temporal grounding, and enough context to stand alone. The resulting units are non-lossy at the session level, atomic for retrieval, and naturally expose event arguments for graph-based associative recall. We instantiate this representation in EMem, which retrieves EDUs with dense representations and relevance filtering based on large language models, and EMem-G, which further organizes sessions, EDUs, and arguments in an event graph and applies Personalized PageRank. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval_S benchmarks, our methods improve over prior state-of-the-art by up to 21.3% while using up to 7\times shorter effective context.

paper.title: AQS: MoCA-Guided Adaptive Questioning with Learned Stopping for Efficient Cognitive Impairment Screening
paper.abstract: Fixed-item cognitive screening tools such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) may ask redundant questions and increase patient burden. We propose AQS, an adaptive cognitive screening framework that selects questions and stops assessment according to an evolving cognitive state. Using ADNI-derived MoCA records, we construct an expanded question bank and an 8-dimensional state space, where free-form responses are mapped to discrete severity signals for online impairment updating. We compare handcrafted adaptive selection, fixed stopping, and reinforcement learning (RL) policies. Results show that combining a structured adaptive selector with an RL-based stopping policy yields the best performance–efficiency trade-off. Compared with the classical FisherInfo strategy, it improves Acc from 0.682 to 0.715 and AUC from 0.762 to 0.771, while reducing the average number of questions from 14.43 to 9.78. It also concentrates assessments in a more balanced question-count range and reduces excessive long-tail testing. Analysis further suggests that question selection and stopping are better treated as decoupled decisions, since naive joint RL leads to unstable optimization. These findings provide a simulation-grounded offline framework for efficient cognitive screening under data-scarce medical settings.

paper.title: GRAIL: Gradient-Reward Aligned Initialization for LoRA-based GRPO
paper.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves LLM reasoning, but LoRA-based GRPO can underperform when the initialized adapter subspace is poorly aligned with reward-induced gradients. We propose GRAIL, Gradient-Reward Aligned Initialization for LoRA-based GRPO, which estimates reward-aligned gradients from grouped rollouts before policy optimization and uses them to construct LoRA factors. The full GRAIL configuration includes a reference-solution fallback only for all-zero-correctness groups during calibration; after initialization, all models use the standard GRPO objective without extra trainable parameters or loss changes. We also study Degenerate-Group Reflection Resampling (DGRR) as an optional extension that resamples all-zero-correctness groups after self-reflection without exposing reference solutions. Across Qwen2.5, Phi-3.5, and Gemma-2 backbones on GSM8K and MATH500, GRAIL consistently improves LoRA-based GRPO, with particularly strong gains on smaller Qwen and Gemma models. Analyses attribute these gains to stronger GRPO-gradient capture, smaller principal angles, and better handling of correctness-degenerate groups.

paper.title: LegalOne: A Family of Foundation Models for Reliable Legal Reasoning
paper.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive general capabilities, their direct application in the legal domain is often hindered by a lack of precise domain knowledge and complexity of performing rigorous multi-step judicial reasoning. To address this gap, we present LegalOne, a family of foundational models specifically tailored for the Chinese legal domain. LegalOne is developed through a comprehensive three-phase pipeline designed to master legal reasoning. First, during mid-training phase, we propose Plasticity-Adjusted Sampling (PAS) to address the challenge of domain adaptation. This perplexity-based scheduler strikes a balance between the acquisition of new knowledge and the retention of original capabilities, effectively establishing a robust legal foundation. Second, during supervised fine-tuning, we employ Legal Agentic CoT Distillation (LEAD) to distill explicit reasoning from raw legal texts. Unlike naive distillation, LEAD utilizes an agentic workflow to convert complex judicial processes into structured reasoning trajectories, thereby enforcing factual grounding and logical rigor. Finally, we implement a Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (RL) strategy. Through a progressive reinforcement process spanning memorization, understanding, and reasoning, LegalOne evolves from simple pattern matching to autonomous and reliable legal reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that LegalOne achieves state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of legal tasks, surpassing general-purpose LLMs with vastly larger parameter counts through enhanced knowledge density and efficiency.

paper.title: The Shape of Power: A Multilingual Framework for Social Power Reasoning in Dialogues

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Social power plays a fundamental role in shaping human interaction, yet computational studies of power remain limited to narrow linguistic and cultural settings. Existing datasets further lack the demographic and relational depth needed for robust cross-cultural analysis. To address this gap, we introduce a theoretically grounded framework for studying social power in naturalistic multilingual dialog through movie screenplays. The framework integrates a schema informed by social science theory, a native speaker annotation pipeline refined through pilot studies, and a custom interface for scalable cross-lingual analysis. Using this framework, we constructed an initial corpus containing 15,836 annotated instances from 100 scenes in French and Egyptian Arabic movies. Our analysis reveals strong agreement on observable demographic and contextual attributes, while socially interpretive aspects, such as power asymmetry and intention alignment, remain more contested, highlighting the complexity of social power across cultures. We evaluated 6 Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal LLMs on cross-cultural social power reasoning, finding persistent gaps between human and model agreement in relational and theory-of-mind reasoning. Our work introduces the first extensible multilingual framework for studying social power in dialogues and provides an initial evaluation setting for studying cross-cultural social reasoning.

paper.title: Think Before You Prune: Selective Self-Generated Calibration for Pruning Large Reasoning Models

author.affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on complex reasoning benchmarks. However, their long chain-of-thought reasoning processes incur significant inference overhead. Pruning has emerged as a promising approach to reducing computational costs. However, existing efforts have primarily focused on large language models (LLMs), while pruning LRMs remains unexplored. In this work, we conduct the first empirical study on pruning LRMs and show that directly applying existing pruning techniques fails to yield satisfactory results. Our findings indicate that using self-generated reasoning data for calibration can substantially improve pruning performance. We further investigate how the difficulty and length of reasoning data affect pruning outcomes. Our analysis reveals that challenging and moderately long self-generated reasoning data serve as ideal calibration data. Based on these insights, we propose a Selective Self-Generated Reasoning (SSGR) data construction strategy to provide effective calibration data for pruning LRMs. Experimental results on different model series validate that our strategy improves the reasoning ability of pruned LRMs by 10–13% compared to general pruning methods.

paper.title: ProMediConv: Benchmarking Proactive Conversational Agents in Legal Dispute Mediation

author.affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center

paper.abstract: Dispute mediation is essential for maintaining social harmony and resilience, yet developing skilled mediators is costly and time-consuming. Existing LLM-based mediation research remains limited by unrealistic task formulations, low-fidelity datasets, and coarse evaluation metrics that obscure turn-by-turn dynamics. To address these gaps, we introduce ProMediConv, a novel benchmarking framework that models mediation as a proactive, multi-stage, and party-aware dialogue process incorporating 11 mediation strategies and four party behavior pattern (BP) states. Using 972 complete real-world cases, we construct a high-fidelity mediation dataset with utterance-level annotations of strategies and BP states. Furthermore, to better assess agent impact, we propose MAD (Mean Attribute Difference), a fine-grained metric that captures BP shifts throughout the dialogue. Leveraging this framework, we establish a comprehensive benchmark by evaluating diverse models alongside our tailored baseline ProMediAgent. Extensive empirical analyses reveal critical behavioral phenomena and underscore the persistent challenges current models face in dynamic, multi-party mediation. Ultimately, ProMediConv provides a rigorous foundation and a vital quantitative standard for advancing AI-assisted conflict resolution. Our dataset and codebase are accessible at https://github.com/ZsWei66/ProMediConv_repo.

paper.title: Unlocking the Unsolvable: Teacher-Guided Curriculum for Data-Efficient RLVR
paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown remarkable success in improving the mathematical reasoning of large language models. Yet problems beyond the model’s current capability, where rollouts uniformly fail and no learning signal is produced, are structurally wasted despite marking the most informative training frontier. We show that these otherwise-inert problems can be unlocked via teacher-guided curriculum learning: partial reasoning traces from a stronger model create a graded difficulty landscape, and a backward-chaining curriculum progressively withdraws guidance until the model solves problems unaided. Training on only 128 unsolvable problems matches or exceeds GRPO trained on a full 2,000-problem corpus (~16× data efficiency) on the nine-benchmark average for both base models, while substantially expanding the reasoning boundary measured by pass@k at large k. Furthermore, we identify a distribution-shift cost that is particularly acute in the unsolvable-only regime and propose Monotone Frontier Curriculum (MFC), a method that monotonically drives training toward unguided solving, consistently outperforming existing curriculum methods.

paper.title: EnterpriseBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Enterprise-Level Strategic Reasoning and Decision-Making
paper.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly expected to support enterprise workflows, where tasks often involve missing information, uncertainty, feedback, and long-term trade-offs. However, existing enterprise and financial benchmarks mainly test static capabilities such as information extraction, numerical calculation, domain knowledge, and financial QA, leaving interactive and long-horizon decision-making underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnterpriseBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLM agents across this spectrum, from static question answering to dynamic decision-making. Specifically, EnterpriseBench reorganizes existing enterprise and financial QA datasets into a unified foundational suite annotated by capability and difficulty, and introduces three professional interactive settings: Consulting, based on management-consulting-style business cases for client problem diagnosis through multi-turn information seeking; the Beer Game, adapted from a classic supply-chain management simulation for inventory control under delayed feedback; and Enterprise Digital Twin, a project-based business simulator for workforce, risk, and project planning. Experiments with nine agent methods under two backbone models show that current agents have not yet achieved stable, comprehensive, and cross-task reliability in enterprise scenarios. These results show that EnterpriseBench provides a practical benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in realistic enterprise strategic reasoning and decision-making. Our codes and benchmark implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/sduyangmin/FirmBench.

paper.title: How You Ask Shapes What You Get: A Theory-Seeded Measurement of Articulation in Advice-Seeking LLM Conversations

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: Users articulate the same advice-seeking request in different ways: some specify detailed constraints, others gesture at a vague need. Prior work treats this variation as noise to be averaged away; we instead treat it as a stable, measurable structure in the input distribution. We ask whether articulation (how people ask) forms latent dimensions separable from topic (what they ask about), and whether it is associated with how language models respond. We extract interpretable features from 16,447 advice-seeking prompts pooled from public chat corpora (WildChat, LMSYS, and ShareChat) and recover a small set of latent articulation factors that replicate across train/test splits and across corpora. Because this structure is largely separable from topic, the populations it defines cut across topics and stay invisible to topic- or task-based evaluation. The factors define a handful of recurring articulation styles, one of which stands out: a long-form but information-poor style, roughly one in six prompts in the largest corpus, where models return shorter, vaguer answers and do not ask for clarification even though under-specification is exactly the condition that warrants it. The contrast holds within every topic group and length quintile, and is not under-specification alone: a second, equally under-specified style does draw clarifying questions. Two independent human annotators reproduce this contrast. We argue that benchmarks should stratify on articulation, and we offer the extracted structure as a measurement instrument for doing so.

paper.title: Skip-Connected Rollouts for Mid-Trajectory Rewards in GRPO

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and its variants have proven effective for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards through outcome-based feedback. Incorporating intermediate credit, however, remains challenging. We show that, under practical sampling budgets, token-level Monte Carlo estimates at early reasoning positions have high variance, which can cause frequent advantage-sign errors after group-relative normalization and yield wrong-direction token-level gradient contributions. At later positions, these estimates increasingly resemble the terminal outcome reward and provide limited additional information.We propose SCRoll, a rollout-side module that augments group-relative policy optimizers with randomized single-boundary segment-level rewards while leaving the downstream optimizer interface unchanged. SCRoll uses a skip-connected two-stream rollout. An upstream stream generates an early-stopped reasoning segment s, while a downstream stream samples G continuations conditioned on [s,q], which places the segment before the original problem. This construction retains the segment as preceding reasoning context while mitigating the reward homogenization associated with pure-prefix continuation. The same downstream group supplies terminal outcomes for the standard group-relative objective and a Monte Carlo aggregate used as the upstream segment reward, avoiding a separate objective-specific rollout group. The upstream segment is optimized with a sample-efficient single-stream objective.Across Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, pairing SCRoll with four representative group-relative optimizers improves performance in most evaluated settings. The clearest gains occur with CISPO, with smaller positive average gains for GRPO and DAPO and marginal gains for GSPO. A decoupled two-process baseline can achieve comparable performance with substantially more generated tokens, while SCRoll performs better under a matched generated-token budget, supporting the sample-efficiency benefit of rollout reuse.

paper.title: SYMMETRA : Semantic prompt sanitization for end-to-end utility-preserving privacy protection in LLM interactions
paper.abstract: External LLM services provide strong generation capabilities but require users to send prompts that may contain sensitive information. Existing prompt-protection methods focus on masking, perturbing, or rewriting the input prompt itself; however, these transformations can degrade response quality by removing task-relevant context or leave sensitive cues recoverable from the sanitized prompt. We present SYMMETRA, an end-to-end prompt-response protection framework based on semantic prompt sanitization. SYMMETRA detects context-dependent sensitive spans, selects response-aware replacements, and locally reconstructs responses with session memory and post-editing. We also introduce a synthetic prompt-domain dataset with an extended taxonomy and span-level annotations. Our evaluation shows that SYMMETRA improves the privacy–utility trade-off, reducing direct leakage to 0.13 and adversarial recovery to 0.42 while preserving a response similarity of 0.82 and restoring task-specific references in final user-facing responses after external inference.

paper.title: Test-Time Training with Next-Token Prediction

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Wisconsin - Madison

paper.abstract: Next-token prediction is the self-supervised signal that trains language models, and every observed prompt token provides the same signal at test time. We study whether this signal can define the inner-loop objective for test-time training (TTT) in pretrained long-context language models. Existing in-place TTT methods store prompt information in fast weights, but they train each write to match a learned shortcut target: an internal pattern that may be easy to predict, yet is not the trajectory the model uses to form its next-token distribution. We introduce Test-Time Training with Next-Token Prediction (TTT-NTP), a drop-in fast-weight adaptation method for pretrained LLMs that instead supervises updates using the model’s own next contextual hidden state. This makes each local write follow the same causal computation that supports next-token prediction, without aggregating over a neighborhood of positions: the value target is a pointwise linear projection of a single next-position contextual state. Across four backbones from three model families, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-0.6B, TTT-NTP is the only method that consistently improves RULER Full-13 over the released backbone, by 2.9 to 4.1 points, while aggregate commonsense and knowledge performance is preserved. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yancyou/TTT-NTP.

paper.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.

paper.title: The Target Is a Predicate: Predicate-State Grounding for Semantic-Level Video Reasoning Segmentation
paper.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate P(o,t) over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 \mathcal{J} \mathcal{F} on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.

paper.title: LongMem-RAT: Long-Term Memory for Cross-Session Red Teaming

author.affiliation: Ben Gurion University of the Negev
Ben Gurion University of the Negev
Ben Gurion University of the Negev
Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Technion
Ben Gurion University of the Negev

paper.abstract: Red-teaming has become a standard tool for probing alignment and safety weaknesses in large language models, but most existing methods treat each attack session in isolation and discard what was learned once the dialogue ends. We introduce **LongMem-RAT**, a multi-agent red-teaming framework equipped with long-term memory that accumulates, consolidates, and reuses insights from past attacks across sessions. This design enables cross-session generalization, reduces redundant exploration, and focuses new attacks on fragile alignment behaviors. Across multiple proprietary and open-weight models, LongMem-RAT improves Attack Success Rate (ASR) over a fully reproduced X-Teaming baseline by **21.73 percentage points on HarmBench and 18.40 points on AdvBench** (20.06 points on average). Memory ablations show that long-term memory improves ASR by 13.23 and 6.07 points and reduces Average Turns to Success (ATtS) by 0.37 and 1.92 turns on HarmBench and AdvBench, respectively, averaging a 9.65-point ASR gain and a 1.14-turn ATtS reduction.

paper.title: Triplet-Block Diffusion RWKV

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Causal Transformer language models suffer from strictly sequential decoding and a quadratic per-step attention cost, resulting in expensive inference and an inability to revise previous tokens during text generation. While linear-time causal models and discrete diffusion models each address these weaknesses, their integration remains inherently inconsistent and underdeveloped. In this work, we propose B3D-RWKV, a diffusion-based RWKV variant that integrates the model’s \mathcal{O}(L) inference efficiency with parallel, bidirectional discrete-diffusion through a triplet-block layout method. B3D-RWKV-7.2B reaches comparable accuracy on an 8-task suite versus existing models while significantly outperforming baselines in decoding throughput with an average of 1.6\times speedup. Code is available at https://github.com/leonardodalinky/B3D-RWKV.

paper.title: How to Score Experts for One-Shot MoE Expert Pruning: A Systematic Formulation and Selection Principle

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Carnegie Mellon University

paper.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models reduce per-token computation through sparse expert activation, yet deployment still requires storing the full expert pool, making one-shot expert pruning a practical approach for reducing memory usage. Although effective, existing criteria are largely heuristic, and no single criterion is universally optimal. Thus, establishing a principle for selecting pruning criteria suited to different deployment objectives remains an important yet largely underexplored problem in one-shot expert pruning. To this end, we introduce a systematic formulation for one-shot MoE expert pruning organized around three factors: routing frequency, gate weighting, and activation strength. The formulation yields a criteria selection principle: task-agnostic pruning should favor routed-token-averaged, gate-free activation-based criteria, whereas task-specific pruning can benefit from retaining routing-frequency and gate-weight information. Beyond this principle, the formulation also provides a systematic view of existing heuristic criteria and gives rise to two new task-agnostic criteria, Mean Activation Norm (MAN) and Mean Squared Activation Norm (MSAN). Across four representative MoE models and 16 diverse benchmarks, MAN and MSAN are consistently strong in the task-agnostic setting, obtain the top-two average ranks, and improve average performance by 4.0 points on average and up to 8.8 points over the strongest baseline.

paper.title: Rank4Gen: RAG-Preference-Aligned Document Set Selection and Ranking

author.affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
East China University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: In the RAG paradigm, document ranking determines the evidence available to downstream generators. Through controlled analysis, we identify two phenomena underexplored by existing rankers: (i) downstream response quality depends not only on relevance but also on the composition and ordering of selected documents, and (ii) such preferences differ systematically across generators. However, existing rankers are trained purely on query–document relevance, leaving both phenomena unmodeled. To close this gap, we construct PRISM, a bilingual preference-aligned dataset built through a four-stage pipeline that compresses the combinatorial subset-and-ordering space by roughly four orders of magnitude and produces response-quality preference supervision conditioned on seven downstream generators. On a 13k-query subset of PRISM, we train Rank4Gen, a generator-aware ranker that performs joint document set selection and ordering. Experiments on five challenging RAG benchmarks show that Rank4Gen improves downstream QA quality on most evaluated generators, with per-generator F1 gains of up to +2.08 over the strongest set-selection baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/JOHNNY-fans/Rank4Gen.

paper.title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts

author.affiliation: Amazon and Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
New York University and United Nations
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00–45.67%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea’s Proprietary AI Foundation Model program achieve at most 10.33%. We further construct a 100-problem Synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code at https://github.com/prometheus-eval/K-BrowseComp.

paper.title: TypoCD: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Typographic Defense in Large Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain highly sensitive to text embedded in images: a misleading word printed, painted, or pasted onto an object can override visual evidence and flip the model’s answer. Existing defenses are often tied to specific vision encoders, require training or feature-level intervention, or do not operate on the autoregressive decoding interface of modern LVLMs. We propose TypoCD, a training-free contrastive decoding method for typographic robustness. TypoCD constructs a text-localized counterfactual view by detecting visible text regions and inpainting only the typographic content, then contrasts the attacked-image and typography-removed logits during decoding. This localized contrastive direction targets the attacker’s textual signal while preserving unrelated visual content, allowing TypoCD to subtract the typography-induced logit shift without modifying model parameters or internal features. Across three open-source LVLM backbones and synthetic, real-world, and safety-oriented typographic benchmarks, TypoCD recovers attacked-image accuracy to within a few percentage points of clean-image performance without per-backbone tuning, closing a gap that often exceeds 40 percentage points under attack. When combined with a simple prompt prefix, TypoCD also substantially reduces jailbreak attack success on safety-oriented typographic attacks.

paper.title: AdaptInfer: Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision Language Model Inference via Dynamical Text Guidance

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) have achieved impressive performance on multimodal inference tasks, but the cost remains a significant challenge due to the large number of vision tokens processed during the prefill stage. Existing token pruning methods often rely on utilizing the static attention patterns directly, failing to exploit the dynamic internal signals within VLMs. To address the issue, we propose AdaptInfer, a novel plug-and-play framework for vision token pruning. First, we introduce a dynamic text-guided pruning mechanism that construct soft priors over text-token importance on each pruning layer, allowing more informed scoring of vision tokens at each stage. Second, we observe a highly consistent distribution of cross-modal attention shifts by architecture, which inspires us to introduce a efficient data-driven schedule which determines the pruning locations automatically. Experimental results have verified the effectiveness and generalization of the proposed method. Under the same token budget, AdaptInfer surpasses existing approaches in accuracy. For instance, AdaptInfer maintains averagely 99.4% accuracy on Qwen2-VL while 70% of the prefilling vision token overhead is reduced. The source code is available on: https://github.com/weiczh02/AdaptInfer-base.

paper.title: EgoErrorVQA: Assess Egocentric Comprehension Capabilities through Procedural Errors for Ego-Agentic AI
paper.abstract: The majority of our everyday activities are procedural and consist of sequences of interdependent steps. However, existing benchmarks for Visual Agents and Visual Language Models (VLMs) overlook the evaluation of their procedural comprehension ability from an egocentric visual perspective, particularly for detecting procedural errors, a critical capability for everyday assistance. To bridge this gap, the EgoErrorVQA task is firstly proposed for egocentric procedural comprehension with explicit procedural errors modeling. Besides, we develop a user-friendly evaluator agent based on the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, enabling rigorous and standardized evaluation of visual agents through VQA-based interaction. A range of models are evaluated using both open-ended and multiple-choice questions, revealing persistent weaknesses in handling procedural errors and error types. Moreover, we introduce Ego-ADR, an Adaptive Decoupled Reasoning framework that decouples complex procedural reasoning to enhance models’ understanding of procedural errors. It achieves consistent performance gains over the selected baselines and attains state-of-the-art results on several metrics under comparable settings. Code: https://github.com/z1oong/EgoErrorVQA

paper.title: MemPulse: Memory Pulse-Driven Adaptive Long-Context Reasoning with Fact-based Hypergraph
paper.abstract: Memory-augmented long-context reasoning boosts LLMs’ complex task solving via external knowledge, yet current methods suffer from disjointed memory retrieval-induced context drift and aimless iterations causing premature convergence or redundant computation. We present MemPulse, integrating fact-based memory hypergraphs and pulse-driven adaptive iteration. It builds hypergraphs with facts as hyperedges to gather scattered information and sustain coherent context evolution. Its memory pulse engine computes agent confidence and structural novelty to output dynamic control signals, adjusting retrieval range and stopping criteria for logical reasoning with minimal overhead. Evaluated on Locomo, MemPulse surpasses mainstream baselines in reasoning accuracy and efficiency.

paper.title: Function-Level Execution Feedback for Code Preference Optimization

author.affiliation: Seoul National University and Telecom SudParis

paper.abstract: Process supervision has improved mathematical reasoning, where intermediate steps are naturally expressed as chains of thought. In code generation, however, process supervision remains underexplored because there is no standard notion of a step. Supervision can target lines, reasoning traces, or program states, making it unclear what to label and optimize. We propose STEP-KTODER, a framework for code preference optimization that defines steps as module-level functions in decomposed multi-function programs and assigns binary correctness labels via automatically generated unit tests. Our method provides a code-specific instantiation of stepwise KTO, combining function-level process supervision with outcome-level feedback on the full program. We evaluate on HumanEval(+), MBPP(+), BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench, showing that STEP-KTODER improves over outcome-only KTO and DPO. Further analysis shows that execution-based labels are essential: LLM-as-a-judge annotations systematically over-predict function failures, corrupt positive step labels, and degrade downstream preference optimization. Code is available at: https://github.com/inechnech/STEP-KTODER

paper.title: MI-Distillation: Selecting from Model-Interpolated Instruct-Reasoning Data Spectrum for Chain-of-Thought Distillation

author.affiliation: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown strong performance on complex problems through long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning. However, distilling such trajectories into smaller student models remains challenging: direct Long CoT supervision often provides limited gains and can be less effective than concise Short CoT rationales. In this work, we investigate this phenomenon from a gradient-centric perspective. Our analysis shows that Long CoT induces larger gradient magnitudes and more concentrated update directions than Short CoT, with this effect becoming more pronounced as student model capacity increases. These findings suggest that effective Long CoT distillation requires balancing the reasoning information density of reasoning trajectories with their distributional alignment to the student model. Motivated by this insight, we propose Model Interporlation Distillation (MI-Distillation), a framework that constructs a continuous Instruct-Reasoning data spectrum through model interpolation. To select suitable trajectories from this spectrum, we further introduce Sequential Learnable Surprisal Score (SeqLSS), which favors reasoning paths that are both informative and learnable for the student. Extensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that MI-Distillation consistently improves small model CoT distillation over strong Long CoT baselines.

paper.title: Improving Synthetic Data Generation for Argument Mining via Adversarial Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Argument Mining (AM) is fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of high-quality structure-annotated datasets. While LLMs have shown promise in synthetic data generation, producing synthetic AM data that is both structurally accurate and sufficiently diverse remains a challenging problem. To address this problem, we revisit synthetic data generation for AM from a new perspective and propose a novel Adversarial Reinforcement Learning framework for Data Synthesis. The proposed framework jointly optimizes the generator and the discriminator in an adversarial loop, in which the generator produces structured AM instances, and the discriminator provides learning signals by distinguishing real data from synthetic candidates. This enables the generator to progressively improve both the structural accuracy of generated argument data while maintaining diversity through adversarial feedback.
