The method targets datasets whose underlying information needs already exist in public knowledge sources (e.g., knowledge available on the web and used by public-facing services). We further provide explicit applicability conditions showing that declassification succeeds when sufficient semantic overlap exists between proprietary and public corpora, and degrades predictably when it does not.

paper.title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
paper.abstract: Time series analysis in high-stakes domains relies on recurring data releases, where new observations can alter the evidence base and the validity of later conclusions. Existing time series QA benchmarks mostly rely on fixed snapshots, leaving temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use unevaluated. We introduce TimeSage-EV, a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis in evolving environments. It tracks 60 real institutional scenarios across 6 domains, comprising 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026 and spanning monthly, weekly, daily, and irregular release cadences. At each period, large language model (LLM) agents receive time series data and source reports, while the withheld target release provides ground truth. TimeSage-EV evaluates state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a novel self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, reveal significant performance gaps across model tiers and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation. We release TimeSage-EV as a research resource with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses.

paper.title: Robust Code RL via Faulty-Code-Driven Test case Synthesis and Dense Reward Shaping
paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is pivotal for enhancing LLM code generation, yet its efficacy is often hindered by insufficient test case coverage, leading to reward hacking and policy degradation. To address this, we propose RobustTests, a framework featuring a faulty-code-driven test case synthesis strategy. By leveraging "near-correct" faulty codes, RobustTests captures latent logical discrepancies and employs validator agents with behavioral feature clustering to filter invalid or redundant test cases. Additionally, a stepwise dense reward function based on pass rates is introduced to mitigate false negatives and enhance training robustness. Using this pipeline, we construct an augmented version of the CodeContests+ dataset with superior diagnostic utility. Experimental results show that RL fine-tuning of Qwen3-32B via RobustTests achieves a 3% absolute gain on LiveCodeBench, demonstrating its effectiveness in advancing LLM code generation proficiency. Codes and data are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sid6/RobustTests.

paper.title: Is Multilingual LLM Watermarking Truly Multilingual? Scaling Robustness to 100+ Languages via Back-Translation
paper.abstract: Multilingual watermarking aims to make large language model (LLM) outputs traceable across languages, yet current methods still fall short. Despite claims of cross-lingual robustness, they are evaluated only on high-resource languages. We show that existing multilingual watermarking methods are not truly multilingual: they fail to remain robust under translation attacks in medium- and low-resource languages. We trace this failure to semantic clustering, which fails when the tokenizer vocabulary contains too few full-word tokens for a given language. To address this, we introduce STEAM, a detection method that uses Bayesian optimisation to search among 126 candidate languages for the back-translation that best recovers the watermark strength. It is compatible with any watermarking method, robust across different tokenizers and languages, non-invasive, and easily extendable to new languages. With average gains of +0.23 AUC and +37%p TPR@1%, STEAM provides a scalable approach toward fairer watermarking across the diversity of languages.

paper.title: RIFT-Bench: Dynamic Red-teaming For Agentic AI Systems

author.affiliation: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Tel Aviv University and Fujitsu Research of Europe
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.

paper.abstract: Agentic AI systems powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving into autonomous decision-making systems, exposing attack vectors beyond those of traditional LLM vulnerabilities. Existing security evaluations are often tied to specific implementations or domains, limiting unified comparison across heterogeneous systems. To address this gap, we introduce RIFT-Bench, a representation-driven methodology for dynamic red-teaming that enables unified evaluations across diverse agentic architectures. Building on a novel hierarchical representation, RIFT-Bench operates in two automated phases: Discovery, which extracts system structure, and Scanning, which executes adaptive adversarial attacks. It directly evaluates the examined system using 105 adaptive adversarial probes spanning diverse attack vectors and objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed evaluation pipeline across 45 agentic systems spanning a diverse range of implementations, showing that the approach generalizes effectively to heterogeneous agentic architectures. Beyond systems and attacks, RIFT-Bench also supports direct evaluation of mitigation strategies. These key capabilities make RIFT-Bench a scalable foundation for security evaluation of agentic AI systems in practice. Infrastructure code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/RIFT-Bench.

paper.title: \lambda-Diffusion Language Models: Controllable Generalization of Continuous and Discrete Diffusion Dynamics

author.affiliation: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models. While discrete DLMs achieve strong performance across language generation tasks, continuous DLMs remain relatively underexplored despite their smooth latent-space dynamics. In this work, we present a unified embedding-space interpretation of continuous and discrete DLMs. Within this framework, we analyze continuous diffusion dynamics as a retention channel that preserves intermediate denoising information during sampling. Motivated by this perspective, we propose \lambda-DLM, which smoothly interpolates between continuous and discrete diffusion dynamics through a controllable parameter \lambda. By training with randomly sampled \lambda, a single model generalizes across continuous, discrete, and intermediate diffusion dynamics, unifying diverse retention behaviors within one framework. Unlike prior methods that rely on fixed or self-confidence-guided diffusion dynamics, \lambda-DLM enables controllable exploitation–exploration trade-offs without retraining. Experiments on LM1B and OWT unconditional generation benchmarks show that \lambda-DLM consistently outperforms strong baselines. Moreover, varying \lambda enables semantically diverse generation without additional training. Compared with temperature sweeps, varying \lambda shows a more structured relationship between lexical diversity and sentence-embedding-based mode coverage.

paper.title: AdaMemPIP: Adaptive Memory Pipeline Orchestration for LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly depend on external memory to support long-horizon interaction. Yet many current memory systems still rely on largely fixed default rules once their pipelines are configured. They often apply the same extraction, retrieval, and evidence-organization choices across inputs. This is restrictive. Different memory needs require different choices. We propose AdaMemPIP, an adaptive memory orchestration framework for LLM agents. AdaMemPIP uses an LLM to route both memory storage and memory usage. For storage, it selects extractors for each new batch of dialogue records and writes the extracted items to matched memory libraries. For usage, it selects retrieval methods, target libraries, and organization strategies for each query, then executes the resulting pipeline. The framework is also extensible: new extractors, retrievers, stores, and organizers can be added without changing the overall control logic. This makes AdaMemPIP a flexible framework to long-term agent memory.

paper.title: Plan, Verify and Fill: A Structured Parallel Decoding Approach for Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) enable parallel text generation by denoising multiple masked positions in a single pass, but confidence-threshold decoding often commits only the safest predictions, leaving informative uncertainty underused. We propose Plan-Verify-Fill (PVF), a training-free draft-and-verification decoding strategy that preserves the high-confidence decoding backbone while selectively testing lower-confidence candidates with high expected verified utility. PVF uses a calibrated planning-token vocabulary to allocate its limited verification budget, accepts proposed drafts only when they remain consistent with the backbone trajectory, and otherwise defaults to conservative confidence-gated unmasking. Across mathematical reasoning, knowledge, and code-generation benchmarks on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, PVF maintains comparable accuracy while delivering up to 2.3\times higher throughput than baseline methods.

paper.title: Improving Speech Generation via Multi-Neighbor Token Prediction for Neural Codec Language Models
paper.abstract: Inspired by Large Language Models (LLMs), codec-based TTS systems have achieved remarkable success in high-fidelity speech generation by directly adopting the standard Cross-Entropy (CE) objective to predict sequences of discrete speech tokens from neural audio codecs. However, this practice overlooks the geometric structure of codec token spaces: tokens that are close in the codec codebook embedding space often correspond to acoustically similar speech realizations and can serve as perceptually plausible alternatives. We term this observation the Neighboring Token Phenomenon. The one-hot CE objective is agnostic to such structure, as it penalizes all non-target tokens equally, including these close neighbors, creating a mismatch between the structured codec latent space and the learning objective. In this paper, we quantitatively analyze the neighboring token phenomenon in both reconstruction and generation settings. To address the mismatch, we propose Multi-Neighbor Cross-Entropy (MNCE) loss function, which generalizes the one-hot target of CE loss into a positive set containing the ground-truth token and its nearest neighbors, encouraging the model to treat neighbor predictions as partially correct. As a result, even when the model misses the exact target token, it is more likely to predict a close neighbor rather than an unrelated token, reducing perceptually harmful errors in synthesized speech. Experiments demonstrate that MNCE is effective and generalizable across diverse codec-based TTS systems, improving quality and robustness. Moreover, scaling training to 20,000 hours further validates the scalability of our approach.

paper.title: Modular Expert Merging for Biomedical Retrieval

author.affiliation: Institute for AI in Medicine (IKIM), University Medicine Essen

paper.abstract: Adapting general-purpose LLMs into domain-specialized dense retrievers typically requires large-scale training on mixed-domain data. We show that merging independently trained domain-specialized experts consistently exceeds this approach across four decoder-only LLM families (0.6B–7B), four merging methods, and twelve medical and general retrieval tasks from MTEB, suggesting that parameter-space composition captures complementary domain strengths that large-scale mixed-domain training averages out. To further maximize expert quality, we introduce Synthesize-Train-Merge (STM), a modular framework that synthesizes hard negatives with a top-tier LLM and fine-tunes domain-specialized experts via LoRA before merging them, without continual pre-training. Synthesized hard negatives yield the largest gains for smaller models, and STM achieves strong performance on biomedical retrieval tasks while maintaining competitive general-domain results across all four backbone families.

paper.title: PerturbPrune: Guiding Sparsity Allocation by Probing Layer Stability Along Principal Directions
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, motivating non-uniform pruning for efficient compression. However, existing sparsity allocation methods rely on indirect statistical heuristics derived from weight magnitudes or activation distributions, without directly assessing how robustly each layer preserves semantic information under input variation. We propose PerturbPrune, a framework that allocates layer-wise sparsity by probing the intrinsic stability of hidden representations. PerturbPrune estimates the principal subspace of each layer’s activations via PCA and injects structured perturbations along these directions. Layer sensitivity is quantified through matrix difference entropy (DiME): stable layers are identified as encoding compact, essential features and thus preserved, while highly sensitive layers are deemed over-parameterized and pruned more aggressively. Extensive experiments across diverse LLM families (LLaMA, LLaMA-2, Qwen, OPT) demonstrate that PerturbPrune broadly matches or outperforms existing non-uniform methods. Compared to uniform pruning, it prevents catastrophic collapse, reducing perplexity by up to 99.7% and improving zero-shot accuracy by up to 22.7%. The method is also highly efficient, completing sparsity allocation on Qwen3.5-9B in 7 minutes—achieving 24\times and 17.4\times speedups over AlphaPruning and MRP. Finally, PerturbPrune generalizes to Mixture-of-Experts architectures, achieving up to 19.3% perplexity reduction on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.

paper.title: Compile, Don’t Memorize: A Context Compilation Architecture (CCA) for In-Context Learning

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong and Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly handle in-context learning (ICL) tasks where a long, novel context defines the rules, knowledge, and output schema for a series of questions. On benchmarks that grade against every detail of the context, even strong open-weights models pass only 12-16% of tasks: a single overlooked rule fails the whole response. We argue this brittleness is structural—the dominant "read-and-reason" paradigm asks the model to extract, plan, generate, and self-verify in one forward pass—and ask whether explicit context compilation can fix it, how it compares to existing long-context strategies (gist retrieval, multi-agent self-play), and where the resulting harness benefit holds across task structure and model scale. We propose the Context Compilation Architecture (CCA): compile the given context into a structured IR of rules, schemas, and exact terms; generate executable verifiers from the IR; run a checked reasoning loop that corrects any violation those verifiers flag. On CL-bench (1,899 tasks across 4 open base models), CCA outperforms vanilla prompting and two long-context baselines (ReadAgent-P, Ctx2Skill) on every base model, lifting Kimi K2.5 from 15.4% to 21.4% with gains concentrated on rule-dense sub-categories.

paper.title: Adversarial Robustness of Activation Steering in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Activation steering has become a popular training-free method to control LLMs’ behavior by injecting precomputed direction vectors into the model’s residual stream at inference time. Yet, its robustness to realistic input variation remains under-explored. We present the first systematic evaluation of activation steering robustness under adversarial text perturbations on the inputs, covering four extraction methods, three attack strategies, six personas from the Anthropic Model-Written Evaluations dataset, and five models ranging from 1.5B to 30B parameters. Attacks succeed broadly across all settings: directional robustness drops by up to 64%, post-attack confidence collapses near or below 0.25 across all methods and models, and steering strength degrades on nearly every steerable input. Layer selection is equally fragile, with the optimal layer identified by an automated method on clean inputs shifting by up to 17 positions under perturbation, a failure that compounds the vector-level breakdown. Extracting vectors from adversarially perturbed inputs partially recovers steerability for PCA and MD on mid-to-large models, but they consistently fail to locate the improved optimal layer, limiting the practical benefit of this mitigation. Together, these findings reveal that the brittleness of activation steering is structural rather than method-specific, and that current layer selection strategies are not robust enough for real-world deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/kien206/steering-adv-robustness.

paper.title: AeroVerifier: A Typed Spatial Verifier for Frozen Vision-Language Models in Aerial Visual Question Answering

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Drone-based applications such as navigation, inspection, and search depend on vision-language models (VLMs) that can answer spatial visual questions. The VLM faces three challenging tasks: grounding each referenced phrase to a scene object, choosing a viewpoint for spatial relations, and verifying the relation against accurate 3D geometry. In current frozen VLMs, all three tasks happen inside a single forward pass, and only the final answer is visible from outside. As a result, when that answer is wrong, we cannot tell which task failed. To address this, we introduce AeroVerifier, which exposes each of these three tasks as an explicit and checkable interface. Given a question, AeroVerifier compiles it into an executable typed program, runs the program over object-level 3D evidence, and returns the program answer together with stage-wise diagnostic signals to the base VLM as single-step revision feedback. On a 1000-row Open3D-VQA subset, both AeroVerifier’s program answer and its revision feedback yield higher answer accuracy than the Qwen2.5-VL-7B and GPT-5.4 API baselines.

paper.title: Exploring Language-Agnosticity in Function Vectors: A Case Study in Machine Translation

author.affiliation: Cantina AI and Universidad Politécnica de Cataluna
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Function vectors (FVs) are vector representations of tasks extracted from model activations during in-context learning. While prior work has shown that multilingual model representations can be language-agnostic, it remains unclear whether the same holds for function vectors. We study whether FVs exhibit language-agnosticity, using word-level machine translation as a case study. Across three decoder-only multilingual LLMs, we find that translation FVs extracted from word-to-word prompts in a single English\toX direction transfer to other target languages, consistently improving the rank of correct translation tokens across multiple unseen languages. We further find that the highest-gain tokens span multiple languages and that translation FVs across directions share most of their top-ranked heads, indicating that the FV encodes a largely language-agnostic translation signal.

paper.title: SWITCH: Benchmarking Modeling and Handling of Tangible Interfaces in Long-horizon Embodied Scenarios

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Tangible control interfaces (TCIs), such as appliance panels, remotes, elevators, and embedded GUIs, are a fundamental component of everyday human-built environments. Interacting with these interfaces requires agents not only to ground language in visual observations, but also to execute actions, track temporally evolving state changes, and verify whether intended outcomes have been achieved. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate open-loop perception or single-step action execution, failing to capture this continuous cycle of interaction, feedback, and correction. We introduce SWITCH, a benchmark for closed-loop interactive reasoning with TCIs inrealistic egocentric environments1. SWITCH comprises 1,170 temporally interactive videos across diverse functional categories, providing structured annotations of instructions, actions,state transitions, outcomes, and recovery behaviors over time. To probe generative world modeling, SWITCH also evaluates video generation models on interaction-centered tasks using both LLM-as-judge and human evaluation.Experiments with frontier proprietary and opensource multimodal models reveal persistent weaknesses in fine-grained visual-temporal perception, outcome verification, and error recovery, highlighting SWITCH as a testbed for closed-loop embodied intelligence

paper.title: Every Step Counts: Step-Level Credit Assignment for Tool-Integrated Text-to-SQL
paper.abstract: Tool-integrated reasoning has emerged as a promising paradigm for Text-to-SQL, framing SQL generation as sequential decision-making interleaved with tool execution. However, existing reinforcement learning approaches rely on coarse-grained outcome supervision, creating a credit assignment problem: models receive identical rewards regardless of whether intermediate steps are redundant or erroneous. We observe that tool-integrated reasoning offers a unique opportunity: each tool invocation produces structured, verifiable outputs that can serve as training-free step-level signals, eliminating the need for expensive reward model training. Building on this insight, we propose FineStep, a step-level credit assignment framework that leverages training-free process rewards derived from tool execution feedback. FineStep constructs a dual-channel value estimate for each step, combining backward-propagated outcome value with forward-smoothed process value, and synthesizes them via group-based normalization into a unified step-level advantage for policy optimization. Experiments on Text-to-SQL benchmarks show that FineStep achieves SOTA performance with a 3.25% EX gain over GRPO at the 4B scale, while results on AIME24 demonstrate transferability beyond SQL.

paper.title: StanceAgent-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Zero-Shot Conversational Stance Detection
paper.abstract: Conversational stance detection requires identifying the stance of a current utterance toward a target within its dialogue context. Existing methods often rely on sequential encoding, fixed knowledge-integration pipelines, or uniform reasoning strategies, which limits their ability to capture cross-turn dependencies and adapt to instance-specific needs. We propose StanceAgent-R1, an agentic reinforcement learning framework that adaptively routes each instance to evidence-path selection and/or knowledge elicitation. The model is first warm-started with rejection-sampled expert trajectories and then optimized with a progressive trajectory-faithful reward that encourages correct, well-formed, and route-consistent reasoning. Experiments on ZS-CSD, MT-CSD, and C-MTCSD show that StanceAgent-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance, with further analyses confirming the effectiveness of its agentic design and reward strategy.

paper.title: Reflection Is Not Monolithic: Experience-Driven Control of Recheck in LLM Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by generating long reasoning traces with explicit reflection. However, reflection is not functionally uniform: some reflections revise the reasoning strategy, while others verify previously derived intermediate results. In this work, we examine whether local self-verification can be controlled selectively without suppressing useful reasoning. Through a large-scale analysis of mathematical reasoning traces, we distinguish strategy-level rethink from local self-verification recheck, and further separate rechecks into corrective and confirmatory cases. We find that recheck occurs frequently across models and benchmarks, but most observed rechecks are confirmatory, rarely uncovering errors or changing the reasoning trajectory. Motivated by this finding, we propose Experience-Driven Suppression (EDS), a conservative test-time controller that suppresses a recheck only when historical outcomes of similar episodes suggest low utility. Unlike early-exit or trigger-suppression methods that stop reasoning globally or suppress reflection cues broadly, EDS targets local recheck while preserving later rethink. Experiments show that EDS yields moderate reasoning-length reductions with limited accuracy changes, supporting behavior-specific rather than monolithic reflection control.

paper.title: SYNAPSE: Neuro-Symbolic Visual Thought-to-Text Decoding via Topological Semantic Denoising
paper.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have accelerated open-vocabulary EEG-to-imagined-text decoding, where non-invasive neural activity recorded during visual perception is translated into coherent natural language descriptions of viewed stimuli. However, existing systems remain highly vulnerable to biological noise, where corrupted neural projections induce hallucinated or semantically unstable generation in frozen language models. We introduce SYNAPSE (Symbolic Neural Alignment for Precise Semantic Extraction), a lightweight neuro-symbolic framework that stabilizes neural text generation through inference-time symbolic regularization. By purifying EEG-derived semantic candidates using commonsense graph structure and latent exemplars, SYNAPSE improves semantic stability without end-to-end LLM fine-tuning. Experiments across popular EEG decoding benchmarks and multiple frozen LLM backends demonstrate consistent gains over unconstrained prompting baselines, robustness under object-label ablation, and performance commensurate with substantially more resource-intensive fine-tuned systems, while preserving biometric privacy by localizing raw EEG processing entirely within the encoder stack.

paper.title: RecToolBench: Benchmarking Recommendation-Specific Tool Orchestration under Fuzzy User Intent
paper.abstract: Recent advances in agentic recommender systems are shifting recommender systems from passive filtering engines to instruction-following agents that use external tools to resolve user intent. However, existing benchmarks often assume explicit user intent, simplified tool environments, or isolated function calls, leaving realistic tool orchestration for recommendation underexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose RecToolBench, a Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based benchmark for evaluating tool-using recommender agents under fuzzy user instructions. RecToolBench contains more than 1,200 executable tasks across three recommendation domains, 13 MCP servers, and 32 tools, spanning single-tool calls, parallel tool calls, sequential tool chains, and hybrid tool orchestration. We construct RecToolBench with a scalable synthesize–fuzzify–judge pipeline that generates executable fuzzy recommendation tasks, and evaluates agent trajectories using rule-based execution checks and rubric-based LLM evaluation. Experiments on representative LLMs show that syntactically valid tool calls do not guarantee successful recommendations. Models struggle with semantic parameter grounding, multi-step evidence integration, and grounded final recommendations, especially as orchestration complexity increases. Our results identify tool orchestration under fuzzy user intent as a major bottleneck for agentic recommender systems. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/ShawnChenn/RecToolBench.

paper.title: Are Large Language Models Suitable for Graph Computation? Progress and Prospects

author.affiliation: Edith Cowan University and University of Technology Sydney
the university of new south wales

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly explored for graph computation, where tasks require reasoning over structured relationships and algorithmic operations. Yet, it remains unclear when LLMs can reliably support such computation and how they should be incorporated into graph-solving pipelines. Existing surveys at the intersection of LLMs and graphs primarily focus on graph learning, text-attributed graphs, or graph-language modeling. To bridge this gap, we provide a comprehensive review of LLMs for graph computation through a role-based taxonomy. Specifically, we identify two major paradigms: i) LLMs as executors, where models directly solve graph tasks from graph descriptions and instructions; and ii) LLMs as planners, where models formulate problems, decompose reasoning steps, and invoke external tools or agents for execution. Based on this taxonomy, we analyze the strengths and limitations of current methods. Our review indicates that LLMs are promising for simple, small-scale tasks, but remain unreliable for large-scale and exactness-demanding tasks. Finally, we summarize available datasets and suggest four future directions.

paper.title: EvalMem: An Operation-Level Diagnostic Framework for Long-Term Memory Systems
paper.abstract: Long-horizon interactions with LLM-based assistants require memory systems that preserve and update user states, preferences, and interaction histories. Existing evaluations report end-to-end QA accuracy and cannot determine whether errors arise from encoding, retrieval, or generation. We introduce **EvalMem**, an operation-level diagnostic framework with three parallel Examiners. For each query, the Encoding Examiner checks whether the target fact is stored, the Retrieval Examiner assesses whether the native retriever returns usable evidence, and the Generation Examiner tests whether the model can answer from oracle evidence. Their outputs form fine-grained multi-label defect codes. To improve store-level diagnosis, we adapt agentic RAG with a recall-first strategy that searches using both the query and source evidence, increasing recall of present evidence on LoCoMo from 70.2% to 95.6%. Evaluations of seven memory systems on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and dynamic DynaMem-Bench identify retrieval as the most frequently attributed failure layer; in default LoCoMo, retrieval defects reach 22.1%, compared with 7.7% for encoding and 6.5% for generation. Guided by this diagnosis, **MemWiki**, a search-friendly auxiliary structure built from each system’s memory export, improves mean accuracy by 2.5 and 2.3 percentage points on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, respectively.

paper.title: Probe to Act: Elevating Browser-Use Agent via Active Visual Probing

author.affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Browser-use agents require seamless alignment between structured web metadata and visual information, while preserving relevant context across long interactions. Existing interfaces often rely on either screenshot-level action prediction or static Set-of-Marks overlays, leaving the model to resolve dense DOM-pixel alignment before every operation. We introduce Probe to Act (P2A), an active probing framework for the browser-agent loop that moves this alignment into decision time. P2A addresses an asymmetric bridge between symbolic DOM hypotheses and screenshot layout by rendering on-demand symbolic DOM structure back into pixels. Before committing a state-changing browser operation, the agent can issue lightweight probes to translate DOM handles into pixel evidence, map screen regions back to DOM candidates, register visual-only targets, and commit verified notes. These interleaved processes naturally produce evidence-based memory: only probed, acted-on, or explicitly committed observations are kept across steps, preserving only decision-critical evidence in long-horizon contexts. P2A can be used as a prompting strategy for proprietary models under the standard DOM+SoM interface, and can be distilled into open-weight models through cold-start synthesis and self-bootstrapped SFT. Across three browser-use benchmarks, P2A shows clear gains on task success rate for both proprietary and fine-tuned models; on VisualWebArena, for example, it improves Gemini-3-Pro from 54.1% to 61.2% and Qwen3-VL-8B from 24.6% to 32.9%, while matching the costly full-observation history (3̃×) at near context cost of action-only history (1̃.2×).

paper.title: EgoActor: Grounding Task Planning into Spatial-aware Egocentric Actions for Humanoid Robots via Visual-Language Models
paper.abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments requires tightly integrating perception, locomotion, and manipulation under partial observations, dynamic changes, and frequent transitions across heterogeneous sub-tasks. Towards this challenge, we propose EgoActing, a new task that grounds high-level instructions into diverse, precise, and spatially aware humanoid actions. We instantiate it with EgoActor, a hierarchical humanoid system centered on a vision-language model that predicts egocentric textual actions from monocular RGB observations. Among the actions, parameterized movement and viewpoint actions are mapped to locomotion and head controllers, while manipulation and human-interaction actions are routed to downstream skills via lightweight parsing. Trained with broad supervision from real-world egocentric demonstrations, spatial reasoning QA, and simulated demonstrations, EgoActor makes robust, context-aware decisions with a sub-second VLM forward pass for both 8B and 4B variants, while the current cloud-deployed robot loop takes 3–8 seconds end-to-end. Extensive simulated and real-world evaluations show that EgoActor bridges abstract task planning and concrete motor execution, generalizing across diverse tasks and unseen environments. Code and models are released at https://baai-agents.github.io/RoboNoid/EgoActor/.

paper.title: Difficulty-Adaptive Tree-Structured Policy Optimization for Expanding Reasoning Coverage in RLVR

author.affiliation: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been central to the recent success of Large Reasoning Models. However, while RLVR significantly improves single-sample accuracy, it often fails to expand the model’s intrinsic reasoning coverage (pass@k) due to limited exploration during training. To address this, we optimize the structural design of train-time rollouts to enhance pass@k. Our analysis identifies three key design principles: (1) difficulty-adaptive rollout can play an important role in expanding pass@k, beyond serving as an efficiency heuristic; (2) tree-based rollout outperforms parallel sampling in discovering correct answers; and (3) sentence-entropy-guided forking overcomes the localization phenomenon of token-level branching to maximize semantic diversity. Building on these insights, we propose DATPO (Difficulty-Adaptive Sentence-entropy-guided Tree-structured Policy Optimization). DATPO integrates difficulty-adaptive tree search with a sibling-diversity advantage term, explicitly promoting semantic diversity to expand reasoning coverage during training. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DATPO outperforms baselines especially in pass@k, which directly translates to superior test-time scaling performance.

paper.title: PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference
paper.abstract: ision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate exceptional visual reasoning capabilities, yet their inference costs escalate rapidly with the proliferation of visual tokens. Existing visual token pruning methods exhibit two fundamental limitations. First, most approaches operate exclusively post-vision encoder, leaving the substantial latency of the visual encoding phase unoptimized. Second, under strict token budgets, these methods often fail to jointly preserve holistic visual contexts and fine-grained details, leading to performance degradation. To address these bottlenecks, we propose PACE (Pixel-Adaptive Condense and Extract), a training-free inference framework that accelerates both the vision encoder and the Large Language Model (LLM) via a unified Condense-and-Extract paradigm. During the Condense stage, an Adaptive Pixel Compressor (APC) evaluates visual information density prior to encoding, adaptively downsampling redundant inputs, curtailing encoder computation while preserving global context and essential visual cues. In the Extract stage, a Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor (DDAE) selectively retains visual tokens via a fusion of internal visual signals from the encoder and semantic signals from the LLM, safeguarding task-critical details. By integrating PACE into Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the model retains 93.8% of its original performance while utilizing only 10% of the visual tokens, yielding a 3.1× speedup in time to first token (TTFT). Our code is available at https://github.com/jjL357/PACE

paper.title: Where Identity Lives: Localized, Retain-Free Identity Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Removing a specific individual’s information from multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is often needed after deployment, but existing methods rely on a retain set, which is hardest to obtain at that point, and rebuilding it recreates the privacy exposure that unlearning aims to remove. Forgetting from the forget set alone instead damages the shared visual-language computation, harming perception. We cast retain-free unlearning as a localization problem: causal tracing, weight transplant, and Fisher overlap all point to early-to-mid decoder MLPs as the layers where identity information is stored and, unlike other module families, can be modified without substantially disrupting vision. We turn this into Pathway-Aware Visual-attribute Anchoring (PAVA), which confines updates to these layers and pairs a forget loss with a visual-attribute anchor that preserves image-grounded behavior by distilling the model’s own pre-unlearning answers from the forget images alone. On MLLMU-Bench and ReMem, PAVA gives the strongest forget-retain trade-off among forget-set-only methods and remains competitive with retain-based baselines.

paper.title: Beyond Trajectory Rewards: Step-level Credit Assignment for Agentic Search via Graph Modeling

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunication

paper.abstract: In Agentic Search, trajectory-level outcome rewards fail to quantify the behavioral contributions of individual steps, while existing step-level reward methods typically rely on costly tree sampling. We view world knowledge as a latent world graph and each IS task as search within a latent task graph, where effective steps should make graph progress toward the answer node. Based on this prior, we propose Graph-Distance Contribution Reward (GDCR), a step-level process reward that scores newly-retrieved and newly-cited entities by their distance to the answer node in a training-time Entity-Relation (ER) graph. We further propose Step Advantage Policy Optimization (SAPO), which converts GDCR into step-level advantages and combines them with trajectory-level outcome advantages. Experiments on four challenging benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method.

paper.title: When Not to Imitate: Boundary-Aware Skill Memory for Reliable Tool-Use LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Extracting skills from past successes is critical for the efficient evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Prevailing agent self-evolution paradigms typically rely on a core assumption: equipping LLMs with skill memories derived from successful trajectories will monotonically improve their problem-solving capabilities. However, probe analyses reveal that extracting skills solely from successful trajectories traps the model in a Skill Imitation Trap. For tasks that resemble past successes but require different tools, retrieving more skills paradoxically increases the model’s confidence in wrong tool calls—procedure skills raise the wrong-tool margin by 47% over a memory-free baseline. To overcome this limitation, we propose Boundary-Aware Skill Memory (BASM), which augments each skill with explicit boundary fields—applicability conditions, risk cues, avoidance rules, and recovery notes. These fields transform each retrieved skill from an unconditional action template into state-conditioned guidance: the agent applies the skill when its conditions hold, suppresses inapplicable tool calls when they do not, and issues targeted repairs when execution fails. Across three agent benchmarks and four model scales, BASM consistently outperforms success-distilled skill-memory baselines: it improves task success rate by up to 23.8% on AppWorld, accuracy by up to 5.0% on BFCL, and reduces attack success rate by 4.6% on AgentDojo, while simultaneously reducing average AppWorld steps by up to 6.6% relative to the memory-free baseline.

paper.title: Remembering Facts, Updating Minds: Personal-Factual Adaptive Memory for Multi-Turn Emotional Support
paper.abstract: Emotional Support Conversation (ESC) systems help seekers understand and cope with distress through multi-turn interaction. Existing ESC systems typically improve responses by adding auxiliary support knowledge or prompting LLMs to reason over dialogue context. However, they usually pass inferred seeker information to the generator as a single state, so factual circumstances and mental state inferences are stored, selected, and updated in the same way. This blurs the difference between persistent facts and transient personal states, making it difficult to retain stable grounding while adapting to psychological changes across turns. Therefore, in this paper, we propose MIA, a Personal-Factual Adaptive Memory framework for multi-turn emotional support conversation. MIA first infers Emotional Theory-of-Mind factors and separates them into factual and personal states. It then uses a Personal-Factual Discriminator to decide which state should guide the next response, and an Obsolescence Removal Mechanism to remove outdated memory before generation. This design enables the generator to preserve factual grounding, focus on the turn-relevant support orientation, and avoid stale psychological assumptions. Experiments on ESConv and CPsyCounD show that MIA better understands the seeker’s situation, provides more constructive guidance, and maintains more coherent support across turns. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/ Wh2018/MIA.

paper.title: Evaluate-as-Action: Self-Evaluated Process Rewards for Retrieval-Augmented Agents

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented agents can query external evidence, yet their reliability in multi-step reasoning remains limited: noisy retrieval may derail multi-hop question answering, while outcome-only reinforcement learning provides credit signals that are too coarse to optimize intermediate steps. To address these limitations, we propose EvalAct (Evaluate-as-Action), which converts implicit retrieval quality assessment into an explicit action and enforces a coupled Search-to-Evaluate protocol so that each retrieval is immediately followed by an explicit evaluation score, yielding process signals aligned with the interaction trajectory. To leverage these signals, we introduce Process-Calibrated Advantage Rescaling (PCAR), a GRPO-based optimization method that rescales advantages at the segment level according to evaluation scores, emphasizing reliable segments while updating uncertain ones conservatively. Experiments on seven open-domain QA benchmarks show that EvalAct achieves the best average EM across multiple model scales, with the largest gains on multi-hop tasks. Ablations verify that the explicit evaluation loop drives the primary improvements, while PCAR provides consistent additional benefits. Code is available at https://github.com/DBMing/EvalAct.

paper.title: SFAD: Speculative Factuality-Aware Decoding

author.affiliation: Alibaba Group and University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: As one of the most critical challenges in large language models, contextual faithfulness directly determines their reliability in knowledge-intensive applications. This task is particularly challenging as it requires balancing factual consistency with generation efficiency. Contrastive decoding methods require dual forward passes (with and without context) to compare model outputs, doubling inference computational overhead, while post-training alignment demands extensive reinforcement learning with substantial computational overhead. To address this challenge, we present SFAD, a speculative decoding framework that enhances contextual faithfulness without inference degradation. We first construct ConFide, a preference dataset with fine-grained atomic perturbations, to train a context-faithful draft model via Direct Preference Optimization. During inference, Epistemic Friction detects potential hallucinations by quantifying distributional tension weighted by specialist certainty. When friction exceeds the threshold, Asymmetric Logit Steering refines the target distribution through residual-based logit injection; otherwise, standard speculation proceeds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFAD substantially improves faithfulness while achieving 2.48× speedup, offering a practical solution for efficient LLMs.

paper.title: JaggedBench: Measuring Reasoning Invariance via Automated Weakness Exploration

author.affiliation: Department of Precision Instrument, Tsinghua University, Tsinghua University
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Strong large language models (LLMs) often achieve high scores on many benchmarks, yet can fail on closely related, sometimes easier, problems near their apparent capability boundary, a phenomenon known as jagged intelligence that reveals reasoning weaknesses masked by aggregate scores. Existing evaluations of jagged intelligence rely on manually designed benchmark-adjacent rewrites, which are hard to scale and quickly saturate as models improve. To address this challenge, we propose Automated Weakness Exploration (AWE), a fully automated framework for constructing and maintaining jaggedness evaluations. Using AWE, we construct JaggedBench with 1,142 verified capability-adjacent variants and evaluate 24 state-of-the-art models. On the primary evaluation set AIME 2025, benchmark-adjacent rewrites induce an average OG-to-RW relative drop of approximately 25% in Avg@k across 24 models, with consistent degradation observed across math, code, science, and knowledge domains. We identify 18 recurring failure modes. Our analysis shows that increasing reasoning intensity and scaling model size improve average performance and reduce failure frequency, yet the underlying failure-mode categories largely persist. Overall, these findings indicate that standard benchmark scores can present an overly optimistic view of reliability near the capability boundary. JaggedBench provides a more faithful and scalable lens for evaluating boundary robustness, enabling systematic diagnosis of boundary failures and longitudinal tracking of persistent weaknesses as models evolve. We release the benchmark, code, and subsequent updates at https://jaggedbench.github.io/.

paper.title: BDI-batch: Leveraging Standardized Clinical Questionnaires for Contrastive Learning in Psychological Marker Retrieval
paper.abstract: Automatic detection of signs of depression has received increasing attention in recent years, evolving from user-level classification (binary) to fine-grained symptom detection. Despite recent advances, state-of-the-art sentence retrieval models still struggle to discriminate between sentences associated with closely related symptoms. In this work, we propose BDI-batch, a novel contrastive learning method that leverages clinically grounded sentence pairs to encode fine-grained distinctions among depression-related symptoms. The method exploits a standardized clinical questionnaire and does not rely on annotated data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two early risk detection datasets and under multiple retrieval strategies. Additionally, we explore the use of LLMs to generate synthetic contrastive samples and observe that their performance falls short of questionnaire-derived pairs. Finally, we conduct an error analysis that reveals the most common errors of the sentence retrievers.

paper.title: SemFed: Semantic Federated Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Training Large Language Model (LLM) agents via Reinforcement Learning (RL) in federated settings faces fundamental challenges, including model heterogeneity across clients, prohibitive communication costs and severe data heterogeneity. We propose a semantic federated learning framework called SemFed that addresses all challenges by communicating behavioral patterns rather than model parameters. Each client extracts compact semantic policy summaries from local training trajectories, which are aggregated at the server into shared, elite and anti-patterns. These aggregated patterns are injected back into local training through different complementary channels. Since the communicated objects are structured behavioral abstractions, SemFed supports heterogeneous model architectures while reducing per-round communication to kilobytes. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across multiple heterogeneous LLM backbones demonstrate that SemFed consistently surpasses strong federated baselines in task success while reducing communication overhead by orders of magnitude.

paper.title: STAGE: Diagnosing Semantic Transfer at Grounded Execution in Embodied Agents
paper.abstract: Embodied language grounding requires more than identifying the referent of an instruction: recovered semantics must also control the action an agent exposes. We study this missing link as a semantic–action gap, where instruction semantics are recoverable but weakly expressed in native continuous actions. We introduce SAT-Bench, a fixed-observation counterfactual benchmark that holds the visual scene and agent state fixed while changing only instruction semantics. On LIBERO target-name and pixel-grounded relation swaps, target recovery reaches 100.0% and 95.8%, whereas OpenVLA action sensitivity remains only 6.8% and 7.7%. The gap persists across 1,000 additional compositional and temporal/procedural counterfactuals, with overall action sensitivity of 6.1%. Hidden-state, threshold-free, cross-policy, and rollout diagnostics further support this semantic–action transfer failure. We introduce VISA, a lightweight execution-time interface that converts recovered semantics into ALLOW, DEFER, target-consistency, and verified-selection decisions. VISA reduces invalid-instruction blind execution from 92.7% to 2.8% while preserving 94.0% of normal commands, and verified selection further improves target-consistent action exposure without updating the underlying policy. Overall, embodied language evaluation should measure semantic–action transfer, not semantic parsing alone.

paper.title: Asking the Right Questions: Ontology-Grounded Interpretable Embeddings for Biomedical Text
paper.abstract: While dense biomedical embeddings achieve strong performance, their opaque dimensions limit transparency in biomedical NLP. Recent question-based interpretable embeddings represent text through binary answers to natural-language questions, but existing approaches rely primarily on corpus-driven signals, often capturing topical or stylistic differences rather than fine-grained biomedical distinctions. We propose QIME, an ontology-grounded framework for interpretable biomedical text embeddings in which each dimension corresponds to an explicit biomedical-domain yes/no question. QIME leverages a biomedical ontology to guide contrastive question generation from semantic clusters, producing atomic, domain-grounded questions. It constructs embeddings via similarity-based semantic activation with MMR-based diversity-aware dimension selection, yielding sparse representations efficiently. Experiments on biomedical clustering, STS and retrieval benchmarks show that QIME consistently outperforms prior interpretable embedding methods and substantially narrows the gap to strong black-box biomedical encoders. It also imposes substantially lower cognitive burden than existing methods, providing concise and domain-specific interpretations. The code is available at https://github.com/L1nzh/QIME.

paper.title: Diagnosing Decision-Boundary Induction in Few-Shot In-Context Learning
paper.abstract: Few-shot in-context learning is usually evaluated by final accuracy, but correct predictions do not guarantee recovery of the intended task boundary. We formulate few-shot ICL as decision-boundary induction and decompose performance into boundary induction and rule execution. Using controlled binary verification tasks with decomposable boundaries, we diagnose which necessary components are behaviorally enforced and, under chain-of-thought, explicitly recognized. Across three tasks and multiple model families, we show that few-shot ICL often induces component-biased verifiers rather than the full target boundary. Stronger models are more robust to this bias, while chain-of-thought reshapes rather than uniformly improves boundary recovery. An explicit-rule intervention further shows that improvements come from both recovering missing boundary components and executing recognized ones more reliably. These results suggest that evaluating few-shot ICL should go beyond aggregate accuracy and directly test boundary recovery. Code is available at https://github.com/limy805/boundary-icl.

paper.title: InSight-doc: Agentic Visual Perception for Long-Document Understanding

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Long-document understanding often requires reasoning over many visually rich pages, making inference costly and prone to context rot. In this work, we propose InSight-doc, an agentic visual perception framework that treats visual resolution as an adaptive reasoning-time resource. InSight-doc starts from low resolution and selectively zooms into high-resolution regions for finer evidence, without relying on any external retriever. To train such an agent, we construct an active-perception corpus of 17.9K high-quality SFT examples with region-level zoom-in trajectories, accompanied by 19.2K hard RL examples. Through SFT+RL, InSight-doc-8B improves the baseline by 4.3–16.4 accuracy points over document VQA benchmarks. On long documents, it reduces hallucination by more than 40% and inference latency by 41%–68% while maintaining an accuracy lead. Our code, datasets, and model are released at https://github.com/m-Just/InSight-doc.

paper.title: Tracing Query Expansion Effects through Sparse Autoencoder Features
paper.abstract: Query expansion (QE) is a critical technique in information retrieval that enriches underspecified queries with additional textual context. However, its effect is often unreliable in modern dense retrieval, especially for strong off-the-shelf retrievers without retraining. Existing studies mainly examine expansion quality, semantic drift, or retrieval outcomes, but rarely explain how QE changes dense retrievers internally. In this work, we trace QE effects through sparse autoencoder (SAE) features. Using paired original and expanded queries, we decompose layer-wise retriever representations into sparse latent activations, identify QE-related latents from expansion-induced activation shifts, and interpret them with natural-language descriptions and retrieval cases. Our analysis shows that effective QE induces layer-concentrated changes in sparse latents aligned with retrieval intent and entity attributes, rather than only perturbing final query embeddings. SAE-based activation steering further validates these latents improve retrieval more consistently than random interventions or vanilla QE across four benchmarks, suggesting that SAEs can explain QE effects and offer a lightweight option for precise retrieval behavior modulation without query rewriting or retriever fine-tuning.

paper.title: A Controlled Study of Auxiliary Supervision for Low-Resource Emotion Classification
paper.abstract: We present a controlled empirical study of auxiliary supervision for low-resource emotion classification. Using a shared-encoder multi-task learning framework, we compare three auxiliary objectives - coarse affective valence, valence-activation structure, and positive-affect detection - across three supervision sources: aligned labels deterministically derived from gold emotion annotations, rule-based weak labels generated with VADER, and synthetic labels generated by Qwen2.5-14B. We evaluate on MELD, GoEmotions, and DAIR-AI Emotion under matched training procedures and multiple data regimes. Auxiliary supervision yields its clearest, though modest, gains in low-resource settings, especially on MELD and GoEmotions, while improvements on DAIR-AI Emotion are smaller and less consistent. Error and per-class analyses suggest that gains concentrate in semantically overlapping or low-frequency categories such as anger/disgust, fear/sadness, remorse, and embarrassment. We further find that agreement with aligned auxiliary labels is only weakly associated with downstream transfer, suggesting that useful auxiliary supervision need not exactly reproduce gold-derived affective mappings. Overall, our results support auxiliary supervision as a lightweight inductive bias for low-resource emotion classification, while also showing that its benefits are dataset-dependent and sensitive to auxiliary-task design.

paper.title: DeepDiver-DR: Empowering LLMs for Deep Research via Specialized Multi-Agent Collaboration
paper.abstract: Deep Research (DR) systems iteratively plan, retrieve evidence, and synthesize long-form reports in response to complex, open-ended queries. Existing approaches suffer from context overload, role entanglement, and error propagation over long horizons, while the most capable DR systems remain locked behind massive proprietary models. We present DeepDiver-DR (DD-DR), a multi-agent framework that decomposes the DR process into three specialized roles—planner, information seeker, and writer—coordinated through a persistent, file-based shared workspace. Each role is further equipped with fine-grained, DR-specific tools. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce RubricWrite-Bench (RW-Bench), a benchmark of 100 rubric-based writing queries with a two-phase assessment of global report quality and point-level rubric fulfillment. Experiments show that DD-DR (30B) establishes a new state of the art among models at the same parameter scale on the DeepResearch Bench, and achieves performance competitive with leading proprietary DR systems on RW-Bench. Ablations further confirm the contribution of the architectural components.

paper.title: On Large Language Models for Effective Red Teaming

author.affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Red teaming attacks are a well-established approach for identifying weaknesses in large language models (LLMs). As the generative capabilities of LLMs continue to improve, researchers have increasingly leveraged them to automatically generate red teaming attacks, often by crafting adversarial prompts that target other LLMs. Despite this progress, there is currently no effective strategy for selecting suitable LLMs to serve as red teaming agents. In this work, we propose a systematic framework to investigate how various factors of LLMs influence their effectiveness in generating red teaming attacks, including model security, general capability, and parameter scale. The goal of this study is to understand the mechanisms behind the effectiveness of red teaming LLMs and to provide principled guidance for selecting appropriate red teaming LLM.

paper.title: Beyond Visual Neglect: Context-Preference Activation Steering for Mitigating MLLM Hallucinations
paper.abstract: Object hallucination remains a primary obstacle to the reliable deployment of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Current inference-time mitigation methods mainly assume that hallucinations stem from visual neglect and therefore steer models toward greater visual reliance. In contrast, our systematic interventions on multiple MLLMs show that increasing visual reliance may exacerbate hallucinations on some models, whereas reducing it may mitigate them. This result suggests that visual neglect alone provides an incomplete explanation of hallucination. We characterize the image as a context that competes with both the model’s parametric knowledge and its textual context. Based on this characterization, we propose a training-free framework, Context-Preference Activation Steering (CAS). CAS extracts two Context Preference Vectors (CPVs), designed to capture different context-preference relationships, from two small sets of conflict samples and injects signed residuals into the MLP-sublayer outputs before residual addition at four mid-early layers in a single forward pass. Experiments show that CAS substantially mitigates object hallucinations with negligible decoding overhead while maintaining F1, lexical diversity, and repetition rates close to those of the base models. Code and data are available at https://github.com/wss7/CAS.

paper.title: Evaluating Demographics Effect in Policy-Governed Tool-Using Agents Across Real-World Service Domains
paper.abstract: Imagine two users contacting the same AI travel agent on the same day, making the same request under identical policy conditions, differing only in the demographic information they provide. The governing policy is explicit and contains no demographic distinction. Should the agent respond identically? We present an empirical study of how demographic context influences the behaviour of policy-governed LLM agents. Building on an existing agentic evaluation framework, we augment policy-governed tasks with controlled demographic cues while keeping policies and task environments fixed, enabling behavioural differences to be attributed solely to demographic signals. To evaluate procedural fairness, we introduce three procedural dimensions: Policy Application Fairness (PAF), Procedural Effort Equity (PEE), and User Fulfillment Parity (UFP), unified into the Demographic Policy Fairness Index (DPFI). Across more than twenty thousand simulated interactions spanning multiple service domains and frontier models, all evaluated systems exhibit systematic demographic disparities that conventional task-success metrics fail to capture. Our analysis identifies three distinct failure modes with different procedural dynamics, demonstrating that aggregate success metrics can obscure how disparities emerge. Overall, the findings suggest that demographic bias in policy-governed LLM agents manifests through procedural behaviour rather than a single uniform failure pattern. The proposed framework provides a foundation for systematically auditing procedural fairness in policy-driven LLM agents.

paper.title: VisMind: Stateful Synthetic Dialogue for Visual Mid-Training
paper.abstract: The mid-training phase has emerged as a critical bridge for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the scarcity of high-quality visual reasoning data. While data synthesis offers a promising alternative, conventional stateless synthesis paradigms produce shallow trajectories that quickly succumb to utility plateaus. To overcome this, we propose VisMind, a novel multi-agent collaborative framework that generates deep-reasoning Stateful Synthetic Dialogue (SSD) from visual inputs. By orchestrating iterative problem-solving, where peer student agents engage in bidirectional critique under the ground-truth-anchored guidance of a teacher, VisMind transforms static, fragmented responses into rich, multi-turn logical derivations. Utilizing this interactive paradigm, we construct a dense mid-training corpus of approximately 1.14B tokens. Extensive experiments across the Qwen2-VL and InternVL3 model families demonstrate that applying this corpus via Continued Pretraining consistently outperforms a representative stateless synthesis approach and elevates standard baselines by up to a 2.24% absolute average gain across comprehensive mathematical and logical benchmarks. Furthermore, in-depth analysis reveals that the SSD paradigm exhibits continuous linear scaling without early saturation, fosters intrinsic reasoning generalization, and establishes a robust cognitive foundation that enhances the efficacy of subsequent Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards.

paper.title: EDRAC: Benchmarking Arabic Dialect Reading Comprehension

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Alexandria University and New York University, Abu Dhabi
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Dialectal Arabic (DA) remains under-resourced compared to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), particularly for machine reading comprehension (MRC) and question answering (QA). Existing Arabic QA benchmarks primarily focus on formal written MSA or multiple-choice QA, with limited coverage of naturally spoken dialects. Here, we aim to bridge this gap. We introduce EDRAC, the first large-scale benchmark for dialectal Arabic machine reading comprehension (MRC) and generative QA, covering five major dialects: Egyptian, Moroccan, Emirati, Syrian, and Saudi Arabic. EDRAC contains 499 passages derived from naturally occurring spoken interactions and 4,977 corresponding QA pairs generated through a human–LLM collaborative pipeline combining iterative generation, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human verification. We benchmark Arabic-centric and multilingual LLMs on EDRAC using lexical and semantic metrics. Our results reveal substantial gaps between semantic answer quality and dialectal fidelity, highlighting the limitations of existing evaluation metrics for dialectal Arabic generation. EDRAC provides a realistic and challenging MRC benchmark for future research on dialectal Arabic NLP.

paper.title: RoleArena: Autonomous Plot Progression for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Role-Playing

author.affiliation: University of British Columbia and Tencent
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Improving the plot progression ability of role-playing language agents (RPLAs) plays a critical role in enhancing user experience and dialogue immersion. However, research on plot progression in role-playing language agents is still limited. Existing datasets often contain too few dialogue turns and lack large-scale sentences with clear deterministic plot turns, which restricts further model development and evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose RoleArena, an innovative multi-agent role-playing environment. By introducing a critic agent and combining discrete plot lines with environment-agent-based dynamic judgments, the system generates long multi-turn dialogues with key markers for plot progression. Based on RoleArena, we construct the PlotStream dataset, which contains 39.3k characters and 170k dialogues, with annotations for key plot progression sentences. In addition, based on PlotStream, we further develop PlotRole-7B and PlotRole-72B, RPLAs built upon the Qwen2.5 model and specialized in plot progression capabilities. Extensive experiments show that RoleArena and PlotRole improve dialogue generation with plot progression and strengthen the ability of plot progression.

paper.title: DARTS: Diversity-Aware Reasoning Tree Search for Test-Time Scaling

author.affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Harbin Institute of Technology
University of Hong Kong and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory

paper.abstract: Test-time tree search improves the reasoning capability of large language models under fixed inference budgets. However, existing solution-level MCTS often suffers from local homogenization: once a promising solution pattern is found, subsequent search tends to refine nearby variants rather than explore distinct reasoning paths. This wastes computation on redundant candidates and limits solution-space coverage. To address this problem, we propose Diversity-Aware Reasoning Tree Search (DARTS), a Bayesian tree-search framework that treats reasoning-path diversity as an explicit search objective. DARTS separates expansion into local refinement and orthogonal regeneration, and updates action posteriors using a joint reward over task quality and reasoning-path diversity. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests, DARTS achieves the best exploration performance and produces more diverse correct solutions. With half the budget, it matches or exceeds the strongest tree-search baseline in four of six settings. On molecular optimization tasks, DARTS improves both optimization quality and structural diversity, suggesting cross-domain transfer.

paper.title: Procedural Blind Spots in Agent Evaluation: A Survey, Coverage Analysis, and New Missions for NLP
paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in multi-step, multi-turn settings that combine user interaction, tool use, state changes, and communication. Most agent evaluation still emphasizes task completion, while procedure-aware checks remain fragmented. We conduct a systematic survey and introduce \mathcal{F}^*, a systematic organizing map that maps scattered procedural checks into a shared audit space spanning integrity relations and quality dimensions. Applying this framework to recent agent-evaluation work reveals three procedural blind spots: most work remains outcome-focused or procedurally under-specified, procedure-aware checks mostly remain local spot-checks, and communication grounding lags action compliance. To close these gaps, we propose four new Natural Language Processing (NLP) missions around communication grounding, constraint semantics, reasoning faithfulness, and procedural equity. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of procedure-aware agent evaluation, offering a common vocabulary and coverage map that clarify what current benchmarks can certify and provide clear guidelines for future research.

paper.title: Arabic Sentence Segmentation Across Genres and Punctuation Conditions

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and New York University, Abu Dhabi
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Sentence segmentation in Arabic is challenging due to ambiguous and inconsistent punctuation, with many texts lacking reliable sentence boundary markers. Existing approaches rely heavily on punctuation cues and are typically evaluated on well-formed text, limiting their robustness in realistic Arabic settings. To address this, we introduce AraSEG, a genre-diverse sentence segmentation corpus spanning eight genres and a wide range of punctuation and document structure conditions. Using AraSEG, we evaluate LLMs, lightweight encoder models, and dependency parser-based models under increasingly challenging segmentation settings. Our experiments show that lightweight encoders, and even dependency parser-based models, outperform LLMs under the hardest conditions. We further investigate the effects of training data size and genre diversity, finding that performance eventually saturates and cross-genre generalization remains challenging. We also demonstrate that accurate sentence segmentation substantially improves downstream dependency parsing. We make our code, data, and models publicly available.

paper.title: AutoBackdoor: Automating Backdoor Attacks via LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Backdoor attacks are an important safety risk for large language models (LLMs), yet existing studies often rely on manually crafted triggers and fixed poisoning pipelines. This limits the diversity of attack behaviors and makes it difficult to systematically evaluate defense robustness. We introduce AutoBackdoor, an agent-driven framework for scalable LLM backdoor red-teaming. Given a target scenario, AutoBackdoor automatically generates triggers, constructs poisoned samples, refines them through self-feedback, and produces backdoored models through fine-tuning. We evaluate the framework across four realistic scenarios: Bias Recommendation, Hallucination Injection, Error Code Generation, and Peer Review Manipulation. Experiments on LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and GPT-4o show that AutoBackdoor can achieve over 90% attack success with only a small number of poisoned samples. We further find that existing defenses provide limited protection against these agent-generated attacks. These results suggest that automated red-teaming can serve as a useful tool for stress-testing LLM backdoor defenses and understanding emerging risks from agent-driven model customization pipelines. Our code is available at https://github.com/bboylyg/AutoBackdoor.

paper.title: Prompted Values and Deployed Policies: A Truth–Propriety Diagnostic in Language Models

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Macau University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Prompting a language model to endorse a value does not by itself establish how that value is deployed when responses require tradeoffs. We study this gap in truth–propriety dilemmas, where direct truth-telling can conflict with tact, face-saving, deference, or role-sensitive restraint. We introduce Truth–Propriety Alignment (TPA), a 600-prompt diagnostic benchmark over 100 scenario groups, and conduct a single-model diagnostic evaluation of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under deterministic decoding. The model remains predominantly truth-oriented, but trigger-assigned scenario groups differ sharply in how residual responses are distributed. Because value triggers are fixed within scenario groups, we interpret this pattern as trigger-associated residual composition rather than a causal trigger effect. A small semantic audit shows that compatible residuals are mixed: they include substantive reframings but also tonal and lexical tracking. Finally, a hidden-state probe is nearly matched by an exact-prompt BoW baseline, and deleting the explicit value-trigger sentence does not reduce BoW performance, indicating that behavioral-label predictability is distributed across the prompt surface. We therefore frame TPA as a diagnostic audit of prompt intent, observed behavior, scenario/trigger priors, annotation boundaries, and probe evidence, rather than as evidence for prompt-independent value representations.

paper.title: When Reward-Free Signals Are Not Directions: A Gradient-Level Diagnostic for Test-Time Reasoning Optimization

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: First-order test-time optimization (TTO) updates continuous variables such as logits or latent states for a single input. Successful methods usually rely on external reward models or verifiers to supply a semantic gradient. We ask whether reward-free signals from model distributions or prompted self-verification can supply comparable update directions for reasoning tasks. In logit-space TTO, we compare each reward-free gradient with an operational reward-model reference direction, instantiated as the reward-model gradient on the same logits. Across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, confidence gradients remain nearly orthogonal to the reference, entropy-slope gradients have vanishing scale near greedy rollouts, and terminal answer certainty is sparse and reference-sensitive. Prompted-verifier gradients are more reference-dependent: in a tokenizer-matched Llama diagnostic, four variants attain moderate RM-relative alignment and measurable local RM-score gains. Nevertheless, in end-to-end TTO on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the selected reward-free signals produce no wrong-to-correct flips on MATH-500, AIME-2024, AIME-2025, or GSM8K, while a separate reward-model-guided TTO reproduction provides an external positive control with measurable gains.

paper.title: Scope3Trace: Evidence-Based Identification and Extraction of Scope 3 GHG Emissions from Sustainability Reports
paper.abstract: Scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions account for the majority of corporate carbon footprints, yet remain difficult to analyze at scale due to sparse disclosures, heterogeneous report document formats, and limited evidence traceability. Existing approaches typically rely on large language models to extract emissions information from ESG reports, but often lack explicit evidence grounding or depend on costly manual annotation and verification to ensure extraction reliability.
