To make such methodology-driven planning executable and auditable in heterogeneous settings, we introduce Data2MCP, a router-based orchestration infrastructure that standardizes SQL databases, knowledge graphs, vector stores, and tables as MCP-compatible tools and routes queries dynamically for multi-source retrieval and join-like reasoning. We compare Data2MCP against a RAG baseline and DA-Agent across multi-source retrieval, DAComp, and BIRD MiniDev. In multi-source retrieval, Data2MCP outperforms DA-Agent, and strategy injection benefits both architectures. On DAComp, strategy injection improves DA-Agent from 50.84 to 57.17 (+6.33). The code is available at https://github.com/turambar928/Data2MCP.

paper.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Visual-Prior Conflicts
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must often arbitrate between visual evidence and world-knowledge priors when an image conflicts with commonsense expectations. Existing work has demonstrated that activation steering vectors can bias model outputs toward either source of information, but it remains unclear whether this arbitration mechanism generalizes across languages. To investigate this, we construct a multilingual extension of the Visual CounterFact color split and derive activation steering directions that contrast image-grounded answers with prior-based answers. Across 12 languages, we find that English-derived and shared multilingual steering directions consistently shift model outputs on non-English prompts, suggesting that visual-prior arbitration has a substantial cross-lingual component. At the same time, we find that performance gains on common knowledge questions can come at the cost of image-grounded accuracy, a trade-off that is particularly pronounced for lower-resource languages. Code and data are available at https://github.com/elffiona/cross-lingual-visual-prior-steering.

paper.title: STAIF: A Stage-wise Optimization for Complex Instruction Following

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Following complex instructions with multiple explicit constraints remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods, such as DPO, optimize holistic reward signals that often under-emphasize strict satisfaction of individual constraints, particularly under out-of-distribution or multi-constraint settings. In this paper, we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework that decouples the alignment of subjective (soft) constraints from the optimization of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints. Stage 1 applies preference optimization with multiple negative samples to sharpen the sensitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance with hard constraints. To support this method, we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approximately 31,000 complex multi-constraint instructions. Extensive analyses validate the design of STAIF and show state-of-the-art performance on representative benchmarks against strong baselines, as well as genuine generalization.

paper.title: RUBAS: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning for Agent Safety
paper.abstract: The evolution of LLMs into tool-enabled agents creates a new class of safety challenges associated with real-world execution rather than simple text generation. Existing alignment methods often rely on coarse refusal signals or static supervision, making it difficult to balance safety with useful tool execution across diverse agentic risks. We introduce RUBAS, a rubric-based reinforcement learning framework for agent safety. RUBAS decomposes agent behavior into four dimensions: tool-use safety, argument safety, response safety, and helpfulness. These structured rubrics provide fine-grained and interpretable rewards over complete agent trajectories, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize safe tool use while preserving task completion. Extensive experiments across multiple agent safety benchmarks and models show that RUBAS improves safety over standard alignment baselines, reduces tool-grounded hallucinations, and maintains competitive utility. Our results suggest that multi-dimensional rubric rewards provide an effective training signal for aligning LLM agents in safety-critical tool-use settings.

paper.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science

paper.abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SOURCECLASH, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.

paper.title: ParaCalib: Semantically Calibrated Paralinguistic Modeling for Depression Detection
paper.abstract: Vocal behavior provides important signals for speech-based depression detection, but its interpretation often depends on what is being said and how it functions in context. However, existing methods typically treat acoustic cues as context-independent markers, making it difficult to distinguish vocal form from its context-dependent communicative function. We propose ParaCalib, a framework that semantically calibrates paralinguistic behavior by interpreting vocal patterns relative to utterance-level semantic context and inferred communicative function and representing them in a comparable state space. Concretely, ParaCalib uses an Audio-Language Model (ALM) to generate contextualized vocal descriptions and an LLM-based Paralinguistic State Extractor (PSE) to map these descriptions into a structured Semantically Calibrated Paralinguistic (SC-Para) representation. ParaCalib achieves the highest mean Macro-F1 among the evaluated methods, reaching 71.9% on DAIC-WOZ and 90.5% on MODMA. Our controlled analysis provides direct evidence of semantic calibration at the PSE stage: under a fixed caption-level acoustic description, varying the accompanying semantic context changes the inferred depression-related paralinguistic evidence. Our exploratory analysis further identifies recurring configurations of paralinguistic states associated with depression labels rather than a single uniformly dominant state.

paper.title: GIFT: Reconciling Post-Training Objectives via Variational Finite-Temperature Gibbs Initialization
paper.abstract: The prevailing post-training paradigm for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)—Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) followed by Reinforcement Learning (RL)—suffers from an intrinsic optimization mismatch: the rigid likelihood maximization in SFT induces distributional collapse, thereby exhausting the exploration space necessary for subsequent RL. Motivated by the Gibbs optimum of KL-regularized RL, we derive a token-level variational surrogate that makes the SFT target structurally compatible with the subsequent RL stage, and propose Gibbs Initialization with Finite Temperature (GIFT). Standard SFT emerges as a degenerate zero-temperature limit of this surrogate, while a finite temperature preserves structural diversity. Our experiments demonstrate that GIFT outperforms standard SFT and surpasses competitive baselines when utilized for RL initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/zzy1127/GIFT.

paper.title: Bridging Lexical Divergence: LLM-Assisted, Cost-Efficient, Zero-shot Scientific Entity Linking
paper.abstract: Scientific domain entity linking (EL) differs from general domain EL because mentions and entity names often lack lexical overlap. Another challenge is that specialized terminology is used in the scientific domain, which is rarely encountered in models pretrained on general domains. Therefore, models trained on general domains transfer poorly to scientific domains. To address this, in-domain fine-tuning is the natural remedy. However, many scientific domains lack expert-annotated data, motivating the need for a zero-human-annotation approach. Existing zero-shot methods heavily rely on LLMs to generate aliases across entire mention corpora, which incurs substantial computational cost, and those methods provide no mechanism to filter out noise from LLMs. To address these challenges, we propose Sci-ZSEL, a framework that selectively generates entity aliases with an LLM to control computational cost, and applies an ontology-aware filter to remove aliases that semantically drift toward ontology neighbors. Then, filtered aliases are used to construct pseudo-labeled mention-entity pairs for fine-tuning. To enable evaluation of EL under low lexical overlap, we also release a new animal science EL benchmark linked to three livestock trait ontologies, where mentions and entities exhibit substantially lower lexical overlap than in existing benchmarks. Across five benchmarks, Sci-ZSEL outperforms the non-fine-tuned baseline, is most useful on nonoverlapping mentions, and combining it with curated synonyms gives the best performance in most settings.

paper.title: ARMOR-PRM: Adversarially Robust Process Reward Models via Counterfactual Margins and Invariance Regularization
paper.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are vulnerable to reward hacking: policies exploit surface cues such as confident phrasing or structured formatting in place of logical correctness, which yields an inverted-U collapse under optimization pressure. We propose ARMOR-PRM, which augments standard PRM training with three regularizers: a counterfactual margin loss, an adversarial invariance loss with low-score anchoring, and a gradient penalty on the reward head. On ProcessBench (three splits; "math" excluded due to training data overlap), ARMOR-PRM improves Detection Rate by 14.9 percentage points and AUROC by 4.1 percentage points over Vanilla PRM, and is the only variant whose Best-of-N reranking accuracy improves monotonically through N=128. A domain-shift diagnostic further shows that objective-level robustness and data coverage are distinct but complementary axes: ARMOR-PRM responds best to iterative hard-negative retraining, suggesting a practical two-stage deployment path.

paper.title: Toppling the Hierarchy in Byte-level Language Modeling
paper.abstract: This work examines recent byte-level models and their failure to perfectly manipulate characters. State-of-the-art byte-level models use a hierarchical structure, starting at the byte level, downsampling to the word level, and then upsampling back to bytes. While this improves training and inference efficiency, we find that the hierarchical design itself limits character-level understanding, with pure byte-level models consistently outperforming hierarchical variants on character manipulation tasks. Ablating transformer layers into attention and feed-forward components further reveals that byte-level attention is the primary mechanism driving this behavior. Together, our results provide an explanation for the character-level failures of hierarchical byte models and establish a clear trade-off between computational efficiency and fine-grained character understanding.

paper.title: When Users Don’t Ask: Benchmarking Context-Driven Memory Retrieval in Conversational Agents
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as long-horizon conversational agents, motivating growing interest in memory systems. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate memory through QA-style probing rather than in-situ conversational usage. We introduce LOCOMO-CONV, a conversational memory benchmark derived from LoCoMo with four query styles: dialog, implicit, counterfactual, and composed. Across four representative memory systems, we evaluate both retrieval recall and end-to-end response quality. Our experiments show that conversational framing exposes substantial retrieval gaps overlooked by QA benchmarks, especially on implicit and composed queries, which multi-facet query rewriting narrows for raw-turn but not abstractive memory. We further find that strong retrieval does not fully translate into response quality, and that implicit queries exhibit silent grounding, where memory improves contextual grounding without explicitly surfacing the gold fact. These results point to reasoning-based memory elaboration as a promising direction, and we release auxiliary supportive_memory annotations capturing conversationally useful context beyond the original gold evidence.

paper.title: Guided Permutation Scoring (GPS) : Option-Order Permutation for Multiple-Choice Question Answering

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Stony Brook
State University of New York, Stony Brook
State University of New York at Stony Brook and Academic medical center at State University of New York at Stony Brook

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are sensitive to the order in which answer choices are presented in Multiple-Choice Question Answering. The same question can yield a different prediction when its options are shuffled. Although exhaustive majority voting over all permutations can mitigate this bias, its factorial cost makes it impractical at inference time. We propose GPS (Guided Permutation Scoring), a two-stage inference-time pipeline that selects option orderings more likely to produce correct predictions from a frozen LLM. A sensitivity classifier first identifies which questions are genuinely vulnerable to positional interference; robust questions are answered directly, while sensitive ones are forwarded to a trained permutation scorer that identifies a more position-stable option ordering, promoting better predictions. Unlike prior approaches that either enumerate all permutations uniformly, or require modifying the LLM’s parameters, GPS is the first method to actively select permutations so that the base model can consistently give better answers. GPS steadily improves Accuracy, and Macro F1 across all evaluated model-dataset combinations, with remarkable reductions in positional bias metrics.

paper.title: Reflecting What Matters: Same-Surgery References for Postoperative Clinical Note Generation
paper.abstract: Generating the first postoperative outpatient note requires selecting which information from heterogeneous clinical records should be reflected in the final note, rather than merely summarizing all inputs. We evaluate this task on an original 170-case set of de-identified clinical cases collected at Seoul National University Hospital (SNUH), involving two surgical divisions and five physicians. We then extend the evaluation to 1,329 cases across 10 surgery groups within the same institution to examine whether the main trends persist at a larger scale. We introduce physician- and surgery-specific same-surgery references: structured reflection maps that capture how information is selected and rewritten in prior same-surgery cases. Experiments show that these references become most effective when carried into the merge stage, suggesting that the main bottleneck is deciding what to reflect across records. We further show that cross-patient references can induce unsupported transfer from prior cases. To analyze this trade-off, we use a human-validated two-source FactScore that checks each generated fact against both the source records and the physician-written note. A lightweight grounding constraint reduces hallucination while maintaining or improving alignment with physician-written notes across divisions and LLMs.

paper.title: Do MLLMs Really Understand Space? A Mathematical Spatial Reasoning Evaluation

author.affiliation: Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
NLPR, CASIA and University of Science and Technology of China
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on perception-oriented tasks, yet their ability to perform mathematical spatial reasoning, defined as the capacity to parse and manipulate two- and three-dimensional relations, remains unclear. While humans easily master textbook-style spatial problems, current MLLMs exhibit substantially higher error rates, exposing a fundamental weakness in spatial comprehension. To investigate this gap, we present MathSpatial, the first large-scale and systematic dataset resource dedicated to mathematical spatial reasoning in MLLMs. MathSpatial provides two complementary subsets: MathSpatial-Bench (2,000 problems) for evaluating spatial reasoning isolated from perceptual noise, and MathSpatial-Corpus (8,000 problems) equipped with structured reasoning traces for training. Benchmarking 20+ MLLMs reveals a severe deficit: non-reasoning models largely languish below 60% accuracy, and even the strongest reasoning models fall ~16 percentage points behind human performance (96.3%). Crucially, we demonstrate that fine-tuning on MathSpatial-Corpus yields consistent performance gains across model families. MathSpatial provides a vital resource for diagnosing and advancing spatial reasoning in MLLMs. The dataset and related resources are available at https://github.com/shuolucs/MathSpatial.

paper.title: Agent Tools Orchestration Leaks More: Dataset, Benchmark, and Mitigation
paper.abstract: LLM agents can combine individually non-revealing tool returns and disclose a sensitive conclusion, creating Tools Orchestration Privacy Risk (TOP-R). We formalize TOP-R through three conditions: conclusion sensitivity, single-source non-inferability, and compositional inferability. We introduce Library-Grounded Reverse-Inference Seed Expansion (LRSE), a four-library reverse-construction pipeline, and use it to build TOP-Bench, a 1,000-instance benchmark evaluated under a controlled two-stage tool-use protocol. Across six LLM agents, average task completion, leakage, and H-score are 98.0 percent, 88.6 percent, and 20.4. With native reasoning enabled, four models average 81.4 percent final-response leakage and 82.4 percent reasoning-trace leakage. With reasoning disabled, three prompt-only safeguards improve H-score by an average of about 3.4 points on TOP-Bench. We further propose TOP-Align, an SFT+DPO method for learning safer task-completion boundaries. On a separate post-training evaluation set, TOP-Align improves H-score by 16.2 points over the base model, versus a 5.0-point average gain from prompt-only mitigation on the same set. These results show that TOP-R requires defenses beyond prompting alone. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/1Ponder/TOP-R.

paper.title: CausalPrism: Component-Level Evaluation of Intervention-Based Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Evaluating causal reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is complicated by benchmarks that conflate distinct reasoning operations into aggregate scores. We propose CausalPrism, an evaluation framework grounded in structural causal model semantics and cognitive models of causal inference, which decomposes intervention-based causal reasoning into three functional primitives—Causal Prior, Forward State Tracing, and Belief Updating—plus a consistency primitive, Agency Sensitivity. Primitives are instantiated in directed acyclic graphs and evaluated across three narrative domains of varying semantic richness. Across 14 open-source and frontier LLMs, Belief Updating is the dominant bottleneck: the best model reaches only 0.613 accuracy, while GPT-5.2 and GPT-5-mini score 0.531 and 0.517 despite near-ceiling performance on Causal Prior and Forward State Tracing. Prior exhibits systematic domain sensitivity and over-rejection. Agency framing effects are family-dependent for weaker models. We argue against treating causal reasoning as a unitary capability and motivate targeted evaluation and training along multiple primitive axes.

paper.title: GAMS: Geospatial Knowledge Enhanced Agentic Framework for Urban Human Mobility Behavior Simulation
paper.abstract: Recently, researchers have explored leveraging the commonsense knowledge and reasoning capabilities of large language models to accelerate human mobility simulation. However, these methods suffer from several critical shortcomings, including inadequate modeling of urban spaces, poor integration with individual mobility patterns, and weak alignment with collective mobility distributions. To address these limitations, we propose Geospatial Knowledge Enhanced Agentic framework for Mobility Simulation (GAMS), an agentic framework that leverages the language based geospatial foundation model to simulate human mobility in urban space. GAMS comprises three core modules: MobExtractor, which extracts template-based mobility profiles and synthesizes new ones during simulation; GeoGenerator, which generates trajectory points considering collective mobility knowledge and urban geospatial knowledge; and TrajEnhancer, which captures individual mobility regularities from real-world trajectories and refines to generate style-aligned synthetic trajectories. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that GAMS achieves superior performance over various state-of-the-art methods, with more than a 17% improvement by capturing diverse mobility regularities. Our codes and datasets are open-sourced via https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CAMS-1992/.

paper.title: The Role of Entropy in Visual Grounding: Analysis and Optimization
paper.abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning–based fine-tuning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have highlighted the importance of entropy control for stable optimization. While entropy has been extensively studied in reasoning-centric settings, its behavior and optimization role in perception-oriented tasks remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we reveal that entropy exhibits fundamentally different roles in perception tasks compared to reasoning, particularly under continuous prediction and reward. Using visual grounding as a case study, we show that entropy can remain misaligned with optimization objectives due to persistent low-probability yet high-advantage samples. Building on these findings, we introduce ECVGPO (Entropy Control Visual Grounding Policy Optimization), an interpretable algorithm designed for effective entropy regulation. Through entropy control, the trade-off between exploration and exploitation is better balanced. Experiments show that ECVGPO achieves broad improvements across various benchmarks and models.

paper.title: MIMIC-CTRL-2026: A Realistic Clinical Trial Dataset to Benchmark LLM performance
paper.abstract: Patient recruitment remains a major barrier in clinical trials, as identifying eligible participants often requires manual screening of complex health records, contributing significantly to trial delays and increased costs. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential to automate this process, existing public datasets are overly simplistic in their patient representation: they pair full criterion lists with single-paragraph synthetic summaries, failing to capture the longitudinal complexity of real clinical records. We introduce MIMIC-CTRL-2026, a dataset of 800 manually labeled patient-criterion pairs grounded in real-world longitudinal EHR data from MIMIC-IV, annotated by clinically trained experts. Each instance pairs one eligibility criterion with a full patient record spanning multiple discharge notes, radiology reports, lab values, and medication histories. While simple prompting achieves high performance (κ = 0.84) on existing benchmarks, it collapses (κ = 0.06) on our dataset, revealing a substantial benchmark-difficulty gap between simplified and real-world clinical evaluation. Lastly, we present a framework combining structured pre-processing with a clinician-validated expanded prompt that substantially outperforms naive baselines without any model fine-tuning, establishing a realistic benchmark for automated clinical trial screening on real EHR data. Our dataset and code are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22103011

paper.title: DuCEI: When to Introduce Metadata in Cross-Entity Interaction for Entity Disambiguation

author.affiliation: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Entity disambiguation links mentions in text to the entities they refer to in a knowledge base. Recent cross-entity interaction models improve candidate comparison by jointly encoding multiple candidates, but incorporating entity metadata into this joint encoding is not straightforward. Appending metadata to every candidate forces joint encoding to process longer inputs with detailed distractor information, which can weaken the contrastive cues that make cross-entity interaction effective. We propose DuCEI, a dual-stage framework that avoids this broad metadata interaction by reducing the candidate set before introducing entity metadata. DuCEI first compares all candidates using title-based cross-entity interaction, and then performs metadata-enriched interaction only among the remaining candidates. This design makes metadata use selective at the candidate level, applying detailed evidence only where it is likely to help. Experiments on six standard benchmarks show that DuCEI achieves the best overall performance among models trained solely on AIDA-CoNLL. Further analyses show that confidence-based selective refinement preserves nearly all of the full two-stage performance while applying Stage 2 to only 27.80% of mentions, reducing inference cost from 1.90× to approximately 1.27× that of Stage 1 alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinwoomin/DuCEI.

paper.title: Beyond One-Hot Replay: Self-Distillation Reduces Target Variance in Continual Pre-Training
paper.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts a pretrained language model to a target domain, but it often degrades general capabilities even when general-data replay is used to mitigate forgetting. We revisit this failure through replay supervision: prior CPT replay mainly tunes data mixtures and token budgets while applying one-hot next-token prediction (NTP) uniformly to domain and replay tokens. This target is natural for learning domain text, but on replay tokens it introduces target variance: it is a noisy, corpus-dependent proxy for preserving the frozen base model’s conditional behavior. We study self-distilled replay: domain tokens keep NTP, while replay tokens are trained to match the frozen base model distribution. Diagnostics show that this target substitution lowers target error, produces more directionally consistent replay gradients, and reduces base-behavior drift. Empirically, self-distilled replay improves the SmolLM3 domain–general trade-off over matched NTP replay across diverse token budgets and replay ratios. It also remains effective for Qwen3 models whose pretraining mixtures are unavailable: under the same mismatched, non-source replay setting, it improves both general score and PubMedQA in all eight matched comparisons. Overall, these results suggest supervising CPT replay to preserve base behavior, rather than fit empirical next tokens, as a way to reduce target variance.

paper.title: When Linguistic and Internal Confidence Diverge in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Users often ask large language models (LLMs) to report how confident they are, but it is unclear whether such linguistic confidence tracks the model’s internal confidence. We study this question across 8 classification tasks, 2 generation tasks and 30 models from three families. For classification, we compare linguistic confidence with logits-based confidence along three axes: association, magnitude agreement and calibration. For generation, we test whether linguistic confidence tracks semantic-entropy-based uncertainty. The axes frequently diverge. Instance-level association is weak on average, although it improves on easier items and for stronger base models. Instruction-tuned models often report higher confidence and sometimes show higher association, but they also have larger confidence gaps and worse calibration. Prompt design mostly changes the distribution of reported confidence. Attitude cues inflate confidence without improving alignment, while score exemplars can preserve rank-order signal when they avoid collapsed confidence values. Regression analyses show that distributional properties of confidence scores explain much of the observed alignment pattern, with model metadata playing a smaller role after controls. These results support a lossy-channel view of linguistic confidence. A more dispersed verbal confidence distribution can carry useful rank information, but it does not make the scores calibrated. Linguistic confidence should therefore be evaluated with multi-axis diagnostics before being used in downstream reliability pipelines.

paper.title: Prism: Persistent Faceted File Memory for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
paper.abstract: Coding agents working on sequential maintenance tasks re-read the same files across related tasks, wasting more than a third of their input tokens on redundant context. The natural fix, caching file summaries, fails to reliably reduce cost: tool-use traces are consistent with agents over-relying on generic descriptions, skipping re-reads, and offsetting token savings with less effective downstream decisions, leaving net cost roughly unchanged. We introduce Prism, a content-hash-keyed file memory that augments summaries with bounded facets: identifier-grounded facts distilled from the agent’s own prior reasoning. On 12 SWE-Chain dependency-upgrade chains, Prism reduces cost by 24.9% on GPT-5 and 9.9% on GPT-5.4-mini, while maintaining comparable aggregate Build+Fix F1. Against no memory, a summary-only ablation yields only a nominal 2.4% cost decrease that falls within run-to-run variability, while a static Aider-style repo-map baseline costs substantially more at 13% over no memory. Two controlled ablations isolate the causal contributions: wiping the persistent store before every task raises cost by 37% over no memory, and replacing facets with a 3× larger unstructured summary raises it by 41%. Code: https://github.com/WhiteFlamesCN/Prism-Opencode.

paper.title: EAGER: Enhancing Generative Event Extraction via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

author.affiliation: Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg and German Research Center for AI
German Research Center for AI and Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg

paper.abstract: End-to-end event extraction remains challenging for large language models as it requires simultaneous identification of event triggers, classification of event types, and extraction of schema-grounded argument spans. We present EAGER, a reinforcement learning framework for generative event extraction that combines fine-grained verifiable rewards with Schema-Contrastive Advantage Estimation to alleviate advantage collapse under sparse binary rewards. Our reward design explicitly targets structural validity, extraction accuracy, groundedness, coverage, over-generation, and span precision. Experiments across seven benchmark datasets show that EAGER consistently outperforms prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and prior reinforcement learning baselines, achieving a substantial improvement over the strongest prior method. Results demonstrate that task-aligned verifiable rewards and contrastive advantage estimation substantially improve structured extraction.

paper.title: TICD: Time-Aware Internal Contrastive Decoding for Enhancing Factuality in Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: Beijing Zhongguancun Academy and Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Zhongguancun Academy and Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, but they remain prone to factual errors in knowledge-intensive tasks. Through layer-wise and timestep-wise probing, we observe a spatiotemporal stratification pattern in dLLMs: structural-token predictions tend to converge earlier across layers, whereas factual-token predictions rely more heavily on deep layers and become reliable only after sufficient denoising progress. Motivated by this observation, we propose Time-Aware Internal Contrastive Decoding (TICD), a training-free decoding method that calibrates final-layer predictions using entropy-gated intermediate-layer references only during semantically reliable denoising stages. This design uses reliable final-intermediate prediction gaps as correction signals to strengthen factual predictions at the final layer. Experiments on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across factuality and reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements over vanilla decoding.

paper.title: Evaluating multi-modal LLMs on historical book illustrations
paper.abstract: Historical book illustrations are culturally significant multimodal artifacts that pose distinctive challenges for computational analysis, including sparse visual cues, historical reproduction techniques, and material degradation. We present the first task-specific evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on historical book illustrations, testing five contemporary models on 1,969 children’s book illustrations across a range of visual labeling exercises and caption generation tasks. Frontier models performed strongly against human consensus annotations on concrete tasks, particularly illustration and setting detection, and mirrored human-level disagreement on entity, object and action identification. All model families struggled with accurate emotional intensity estimation. GPT and Gemini produced the strongest captions, with greater than 70% of images exhibiting no factual errors. Finally, frontier models closely recovered human distributions at the corpus level for major visual categories suggesting their appropriateness for use in large-scale studies.

paper.title: Same Ranking, Different Winner: How Scoring Targets Shape LLM Memory Benchmarks
paper.abstract: Conversational-memory systems increasingly transform dialogue history into facts, summaries, timelines, and other source-linked descendants, so a single source turn can coexist with several derived memories in the same retrieval index. This raises an under-specified evaluation question: which stored form should receive retrieval credit? We show that this scoring-target choice is often left implicit and can materially change benchmark conclusions. We present TIAP, a fixed-output audit that rescores saved ranked outputs under three targets—Raw, Source, and Canonical—without rerunning retrieval. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, switching only the credited target changes nDCG on 83.4%–94.0% of shared queries, flips target orderings on Mem0 and MemoryOS transfer runs, and reverses parser-density recommendations. A 1,902-case semantic audit further shows that relaxed source-linked credit is fully justified only 29.2% of the time, despite high rubric reliability in a validation subset. These results reveal target noninvariance: conclusions about memory architectures can silently flip with a single benchmark-design choice. Conversational-memory papers should therefore define and report the scoring target explicitly.

paper.title: Context Modeling for LLM-Based Behavioral Simulation
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for simulating human decision making at scale, yet prompting-based approaches often fail to recover realistic population-level response distributions, particularly for heterogeneous demographic groups and high-entropy questions. This paper introduces context modeling with agentic AI, a structured simulation framework that explicitly constructs latent, individual-level decision contexts prior to response generation. By separating persona construction from decision making and introducing structured stochasticity through context sampling, the method captures within-group heterogeneity and mitigates mode collapse inherent in single-prompt simulations. Extensive empirical evaluation across population-level and group-conditioned settings shows that context modeling consistently improves simulation fidelity, with especially strong gains on high-entropy questions and demographic subpopulations, while preserving performance on low-entropy tasks. Detailed tail analysis further reveals that the primary improvement arises from recovering minority and low-probability response options that are systematically underrepresented by direct prompting. Overall, the results demonstrate that faithful behavioral simulation requires explicit modeling of contextual heterogeneity and structured uncertainty, establishing context modeling as a robust foundation for LLM-based behavioral simulation.

paper.title: Why are all LLMs Obsessed with Japanese Culture? On the Hidden Cultural and Regional Biases of LLMs
paper.abstract: LLMs have limitations when it comes to cultural coverage and competence, and in some cases, show specific cultural biases. Although prior studies have examined the cultural capabilities of LLMs, none have specifically investigated their regional preferences in generic culture-related questions. In this work, we propose a new dataset based on a comprehensive taxonomy of Culture-Related Open Questions (CROQ), with questions available in 24 languages. We evaluate LLMs by prompting them to answer questions from CROQ and provide a sample location. The results show that, contrary to previous cultural bias work, LLMs show a clear tendency towards countries such as Japan in their answers. Moreover, our results show that when prompting in languages such as English or other high-resource ones, LLMs tend to provide more diverse outputs. Low-resource languages, on the other hand, show more inclinations towards answering questions highlighting countries for which the input language is an official language. Finally, we also investigate at which point of LLM training this cultural bias emerges, with our results suggesting that the first clear signs appear after supervised fine-tuning, and not during pre-training. Dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HiTZ/CROQ.

paper.title: AFROSCOPE: A Framework for Studying the Linguistic Landscape of Africa
paper.abstract: Language Identification (LID), the task of determining the language of a given text, is a fundamental preprocessing step for multilingual NLP. While recent work has expanded African LID, existing systems remain limited in both language coverage and fine-grained discrimination among closely related languages and varieties. We introduce AFROSCOPE, a unified framework for African LID that includes AFROSCOPE-DATA, a dataset covering 640 languages, and AFROSCOPE-MODELS, a suite of strong LID models with broad African language coverage. To address persistent confusions among related or geographically proximate languages, we propose a hierarchical classification approach leveraging AFROSCOPE-MIRROR, a specialized embedding model for targeted disambiguation. This approach improves macro-F1 by 4.55 points on a confusable-language subset compared to our strongest base model. We further analyze cross-lingual transfer and domain effects, showing how language-family structure, script compatibility, and domain coverage shape LID performance. Finally, we position African LID as an enabling technology for measuring Africa’s linguistic landscape in digital text and release AFROSCOPE-DATA and AFROSCOPE-MODELS online.

paper.title: VERGE : Formal Refinement and Guidance Engine for Verifiable LLM Reasoning
paper.abstract: Despite the syntactic fluency of Large Language Models (LLMs), ensuring their logical correctness in high-stakes domains remains a fundamental challenge. We present VERGE, a neurosymbolic framework that combines LLMs with SMT solvers to produce verification-guided answers through iterative refinement. VERGE decomposes LLM outputs into atomic claims, autoformalizes them into first-order logic, and verifies their logical consistency using automated theorem proving. VERGE introduce three key innovations: (1) multi-model consensus via formal semantic equivalence checking to ensure logic-level alignment between candidates, eliminating the syntactic bias of surface-form metrics, (2) semantic routing that directs different claim types to appropriate verification strategies: symbolic solvers for logical claims and LLM ensembles for commonsense reasoning, and (3) precise logical error localization via Minimal Correction Subsets (MCS), which pinpoint the exact subset of claims to revise, transforming binary failure signals into actionable feedback. VERGE framework classifies claims by their logical status and aggregates multiple verification signals into a unified score with variance-based penalty. The system iteratively refines answers using structured feedback until acceptance criteria are met or convergence is achieved. This hybrid approach delivers formal guarantees where possible and consensus verification elsewhere, advancing trustworthy AI. With the GPT-OSS-120B model, VERGE demonstrates an average performance uplift of 18.7% at convergence across a set of reasoning benchmarks compared to single-pass approaches.

paper.title: Causal Attribution Meets Impact-aware Verification: Debugging LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Static–Dynamic Synergy

author.affiliation: Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based Multi-Agent Systems (MASs) are vulnerable to stochastic reasoning and coordination failures, yielding verbose, unstructured trajectories that are difficult to debug. Existing debuggers typically rely on either post-hoc static analysis, which suffers from ambiguous causal attribution, or dynamic verification, which incurs prohibitive computational costs and execution instability. To bridge this gap, we propose SynDebug, a static–dynamic synergistic debugging framework. Statically, SynDebug reconstructs execution topologies from flat logs via a Hierarchical Causal Graph and prioritizes root-cause candidates using synthesized Virtual Oracles.Dynamically, it performs targeted interventions on prioritized candidates to progressively recalibrate suspiciousness rankings based on execution impact. Evaluated across three MAS frameworks and four benchmarks, SynDebug outperforms six baselines, improving the repair success rate by 5.59%–81.81% while maintaining competitive efficiency.

paper.title: Cross-Cultural Value Attribution in Large Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: The rapid adoption of large vision-language models (LVLMs) in recent years has been accompanied by growing fairness concerns due to their propensity to reinforce harmful societal stereotypes. While significant attention has been paid to such fairness concerns in the context of social biases, relatively little prior work has examined the presence of stereotypes in LVLMs related to cultural contexts such as religion, nationality, and socioeconomic status. In this work, we aim to narrow this gap by investigating how LVLM judgments about a person’s moral, ethical, and political values vary across cultural contexts presented in images. We conduct a multi-dimensional analysis of such value judgments in popular LVLMs using counterfactual image sets, which depict the same person across different cultural contexts. Our evaluation framework pairs descriptive analyses (Moral Foundations Theory categorization, lexical analyses, and value sensitivity) with a novel grounding analysis that compares LVLM cross-context variation against two large-scale human surveys (MFQ-2 and WVS Wave 7). Across 4.8 million LVLM generations, we identify three survey-grounding bias patterns that replicate across multiple architecturally diverse models. Additional ablations show that nationality grounding is text-dominant while religion and socioeconomic grounding depend strongly on the image, and that image conditioning can amplify survey-grounding bias patterns.

paper.title: Query-Efficient Memory Injection Attacks on LLM Agents

author.affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security

paper.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent, shared memory, turning the memory module into a new attack surface through which attackers can inject malicious text via query-only interaction. Existing query-only attacks, however, remain expensive, requiring multiple bridging injected queries per target and leaving visible directive traces in stored records. We present AMIA (Agent Memory Injection Attack), which improves both query efficiency and stealth through three injection families along a stealth-to-effectiveness axis: prompt injection, semi-instruction that hides the misleading answer in a benign restate or discredit request, and no-instruction that delivers the false claim as the presupposition of a natural follow-up question. We progressively scale AMIA from QA agents on flat key-value memory, to multi-agent shared memory, and to three production-oriented memory architectures (Mem0, A-MEM, MemoryOS), and finally to three non-QA agent classes (clinical support, code summarization, web shopping), where AMIA exceeds prior query-only attacks on most settings while using a fraction of their inject query budget. We further evaluate defenses that mitigate all three attack families across settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/TrustAIRLab/AMIA.

paper.title: DramaSearch: Benchmarking Multimodal Searching Agents in Ultra-long TV Dramas

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
Huawei Technologies Ltd. and Independent Researcher
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Searching agents have achieved significant progress in NLP, yet their multimodal counterparts are constrained by a lack of suitable evaluation benchmarks requiring reasoning over continuous video, audio, and images. We propose long-form TV dramas as a natural solution and introduce DramaSearch, encompassing 3,600 riddles across 9 dramas totaling 239 hours. Our dataset is generated via a graph-constrained pipeline that processes enriched captions into structured events and multi-granularity evidence views. By employing character-to-view and entity-to-view indexing, we ensure controllable clue disclosure and strictly unique answers. The riddles are categorized into multi-clue, multi-hop, and compositional types, requiring agents to aggregate isolated clues and navigate complex dependency chains. Experiments demonstrate that a Qwen3-8B agent, trained on a held-out set using SFT and RL, achieves an accuracy of 48.3%. This result establishes a strong baseline that performs favorably against zero-shot GPT-5 (37.0%), while indicating significant room for future research. All data and code will be publicly released.

paper.title: Scalable Multi-Agent LLMs for Multi-Turn Conversation Bias Detection and Mitigation

author.affiliation: University of North Carolina at Charlotte
University of North Carolina at Charlotte
University of North Carolina at Charlotte
University of North Carolina at Charlotte

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in conversational systems where responses emerge through multi-turn interactions rather than single prompts. We introduce a multi-agent evaluation framework that probes LLMs for bias through multi-turn conversations. We present a framework that orchestrates three roles (target, adversary, and scorer) under diverse normative fairness definitions. Experiments on five widely used LLMs using 100 adversarial prompts show that adversarial multi-turn probing reliably surfaces bias-related responses, with baseline violation rates exceeding 80% across models, while human validation with the scorer (~85% agreement) confirms the scoring reliability. Preventive prompt-conditioning strategies provide limited reduction in violations, while our iterative post-hoc mitigation pipeline substantially reduces scorer-detected violations under the active fairness profile, from over 80% to near-zero. We frame this as scorer-relative violation reduction rather than universal debiasing.

paper.title: DARE: Dialectical Agentic Reasoning for Structured Knowledge Fact Checking

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Structured knowledge fact checking aims to determine the truthfulness of natural language claims by reasoning over structured evidence. Recent program-generation approaches leverage large language models (LLMs) to generate executable graph reasoning programs, achieving strong performance on structured knowledge fact checking benchmarks. However, these methods remain limited by invalid relation generation, single-path reasoning that lacks self-correction, and biased evidence assessment that tends to overestimate supporting signals. We propose Dialectical Agentic REasoning (DARE), a multi-agent framework that formulates structured knowledge fact checking as an iterative retrieve-reason-reflect process. DARE integrates relation-grounded evidence retrieval to constrain reasoning to valid structures, dialectical bidirectional verification to evaluate evidence from both supporting and refuting perspectives, and confidence-driven meta-reflection to dynamically determine whether additional evidence exploration is necessary. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DARE in structured knowledge fact checking, with an 8B backbone achieving 88.12% accuracy and matching or surpassing GPT-4o-based program-generation baselines, which attests to the efficacy of dialectical agentic reasoning in eliciting the latent reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/inflee/DARE.

paper.title: AEL: Evolving Agent Harness in Open-Ended Environments

author.affiliation: SalesForce.com and Rutgers University, New Brunswick
Rutgers University, Rutgers University and Rutgers University

paper.abstract: LLM Agents Harnesses are hand-designed and stay fixed, so agents accumulate experience but never learn how to use it: which memories to retrieve, when retrieved evidence is misleading, and when the retrieval strategy itself should change. We introduce Agent Evolving Learning (AEL), a two-timescale framework that evolves the harness, recasting memory use as online policy selection. A fast Thompson Sampling bandit selects among memory-retrieval policies episode by episode, while slow LLM reflection follows a diagnose-before-prescribe principle: it first explains why performance degraded, then injects a targeted new retrieval policy as a bandit arm when the current pool plateaus. AEL outperforms ten self-improving and nonLLM baselines on a sequential portfolio benchmark, lifting Sharpe by 27% over the strongest memory-only variant with the lowest variance among all stochastic methods, and generalizes to a support-ticket routing stream, where it improves accuracy by 18% over reflectionfree Thompson Sampling and by 51% over the best prior baseline. Mechanism studies further show that the gains are causal: reflection helps precisely when regimes demand different retrieval behavior, and is provably no-harm/nogain when the best policy is stable.

paper.title: CourtGuard-PMPD: Zero-Shot Policy Adaptation in LLM Safety without Fine-Tuning using Prompt-Based Modular Policy Database

author.affiliation: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University and University of Texas at Dallas

paper.abstract: Safety judges are typically optimized for static harm definitions, yet real-world deployment policies evolve rapidly. We present , a model-agnostic safety judging framework that enables zero-shot policy adaptation without model fine-tuning. Rather than relying on static weights or vector-search RAG over raw text chunks, CourtGuard-PMPD introduces a system abstraction that compiles external governance documents into a Prompt-Based Modular Policy Database (PMPD). At inference time, an LLM category mapper routes inputs against active policy modules to lightweight label judges. When policies change, the system updates its decision boundary instantly by swapping database modules. Evaluated on MLCommons intra-domain policy adaptation, CourtGuard-PMPD achieves the highest mean accuracy (0.84) and F1 (0.82) across four staged policy removals, outperforming policy-following baselines without retraining. On a policy-aligned 850-example attack suite and an eight-dataset public benchmark suite, it remains highly competitive (0.915 and 0.871 accuracy, respectively). These results position policy-grounded judging as a controllable and competitive alternative to static safety classifiers and benchmark-oriented generic judges.

paper.title: Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis
paper.abstract: Significant challenges remain in AI-driven educational systems in balancing privacy preservation with accurate cognitive diagnosis. In order to overcome this, we propose a federated inference framework in which several commercial LLM APIs collaborate without requiring access to raw student data or proprietary model internals. Using multiple federated entities, such as LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude-3-Haiku, our framework builds upon the heterogeneous multi-LLM architecture. The predictions generated by these entities are combined with ε-local differential privacy by adding Laplace noise locally to each entity’s prediction output before aggregation, while residual-based aggregation mitigates model heterogeneity. Our approach is predicated on an honest-but-curious trust paradigm in which API providers are presumed not to abuse submitted queries, and our differential privacy mechanism shields the published diagnostic results from external inference. We conduct rigorous privacy–utility analysis showing strong privacy guarantees with minimal accuracy loss, and extensive real-world evaluations across three educational benchmarks confirm the framework’s practical usability and cross-domain generalizability.

paper.title: Query Symbolically or Retrieve Semantically? A Dataset and Method for Semi-Structured Question Answering

author.affiliation: University of Edinburgh and Samsung AI Research Centre

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for question answering typically retrieve evidence by semantic similarity between the query and document chunks. While effective for unstructured text, this approach is less reliable on semi-structured corpora where answering may require exact filtering, aggregation, or exhaustive retrieval over structured attributes across multiple documents. Symbolic approaches support such operations, but they are often brittle on noisy natural-language corpora. We address this gap with DualGraph, a RAG framework that represents documents through two complementary views: a Textual Knowledge Graph for semantic retrieval and a Symbolic Knowledge Graph for symbolic querying over typed subject–predicate–object triples. Building on these two components, we provide multiple strategies for selecting or combining semantic and symbolic evidence. We also introduce SpecsQA, a benchmark from a commercial shopping website with semi-structured product documents and manually curated questions spanning open-ended and specification-oriented retrieval. Experiments show that DualGraph consistently outperforms state-of-the-art dense-retrieval, GraphRAG, symbolic, and table-oriented baselines across question types. Code and data are available at https://github.com/corneliocristina/DualGraphRAG.

paper.title: MedProb: Probing Internal Representations of Vision-Language Models for Medical Question Answering

author.affiliation: University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio

paper.abstract: Medical visual question answering (Med-VQA) is often assumed to require medical fine-tuning, large models, or complex multi-agent pipelines. We revisit this assumption with MedProb, a lightweight probing framework that predicts multiple-choice Med-VQA answers from frozen VLM representations without free-text generation. Across PATH-VQA, SLAKE, and VQA-RAD, MedProb recovers substantially more answer-relevant signal than prompting and performs stronger than medical VLMs and agentic systems. Probing also reduces the apparent gap between small and large models compared to prompting, suggesting that smaller VLMs contain more recoverable Med-VQA signal than generation-based evaluation reveals. Across 14 matched general-purpose and medical VLM pairs, medical adaptation does not consistently improve this linear decodability.

paper.title: Attitude Analysis in Systemic Functional Linguistics: A New Corpus and Benchmark Task
paper.abstract: We introduce a corpus for Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) Appraisal analysis in Chilean Spanish, together with TULIO, a BERT model adapted to Chilean Spanish through continual pre-training. The corpus contains 2,546 texts annotated for the Attitude subsystem, with a focus on negative Judgment, and supports two span-level sequence labeling tasks: Attitude Types, which distinguishes Affect, Judgment, and Appreciation, and Judgment Subtypes, which identifies five finer-grained forms of social evaluation. To reduce the boundary ambiguity reported in prior Appraisal annotation work, we use a two-stage protocol that first marks structural spans and then assigns Attitude labels. Three expert annotators reach almost perfect agreement at the general level (Krippendorff’s α = 0.834) and substantial agreement for Judgment Subtypes (α = 0.647). We benchmark supervised sequence labelers and structured LLM agents. The highest observed F1 scores are 0.554 on Attitude Types from a Flair BiLSTM-CRF with TULIO embeddings and 0.410 on Judgment Subtypes from Qwen 3.6 Plus. Under Twitter-only training, supervised performance is genre-sensitive, with higher F1 on Twitter than on other genres. All model scores remain below expert agreement.

paper.title: Reduced Matrix Multiplication: Input-Adaptive Matrix-Product Reduction for LLM Inference

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Stony Brook

paper.abstract: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur substantial inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. We propose Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a training free, input-adaptive inference method that reduces Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along their contraction dimensions, without modifying model weights. Under a simple retention-ratio control, RMM provides a smooth and predictable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.Across language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, we find that reduction tolerance depends on the model family, task, component, and retention ratio, although it often improves with model scale. Under moderate reduction, RMM remains robust across the evaluated discriminative, autoregressive-generation, and long-context settings. We further show that the same principle extends to multimodal vision–language inference. Mechanistic ablations reveal a structural asymmetry within Transformers: attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components. Finally, wall-clock benchmarks with custom kernels on an NVIDIA A100 show that these computational savings can translate into practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths. Together, these results position RMM as a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization.

paper.title: OISD: On-Policy Internal Self-Distillation of Language Models
paper.abstract: Recent reinforcement learning (RL) post-training approaches primarily optimize the final output policy using sparse outcome-level rewards, while largely overlooking predictive signals encoded in intermediate representations. In this paper, we introduce a new paradigm called on-policy internal self-distillation and propose the OISD framework, which improves reasoning by transferring on-policy predictive signals from the final layer to intermediate representations. During rollout and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimization, the final layer acts as both the policy and a detached internal teacher for selected intermediate layers, which are guided to align with it through two complementary mechanisms: logit alignment, which transfers high-level reasoning behaviors (how to think), and attention alignment, which enforces consistent attention patterns (where to look) from the final layer to the selected intermediate layer, both without requiring external privileged information. Our OISD, together with GRPO, employs signed advantage-weighted Jensen–Shannon alignment to distill informative intermediate representations while preserving policy consistency under a unified acting policy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of OISD, with substantial and consistent improvements over strong reasoning RL baselines across four mathematical reasoning tasks.

paper.title: A Pre-Generation Epistemic Routing Axis in Language Models

author.affiliation: Ontario Tech University and Ontario Tech University

paper.abstract: When answering factual questions, language models may respond correctly, hallucinate, or abstain. We investigate whether this epistemic disposition is encoded in hidden states before any answer token is generated. Using a balanced Wikipedia QA corpus with pre/post article-date splits and rollout-consensus labels, we analyze prompt-only MLP activations from four instruction-tuned 7–9B models. PCA reveals a dominant pre-generation epistemic routing axis that orders outcomes as ABSTAIN, HALLUCINATION, and CORRECT. We then apply activation steering as a bounded causal stress test. Dense residual-write edits can shift many hallucinations toward abstention or correctness, while sparse MLP-intermediate edits localize the steering signal. These results frame the axis as a steering audit: it identifies where fixed edits improve factual behavior and where correct loss or broken outputs call for conditional controllers.

paper.title: CoBRA: Learning Tool-Use Boundaries via Counterfactual Margins
paper.abstract: As large language models increasingly act through external tools, deciding when to call a tool has become a central problem alongside deciding how to use it. Unnecessary tool calls introduce latency, cost, retrieval noise, and error propagation, while missed calls hurt knowledge-intensive queries or questions requiring up-to-date evidence. Existing methods typically trigger tools from absolute query or generation signals, such as difficulty, confidence, or final task reward, and therefore lack an explicit estimate of the instance-level marginal benefit of tool use. We propose CoBRA, a counterfactual boundary-learning framework for tool-augmented language models. CoBRA first constructs internal and external experts from the same base model, collects paired trajectories, and estimates the reward margin between answering with and without tools. This margin partitions data into internal-favored, external-favored, and ambiguous cases. CoBRA then uses clear-margin samples for Boundary-Aware Cold-Start SFT, followed by MARS-RL with reference-split rollouts and counterfactual marginal advantages to optimize boundary decisions. Experiments with retrieval as the main tool on Qwen3-4B show that CoBRA improves tool-use efficiency and boundary-sensitive answer accuracy while maintaining strong performance on tool-dependent out-of-distribution questions.

paper.title: PEAM: Parametric Embodied Agent Memory for Continual Skill Learning via Internalization of Experience in Minecraft

author.affiliation: South China University of Technology and South China University of Technology

paper.abstract: We present PEAM, a Parametric Embodied Agent Memory framework in Minecraft that transforms agent memory from inference-time retrieval into parameter-resident skills internalized through experience. PEAM pairs a slow deliberative LLM for open-ended reasoning with a fast parametric module for reflexive execution of consolidated skills. The fast module is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts LoRA architecture with per-category physically isolated adapters, enabling parameter-level continual learning with structural resistance to cross- category forgetting. We treat failure as a first-class training signal: failure–correction trajectory pairs are internalized through a joint behavioral-cloning and contrastive objective, so the agent learns not only what succeeds but also how corrected actions differ from failed ones. To govern consolidation, PEAM introduces a parameterization-worthiness score for deciding which experience should be internalized, and a scale-free self-triggered consolidation mechanism for deciding when to internalize without task-specific hand-tuned thresholds, making the agent self-evolving as the trigger transfers across task distributions without re-tuning. Experiments in Minecraft show that PEAM improves long-horizon task performance, mitigates forgetting on previously consolidated skills, and improves parametric-versus-retrieval efficiency over retrieval-based embodied agents and parametric memory variants.

paper.title: LEAF: Growing Trees Without Branching for Speech-Aware Large Language Model Post-Training
paper.abstract: State-of-the-art GRPO-style methods for speech-aware large language model post-training suffer from coarse credit assignment, broadcasting the same terminal-reward advantage to every token in a response. This ignores useful structure within rollout batches, where speech-conditioned completions often share prefixes before diverging at important decisions. We propose Low-rank Exploration with Adaptive Forking (LEAF), a retrospective tree-based RL method that recovers this structure without online branching or additional decoding. LEAF samples complete responses, selects high-surprisal boundaries, groups responses by shared prefixes, and assigns span-level advantages using descendant rewards. We theoretically justify LEAF’s span-level credit assignment and boundary-selection design. Empirically, LEAF improves over GRPO across speech question answering and speech translation benchmarks under the same rollout and low-rank adaptation budget. Notably, smaller LEAF-trained models consistently outperform current state-of-art, full-parameter baselines.

paper.title: Refusal Before Decoding: Detecting and Exploiting Refusal Signals in Intermediate LLM Activations

author.affiliation: Universita' di Padova, University of Padua
Örebro University and RISE Research Institutes of Sweden AB
Universita' di Padova, University of Padua

paper.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether refusal behavior can be predicted from LLM intermediate activations before decoding using linear probes trained on residual stream activations at each transformer block. We find that refusal is linearly decodable well before the final layer, indicating that safety-relevant behavior is represented in intermediate activations before output generation. To test whether this signal is actionable, we introduce Mechanistic AutoDAN, a probe-guided variant of AutoDAN that replaces full-model fitness evaluation with partial forward passes and probe-based scoring inside a genetic prompt search loop. Across the evaluated models, our method achieves attack success rates competitive with vanilla AutoDAN while reducing per-iteration search time by up to 72%, and probe-guided prompts match or exceed AutoDAN’s cross-model transfer in several configurations. We further find that the usefulness of probe guidance increases with model scale. Our results suggest that refusal-relevant information is decodable from intermediate activations and can serve as an effective search signal in an AutoDAN-style discrete jailbreak optimization loop, especially for larger and more robust models.

paper.title: Small Cues, Big Consequences: Learning Pivotal Cues for Multimodal Meme Classification

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Guwahati, Indian institute of science, Bangalore

paper.abstract: Memes often derive their harmful, hateful, or sarcastic meaning from small but decisive visual, textual, or cross-modal cues. Existing multimodal classifiers can miss such evidence when relying mainly on global image-text representations. We introduce MemeCF, a cue-focused benchmark of 9,895 memes across harm, hate, and sarcasm, with annotations identifying the modality and rationale of the pivotal evidence. We also propose MemePIVOT, a local-global architecture for meme classification. MemePIVOT uses frozen CLIP features, unbalanced optimal transport to align words with image patches while allowing irrelevant evidence to remain unmatched, and an evidential fusion head to combine local grounding with global meme context under uncertainty. Experiments on HarMeme, PrideMM, and MemeCF show consistent gains over strong text-only, image-only, multimodal, and vision-language baselines. Cross-dataset and ablation results further show that explicit pivotal-evidence modeling improves robustness and contributes meaningfully beyond global multimodal representations. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/AkshitSharma1/MemePIVOT

paper.title: Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention
paper.abstract: Inference with large language models (LLMs) on long sequences is computationally expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host. We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens. This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3\times over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Pulsar Attention outperforms Star Attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens and remains competitive with dense attention across most tasks, with task-dependent absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.

paper.title: Folding Context into Executable States: Structured Strategy Folding for Long-Horizon Reasoning Agent

author.affiliation: City University of Hong Kong and University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Current Large Language Model (LLM) agents struggle with long-horizon reasoning tasks, such as competition-level mathematics, where sustaining precision over hundreds of steps is critical. A primary bottleneck is the reliance on natural language context or summaries to track progress; these linguistic representations are inherently "lossy," introducing semantic drift and accumulating errors that derail the reasoning chain. To address this, we propose Structured Strategy Folding (SSF), a novel paradigm that shifts the agent’s memory mechanism from linguistic description to computational verification. Instead of compressing history into text, SSF "folds" the reasoning trajectory into a sequence of Executable Symbolic States (ESS). Each ESS serves as a verifiable anchor—comprising either executed code artifacts or formally judged symbolic lemmas—generated through a dual-pathway validation mechanism. By interacting with these rigorous state artifacts rather than raw textual history, the agent effectively eliminates ambiguity and prevents error propagation. Experiments on challenging mathematical benchmarks demonstrate that SSF significantly outperforms standard Chain-of-Thought and existing summarization baselines, achieving substantial accuracy improvements while maintaining robust performance over extended reasoning horizons.

paper.title: GROVE: Graph-based Routing Over Variant Experts for Adaptive Two-Stage Training of Reasoning Models
paper.abstract: Post-training reasoning models is computationally expensive, and the allocation between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) substantially affects reasoning quality. Existing methods operate at the training-procedure level and treat the reasoning corpus as homogeneous, ignoring the structural heterogeneity of individual traces. We propose GROVE (Graph-based Routing Over Variant Experts), an adaptive framework that routes each example to SFT or RL based on the structural topology of its reasoning trace. GROVE parses each trace into a Reasoning Tree, scores its complexity via graph entropy, and partitions the corpus through a data-driven Gaussian Mixture Model with no hand-tuned threshold. Low-complexity traces are trained with SFT and high-complexity traces with GRPO as parallel LoRA adapters from a shared frozen base, merged into a single deployable model with no inference-time overhead. Across two training corpora and five reasoning benchmarks, GROVE consistently outperforms single-stage and naive-hybrid baselines, and a reversed-routing ablation confirms that this mapping is intrinsic rather than arbitrary.

paper.title: MTGBench: A Multi-Turn Game Benchmark for Diverse LLM Capability Assessment

author.affiliation: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology and Yandex

paper.abstract: Existing LLM reasoning benchmarks are largely static, single-turn, English-centric, and reliant on biased LLM-as-a-judge scoring. We present MTGBench, a bilingual (English/Russian) suite of seven multi-turn puzzle games—Wordle, Word Chain, Situation Puzzles, 20 Questions, Wheel of Fortune, 20 Features, and Alias—spanning deductive, semantic, lateral, consistency, and knowledge-retrieval reasoning. Four games use algorithmic checkers; the remaining three use a constrained LLM-as-a-rule-enforcer validated against human annotators, and episodes are regenerated natively per language rather than translated. Across 16 frontier models and a human baseline comprising 476 sessions we find that (i) rankings are highly task-dependent, (ii) chain-of-thought is near-essential for letter-level games but uneven on knowledge-driven ones, and (iii) the strongest reasoning-enabled LLMs match or exceed our collected Russian human baseline across the entire suite. Game scores align most consistently with cognitive batteries probing Causal Reasoning, Pragmatics, Planning, and Common-sense Reasoning, though these associations are game-specific rather than a single executive-function signal. Code and data are available in MTGBench github.

paper.title: LaMoC: Loss-Aware Modular Compression for LLMs
paper.abstract: Modular compression has enabled considerable parameter reduction in LLMs while preserving strong language understanding and downstream task accuracy. However, existing joint modular compression methods primarily rely on activation statistics, leaving loss-sensitivity information and its module-level characterization underexplored. We investigate addressing this gap with LaMoC, a loss-aware modular compression methodology that blends activation and Empirical Fisher statistics through gradient-error alignment. LaMoC improves joint compression by selecting compression statistics that better align local module reconstruction error with the downstream loss. Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We characterize the Empirical Fisher as a module-level loss-aware proxy that can be blended with the activation statistics required for compression. (2) We reformulate joint modular compression as a two-tiered optimization problem that minimizes module reconstruction error while tuning the activation and gradient information blending rate. (3) We implement an empirically driven methodology with statistical validation to solve the resulting compression problem. We evaluate LaMoC across four model families spanning eight models. On the 4–8B models, LaMoC achieves an average 2.5% reduction in perplexity and a 1% relative improvement in task accuracy over state-of-the-art modular compression methods.

paper.title: DualGauge: Automated Joint Security-Functionality Benchmarking of Specification-Only Code Generation by LLMs and Coding Agents

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Buffalo
State University of New York at Buffalo
State University of New York at Buffalo
State University of New York at Buffalo

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based coding agents are now used to generate code from natural-language specifications, yet ensuring such code is both functionally correct and secure remains a challenge. We present DualGauge, the first fully automated framework for jointly evaluating correctness and security of specification-only code generation, supported by DualGauge-Bench, a language-agnostic benchmark of 307 coding tasks each paired with functional and security tests derived from the same specification. Evaluating 10 representative LLMs across Python, C++, and JavaScript, we find that functional correctness substantially overestimates reliable code generation: even the strongest model remains below 15% joint security-functionality success in every language. Common model-side factors—scale, extended thinking, quantization, instruction tuning, and code specialization—do not reliably improve joint performance, suggesting secure-and-correct code generation does not simply emerge from stronger coding capability. Evaluation of 3 leading agentic coding systems (Codex, OpenHands, and Claude Code) shows that iterative scaffolding provides no advantage over direct (LLM-based) generation on specification-only tasks.
