We further plan to release the dual-branch graph representations as an additional resource for future research.

paper.title: FServe: FP8-Native W4A8KV4 Quantization and Attention Kernel Optimization for Efficient LLM Serving
paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) scale, inference throughput is increasingly bottlenecked by memory bandwidth. While prior 4-bit quantization schemes promise memory savings, their dequantization overhead often negates these gains. We present FServe, a hardware-software co-designed framework featuring an FP8-native W4A8KV4 scheme that combines channel pre-scaling and group-wise scale relaxation for linear layers with post-RoPE key smoothing that aligns channel-wise means and ranges for attention layers. To translate these memory savings into FP8-native throughput, FServe further extends FlashAttention-3 kernels for prefill with packed-FP16 softmax instruction reordering and multi-warp asynchronous TMA fetching, and introduces a dynamic Stream-KV tile scheduler for decode phase workload imbalance. Our evaluation on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B shows that FServe outperforms AWQ W4A16 and W4A8 baselines on accuracy despite additionally compressing the KV cache to INT4, achieves up to 1.41× TTFT speedup over BF16, and sustains effective decode bandwidth above the H100’s theoretical peak.

paper.title: EviDx: Evidence-Aware Active Diagnosis with Scaffolded LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Shanghai Jiaotong University, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Sensetime

paper.abstract: Clinical diagnosis is an active evidence-seeking process in which clinicians acquire evidence, update competing hypotheses, and decide when the available evidence is sufficient for diagnosis. Yet many medical diagnosis systems built around large language models (LLMs) still formulate diagnosis as static case-to-answer prediction, with limited support for evidence acquisition. Agentic LLMs offer a dynamic alternative through tool use and intermediate diagnostic trajectories, but existing systems often under-specify how patient evidence should be exposed, scaffolded, and controlled at runtime. We introduce EviDx, an evidence-aware active diagnosis framework that pairs patient-specific diagnostic environments with a clinical diagnostic scaffold and an observer-guided runtime harness. In EviDx, \mathcal{E}-Synthesis constructs interactive environments from raw clinical cases; the scaffold organizes role-specialized agents, evidence tools, and evolving evidence states; and the harness regulates diagnostic termination by tracking uncertainty and evidence coverage. A 3-level evaluation pyramid assesses execution robustness, reasoning dynamics, and diagnostic outcomes. Experiments show that EviDx improves diagnostic performance and process stability while revealing model-dependent capability boundaries.

paper.title: Why LLMs Give In: Conversational Factors and Reasoning Behind Medical Sycophancy

author.affiliation: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

paper.abstract: Large language models can answer a medical question correctly and still abandon that answer when a user pushes back. We study this failure as medical sycophancy and ask when models are most likely to give in. Across five open-weight models, 500 MEDQUAD questions, and 1.2 million trials, we use a fully crossed design over four conversational factors: user role, user evidence, interaction structure, and grounding. Medical sycophancy is nearly three times more common when users challenge an answer the model has already given than when the false claim appears in the initial query. Models are also more susceptible to users presented as physicians or medical students. Most strikingly, fabricated evidence has opposite effects across interaction structures. It increases sycophancy in single-turn interactions but reduces it after the model has already answered. Grounding helps, but does not eliminate the behavior. Sycophancy varies more across medical questions than across models, making question selection an important part of benchmark design. Reasoning traces suggest that multi-turn failures are associated with models turning back toward their own prior answer, while fabricated evidence receives more scrutiny after an initial response. Together, the results show that medical sycophancy depends as much on how a model is challenged and evaluated as on which model is tested.

paper.title: SAUL: Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning

author.affiliation: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs) faces a critical trade-off between erasing target knowledge and preserving general utility. We propose SAUL (Sharpness-Aware Augmented-Lagrangian Unlearning), which formulates unlearning as a constrained minimization problem following the principle of “forget enough, but no more than necessary.” At its core, SAUL formulates forgetting as an explicit constraint with a prescribed satisfaction criterion, whereas prior unlearning methods typically specify the desired level of forgetting implicitly through optimization objectives. An augmented Lagrangian controller adaptively adjusts forget-side pressure according to constraint violation and can eventually deactivate the forget-side update as the prescribed criterion remains satisfied. Sharpness-aware updates on both retain and forget objectives, together with a dual-optimizer design that maintains role-separated states, further stabilize the resulting unlearning dynamics. We evaluate SAUL on the TOFU, WMDP, and MUSE benchmarks, demonstrating favorable forgetting–utility trade-offs over representative sharpness- and perturbation-based baselines under benchmark-specific forgetting criteria. Beyond the complete SAUL framework, we further show on TOFU and WMDP that applying the augmented-Lagrangian controller as a drop-in modifier to representative baselines improves their post-forgetting utility, demonstrating the practical value of explicit forgetting control.

paper.title: Communicating Chess Strategies in Natural Language
paper.abstract: Chess engines have long achieved superhuman playing strength. However, the underlying strategy behind their move suggestions is difficult for human players, even skilled ones, to comprehend. Motivated by this, we propose the task of chess *strategy verbalization*, which is to describe chess strategies in natural language. We design (i) a pipeline for verbalizing strategies and (ii) an evaluation framework for objective evaluation of generated strategy descriptions. Our experiments show that natural language is a promising and interpretable medium for communicating strategic information to both human and LLM players. We glean additional interesting insights, including (a) the importance of evaluating strategies beyond the main line, (b) the limitations of pure concept-based descriptions, and (c) the limitations of relying on LLMs rather than humans for evaluation.

paper.title: Visual Representation Regularization for Multimodal Hallucination Mitigation
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal reasoning, yet they still suffer from hallucinations that undermine their reliability. Existing inference-time mitigation methods mainly focus on optimizing decoding strategies or analyzing internal attention mechanisms, while the role of visual representations remains underexplored. In this work, we reveal that visual representations exhibit information dispersion during layer-wise evolution, manifested as a progressive deviation from the initial visual subspace and increasing alignment with the textual subspace. Based on this insight, we propose Visual Representation Regularization (VRR), a training-free method that mitigates hallucinations by regularizing visual representations toward their initial states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VRR consistently reduces hallucinations and is compatible with existing mitigation methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jiarker/VRR.

paper.title: Neuron-Guided Fine-Tuning: Unlocking Efficient Alignment Mechanisms for Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Existing Supervised Fine-Tuning paradigms, particularly Full Parameter Fine-Tuning are often plagued by parameter redundancy, inconsistent data quality, and catastrophic forgetting, which current methods typically address in isolation and lack a unified optimization signal to bridge data selection, parameter updates, and knowledge preservation. To address this, we propose Neuron-Guided Fine-Tuning (NGFT), a holistic framework that leverages neuron activation patterns as a universal proxy to unify the fine-tuning lifecycle. NGFT operates via three synergistic mechanisms: (1) Adaptive Task-Specific Neuron Selection, which identifies essential neurons in a single forward pass to concentrate updates and reduce redundancy; (2) Activation-Based Data Selection, which prioritizes information-dense samples that maximize contribution to key neurons; and (3) Neuron Activation Alignment, a novel loss function that anchors activations to pre-trained states, deepening representation learning and preserving general knowledge. Experimental results across three models across both domain-specific and general benchmarks demonstrate that NGFT significantly outperforms existing mainstream fine-tuning methods in both efficiency and performance, while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

paper.title: Plan the Semantics, Then Render the Signal: A Hybrid State-Space Model for Incomplete Multimodal Learning

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Incomplete multimodal learning seeks robust perception when modalities are absent at training or test time, using available streams to recover the missing ones. Most methods cast this as direct regression in a fixed continuous latent, which (i) collapses many valid solutions into an averaged reconstruction when observations underdetermine the target, and (ii) suffers semantic drift when cross-modal relationships shift with context. We argue that completion should first resolve what is missing and only then render how it appears. We realize this as Semantic-first Completion, instantiated by a Hybrid State-Space Model (HySSM) that decouples semantic intent from signal realization. A frozen omni-modal LLM plans over observation-only evidence, generating an evidence-grounded Markovian trajectory of discrete semantic states that act as a compact information bottleneck for stable cross-modal reasoning. The plan is projected into a coordinate-wise control field that drift-guides a conditional diffusion model, synthesizing missing signals or feature streams as diverse and semantically consistent completions. Across MNIST, Hateful Memes, and CMU-MOSEI, HySSM surpasses recent generative baselines and, under agnostic masking shift, remains robust up to 90% missingness.

paper.title: A Thousand Words or An Image: Studying the Influence of Persona Modality in Multimodal LLMs
paper.abstract: Language models have demonstrated remarkable advancements in embodying diverse personas, enhancing their effectiveness as conversational agents. Simultaneously, there have been significant strides in these models in processing and integrating visual information. However, despite images being a natural carrier of persona attributes (e.g. age, occupation, or location), it remains largely unexplored whether multimodal language models (MLLMs) can faithfully ground visual persona information. In this work, we introduce persona embodiment as a novel diagnostic for visual grounding in MLLMs. Unlike simple visual recognition, this task requires models to extract multiple persona attributes from an image, integrate them into a coherent representation, and apply them to downstream language tasks. To this end, we introduce a modality-parallel dataset of personas, containing 2,400 prompts each represented in four modalities. Across our experiments, we find that models frequently underuse visual information relative to text, and that this neglect persists even when richer visual information is clearly available, highlighting underlying limitations and paving the way for future research to bridge this gap.

paper.title: Learning Structured Emotional Dynamics in Latent Space via Trajectory Modeling and Controlled Transitions
paper.abstract: Emotion understanding from text has been predominantly approached through discrete classification frameworks. However, complementary perspectives in psychology and neuroscience suggest that affective states may also exhibit continuous, context-dependent, and temporally structured properties. Building on this perspective, we investigate emotion representations as latent dynamical trajectories within transformer embedding spaces. Using GoEmotions and MELD across four transformer architectures, we analyze the geometric organization and temporal evolution of learned emotional states. We find that latent trajectories exhibit temporal persistence and structured transition dynamics, while the prediction error increases during emotion shifts, acting as a signal of expectation violation. We additionally introduce trajectory-level latent interventions enabling controllable emotional transitions through directional operations in representation space. Finally, manifold capacity analysis reveals partially aligned and variably separable emotional manifolds, suggesting shared geometric organization across affective representations.

paper.title: Skill-Guided Continuation Distillation for GUI Agents

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology Beijing

paper.abstract: Improving GUI agents typically relies on behavior cloning on expert trajectories. However, as the current policy deviates from the expert policy, it inevitably encounters policy-induced off-trajectory states during closed-loop execution, i.e., states that fall outside the expert trajectories. Since expert trajectories provide no demonstrations for these unseen states, such states receive no effective supervision, leaving the policy unable to select the correct action. To close this supervision gap, we propose Skill-Guided Continuation Distillation (SGCD), an iterative self-improvement framework. SGCD first runs the plain policy without skill guidance for a few steps to reach realistic off-trajectory states. From these states, a skill-guided policy then completes the task and produces successful continuations, which are mixed with expert trajectories to supply supervision over policy-induced off-trajectory states. The skills are extracted from both successful and failed rollouts, consisting of Continuation Plans, Critical Targets, Failure Traps, and Success Criteria. On OSWorld-Verified, SGCD improves the success rate of three base models from the low-30% range to over 50%, demonstrating its effectiveness and generality.

paper.title: SLMFix: Leveraging Small Language Models for Domain Specific Language Error Fixing with Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University and Department of Computer Science, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
University of Illinois, Urbana Champaign and University of Illinois, Urbana Champaign

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in code generation across many programming languages but even state-of-the-art LLMs generate programs that contain syntactic errors and fail to complete the given tasks, especially for low-resource programming languages (LRPLs). In addition, the high cost of training makes finetuning LLMs unaffordable for those with constrained computational resources, further weakening the effectiveness of LLMs for code generation. In this work, we propose SLMFix, a novel code generation pipeline that leverages a small language model (SLM) finetuned using reinforcement learning (RL) techniques to fix syntactic errors in LLM-generated programs for domain-specific languages (DSLs) based on interpreter feedback. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach across multiple DSLs, improving the validator pass rates by 40% on LRPLs and eliminating more than 50% of syntactic errors for high-resource DSLs. Notably, SLMFix brings substantial performance improvement to the base model and outperforms supervised finetuning approach even for 7B models on LRPLs including Ansible and Lean, showing the potential of our approach in improving the quality of LLM-generated programs.

paper.title: CabinProAct: Visually Triggered Proactive Intervention for Intelligent Cabin Agents
paper.abstract: Traditional in-vehicle agents mainly follow an instruction-following paradigm, where actions are executed only after explicit user commands. However, real-world cabin scenarios often require agents to proactively determine whether intervention is necessary by jointly reasoning over visual and state inputs. To address this gap, we propose CabinProAct, a multimodal benchmark for proactive intelligent cabin agents. In this setting, agents must jointly reason over in-cabin and out-cabin visual information, vehicle states, and executable APIs to autonomously decide whether to intervene and generate corresponding actions. We further introduce an execution-verification-based synthetic data generation framework to automatically construct execution-consistent proactive interaction data. We evaluate six state-of-the-art multimodal models. The results indicate that execution-grounded synthetic supervision effectively transfers to real-world in-cabin settings, enabling more robust proactive responses in real-world cabin scenarios.

paper.title: ChipLayoutBench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Semiconductor Layout Understanding

author.affiliation: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Recent multimodal benchmarks have significantly expanded the evaluation of visual reasoning in vision-language models, but they primarily focus on holistic semantic understanding. Engineering problems can instead require models to connect visual regions with exact coordinate-level representations and reason over precise quantities. Semiconductor layout analysis is a representative example, yet this fine-grained multimodal grounding capability remains largely unexplored. We introduce ChipLayoutBench, the first benchmark for general semiconductor layout understanding, with text-only, image+metadata, and multimodal settings across diverse reasoning and grounding tasks. Evaluations of eight recent VLMs show that text-based representations achieve the strongest overall performance, while image+metadata inputs remain substantially more challenging. Moreover, combining both modalities often fails to improve over text alone and can even degrade performance, suggesting persistent difficulties in effectively grounding visual information with structured geometric representations. Dedicated VLM-specific tasks further expose these challenges in fine-grained cross-modal alignment and image-grounded reasoning. Our benchmark provides a domain-grounded testbed for advancing geometric reasoning and fine-grained multimodal grounding over structured engineering data.

paper.title: SocialReasonBench: A Video-QA Benchmark for Social Reasoning with Counterfactual Narrative Videos

author.affiliation: University of Liverpool and Eindhoven University of Technology

paper.abstract: Recent advances in Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have greatly improved video understanding, yet their ability to reason about human-centered social situations remains limited. Existing benchmarks typically rely on videos with a single observed trajectory, making it difficult to determine whether models truly understand social dynamics or merely exploit recurring narrative patterns. We introduce SocialReasonBench, a video multiple-choice QA benchmark for evaluating socially grounded reasoning in scenarios derived from interactive narratives. Built from gameplay videos of Detroit: Become Human, the benchmark leverages branching storylines where player decisions lead to alternative social outcomes that can be checked against the game’s own script, flowchart, and recorded branches. We develop a multi-agent curation pipeline that localizes socially meaningful clips, grounds answer labels in game-state signals, and generates theory-guided questions with diagnostic distractors. SocialReasonBench covers seven reasoning dimensions, including intent recognition, emotional empathy, moral dilemma, counterfactual reasoning, and causal antecedent. Experiments on contemporary LMMs show that models perform reasonably well on basic social understanding but struggle with counterfactual and causal reasoning. Further ablation and diagnostic error analyses reveal that models often depend on incomplete modality cues and fall into reasoning traps such as visual shortcuts, highlighting a gap between observable event recognition and deeper reasoning over latent social states.

paper.title: Self- and Other-Labels Induce Bidirectional Bias in LLM Judges

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Georgia Institute of Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: As LLM-as-a-judge becomes increasingly widespread, self-preference—the tendency of a judge to favor its own outputs—raises growing concerns about evaluation reliability. However, this bias has been studied predominantly on generated text, where stylistic features and response quality are inevitably conflated. As a result, existing measurements cannot separate genuine self-preference from these confounds. We address this limitation by changing the object of evaluation: instead of judging generated text, ten LLMs assess sets of narrative constraints selected from a shared pool, which carry no stylistic fingerprint yet retain a recoverable model-specific signature. Two experiments on this task yield complementary findings. Under blind evaluation, self-preference disappears, with a small effect remaining in the opposite direction once selection quality and judge severity are controlled. Under matched quality, however, self- and other-labels alone—without naming any model—shift scores bidirectionally. LLM judges inflate scores for self-labeled selections and deflate those for other-labeled ones regardless of the selection’s actual source. We make two contributions: 1) authorship attribution is a distinct driver of evaluation bias, and 2) ground-truth-free tasks can serve as controlled instruments for studying LLM judge behavior.

paper.title: PatientAct: Theory-Grounded Mental Health Client Simulation
paper.abstract: LLM-based simulated clients are increasingly used to train novice counselors, evaluate LLM therapists, and generate synthetic data. However, current simulators produce overly cooperative clients that disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. We trace these issues to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. We present PatientAct, a framework for client simulation grounded in established clinical theories. Our profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation, providing causal depth without tying the design to any single therapeutic modality. During simulation, profiles include a dynamic memory layer in which items carry trust thresholds (e.g., symptoms are available early, whereas formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, we model the client’s emotional reaction and behavior before generating a response. If the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance in terms of quantity, content, and style rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern. We evaluate our framework on 40 clinical situations and demonstrate that it generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility. Moreover, PatientAct significantly outperforms the baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism. Our code and data are publicly available via github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

paper.title: RADAM: A Retrieval-Augmented Detection and Mitigation Framework for Faithfulness Hallucinations
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) empowers large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but remains vulnerable to faithfulness hallucinations—answers that contradict retrieved evidence. We introduce RADAM, a lightweight post-processing framework that mitigates this issue via fine-grained hallucination detection and guided revision. RADAM leverages a single diagnostic critic, optimized via preference tuning on taxonomy-guided data, to generate structured critiques encompassing both precise error spans and explicit revision suggestions, which guide the base model toward more faithful outputs. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that RADAM consistently achieves the lowest average hallucination rate across the evaluated methods, while largely preserving response quality and achieving out-of-domain performance comparable to enterprise-grade LLMs.

paper.title: SCP-ISA: Spatial Cross-attention Projection for Textual Spatial Semantic Anomaly Detection and Attribution

author.affiliation: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Textual spatial semantic anomaly detection and attribution requires deciding whether a sentence contains an implausible spatial relation and assigning the corresponding attribution label. Prior prompting and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning methods rely on raw tokenlevel representations, leaving spatial roles and cross-triple conflicts implicit. We propose SCP-ISA, a Spatial Cross-attention Projection (SCP) method with an Inter-Slot Attention (ISA) layer that uses a frozen MacBERT-large encoder to build input-conditioned spatial slots and injects the projected slots into Qwen2.5 as soft prefix embeddings. The ISA layer enables structured cross-slot interaction that collapses co-referring spatial mentions into a shared entity-anchored representation before generation. On the CRSARC benchmark, SCP-ISA improves test cascade attribution F1 (Attr-F1) by 22.7 percentage points (0.509 to 0.736) over Direct LoRA, and detection macro-F1 (Det-F1) from 0.846 to 0.881.

paper.title: Cross-Session Decomposition Attacks: Scaling Risk and Intent-Aligned Retrieval Defense

author.affiliation: Vector Institute and University of Waterloo

paper.abstract: Scaling laws are usually read as a capability story: lower language-modeling loss yields more useful models. We study a safety consequence of this mechanism in cross-session decomposition attacks, where benign-looking subqueries are asked across independent interactions and later recomposed toward a forbidden objective. We formalize this setting as compositional safety risk and prove a conditional risk-transfer bound: when the reference environment already contains dispersed evidence for a risky reconstruction, the gap between deployed composed risk and reference composed risk is controlled by the model’s excess loss on allowed subqueries. Synthetic withholding experiments show that wider transformers assign lower loss to held-out instructions that never appear verbatim in training but are recoverable from injected supporting facts. A 600-intent pretrained-LLM evaluation shows that larger Qwen3 and Gemma3 family members can yield greater harmful-capability uplift under a fixed decomposition-composition pipeline. As a defense, IntentAlign-MiniLM, our 22M intent-aligned retriever, outperforms much larger embedding models on held-out intent retrieval and yields the best learned-retriever harmful recall across tested guardrails.

paper.title: SAFIRE: Safety-Critical Benchmark for Fine-grained Fire and Smoke Understanding in Multimodal LLMs

author.affiliation: Khalifa University of Science, Technology and Research
Khalifa University of Science, Technology and Research
Khalifa University of Science, Technology and Research
Khalifa University of Science, Technology and Research

paper.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong progress on vision-language tasks, yet their reliability in safety-critical settings remains underexplored. Fire-smoke understanding is central to public safety and disaster response, but most existing benchmarks lack diverse real-world scenarios and context-aware evaluation. We introduce SAFIRE, a large-scale benchmark for fire-smoke understanding in MLLMs, comprising 83K captioned images from 20 scenarios and 193K multiple-choice VQA (MCVQA) generated from a 9.7K-image subset, spanning 10 evaluation dimensions from basic perception to higher-order reasoning. A GPT-5.4-assisted multi-stage verification pipeline with MLLM majority voting ensures annotation quality. Evaluating ten open-source MLLMs (8B-38B) yields an average accuracy of 61.9%, exposing major gaps in safety-critical reasoning. We further show that adapting vision encoders with only 7% of our domain-specific data boosts fire-scene classification accuracy from 20.1% to 64.5%, indicating that carefully curated data can yield substantial gains even when data volume is limited. All datasets, models, and code are available at https://risys-lab.github.io/SAFIRE/.

paper.title: Relevant Is Not Warranted: Evidence-Force Calibration for Cited RAG
paper.abstract: Cited RAG evaluation often treats visible sources as a grounding signal, but a real, topically relevant citation can still under-warrant the attached wording. We study this diagnostic failure as citation laundering: a related source is presented as warrant for an over-strong claim. We introduce ForceBench, a contrastive stress test for evidence-force calibration. Each item holds a cited passage fixed and pairs an evidence-calibrated claim with a localized force-raised variant across five operational axes: relation, modality, scope, temporal validity, and numeric specificity. A calibrated evaluator should score the evidence-calibrated claim higher. Headline experiments use a fixed, locality-filtered 198-pair evaluation set. A citation-presence sanity check is uninformative by design; token and entity overlap still violate monotonicity on 32.8–36.4% of pairs. Across four reported model judges, standard generic support prompting is insufficient for this force-calibration stress test (aggregate MVR 47.2%), while explicit warrant-strength prompting lowers MVR to 24.5% but remains imperfect. We release the benchmark, prompts, outputs, and plug-in pipeline so citation evaluators can report monotonicity violation rate and force sensitivity alongside conventional support metrics.

paper.title: LivingRAG: Augmenting Graph RAG with Experience
paper.abstract: Graph-based RAG improves multi-hop question answering by organizing evidence as a knowledge graph. However, most existing RAG systems process each query in isolation and discard useful reasoning from the LLM’s response after inference. As a result, later related queries need to retrieve evidence and reason from scratch. We propose LivingRAG, a Graph RAG framework with writable and reusable reasoning experience. LivingRAG adds a writable experience store to a graph-based retrieval backbone, enabling verified experiences to be reused during inference in two ways. Stored graph signals help retrieval find entities and passages that were useful in earlier related queries. Stored summaries provide a reference reasoning pattern for answer generation. We analyze online QA streams and find reusable signals from shared entities, graph neighborhoods, and question templates. Experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LivingRAG improves accuracy over strong RAG baselines and reduces completion-token use when relevant prior experience is reused.

paper.title: Human Inputs, Model Outputs: Dual Sources of Variability in Stance Mining on Gun Rights/Control
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science, both to analyze human-generated web content and to act as human surrogates capable of answering substantive research questions. As these uses expand, a critical methodological question arises: how stable and reliable are the answers LLMs produce? We examine this question through the lens of stance mining on gun control and gun rights, a mature and widely used NLP task applied to one of the most extensively studied and polarized political issues in the United States. Using a multi-platform dataset spanning diverse online communities, we evaluate the stability of LLM-predicted stance across model families, prompt designs, and conversational contexts. Despite strong expectations of robustness in this setting, we observe substantial variability in predicted stance across LLMs and prompts. To contextualize these findings, we compare model-induced variability with human variability by analyzing annotations from raters with differing political affiliations. We find that political priors and annotator disagreement persist even in this ostensibly straightforward classification task. As a useful resource, we release a stance dataset annotated by raters with diverse political affiliations. Our results show that outcomes in stance mining depend jointly on which LLM is used and which humans provide the inputs, underscoring dual sources of variability that have important implications for using LLMs as research instruments in computational social science.

paper.title: SurrogateKV: Representation-Preserving KV Cache Compression for Long-Context LLMs
paper.abstract: KV cache compression is essential for long-context LLM inference. Most token-level KV compressors reduce cache length by retaining selected token KV entries and evicting the rest. Once evicted, those spans no longer receive attention, even though some may still carry information useful enough to preserve in compact form. We propose SurrogateKV, a training-free, runtime-only method that reframes KV compression as region-level representation allocation. Under the same KV-slot budget, SurrogateKV assigns historical regions to raw KV, surrogate KV, or drop. It does not train a compressor, modify model weights, or introduce a new attention operator. After prefill, SurrogateKV constructs lightweight surrogate entries as ordinary KV pairs, keeping their information available during standard attention decoding. This representation decision is orthogonal to layer- and head-wise budget allocation. We evaluate SurrogateKV-Snap, SurrogateKV-Dynamic, and SurrogateKV-Ada, obtained by applying SurrogateKV to SnapKV, DynamicKV, and Ada-KV, respectively. As representative results, SurrogateKV-Snap raises Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) retrieval accuracy from 87.51 to 98.84 at 128 slots per layer. SurrogateKV-Ada raises the LongBench average score from 40.77 to 41.26 at 512 slots per layer while preserving 98.4% of full-cache performance with only 10.5% of the prefill KV cache. Code is available at https://github.com/kimjunewon/SurrogateKV.

paper.title: DyMT-ESB: Dynamic Multi-Turn Evaluation of Social Bias in User-LLM Interactions

author.affiliation: Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology and Sony Group Corporation
NII LLMC and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Warning: This paper contains examples of stereotypes and social bias. LLMs are increasingly used in interactive settings by the general public, making the evaluation of model behavior in multi-turn conversational scenarios important for safety, including stereotyping-related harms. However, existing multi-turn social bias evaluations often rely on pre-specified or template-based user inputs that do not adapt to model responses and typically assume a fixed dialogue length in advance. In this paper, we study social bias dynamics in response-conditioned multi-turn interactions using a controlled evaluation protocol that generates follow-up user queries from the evolving dialogue history and allows evaluation over variable numbers of turns. Experimental results show that LLMs exhibit social bias even in coherent, response-conditioned multi-turn interactions, revealing late-emerging bias, non-monotonic bias patterns, and bias re-emergence. These results motivate evaluations that extend beyond fixed-turn, pre-scripted protocols. Our findings highlight the importance of analyzing social bias as a turn-level dynamic phenomenon.

paper.title: Skill-MAS: Evolving Meta-Skill for Automatic Multi-Agent Systems

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based automatic Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) generation has become a crucial frontier for tackling complex tasks. However, existing methods face a dilemma between model capability and experience retention. Inference-time MAS leverages frozen frontier LLMs but repeats identical searches without learning from past experience. Conversely, Training-time MAS internalizes experience via gradient updates but is constrained by the low capability ceiling of smaller models, and is hard to scale to large frontier LLMs. To bridge this gap, we propose Skill-MAS, a novel third path that decouples experience retention from parametric updates by conceptualizing the high-level orchestration capability as an evolvable Meta-Skill. Skill-MAS refines this architectural knowledge through a closed optimization loop: (1) Multi-Trajectory Rollout samples a behavioral distribution for each task under the current Meta-Skill; and (2) Selective Reflection adaptively selects priority tasks and applies hierarchical contrastive analysis to distill systemic experience into generalizable, strategy-level principles. Extensive experiments across four complex benchmarks and four distinct LLMs demonstrate that Skill-MAS not only achieves remarkable performance gains but also maintains a favorable cost-performance trade-off. Further analysis reveals that the evolved Meta-Skills are highly robust and exhibit strong transferability across unseen tasks and different LLMs.

paper.title: Not All Components Forget Alike: Component-Level Intervention Profiles in Continual Pretraining
paper.abstract: Continual pretraining adapts a language model to new domains but can degrade performance on earlier domains. We study this degradation through component-level interventions in Transformer blocks. Our main observation is that forgetting interventions have sharply different profiles across Q/K, V/O, and MLP components. In SmolLM2-360M continual pretraining over six domains, V/O rollback improves previous-domain Wiki perplexity while leaving new-domain perplexity nearly unchanged (-5.72 +/- 0.08 Wiki PPL diff; new-domain range -1.06 to +0.76), MLP rollback improves Wiki but severely damages all new domains (-6.29 +/- 0.12 Wiki; +13.95 to +20.75 new-domain damage), and Q/K rollback shows no recovery effect. Training-time V/O freeze reproduces the selective pattern: it reduces Wiki forgetting (-2.98 +/- 0.13, 3 seeds in the stress order; -2.84 +/- 0.29 across 3 seeds x 2 orders) without measurable loss in current-domain learning efficiency and without compensatory MLP/Q/K weight changes. Same-parameter-count Q/K freeze has the opposite direction (+3.17 +/- 2.53), and random attention-subset freeze scales with the included V/O fraction. Finally, inference-time inter-checkpoint activation transplantation modulates forgetting bidirectionally without changing weights (forward -6.27 +/- 0.13, reverse +3.26 +/- 0.09), with the activation-level effect carried primarily by o_proj output rather than by the full V/O projection bundle. We present these results as a robust component-level intervention profile, not as proof that V/O is the unique causal storage site of forgetting.

paper.title: Retrieve Few, Verify Many: Segment-Level Evidence Reuse for Long-Form Factuality Assessment

author.affiliation: Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology

paper.abstract: Existing methods for evaluating the factuality of long-form LLM responses decompose text into atomic claims and verify each independently, retrieving evidence separately for every claim. This atom-independence assumption causes substantial retrieval redundancy, because adjacent claims in coherent text often draw from overlapping sources, a property we term semantic locality. We propose SegmentFact, a deterministic factuality assessor that partitions responses into semantic segments, extracts claims within each segment’s local context, and propagates retrieved evidence forward through a shared pool. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SegmentFact significantly reduces retrieval calls while maintaining accuracy comparable to existing detections.

paper.title: Scaling Multi-Agent Systems with Prospect-State Propagation

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
University of Waterloo and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Current LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) periodically compress intermediate states to reduce inference-time token consumption, thereby attempting to incorporate more agents. However, naive scaling strategies face challenges. For example, in economic simulations, large-scale MAS typically discard semantically rich economic states, i.e., agent behavioral trajectories, which are key drivers of macroeconomic fluctuations. In this paper, we reveal a phenomenon in which agent heterogeneity gradually decreases during simulation, and propose Prospect-State Propagation for Multi-Agent Systems (PspMAS). Inspired by prospect theory, PspMAS decouples each agent’s micro state into a compact Prospect State and an expressive Semantic State. The former records psychological traces through a lightweight, parallelizable propagator and continuously injects heterogeneity into the system. The latter leverages the strong perception, reasoning, planning, and decision-making abilities of LLMs. These two components work complementarily, providing a scalable LLM-based multi-agent simulation solution.

paper.title: Uncovering and Mitigating Aggregation-Induced Reward Hacking in Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning of large language models increasingly adopts multiple reward dimensions, including verifiable rules, task-specific evaluators, and learned reward models, to provide richer supervision across diverse capabilities. These dimensions are commonly scalarized with fixed aggregation weights. We identify a failure mode in which aggregation itself induces reward hacking: static projection aliases qualitatively different reward profiles into a single scalar, steering optimization toward whichever dimensions are easiest, densest, or systematically favored by the reward signal. Over training, this traps the policy in suboptimal profiles and prevents convergence to better-balanced ones that would yield higher task performance. To address this, we propose **Adaptive Multi-Reward Projection (AMRP)**, a lightweight online method that reallocates aggregation weights using three signals—relative shortfall, reward volatility, and recent progress—increasing pressure on lagging, unstable, or stagnant dimensions while relieving saturated ones. Across structured reasoning, citation-grounded generation, and open-ended alignment under GRPO, AMRP consistently improves reward-profile balance and downstream performance over fixed and dynamic weighting baselines; it also remains effective with GDPO and PPO, supporting compatibility across RL algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/yyhappier/AMRP.git.

paper.title: Black-Box Dataset-Level Source Ranking via Context Mixture Factorization
paper.abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) for large language models is dominated by gradient- and retraining-based methods that require model internals, ruling out the most widely deployed closed-weight systems. We study TDA in the strictly black-box setting, observing only input output behavior accessed through retrieval- augmented prompting. We introduce Context Mixture Factorization (CMF), which models the LLM’s output distribution as a mixture of a base component and dataset-specific components and recovers per-dataset contribution weights by regularized matrix factorization via alternating projected least squares. CMF explicitly decomposes background (π0) and dataset- specific influence and requires only K+1 prompts per query for K candidate datasets. As a comparison method we also formulate the Shapley Context Method (SCM), a residual- similarity attribution score aggregated via Shapley values. We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-4, Bloomz, Mistral-7B, Phi-3mini) on BoolQ, a synthetic FakeQ variant, and a post-cutoff Olympic2024 dataset against three baselines (TRAK, ContextCite, retrieval cosine similarity). CMF and SCM recover the ordering predicted by our exposure-proxy setup (BoolQ>FakeQ>Olympic2024); ContextCite shows the opposite ordering, attributing most to Olympic2024 because the model relies on context most when it has no parametric knowledge — supporting the claim that span-level context attribution and dataset-level exposure attribution answer different questions. A synthetic identifiability experiment, controlled fine- tuning sweeps, and a multi-checkpoint unlearning case study provide supporting evidence that the metrics behave as exposure-sensitive source-ranking proxies.

paper.title: Discerning Minds or Generic Tutors? Evaluating Instructional Guidance Capabilities in Socratic LLMs

author.affiliation: Beijing Normal University and Beijing Normal University

paper.abstract: The conversational capabilities of large language models hold significant promise for enabling scalable and interactive tutoring. Prior work has primarily evaluated general instructional competence while overlooking a critical dimension: the ability to adaptively guide learners based on their evolving cognitive states. This study takes instructional guidance as a core capability and asks whether LLMs can emulate expert tutors who dynamically adjust strategies in response to learners’ needs. We introduce GuideEval, a benchmark grounded in authentic educational dialogues that evaluates pedagogical guidance through a three-phase behavioral framework: (i) Assessment, inferring learner states; (ii) Orchestration, adapting instructional strategies; and (iii) Elicitation, stimulating proper reflections. Empirical results indicate that existing LLMs often fail to provide effective adaptive scaffolding when learners experience confusion or require redirection. Complementing quantitative results, we present a detailed failure case analysis, offering intuitive insights into these limitations. We further propose a behavior-guided finetuning strategy based on behavior-prompted instructional dialogues, substantially enhancing guidance performance. By shifting the focus from isolated content correctness to learner-centered state-aware interaction, this work advocates a more dialogic paradigm for evaluating Socratic LLMs.

paper.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant), a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to 2.3\times prefill speedup and 3.5\times memory saving over FP16.

paper.title: Compressing Long Context into Answer-Aligned Memory Embeddings for LLM Inference

author.affiliation: University of Aizu and Pabna University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is constrained by the quadratic scaling of self-attention and the linear scaling of the KV cache, increasing latency, energy consumption, and GPU memory demand as context length scales. Existing soft-compression methods either lack query-guided memory selection at inference time, train without answer-targeted supervision, or couple compression tightly to a specific decoder architecture. We propose a Context-to-Answer-Aligned Memory Compression (CMC) framework, which compresses long input contexts into compact Context Memory Embeddings (CMEs) aligned to any frozen decoder’s embedding space, reducing inference costs without modifying decoder weights. CMC introduces a two-tier KV cache that combines question-guided CME selection with a local context window, and trains the compressor with answer-targeted distillation from a frozen LLM. Experiments across nine encoder-decoder combinations and four QA benchmarks show that CMC consistently outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 7.3 EM and 4.0 F1 point gains on SQuAD, while reducing inference time and energy consumption by up to 20% and peak reserved GPU memory by up to 50% at 3,000 generation tokens. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component and training objective contributes to the performance.

paper.title: Chart-EARL: Improving Chart Reasoning of Vision LLMs via Early Anchoring in Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Chart reasoning poses a significant challenge for Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs). While Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a promising solution, existing outcome-based RL methods overlook intermediate errors, whereas process-based approaches remain difficult in verifying abstract logical steps. We therefore analyze chart-reasoning failures to identify an intermediate supervision signal that is both relevant to the task and amenable to objective verification. Our pilot study suggests that early visual-perception errors constitute a prominent source of failure in the chart-reasoning setting. Guided by this insight, we propose Chart-EARL, which constructs verifiable early visual anchors for targeted chart-reasoning supervision. We first build a structured training corpus that explicitly decouples visual perception from logical deduction. Building upon this structure, our approach optimizes the model with rewards for both accurate extraction of descriptive visual features and final-answer correctness. This strategy provides direct and verifiable feedback on early visual grounding while keeping supervision on the final reasoning objective. Experiments show clear performance improvements on complex chart reasoning benchmarks.

paper.title: IALR: Instance-Adaptive Legal Rubric Supervision for Legal Judgment Prediction

author.affiliation: Zhongguancun Laboratory and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Legal judgment prediction (LJP) is important for supporting judicial decision-making and improving judicial efficiency. Existing LLM-based approaches often rely on manually specified reasoning pipelines or external legal structures, while feedback-based methods typically provide generic signals of correctness or coherence rather than case-specific legal supervision. We propose IALR: Instance-Adaptive Legal Rubric Supervision for Legal Judgment Prediction. For each training instance, IALR contrasts model responses of varying quality and distills their legally consequential failures into a weighted Instance-Adaptive Legal Rubric. These rubrics convert judgment-relevant conditions into discriminative preference signals for Direct Preference Optimization, enabling the model to learn charge prediction without following a predefined reasoning paradigm. At inference time, IALR requires no additional evaluator or correction module. Experiments on four Chinese criminal charge-prediction benchmarks show that IALR consistently improves Qwen2.5-7B, yielding average absolute accuracy gains of 5.68% in-domain and 8.73% out-of-domain. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and cross-domain transferability of Instance-Adaptive Legal Rubric supervision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Baii668/IALR.git.

paper.title: From Base Rollouts to RL Reasoning: A Budgeted Search Perspective
paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning, but how these gains relate to inference-time decoding and search remains unclear. Does RL produce reasoning behavior the base model does not have, or does it shift the rollout distribution toward trajectories the base model can already reach but rarely samples? We study this behaviorally with a Unified Decoding Framework (UDF), which expresses token-level sampling, beam-like search, tree search and sequence-level resampling as executable policies over a shared budgeted operating space. Operating points are scored after generation with pass@k, self-consistency, best-of-N and first-finish success, so the generation policy stays separate from the evaluation metric.Using paired Base/RL checkpoints from SimpleRL-Zoo, we ask whether an RL default-policy curve can be approximated by a structured path of Base operating points (\pi, N_{\mathrm{Base}}) rather than by post-hoc per-budget matching. On Math500, AIME, GPQA and IFEval, the pass@k recovery path follows a Budgeted Operating-Point Transition Rule (BOPTR), N_{\mathrm{Base}} \approx \alpha N_{\mathrm{RL}}^{\beta}, with benchmark-conditioned exponents. On Qwen2.5-7B, BOPTR gives the lowest transfer error among the non-oracle rules we test, 3.41 pp. Across models the rule family remains informative, but its parameters and selected policies are model-specific: Qwen models trained on the same difficulty split share operating-point structure, while cross-family models and different training distributions mark the limits of direct transfer.These results support a qualified internalized-search reading: under the recipe we test, much of the measured RL gain corresponds to a change in sampling efficiency, toward operating points the base model can already reach under search. We treat the benchmark-wise scaling patterns as descriptive of this recipe and cohort, report the cases in which they break down, and use UDF and BOPTR as behavioral diagnostics rather than as evidence of parameter-level equivalence or as general predictors of post-RL performance.

paper.title: Scaled Autoregressive Projection Steering (SAPS): Token-level Steering to Induce Sarcasm and Humblebrag in Text
paper.abstract: We propose Scaled Autoregressive Projection Steering (SAPS) for generating incongruity-based figurative language from literal inputs, extending contrastive paraphrasing-based steering vectors by autoregressively recomputing projection coefficients during decoding. SAPS comprises two novel components: (A) Autoregressive Projection Steering (APS), which recomputes the projection coefficient (c_t) at each decoding step t, adapting the steering signal to the evolving token distribution, and (B) a scaling coefficient \alpha whose effective range is layer-agnostic, enabling compact tuning of figurative intensity. Experiments across three instruction-tuned language models show that APS improves grammatical stability over fixed sentence-level steering while \alpha enables fine-grained figurative control, together yielding gains over prior steering methods and significantly increasing robustness to layer selection and steering strength. Cross-dataset experiments further confirm that steering directions generalize across domains. This is the first work to apply activation steering to incongruity-based figurative language generation. Our code is available at: https://github.com/SharathHN/saps-steering.

paper.title: Learning to Predict Future-Aligned Research Proposals with Language Models
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist ideation in research, but evaluating the quality of LLM-generated research proposals remains difficult: novelty and soundness are hard to measure automatically, and large-scale human evaluation is costly. We propose a verifiable alternative by reframing proposal generation as a time-sliced scientific forecasting problem. Given a research question and inspiring papers available before a cutoff time, the model generates a structured proposal and is evaluated by whether it anticipates research directions that appear in papers published after the time. We operationalize this objective with the Future Alignment Score (FAS), computed via retrieval and LLM-based semantic scoring against a held-out future corpus. To train models, we build a time-consistent dataset of 21,835 paper occurrences across 3,642 instances from targets and their pre-cutoff citations, and synthesize reasoning traces that teach gap identification and inspiration borrowing. Across Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5 models, future-aligned tuning improves future alignment over unaligned baselines (up to +10.6% overall FAS), and domain-expert human evaluation corroborates improved proposal quality. Finally, we demonstrate practical impact by implementing two model-generated proposals with a code agent, obtaining 4.17% accuracy gain on MATH from a new prompting strategy and consistent improvements for a novel model-merging method.

paper.title: Quantifying and Mitigating Default Behaviors in Text-to-Image Models

author.affiliation: Bar-Ilan University and Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models consistently collapse to stereotypical attribute values when prompts leave concepts underspecified, a phenomenon we term default behaviors. We conduct a large-scale empirical study using , an LLM-driven measurement approach that quantifies diversity at the level of individual concept attributes. We find pervasive default behaviors across all evaluated T2I models, with stronger models tending to exhibit less diversity. We trace these defaults to reporting bias in training captions: when captions omit common attributes, the accompanying images are dominated by a narrow set of values, and model outputs closely mirror this skew. We confirm this link causally with controlled fine-tuning interventions. As a proof of concept, we show that making sampled attribute values explicit broadens outputs, with some loss of faithfulness to secondary prompt details. Together, our results recast low diversity not as an inherent limitation of T2I models, but as a measurable and steerable consequence of what their training captions leave unsaid. Code and data available at: https://royira.github.io/GRADE.

paper.title: SPUR-XMC: Context-Adaptive Spurious Correlation Mitigation for Extreme Multi-Label Classification of Biomedical Literature
paper.abstract: Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) of biomedical literature aims to classify articles into a set of pre-defined labels from a large and highly skewed label distribution space. While recent pretrained language model (PLM)-based XMTC approaches have made substantial advances, they still struggle to generalize to tail labels representing concepts of high biomedical significance (e.g., rare diseases). A key factor contributing to poor tail-label performance is the presence of spurious correlations, where models inadvertently learn non-informative feature-label associations. To address this issue, we propose a novel context-adaptive spurious correlation mitigation technique, SPUR-XMC, which selectively attenuates spurious influences according to the context of the input article. A unique advantage of the proposed framework is that it does not modify existing PLM architectures for XMTC and instead operates as an add-on enhancement module. Extensive experiments across benchmark biomedical literature datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paper.title: HarmMetric Eval: Benchmarking Metrics and Judges for LLM Harmfulness Assessment

author.affiliation: The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study, Zhejiang University, The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

paper.abstract: Automatic harmfulness metrics and LLM-based judges are central to LLM safety assessment, yet differences in evaluation criteria, methodologies, and output formats may yield inconsistent judgments for the same model response. The lack of systematic research on these evaluators undermines the credibility and consistency of LLM safety assessments. To bridge this gap, we introduce HarmMetric Eval, a benchmark for both overall and fine-grained assessment of harmfulness evaluators. We construct a dataset of representative harmful prompts paired with diverse harmful responses and non-harmful counterparts across multiple categories. We propose a flexible scoring mechanism that rewards metrics for correctly ranking harmful responses above non-harmful ones, making it applicable to nearly all metrics and judges with varying output formats and scoring scales. Using HarmMetric Eval, we find that conventional reference-based metrics such as ROUGE and METEOR can outperform existing LLM-based judges in fine-grained harmfulness evaluation, challenging prevailing assumptions about LLM superiority. Fine-grained analysis reveals that LLM judges tend to overestimate irrelevant and useless responses. Furthermore, we build a new harmfulness judge by incorporating fine-grained criteria into its prompt template and leveraging reference-based metrics to fine-tune its base LLM. The resulting judge demonstrates leading performance on HarmMetric Eval and two external human-labeled datasets.

paper.title: A Survey on Rubric-guided Reinforcement Learning for Language Models
paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become the dominant paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, traditional RLHF relies on scalar reward signals that lack interpretability and fail to capture the multifaceted nature of response quality. Rubric-guided reinforcement learning addresses these limitations by introducing structured, interpretable evaluation criteria, or rubrics, as the backbone of reward design, feedback generation, and policy optimization. In this survey, we introduce a Bayesian framework that defines constitutions as prior distributions P(\mathcal{R}) over evaluation criteria and rubrics as conditional instantiations \mathcal{R}_x \sim P(\mathcal{R}|x). Under this unified view, we present a taxonomy of rubric-guided RL along the prior-posterior axis, covering constitutional AI, instance-specific rubrics, process-level supervision, self-evolving rubrics, and their agentic and multimodal extensions. Furthermore, as rubrics are natural-language artifacts, we present a linguistic analysis of how granularity trade-offs, semantic drift, and linguistic reward hacking impact alignment reliability, identifying key open problems for future research.

paper.title: Revising Context, Shifting Simulated Stance: Auditing LLM-Based Stance Simulation in Online Discussions
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate social media users and infer how individuals may respond to online discussions. However, it remains unclear whether these simulations reflect precise user-specific beliefs or whether they are highly sensitive to semantically independent changes in conversational contexts. In this work, we study counterfactual context revision as a framework for auditing LLM-based stance simulation. Given an original online conversation, we first infer a target user’s stance toward a specific topic. We then apply controlled revision strategies to the conversational context and simulate the user’s stance again under the revised context. We compare text-only revision strategies with a multimodal one that incorporates meme-based context and evaluate two main effectiveness metrics, i.e., average directional stance shift and stance transition rate. The results reveal effective and robust stance transitions in both text-only and multimodal strategies across different polarization-preference mechanisms. Our study contributes an evaluation framework for understanding the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation (https://github.com/STARResearchLab/StanceShift). More broadly, it highlights both the promise and risk of using LLMs as proxies for social media users in social simulation.

paper.title: MedCPEnv: A Reproducible Cost-Aware Simulated Hospital for Benchmarking and Training Medical LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Real-world clinical competence demands more than answering medical knowledge questions—it requires proactively gathering incomplete patient information, selecting appropriate examinations, and formulating safe, cost-conscious treatment plans through multi-turn interaction. Existing medical LLM benchmarks rely predominantly on static QA formats, failing to assess interactive information acquisition, tool use, or cost–quality tradeoffs. We propose MedCPEnv, a reproducible, cost-aware simulated hospital environment for evaluating and training medical LLM agents. Built from MIMIC-IV-NOTE discharge notes, MedCPEnv comprises 48,803 curated cases, a 1,000-case benchmark, and a 371,550-entry medical QA knowledge base, exposing four deterministic action types (ASK, EXAM, KNOWLEDGE, FINAL) to eliminate high-variance LLM role-playing artifacts. Evaluating eight frontier models, GPT-5.4 achieves the highest composite score (3.69/5) and diagnostic accuracy (60.3%), yet treatment accuracy remains only 19.4%, identifying treatment plan generation as the primary bottleneck. Substantial inter-model variation in the cost–quality tradeoff further demonstrates that clinical correctness alone is insufficient to characterize agent behavior. GRPO-based Agentic RL on Qwen3-4B shows that medical quality rewards consistently improve tool-use strategies, raising the composite score from 2.97 to 3.14 and diagnostic accuracy from 26.0% to 31.2%, establishing MedCPEnv as both a rigorous evaluation benchmark and a reproducible training environment for medical agent research.

paper.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: A Three-Stage Analysis of How SFT, RL, and OPD Shape CoT Calibration
paper.abstract: Large language models have made strong reasoning gains through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, yet these post-training methods are usually evaluated only by final-answer accuracy. We study how they reshape confidence during reasoning. We introduce a three-stage calibration framework that evaluates confidence before, during, and after chain-of-thought generation, corresponding to difficulty estimation, early termination, and answer aggregation. Through a controlled comparison on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we find that OPD provides the most useful pre-reasoning confidence, SFT gives the strongest online signal for early stopping, and RL produces the most reliable trace-level signal for aggregation. We further show that confidence reliability is position-dependent: RL confidence becomes informative after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later. Based on this observation, we propose PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that uses confidence only from reliable relative-position intervals. PosConf improves RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points over majority voting and consistently improves OPD early stopping under tight token budgets, with gains up to 4.3 points by avoiding its later inverse-calibration region, showing that confidence in reasoning models should be used both stage-wise and position-awarely. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Post-Training-Calibration.

paper.title: CultureVLM: Characterizing and Improving Cultural Understanding of Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced human-AI interaction but struggle with cultural understanding, often misinterpreting symbols, gestures, and artifacts due to biases in predominantly Western-centric training data. In this paper, we construct CultureVerse, a large-scale multimodal benchmark covering 19,682 cultural concepts, 188 countries/regions, 15 cultural topics, and 3 question types, with the aim of characterizing and improving VLMs’ multicultural understanding capabilities. Then, we propose CultureVLM, a series of VLMs fine-tuned on our dataset to achieve significant performance improvement in cultural understanding. Our evaluation of 16 models reveals significant disparities, with a stronger performance in Western concepts and weaker results in African and Asian contexts. Fine-tuning on our CultureVerse training set enhances cultural perception, demonstrating cross-cultural, cross-continent, and cross-dataset generalization without sacrificing performance on models’ general VLM benchmarks. We further present insights on cultural generalization and forgetting. We hope that this work could lay the foundation for more equitable and culturally aware multimodal AI systems.

paper.title: Taming the Thinker: Conditional Entropy Shaping for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
paper.abstract: Entropy-based deep reasoning has emerged as a promising direction for improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing methods often either increase response length indiscriminately or shorten responses at the cost of accuracy. To better balance this trade-off, we introduce Conditional Entropy Shaping (CES), a framework that dynamically controls token-level response entropy, enabling LLMs to produce concise solutions on simple problems while encouraging deeper exploration on hard ones. Built on DAPO, CES uses token-level entropy as an uncertainty signal and applies a conditional bidirectional policy: it penalizes high-entropy "forking point" tokens on correct reasoning paths to improve conciseness, and rewards them on incorrect paths to encourage exploration and error correction. We implement CES on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and evaluate it on 12 mathematical benchmarks. CES consistently improves average accuracy while reducing response length relative to DAPO, and supplementary experiments show similar trends on a smaller 1.5B backbone and on out-of-domain benchmarks.

paper.title: Thought-Aware KV Cache Compaction for Reasoning via Adaptive Attention Matching

author.affiliation: Fullive Innovation (Beijing) AI Technology Co., Ltd.
Fullive Innovation (Beijing) AI Technology Co., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Reasoning language models generate lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences whose key-value (KV) cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat reasoning trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning where different steps vary drastically in importance. We propose Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM), which exploits this structure through three mechanisms: (i)thought segmentation that decomposes the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii)adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget based on each segment’s importance and size, and (iii)pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. We prove that the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded. Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show that TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint, with periodic compaction bounding peak memory to 3.1–3.2,GB (a 65% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paper.title: Revisiting Task Vectors: A Structural Analysis of Their Limits

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology

paper.abstract: To mitigate high inference costs for in-context learning, prior works have proposed activation-space task vectors that encapsulate demonstration contexts into static representations. However, performance occasionally degrades across tasks, leaving it unclear whether this stems from sub-optimal extraction heuristics or fundamental limitations. We resolve this by decomposing Transformer self-attention to establish a theoretical best-case approximation: the Minimal-Gap Approximation. By isolating structural constraints from heuristic flaws, the Minimal-Gap Approximation reveals that task vectors are fundamentally bottlenecked by attention and length gaps. Specifically, because task vectors lock contextual information to fixed attention maps and positional alignments, they structurally fail under dynamic routing, length mismatches, and multi-token generation. We further show that these findings consistently hold across training-free extract-and-inject task vector methods, model architectures, and model scales.

paper.title: Does Reasoning Preserve Alignment? On the Trustworthiness of Large Reasoning Models

author.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology and University of Maryland, College Park
Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and University of Colorado at Boulder

paper.abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs are increasingly converted into reasoning models through post-training to improve multi-step task performance. This conversion is usually optimized for reasoning accuracy, without explicitly preserving the instruction-tuned model’s alignment behavior, such as safe refusal, bias avoidance, and privacy protection. We ask: does this conversion preserve alignment? We study this question through a trustworthiness audit and find that it is not behavior-preserving by default. For a systematic analysis, we compare reasoning models produced via supervised fine-tuning, RL-based post-training, and distillation against matched instruction-tuned baselines across six trustworthiness dimensions: safety, toxicity, stereotyping and bias, machine ethics, privacy, and out-of-distribution robustness. We observe that reasoning models often improve on mathematical reasoning benchmarks but exhibit alignment regressions, including increased toxicity, amplified stereotyping, miscalibrated refusal, and contextual privacy leakage. These regressions are consistent with behavioral drift from the instruction-tuned baseline, measured by KL divergence. Our results show that reasoning-model releases should report trustworthiness metrics alongside capability gains.

paper.title: From Narrative to Auditable Forecasts: A Structured Scaffold for Agentic Forecasting
paper.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for live forecasting, where they retrieve up-to-date information and produce estimates for unresolved future events. However, current agentic forecasting often relies on implicit narrative aggregation: agents collect evidence, discuss it in prose, and often assign a probability without an explicit update path from evidence to forecast. This limits both forecasting accuracy and auditability. We propose AuditForecast, an agentic scaffold for structured probabilistic forecasting. AuditForecast first anchors the forecast with a suitable quantitative baseline model, uses model-guided data retrieval to derive a base probability, and then applies situational factor updates outside the model’s scope through mechanical aggregation in odds space. This turns forecasting from a prose-based judgment into a structured process with explicit intermediate objects. Across multiple live forecasting benchmarks, AuditForecast improves forecasting accuracy and calibration relative to strong agentic baselines, surpasses market-implied references in several settings, and outperforms substantially more expensive deep-research agents while remaining Pareto-dominant in the cost–accuracy tradeoff. Beyond performance gains, AuditForecast produces an auditable forecasting report that makes forecast construction explicit and supports systematic post hoc analysis.

paper.title: RAMP: Regime-Aware Merge-Prune Token Compression for ASR-Oriented Audio-Language Models
paper.abstract: ASR-oriented audio-language models (ALMs) encode speech into long audio token sequences for LLM decoding, substantially increasing the inference cost of transcription. This motivates token compression methods that reduce audio token sequence length while preserving the acoustic evidence needed for transcription. However, existing compression methods often inherit vision-language criteria that are poorly matched to temporally ordered audio representations, or require attention-map access outside the standard FlashAttention path. Through a multi-axis geometric analysis, we show that ALM audio representations exhibit two distinct representation regimes: a locally redundant encoder regime and a dispersed post-projector regime. Motivated by this geometric shift, we propose **RAMP** (**R**egime-**A**ware **M**erge-**P**rune), a training-free method for FlashAttention-compatible audio token compression that applies bipartite L_2 merging in the encoder and centroid-distance-guided pruning after the projector. Across seven ASR benchmarks and two primary ALMs, RAMP achieves the lowest average WER multiplier among the evaluated training-free compression baselines at every evaluated retention ratio. At the most aggressive setting (r=0.4) on Audio-Flamingo-3, RAMP attains a 2.36\times average WER multiplier, compared with 4.26\times for the best non-RAMP baseline, while reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 24.8% over Vanilla.

paper.title: RADAR: Accelerate Large Language Model Inference with RL-Based Dynamic Draft Trees

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Inference with modern Large Language Models (LLMs) is expensive and slow, and speculative sampling has emerged as an effective solution to this problem.
