However, the number of calls to the draft model for generating candidate tokens in speculative sampling is a preset hyperparameter, lacking flexibility. To generate and utilize the candidate tokens more effectively, we propose RADAR, a novel speculative sampling method with RL-based dynamic draft trees. RADAR formulates the draft tree generation process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and employs offline reinforcement learning to train a prediction model, which enables real-time decisions on calls to the draft model, reducing redundant computations and further accelerating inference. Evaluations across three LLMs and four tasks show that RADAR achieves a speedup of 3.17x-4.82x over the auto-regressive decoding baseline.

paper.title: DeepResearch RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Deep Research Report
paper.abstract: Empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs), deep research systems integrate online information into research reports through multi-step web searching and information synthesis. Evaluating these reports presents a significant challenge due to their long context, high information density, and domain specificity, necessitating the use of AI evaluation as a substitute for prohibitively expensive human assessment. However, few studies have examined the effectiveness of existing reward models or LLMs in understanding and evaluating such research reports. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepResearch RewardBench, the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating reward modeling for research reports. We collect diverse report candidates from multiple agents or tool-augmented LLMs. These candidates are scored using query-specific rubrics and judged LLMs, and we ensure data quality and difficulty through a combination of multi-round filtering and human verification. Our benchmark comprises preference datasets formatted as pairs, triplets, and quadruplets to test ranking capabilities across varying levels of difficulty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current reward models handle general coherence effectively, their performance significantly degrades when evaluating research reports. In contrast, generative LLMs acting as judges demonstrate comprehensive superiority in this domain, with comparative evaluation proving more effective than direct scoring methods. We anticipate that this benchmark will serve as a vital testbed for the evaluation and advancement of research agents.

paper.title: Not All Tokens See Equally: Perception-Grounded Policy Optimization for Large Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: While Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has advanced reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), prevailing frameworks suffer from a foundational methodological flaw: by distributing identical advantages across all generated tokens, these methods inherently dilute the learning signals essential for optimizing the critical, visually-grounded steps of multimodal reasoning. To bridge this gap, we formulate Token Visual Dependency, quantifying the causal information gain of visual inputs via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between visual-conditioned and text-only predictive distributions. Revealing that this dependency is highly sparse and semantically pivotal, we introduce Perception-Grounded Policy Optimization (PGPO), which is a novel fine-grained credit assignment framework that dynamically reshapes advantages at the token level. Through a threshold-gated, mass-conserving mechanism, PGPO actively amplifies learning signals for visually-dependent tokens while suppressing gradient noise from linguistic priors. Extensive experiments based on the Qwen2.5-VL series across seven challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PGPO boosts models by 18.7% on average. Both theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that PGPO effectively reduces gradient variance, prevents training collapse, and acts as a potent regularizer for robust, perception-grounded multimodal reasoning.

paper.title: Social Caption: Evaluating Social Understanding in Multimodal Models
paper.abstract: Social understanding abilities are crucial for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to interpret human social interactions. We introduce Social Caption, a framework grounded in interaction theory to evaluate social understanding abilities of MLLMs along three dimensions: Social Inference (SI), the ability to make accurate inferences about interactions; Holistic Social Analysis (HSA), the ability to generate comprehensive descriptions of interactions; Directed Social Analysis (DSA), the ability to generate relevant information from interactions. We analyze factors influencing model performance in social understanding, such as scale, architectural design, and spoken context. Experiments with MLLM judges demonstrate a path towards scaling automated evaluation of multimodal social understanding.

paper.title: ZipRL: Adaptive Multi-Turn Context Compression with Hindsight Response Replay
paper.abstract: Adaptive context compression is vital for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to complex, multi-turn agent tasks. However, rule-based compression methods may discard task-critical nuances, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches usually struggle to balance information retention and token efficiency under the sparse rewards inherent to long-horizon workflows. To bridge this gap, we propose ZipRL, a novel adaptive compression framework tailored for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). ZipRL features a multi-granularity compression mechanism for active, non-uniform information reduction, coupled with Hindsight Response Replay (HRR)—a technique designed to densify training signals during RLVR optimization. Theoretically, we prove ZipRL’s superior task-relevant utility over uniform methods. Concretely, ZipRL utilizes coarse-to-fine prompts for macro-compression and incorporates HRR into GRPO via generalized advantage reshaping. Multiple models of varying versions and parameter scales validate the effectiveness of our approach. Benchmarks on five agent tasks show ZipRL outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by 27.9% and 34.7% across Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models, while maintaining exceptional token efficiency and robustness under extreme 256-turn extrapolation stress tests. Our code is available at https://github.com/huzhexin/ZipRL.

paper.title: ProofFrontier: Turning Verified Proofs into Boundary-hard Tasks for Formal Theorem Proving

author.affiliation: Alibaba Group and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Formal theorem proving provides executable verification signals from proof assistants, making it a key domain for improving the reliable reasoning ability of large language models through reinforcement learning (RL). However, RL-based prover training is increasingly bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality hard tasks: many existing Lean instances are either already solvable by current provers or too uninformative to drive further improvement. We propose ProofFrontier, a proof-structure-guided method for generating statement-preserving boundary-hard training tasks from verified Lean proofs. Instead of synthesizing open-ended problems that may be ill-posed or unverifiable, ProofFrontier starts from existing theorems with Lean-certified proofs, preserving task completeness and formal verifiability. It selectively withholds proof-structural guidance around important local nodes, encouraging the prover to rediscover nontrivial intermediate reasoning while keeping the original theorem statement unchanged. We further introduce capability-aware filtering to retain tasks that are solvable in principle but not easily solved by the base prover, yielding hard yet rewardable RL data. Training with GRPO on ProofFrontier-generated tasks consistently improves DeepSeek-Prover-V2 and Goedel-Prover-V2 on miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench. Notably, these gains are achieved using only hundreds of synthesized tasks, showing that complete boundary-hard tasks can be more data-efficient than simply scaling weak or already-solved proof data for theorem-proving RL.

paper.title: You Frame It: How Conceptual Representations Shape LLM Detection and Reasoning about Antisemitism

author.affiliation: Universität Hildesheim and Johann Wolfgang Goethe Universität Frankfurt am Main
Hochschule für Technik und Wirtschaft Berlin

paper.abstract: LLMs enable the integration of external conceptual resources at inference time, creating new opportunities for detecting ideologically and historically complex phenomena such as antisemitism. We investigate how different forms of conceptual grounding affect antisemitism detection and explanation behavior across four state-of-the-art LLMs. Using two expert-annotated datasets, we compare definitional, fine-grained taxonomic, example-augmented, and large-context representations of antisemitism. We find that fine-grained taxonomic representations substantially improve recall, while simultaneously reducing precision. Surprisingly, supplying substantially larger conceptual resources yields no additional quantitative benefit. Post-Holocaust antisemitism poses the most persistent challenge across models and configurations. Analysis of explanations further reveals systematic limitations including overproduction of conceptual references, reliance on lexical cues, overconfidence, and difficulties with subtle or justificatory forms of antisemitism. Our findings highlight both the potential and the remaining limitations of conceptually grounded LLMs for antisemitism detection and reasoning.

paper.title: Learning When to Think: Utility-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Efficient Text Retrieval

author.affiliation: Arm Holdings plc, School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University and CMU, Carnegie Mellon University

paper.abstract: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can improve retrieval by progressively refining semantic constraints. However, additional reasoning may introduce over-generalized or semantically noisy abstractions that weaken retrieval specificity. Existing methods largely supervise reasoning through final retrieval outcomes, providing limited guidance over the refinement process itself. We propose AURA, a framework that directly supervises intermediate reasoning states according to how well they separate relevant documents from hard distractors. AURA further trains a lightweight utility estimator over prefix-conditioned embeddings to adapt reasoning depth at inference time. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, AURA-4B achieves 34.7 average nDCG@10 while using 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query. Under matched deployment conditions, adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds relative to full-trajectory reasoning. Results on MS MARCO further suggest that this specialization need not substantially degrade conventional in-domain retrieval.

paper.title: MMRad-22K: A Structured Multimodal Evidence Dataset for Chest X-ray Report Generation

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) reporting follows a region-based clinical workflow in which radiologists inspect anatomical regions and integrate localized findings into a final report. However, existing resources for CXR report generation provide these supervision signals in fragmented forms. We introduce MMRad-22K, a dataset that organizes regional textual observations, anatomical grounding coordinates, localized image evidence, and report targets into structured multimodal evidence units for CXR report generation. To motivate this formulation, we first compare different evidence formats for report generation and find that structured multimodal evidence is generally more useful than text-only or bounding box-based evidence. We then adapt a unified LVLM backbone using MMRad-22K and show that adaptation with multimodal evidence outperforms both textual-evidence adaptation and end-to-end adaptation on language and clinically oriented metrics. Under the same evaluation protocol, the adapted model also reaches a performance level comparable to several open-source LVLM references. Together, these results support MMRad-22K as a practical structured multimodal resource for training and evaluating CXR report generation aligned with clinical reading workflows. The code is available at https://github.com/qiuzyc/MMRad.

paper.title: LSH-RL: Long-Short Horizon Reinforcement Learning for Persona-Level Role-Playing Agents
paper.abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) must sustain persona fidelity, natural interaction, and scene progression across multi-turn trajectories. However, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and coarse episode-level RL can over-reinforce safe stylized responses that appear in-character but are repetitive, low-information, or weakly grounded in the evolving scene. We propose LSH-RL, a Long-Short Horizon Reinforcement Learning framework for persona-level RPAs. LSH-RL trains a shared policy through dynamic multi-role self-play, combining short-horizon utterance/action rewards with long-horizon character-trajectory rewards. A gated trajectory-to-turn reward fusion mechanism prevents locally degenerate turns from receiving undeserved long-horizon credit, while a dialogue-action curriculum supports staged optimization. Experiments on PersonaArena and CharacterBox show that LSH-RL improves over SFT and DPO in both dialogue-only and full interaction settings. Further analyses show reduced repetition and stronger human preferences, suggesting a path toward more coherent and interaction-rich persona-level RPAs. The source code is available at https://github.com/Shiwenlong-source/LSH-RL.

paper.title: PrivAgentFlow: Agentic Workflow for Automating Privacy Preservation in Web Agents
paper.abstract: Autonomous web agents increasingly operate over sensitive personal data, yet existing privacy-preserving approaches rely on static filtering and globally enforced safeguards misaligned with compositional agent execution. We introduce PrivAgentFlow, a memory-guided agentic workflow framework that formulates privacy preservation as adaptive node-level governance over compositional web-agent workflows. PrivAgentFlow decomposes complex tasks into compositional workflow nodes, where each node operates under a distinct privacy policy conditioned on its execution role and information access requirements, enabling privacy governance to be localized at the execution level rather than globally enforced. Such localized governance is refined through execution memory, where historical task failures and privacy violations serve as corrective signals for improving node-level privacy control without exposing raw user data during planning. We provide theoretical insights showing that compositional web-agent workflows induce subtask-specific privacy–utility trade-offs, formally characterizing the advantage of heterogeneous node-level governance over uniform privacy control. Across 246 web-agent tasks on three platforms, PrivAgentFlow improves task utility by 23.1 percentage points (0.415→0.646), cuts environment-level privacy leakage by 92.3% (0.366→0.028), and reduces API-level leakage from 100% to 3.7% over the strongest prior baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/haorentang/PrivAgentFlow.

paper.title: REALM: Reliable Expertise-Aware Language Model Fine-Tuning from Noisy Annotations

author.affiliation: Higharc and University of California, Santa Barbara

paper.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of large language models relies on human-annotated data, yet annotation pipelines routinely involve multiple crowdworkers of heterogeneous expertise. Standard practice aggregates labels via majority vote or simple averaging, discarding annotator identity and causing the model to absorb the errors of unreliable annotators into its parameters. We propose REALM, which jointly learns the model parameters and a scalar expertise value for each annotator, entirely unsupervised and requiring nothing beyond annotator identity. The key idea is to model each observed label as a mixture between the model’s prediction and a uniform random guess, weighted by the annotator’s learned expertise. REALM applies to any task with a fixed label set, and extends to multiple tasks via a learned expertise matrix. On four text-classification datasets with real crowdsourced annotations, REALM is the best method in all 12 configurations of the three heterogeneous-annotator datasets, improving on the strongest applicable baseline, including majority vote and Dawid–Skene aggregation, by +2.9 points on average. On five question answering benchmarks with simulated noisy labels, it outperforms naive noisy fine-tuning in 152 of 162 configurations, by +5.0 points on average, with gains that grow with model capacity. The learned expertise additionally recovers annotator reliability without ever observing it. Our code is available at https://github.com/sajjad-ucsb/REALM.

paper.title: Data-Driven Red-Teaming: Reusing Adversarial Attacks via Metadata-Aware Retrieval

author.affiliation: MATS Research, Doctoral School Information and Biomedical Technologies Polish Academy of Sciences and NASK - National Research Institute
NASK - National Research Institute, Mila - Quebec AI Institute and Jagiellonian University
NASK - National Research Institute and Gdańsk University of Techonology

paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world systems, red-teaming has become a critical tool for identifying safety vulnerabilities. However, existing approaches remain largely stateless and inefficient, repeatedly rediscovering similar failure modes for each new model. In this work, we propose a data-driven paradigm for red-teaming that enables the accumulation and reuse of adversarial knowledge across models. We introduce a framework for generating and collecting adversarial attacks enriched with structured metadata, including attack strategies, risk categories, and diagnostic feedback signals. Leveraging this resource, we demonstrate that metadata-aware retrieval significantly improves the efficiency of discovering successful attacks on unseen models, reducing reliance on purely generative search. To support further research, we release a large-scale dataset comprising >188k successful attacks across 8 models, together with rich metadata annotations.

paper.title: STAR-Table: Spatial Textual Anchoring and Reconstruction for Hierarchical Table Reasoning via OCR
paper.abstract: Tables are widespread in real-world scenarios. In particular, hierarchical tables encode much richer structural semantics; however, their complex layouts pose severe challenges to Large Language Models (LLMs). The core difficulty lies in precisely aligning complex topological structures with multi-level semantic dependencies, where alignment failures often lead to cross-level aggregation errors and hallucinations. To address this challenge, we propose STAR-Table, a framework that synergizes visual perception with symbolic reasoning. Unlike traditional text-only approaches, STAR-Table leverages OCR models to extract pixel-level spatial coordinates, thereby establishing explicit Spatial-Textual AnchoRs. These anchored spatial priors are formulated as explicit structural hints to guide LLMs in reconstructing the hierarchical topology of tables. Based on the reconstructed topology, complex visual layouts are decomposed into one or more distinct sub-tables, each of which is further mapped into a deterministic flattened database. Finally, we design an adaptive QA module that fuses Vision-Language Model (VLM) semantic summaries with multi-step SQL execution to support robust table-based reasoning. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-Table achieves superior performance, significantly outperforming specialized fine-tuned models and advanced in-context learning paradigms.

paper.title: Training-Free Policy Violation Detection via Activation-Space Whitening in LLM

author.affiliation: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Tel Aviv University and Fujitsu Research of Europe
Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Technion
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.

paper.abstract: As organizations increasingly deploy LLMs in sensitive domains such as legal, financial, and medical settings, ensuring alignment with internal organizational policies has become a priority. Existing content moderation frameworks remain largely confined to the safety domain and lack the robustness to capture nuanced organizational policies. LLM-as-a-judge and fine-tuning approaches, though flexible, introduce significant latency and training cost. To address these limitations, we frame policy violation detection as an out-of-distribution (OOD) problem in the model’s activation space. We propose a training-free method that operates directly on the LLM internal representations, leveraging prior evidence that decision-relevant information is encoded within them. Inspired by whitening techniques, we derive policy-violation scores directly from normalized representations of LLM hidden activations. Our method requires only the policy text and a small number of illustrative samples, making it lightweight and easily deployable. We extensively evaluate our method across multiple LLMs and challenging policy benchmarks. It achieves up to 86.0% F1, outperforming both fine-tuned and LLM-as-a-judge baselines while requiring substantially less computation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/LLM-policy-violation-detection.

paper.title: ASSAY: Reconciling Stability and Validity in Reference-Free Scientific LLM Judges
paper.abstract: LLM judges have emerged as a key approach to evaluating open-ended scientific outputs that resist automated verification, yet their faithfulness in reference-free settings remains underexplored, particularly for fields such as novel materials synthesis where no ground-truth reference exists. Such judges produce false positives that accept scientifically invalid recipes and false negatives that penalize semantically equivalent ones in unfamiliar notation. We introduce ASSAY, a probe suite built on domain-grounded augmentations of ground-truth synthesis recipes, and reveal that these two failure modes form a systematic Stability–Validity trade-off across thirteen judge models. To resolve this trade-off, we train SynthJudge-8B via DPO on contrastive pairs derived from the same augmentations, improving judgment accuracy from 51.4% to 85.1% while maintaining agreement with domain experts. We release our probe suite and trained model to support faithful automated evaluation in scientific fields beyond materials synthesis at https://github.com/SoyeonHH/ASSAY.

paper.title: Fusian: Multi-LoRA Fusion for Fine-Grained Continuous MBTI Personality Control in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in simulating diverse human behaviors and personalities. However, existing methods for personality control, which include prompt engineering and standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), typically treat personality traits as discrete categories (e.g., "Extroverted" vs. "Introverted"), lacking the ability to precisely control the intensity of a trait on a continuous spectrum. In this paper, we introduce Fusian, a novel framework for fine-grained, continuous personality control in LLMs. Fusian operates in two stages: (1) Trajectory Collection, where we capture the dynamic evolution of personality adoption during SFT by saving a sequence of LoRA adapters, effectively mapping the continuous manifold of a trait; and (2) RL-based Dynamic Fusion, where we train a policy network using Reinforcement Learning to dynamically compute mixing weights for these frozen adapters. By sampling from a Dirichlet distribution parameterized by the policy network, Fusian fuses multiple adapters to align the model’s output with a specific numerical target intensity. Experiments on the Qwen3-14B model demonstrate that Fusian achieves high precision in personality control, significantly outperforming baseline methods in aligning with user-specified trait intensities.

paper.title: PRISM: Multidimensional Safety Risk Detection and Measurement Beyond Superficial Compliance for LLMs

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Existing LLM safety measures operate as black boxes, lacking categorical precision and calibrated severity assessment. We propose **PRISM** (**P**rototypical **R**epresentation for **I**nternal **S**afety **M**apping), a fine-grained two-stage safety auditing framework grounded in internal mechanistic representations. Stage I localizes functional safety zones via spectral analysis and maps internal activations onto concept prototypes for camouflage-resilient categorical risk identification. Stage II decomposes violation severity across orthogonal dimensions through structured CoT reasoning, producing calibrated human-auditable ordinal verdicts. PRISM achieves a new best F1 of 77.60% on the adversarial ToxicChat benchmark and approaches 671B frontier judges within a 2.3% margin on severity calibration, demonstrating that mechanistic grounding and principled task formulation can substitute for scale in fine-grained safety governance.

paper.title: Text Attribution as Continuous Trajectories: Paired AUC Metrics and Mid-Layer Allocation-Effect Decomposition

author.affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Attribution aims to identify which input tokens are responsible for a language model’s predictions, yet its evaluation in NLP remains dominated by discrete Top-k removal tests that poorly reflect global importance and interaction effects. In this work, we reformulate text attribution evaluation as a continuous functional over attribution-induced trajectories and introduce two complementary AUC-based metrics tailored to autoregressive models. Perturbation AUC measures token necessity via progressive embedding-level corruption with a stable logit-based signal, while Recovery AUC evaluates sufficiency by tracking the restoration of internal representations in hidden-state space. Together, these metrics subsume Top- tests and enable principled, ordering-sensitive assessment of attribution quality. Using these diagnostics, we show that most existing attribution methods collapse to near-random rankings under continuous evaluation and fail to capture even first-order interaction effects. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose a mid-layer attribution framework that exploits a layer-wise saturation property of transformer computation to decompose attribution into information allocation and causal effect. Across multiple models and tasks, our method consistently outperforms existing baselines under both Perturbation and Recovery AUC, yielding more faithful and interaction-aware explanations of language model behavior.

paper.title: From Detection to Refusal: Safer LLMs via Circuit-Guided Weight Scaling

author.affiliation: Computer Science and Engineering Department, University of California, San Diego

paper.abstract: Despite extensive alignment efforts, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to generating unsafe content under adversarial prompting, yet the internal mechanisms by which safety behaviors are implemented remain poorly understood. We study LLM safety from a mechanistic interpretability perspective and characterize a multi-stage *safety circuit* that organizes refusal behavior, consisting of (i) \textbf{Harmful Detection Heads} that respond to harmful inputs, (ii) \textbf{Safety Neurons} that mediate and stabilize safety signals in the residual stream, and (iii) \textbf{Refusal Heads} that translate these signals into safe response generation. Using targeted attention-head and neuron-level interventions, we provide causal evidence consistent with this circuit organization, showing that suppressing upstream Harmful Detection Heads disrupts downstream refusal behavior and that safety neurons mediate this interaction. We validate that this decomposition recurs across multiple LLM architectures and adversarial attack settings, and use simple, architecture-preserving weight scaling as a mechanistic probe to test its functional relevance. Across six LLMs, circuit-guided scaling improves safety rates under attacks by 26.5%, while incurring only a 1.7% accuracy drop across four standard benchmarks. Overall, our results support a circuit-level interpretation of LLM safety and suggest that mechanistic abstractions can reveal stable and transferable patterns underlying aligned behavior.

paper.title: NDD-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal LLMs to Understand Communication in Non- and Minimally-Speaking Autistic Individuals
paper.abstract: Over 30% of autistic individuals are non- or minimally-speaking, relying on a complex, idiosyncratic repertoire of multimodal behaviors to communicate. Recognizing these intentional communicative acts in naturalistic environments remains a significant challenge for current multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which often struggle with the inference of subtle nonverbal cues in this domain. We introduce NDD-R1, a multi-stage reasoning framework that adapts a general-purpose MLLM for multi-view communication understanding for this population. Our approach employs a four-stage curriculum alternating between supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning (\text{SFT}_1 \rightarrow \text{GRPO}_1 \rightarrow \text{SFT}_2 \rightarrow \text{GRPO}_2), integrating label-guided distillation, temperature-escalated self-distillation, and difficulty-tiered reward optimization. We evaluate NDD-R1 on an initial dataset collected through the Rapid Online Sample of Communication (ROSCO) protocol, comprising 2,582 caregiver-annotated multi-view videos of 27 non- and minimally-speaking autistic individuals. NDD-R1 outperforms baselines on action and joint classification tasks, achieving competitive function classification performance relative to Gemini, exhibiting strong multi-view scaling and generalization across unseen sessions. Our code is available at https://github.com/SiddhantBikram/NDD-R1.

paper.title: Preserving General Capability in Personality-Aligned LLMs via Orthogonal Gradient Projection
paper.abstract: Personality alignment tailors Large Language Models (LLMs) for personalized interactions. Most existing studies focus on prompting, post- training, or representation steering to elicit trait expression, but they often compromise the general capabilities like reasoning and truthfulness. In this work, we empirically verified the existence of the Personality Alignment Tax (PAT) that distribution shifts and conflicting objectives during personality updates overwrite pre-trained competencies. To mitigate this tax, we propose a Personality-Orthogonal Gradient Projection (POGP) plug-in that preserves the capability in personality alignment. Specifically, POGP estimates the general-capability subspace from capability reference benchmarks and projects personality gradients onto the orthogonal complement before updating. This isolates and neutralizes conflicting gradients while maintaining the pre-trained reasoning capabilities. Experiments on the BIG5-CHAT dataset with two backbone LLMs demonstrate that POGP achieves a stronger personality plasticity and capability stability trade-off than baselines.

paper.title: EviGen: Predictive Evidence Scaffolding for Verifiable Clinical Rationale Generation
paper.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) capture years of patient history across notes, codes, labs, and procedures, and contain evidence needed to reason about likely clinical outcomes. However, comprehensive clinician review of these records is impractical, and LLM-based processing is costly and often unreliable, missing some relevant observations while hallucinating others. We therefore propose **EviGen**, a three-layer framework for verifiable clinical rationale generation that addresses these challenges. The **first layer** is a patient-conditioned retriever that uses learnable queries to find evidence predictive of, not just textually relevant to, a clinical outcome and ranks it by prediction attribution scores. The **second layer** is an LLM generator that consumes this ranked evidence as a scaffold to produce a clinical rationale grounded in the retrieved spans. The **third layer** is a process-supervised verifier that checks the generated rationale at the reasoning-step level, flagging unreliable claims. Across three medical prediction datasets, EviGen improves prediction performance and rationale faithfulness over full-context LLM and RAG baselines, and is preferred by clinical reviewers in a usability evaluation.

paper.title: Mirror, Mirror on the Wall: Prompt Echoing in Instruct Language Models

author.affiliation: Warsaw University of Technology and Adam Mickiewicz University of Poznan
Institute of Fundamental Technological Research, Polish Academy of Sciences and Warsaw University of Technology

paper.abstract: Prompt echoing is a recognized failure mode of instruct language models, in which a model instead of generating a response, mirrors the provided prompt, even though it did not receive a specific instruction to do so. Is this phenomenon a sign of the model leaking the content of its training dataset, or is it rather caused by a misaligned behavior of the internal induction/copying mechanisms? We investigate prompt echoing small language models from different families (Gemma, Llama, Qwen, SmolLM and OLMo) and show that echoing prompts are likely to have partial overlap with the training dataset but the phenomenon is primarily driven by the model’s induction heads.

paper.title: Learning to Code by Learning to Verify: Execution-Grounded Co-Evolution of Code Generation and Self-Verification for Reliable Code LLMs

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made rapid progress in code generation, yet their ability to verify whether a program is correct has not necessarily improved at the same pace. We identify a generation-verification gap in code LLMs, where scaling substantially improves test-passing code generation, while execution-free correctness reasoning improves much more slowly. This gap challenges existing self-rewarding approaches, which often implicitly assume that a stronger generator also serves as a better judge. To bridge this gap, we propose CoVera, an execution-grounded co-evolution framework that jointly trains a code LLM to generate code and to verify code correctness. In generator mode, the model produces candidate programs and receives execution-based rewards from available tests. In verifier mode, the same model reads a problem-program pair, produces a reasoning trace, and predicts a correctness judgment, which is rewarded according to agreement with execution-derived labels. The calibrated verifier is then used as an auxiliary self-verification signal for generation, while the evolving generator continuously supplies increasingly challenging candidates for verifier training. This co-evolution enables an on-policy curriculum for correctness reasoning and grounds self-verification in execution feedback, without requiring exhaustive test suites or golden reference solutions. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and model scales show that CoVera improves both code generation and intrinsic correctness verification, outperforming representative baselines from diverse code-learning paradigms.

paper.title: Cost-efficient Active Learning for Referring Image Segmentation and Grounding

author.affiliation: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology
Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Collecting natural-language referring expressions along with region annotations, such as masks or boxes, is a major bottleneck in visual grounding (VG), as annotators must write descriptions that distinguish target regions from visually similar ones. We tackle this by formulating active learning (AL) for VG under the realistic setting where only raw images are available without accompanying text. Since ground-truth text is unavailable, sample selection must estimate which images contain ambiguous regions that would require discriminative referring expressions. To address this, we generate auxiliary region-text pairs using foundation models, and introduce Referred Region Ambiguity, a new acquisition function that measures whether the model’s confidence collapses onto a single region or disperses across multiple candidates. It allows our method to prioritize images with strong cross-region competition, which are more informative due to their visual ambiguity. We also design a referring-expression annotation interface that helps annotators quickly focus on writing discriminative language with a few clicks. Experiments on RIS and REC benchmarks show that our AL framework consistently outperforms several AL baselines, while a user study shows up to 1.6\times faster description labeling of ours.

paper.title: Gaming the Judge: How Unfaithful Chain-of-Thought Can Undermine Agent Evaluation

author.affiliation: NVIDIA and University of Michigan - Ann Arbor
LG Corporation and University of Illinois, Chicago
University of Michigan - Ann Arbor and LG AI Research

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance, particularly in non-verifiable settings where judgments rely on agent trajectories including chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. This paradigm implicitly assumes that the agent’s CoT faithfully reflects both its internal reasoning and the underlying environment state. We show this assumption is brittle: LLM judges are highly susceptible to manipulation of agent reasoning traces. By systematically rewriting agent CoTs while holding actions and observations fixed, we demonstrate that manipulated reasoning alone can increase false positive rates of state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM) judges by up to 117% relative to the unmanipulated baseline across 800 trajectories spanning diverse web tasks. We study manipulation strategies spanning style-based approaches that alter only the presentation of reasoning and content-based approaches that fabricate signals of task progress, and find that content-based manipulations are consistently more effective. We evaluate mitigation strategies including manipulation-aware prompting and judge-time scaling, which can reduce but do not eliminate the vulnerability. Our findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability in LLM-based evaluation and highlight the need for judging mechanisms that verify reasoning claims against observable evidence.

paper.title: From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Existing memory systems for long-horizon LLM agents often retrieve prior traces as passive context rather than converting them into executable capabilities. In this paper, we propose MSCE, a training-free Memory–Skill Co-Evolution framework that organizes agent experience into grounded step traces, reusable procedural policies, and declarative environmental cognition. MSCE crystallizes evidence-backed L2 policies with positive estimated gain into callable skills that retain evidence links, applicability boundaries, decision guidance, verification rules, and reliability estimates. It further introduces reflection-weighted value backfilling, which propagates sparse terminal feedback through dense local self-reflections to produce evidence-calibrated trace values for governing memory and skill evolution. Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo show that MSCE achieves the best aggregate performance among the evaluated skill-augmented and memory-driven baselines, with statistically supported aggregate gains, positive cross-domain transfer, and continual improvement as online experience accumulates. Our code is available at https://github.com/MemTensor/MemOS/tree/main/apps/memos-local-plugin.

paper.title: Is LoRA Robust to Adversarial Attacks? Expectation-Based Regularization for Parameter-Efficient Adversarial Training
paper.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet its robustness to textual adversarial perturbations remains understudied. Existing adversarial training methods often improve robustness by solving costly min-max objectives with inner perturbation optimization with suboptimal results. In this research, we propose Expectation-Regularized LoRA (ER-LoRA), a simple expectation-based regularization approach that improves the robustness of LoRA without requiring inner maximization or adversarial example generation. ER-LoRA smooths predictions over a LoRA-aware low-dimensional perturbation distribution and admits a closed-form curvature-aware objective via a local Gaussian approximation. It adds no trainable parameters and keeps the LoRA architecture unchanged. Experiments on adversarial NLP benchmarks and textual attacks show that ER-LoRA improves robustness while preserving clean accuracy and parameter efficiency.

paper.title: HINTBench: Horizon-agent Intrinsic Non-attack Trajectory Benchmark
paper.abstract: Existing agent-safety evaluation has focused mainly on externally induced risks. Yet agents may still enter unsafe trajectories under benign conditions. We study this complementary but underexplored setting through the lens of intrinsic risk, where intrinsic failures remain latent, propagate across long-horizon execution, and eventually lead to high-consequence outcomes. To evaluate this setting, we introduce non-attack intrinsic risk auditing, a guard-oriented safety evaluation task, and present HINTBench, a benchmark of 596 agent trajectories, comprising 400 synthetic risky trajectories, 136 synthetic safe trajectories, 30 reconstructed real-world risky trajectories, and 30 reconstructed real-world safe trajectories, with an average length of 24.0 steps. HINTBench supports three tasks: risk detection, risk-step localization, and intrinsic failure-type identification, with annotations organized under a unified five-constraint taxonomy. Experiments reveal a substantial capability gap: strong LLMs perform well on trajectory-level risk detection, but the best model remains below 37 on fine-grained Strict-F1 for risk-step localization. Existing off-the-shelf guard models evaluated under their native prompts transfer poorly to this setting. These findings establish intrinsic risk auditing as an open challenge for agent safety.

paper.title: CODEPIVOT: Bootstrapping Multilingual Transpilation in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning with Reduced Reliance on Parallel Corpora

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Fudan University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Transpilation, or code translation, aims to convert source code from one programming language (PL) to another. Recent large language model (LLM)-based approaches have demonstrated immense potential for code translation. Training-based methods are important because LLMs currently do not effectively adapt to domain-specific settings that suffer from a lack of knowledge without targeted training. However, existing training-based approaches rely on a pairwise transpilation paradigm, making it impractical to support a diverse range of PLs. Furthermore, these methods shape the reinforcement learning (RL) reward linearly in the test-case pass rate, which underweights the earliest partial progress. To address these limitations, we propose CodePivot, a training framework that leverages Python as an intermediate representation (IR), augmented by a novel RL reward mechanism, Aggressive-Partial-Functional reward, to bootstrap the model’s multilingual transpilation ability with reduced reliance on parallel corpora. Experiments involving 10 PLs show that the resulting 7B model, trained on Python-to-Others tasks, consistently improves performance across both general and low-resource PL-related transpilation tasks. It outperforms substantially larger mainstream models with hundreds of billions more parameters, such as DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, on Python-to-Others tasks and Others-to-All tasks, respectively, and surpasses its counterpart trained directly on Any-to-Any tasks on general transpilation tasks. Code and data: https://github.com/lishangyu-hkust/CodePivot.

paper.title: MetaGAI: A Large-Scale and High-Quality Benchmark for Generative AI Model and Data Card Generation
paper.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative AI has created a pressing need for rigorous documentation standards that support transparency and governance. Manual creation of Model and Data Cards, however, is difficult to scale, and automated approaches lack the large-scale, high-fidelity benchmarks required for systematic evaluation. We introduce MetaGAI, a benchmark of 2,541 semantically matched document triplets constructed from academic papers, GitHub repositories, and Hugging Face artifacts. Reference cards are produced by a multi-agent pipeline of specialized Retriever, Generator, and Editor agents, and the pipeline is assessed through a four-part validation protocol. We further propose an evaluation framework that combines reference-based automated metrics with a multi-model LLM-as-a-Judge protocol, together with explicit agreement and sensitivity analyses. Among the evaluated baselines, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct achieves the best observed cost–quality trade-off, and the results reveal a recurring tension between faithfulness and completeness. MetaGAI provides a testbed for benchmarking, training, and analyzing automated Model and Data Card generation at scale. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/haoxuan-unt2024/MetaGAI-Benchmark.

paper.title: Before the Script, Set the Stage: How Worldview Simulation Amplifies Psychologically Grounded Persuasion in Multi-Turn Jailbreaking
paper.abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks demonstrate that harmful intent can be distributed across dialogue, yet existing methods obscure what conversational mechanisms drive vulnerability. We introduce Blueprint, a safety-evaluation framework that separates a factorized social-influence strategy space from WorldviewSim, a cross-turn situational context module. Monte Carlo Tree Search optimizes turn-level combinations of 18 theory-grounded influence factors across a four-turn trajectory. Across six frontier models, Blueprint achieves near-ceiling attack success rates on major open-weight and proprietary models, while requiring the fewest average queries (2.46). The resulting trajectories further reveal model-specific vulnerability among resistant targets: each responds to distinct influence factors and strategy transitions, yet all share a common recovery pathway. Specifically, shifting toward concrete, executable task framing consistently escapes hard-refusal states. Ablations confirm that operational cues matter most: making requests actionable has the largest impact, gain framing is unusually potent, and some legitimacy appeals can backfire. These findings suggest that robust multi-turn safety requires monitoring not only harmful content, but also how dialogue state makes unsafe requests appear concrete and locally executable. The code is open-sourced at: https://github.com/charlottec1583/Blueprint.

paper.title: Frames2LoRA: Parametric Video Internalization for Vision-Language Models

author.affiliation: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology

paper.abstract: Processing video in vision-language models is expensive: each frame occupies hundreds of tokens, and inference cost scales with every frame and every repeated query. We introduce Frames2LoRA, a method for parametric video internalization. A perceiver hypernetwork reads the intermediate representations produced layer-by-layer as a frozen VLM encodes a video, and generates a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter in a single forward pass. Unlike standard LoRA fine-tuning, which requires iterative gradient updates, Frames2LoRA predicts these weights directly from the video. Trained for SmolVLM2 500M and 2.2B on video summarization and captioning, Frames2LoRA enables the same frozen VLM to answer queries from the adapter alone, with zero visual tokens in its context at query time. Frames2LoRA is statistically non-inferior and equivalent to direct video-in-context inference across all five captioning benchmarks at both model scales, and across seven of eight video question answering benchmark-scale pairings. Although trained only on 12 frames at 384px, it remains stable up to 1,024 frames and 1024px, where direct video-in-context inference often degenerates. Across this sweep, it reduces answer-time visual-token load by up to 1,500x and query TTFT by 6-80x, while preserving video-faithful outputs. We also find that independently generated adapters for non-overlapping video segments can compose in rank space, suggesting a path toward chunked long-video internalization.

paper.title: When Should Queries Be Decomposed? A Stage-Aware Study of Query Decomposition for Multi-Condition Retrieval
paper.abstract: Multi-condition retrieval requires systems to identify documents that satisfy multiple distinct constraints, moving beyond mere topical relevance. While query decomposition is widely adopted as an intuitive remedy, its effectiveness across different retrieval pipeline stages remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a stage-aware empirical study and uncover a stark, stage-dependent effect: decomposition during initial retrieval frequently harms retrieval performance due to semantic dilution, yet substantially improves reranking by enabling more fine-grained constraint verification. Motivated by these insights, we propose a principled Stage-Aware Decomposition framework that retains the monolithic query during initial retrieval to preserve global semantic context, while employing sub-queries exclusively during reranking for fine-grained constraint matching. Extensive evaluations on the MultiConIR and SSRB benchmarks demonstrate that our framework consistently improves ranking performance for compositional queries across multiple retrieval and reranking models.

paper.title: Puzzles to Paradigms: A Survey of Human–Agent Collaboration in Scientific Innovation
paper.abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly embedded in scientific workflows, including literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, tool use, writing, and peer review. However, existing surveys and evaluations often emphasize task performance while underexamining how humans and agents coordinate under different epistemic conditions of scientific work. This survey introduces **CSCW**\times**Kuhn**, a coordination-aware framework that connects computer-supported cooperative work dimensions with distinct scientific contexts. Using this framework, we synthesize recent human–agent systems and benchmarks to examine how coordination demands and failure risks may vary across contexts. Our synthesis identifies five recurring failure modes: procedural drift, grounding substitution, evaluative flattening, proxy optimization, and epistemic black-boxing, and argues for evaluations that move beyond task accuracy and toward grounding, provenance, disagreement preservation, and long-horizon scientific reliability. Our corpus and coding artifact are available at https://github.com/jenlia024/CSCWxKuhn-artifact.

paper.title: TALIM: A Benchmark Dataset for Tajik Academic Language Intelligence Measurement

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: We introduce TALIM (Tajik Academic Language Intelligence Measurement), a large-scale academic benchmark for evaluating academic reasoning and language understanding in Tajik. TALIM spans nine subjects and three question formats, multiple-choice, matching, and free-response, sourced natively from the Tajik national curriculum rather than translated from existing benchmarks. We evaluate nine LLMs, both proprietary and open-weight models, finding that proprietary models substantially outperform open-weight models across all subjects and question types. Grammar is the weakest subject across all models, while physics is consistently the strongest. English translation substantially improves open-weight performance while Farsi transliteration yields only marginal gains, indicating that failures stem from data scarcity rather than script unfamiliarity. Chain-of-thought analysis reveals several systematic failure modes: hallucination, reasoning process failures, and grammatical category confusion. We hope TALIM will serve as a resource for assessing Tajik language capabilities of frontier models and motivate similar native benchmark construction efforts for other low-resource languages.

paper.title: Hybrid PIR: Balancing Token Compression and Structural Invariance via Pāṇinian Role Assignment
paper.abstract: Neural text representations often lack structural guarantees for syntactic variations, relying instead on statistical interpolation to recognize paraphrases. We introduce the Pāṇinian Intermediate Representation (PIR), a deterministic compiler that maps English sentences to role-tagged canonical sequences using Universal Dependency parses. Unlike heuristic methods such as stopword removal, the PIR compiler is deterministic: given a correct dependency parse, syntactically equivalent paraphrases compile to identical strings. On a 200-pair diagnostic suite of templated syntactic alternations spanning active/passive voice, dative shift, and topicalization, the compiler produces identical strings for 196 pairs; all four failures are structurally typed and traced to known parser limitations. Stopword removal produces identical strings for 0 of 200 pairs. To bridge the performance gap in downstream tasks, we propose Hybrid PIR, which selectively restores lexical content through a deduplication mechanism. Hybrid PIR achieves similarity performance comparable to stopword removal (0.8130 vs. 0.8154 average ρ; bootstrap 95% CI on the difference includes zero) at 43.8% token compression, while providing structural guarantees that surface-level methods cannot. On retrieval benchmarks, Hybrid PIR reaches 80% of the English baseline nDCG@10 on BEIR SciFact and 86% of MRR@10 on MS MARCO QA at 39.0% compression. A three-variant representation ablation validates our deduplication design: removing this mechanism degrades retrieval performance by 3.5 points and turns the compression benefit negative (-3.0%). In a QQP-validation duplicate-detection use case (40,430 pairs), Hybrid PIR reaches precision 0.861 with no tuning, matching a tuned embedding threshold and validating the intended deployment as an offline canonicalization tool for deduplication and index construction.

paper.title: Linearly Readable, Not Robust: How Linear Jailbreak Probes Conflate Benign Register with Adversarial Intent
paper.abstract: A cheap, now-standard safety filter attaches a linear probe to a frozen LLM’s hidden states to flag jailbreak prompts before generation, reaching near-perfect in-distribution accuracy at negligible cost. We show this single-layer probe is not a usable real-time filter, explain why, and give a fix. Across two model families, five attack types, ten languages, and three sets of hard-but-benign prompts, we find: (i) published probes are badly miscalibrated, so the headline 98–100% detection is an artifact of the chosen threshold (expected calibration error 0.20–0.33, and 0.07–0.20 even after a leakage-controlled retraining); (ii) most of the signal is benign writing style—its "register"—since a model-free style classifier reproduces ~0.92 of the probe’s accuracy; (iii) a 5% false-positive guarantee set on in-distribution benign prompts rises to 68–98% on diverse traffic; and (iv) a single 20-token suffix drops recall to near zero. Going beyond correlational "shortcut" diagnoses, we use concept erasure (LEACE) to causally remove a 3-dimensional register subspace: this cuts ~60 points of over-refusal (false flags on benign prompts) while leaving detection essentially intact (AUC drop ≤0.003), and the same subspace recurs across three architectures (verified against a shuffled-source-label null). Our recipe—register erasure plus deployment-time distribution-free calibration—achieves a guaranteed ≤5% false-positive rate on held-out diverse benign prompts at 0.945–0.961 recall, versus 0.18–0.29 for the un-erased probe. Cheap probing is a measurement instrument, deployable as a filter only via this recipe.

paper.title: EvoCurr: Self-evolving Curriculum with Behavior Code Generation for Complex Decision-making

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
Zhongguancun Academy and Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Beijing Zhongguancun Academy

paper.abstract: Complex decision-making often requires agents to progress through intermediate tasks rather than solve the final target directly. Existing LLM self-refinement methods typically iterate on a fixed target, while curriculum-learning methods often rely on hand-designed schedules, training-time optimization, or domain-specific difficulty metrics. To smooth the learning curve through adaptive curriculum design, we introduce EvoCurr, a general inference-time framework that co-evolves curricula and executable policies. A Designer proposes verifiable intermediate tasks from the latest accepted progress and recent failures, while a Solver generates or trains policies for these tasks. A task-policy pair is accepted only when it passes hard feasibility checks and reaches a specified performance threshold; meanwhile, an accepted-floor constraint preserves the latest verified checkpoint and prevents failed harder attempts from overwriting mastered behavior. We evaluate EvoCurr across code-as-policy and closed-loop MARL settings, using StarCraft II super-late-game micromanagement as our hardest stress test. EvoCurr demonstrates effective micromanagement across three LLM backbones without LLM parameter training. Improvements in additional experiments on Flatland, POGEMA, Overcooked, and LiveCodeBench Hard demonstrate the generality of EvoCurr.

paper.title: UniSurgBench: Benchmarking Surgical Video Understanding with Step-wise Reasoning and Workflow Aligned Evaluation

author.affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made substantial progress in medical visual understanding, but temporal reasoning and knowledge-guided reasoning over real surgical videos remain underexplored. Existing surgical benchmarks mainly focus on static frames, single procedures, or simple questions, which limits their ability to capture the complexity of real clinical workflows. To address this gap, we introduce UniSurgBench, a unified benchmark for open-ended surgical video reasoning, comprising 2,302 question-answer samples collected from real surgical videos spanning 45 procedures and 29 anatomical structures. Each sample is annotated with temporally grounded evidence and structured reasoning steps. We also propose SurgExpEval, a two-stage evaluation protocol that extracts structured reasoning components from free-form model outputs and jointly assesses answer accuracy, reasoning quality, and temporal grounding. Evaluations with 23 proprietary, open-source, and medical-related MLLMs show that MLLMs can produce clinically reasonable and causally coherent responses. However, they often fail to associate these responses with fine-grained visual evidence, highlighting evidence-level visual grounding as a key bottleneck for reliable surgical intelligence.

paper.title: How do World Models and Policies Compose in LLM Agents? A Joint Spectral and Behavioral Account

author.affiliation: Dartmouth College and Massachusetts Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: How do LLM agents come to both understand environments they act in and master tasks set within them? Through controlled experiments combining world-model training (next-state prediction) and policy training (reward maximization), we investigate this question. We dissect the resulting models through their additive parameter updates. Geometrically, we find effective world-model updates are low-rank and share an input-feature subspace with policy updates while writing to nearly orthogonal output directions, whether trained separately or sequentially. However, we find that, in projection interventions, the sequential update induces more robustness than separate policy RL when removing the world model’s leading input directions, suggesting that it has learned alternative input pathways. Behaviorally, we find the sequentially trained agent explores a wider range of states and actions. Based on this, we ask: does policy training preserve world knowledge as well as it could? We probe this with training-free merging built on the geometrically motivated input basis plus an online world-model loss during policy RL, and show both improve over the untreated baseline. Our findings suggest world knowledge and task-directed ability can be learned in geometrically complementary forms, and that future post-training pipelines should consider how best to engineer the interface between them.

paper.title: Bridging SLMs and LLMs: A Lightweight Framework for Knowledge Injection
paper.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) show immense potential in specialized domains, their adaptation is often hindered by limited access to domain-specific data and the high computational cost of model training. To address these challenges, we propose a lightweight knowledge injection framework. Instead of sharing raw data directly, our approach fine-tunes a small model and transfers its knowledge vectors to the target LLM for knowledge injection, thereby reducing data exposure and computational overhead. To mitigate the knowledge loss incurred during the injection process, we further introduce an iterative knowledge calibration strategy. We theoretically bound the error of the transformation matrix and prove the stability and linear convergence of the calibration process. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms parameter-efficient baselines and achieves performance comparable to full-parameter fine-tuning, while consuming only 28% of the GPU memory and 3% of the raw training data. Code is available at https://github.com/Yuhanleeee/LiSKI.

paper.title: QO-Bench: Diagnosing Query-Operator-Preserving Retrieval over Typed Event Tuples
paper.abstract: Many real-world questions over business, legal, and scientific corpora are natural-language versions of database-style queries over records latent in text. Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are optimized primarily for semantic relevance, but retrieving plausible passages does not guarantee correct query execution. We introduce QO-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for query-operator question answering over typed event tuples. The benchmark covers 22,984 news articles and 614 corporate events, with 18 query templates instantiating 785 questions. Each gold answer is deterministically computed from typed event tuples and scored by recall, with answers matched to the gold tuples by exact match rather than an LLM judge. This design enables operator-level diagnosis such as joins and intersection. We evaluate RAG, ReAct RAG, GraphRAG, and information-extraction-to-SQL under matched conditions, with a long-context oracle ceiling to isolate retrieval failure. A two-axis framework—index-time preservation versus query-time execution—predicts where each paradigm fails, and the results bear it out: systems retrieve relevant text but discard the typed values operators need, and the deployable paradigm ranking inverts across operators, with similarity retrieval leading on filter/project and extraction-to-SQL on intersection and counting. Even given the gold evidence, a long-context oracle stays far from saturated, so operator execution—not retrieval alone—is a core bottleneck that a stronger answer model does not remove. QO-Bench reframes the goal from passage relevance to query-operator-preserving retrieval. The benchmark, predictions, and code are released at https://github.com/ZHANG-MENGAO/qo-bench.

paper.title: Inside the LLM Word Factory
paper.abstract: Transformer language models process input provided as subword fragments, but natural language semantics usually rely on word-level concepts. Detokenization is the process where models reconcile these two facts, aggregating subwords into word-level representations through their computation. Prior work has found that this takes place mostly in early-to-middle layers, but so far the exact mechanics of the process have not been pinned down. We venture deep into detokenization using activation patching in controlled paired experiments that isolate the contribution of different model components, localizing English detokenization in Llama2-7B to a two-stage process at Layer 1. Attention transmits a token-specific signal from nonfinal subwords, using sequential relays if necessary, while the MLP composes it with the local embedding. This two-stage structure generalizes to twelve models from eight families, but the depth over which it takes place depends on the flavor of positional encoding: RoPE-based models detokenize over 1 to 5 layers, while learned-absolute models take 5 to 10. Finally, we provide a probe for determining the success of the detokenization process based on early-layer activations alone, performing at 0.94-0.97 AUROC depending on the amount of context.

paper.title: Evaluating Cross-lingual Knowledge Consistency in Code-Mixed vis-a-vis Indian Languages using IndicKLAR
paper.abstract: Large language models often exhibit a substantial gap between their performance in English and in lower-resourced languages on equivalent knowledge queries—a cross-lingual consistency issue that remains underexplored for Indian languages and their code-mixed counterparts. To study this gap, we introduce IndicKLAR, an Indic extension of the KLAR-CLC benchmark covering 18 of the 22 scheduled Indian languages. For 11 widely used language pairs, we additionally provide code-mixed variants. Both monolingual and code-mixed inputs verified by native speakers. This three-way alignment enables us to examine how knowledge recall consistency varies across English, code-mixed, and native Indian language inputs. Across nine open-weight models, we find that the accuracy gap between native-language and English inputs can reach \sim0.50, while code-mixed inputs substantially reduce this gap, bringing performance within \sim0.05 of English without any model-level intervention. Motivated by this finding, we evaluate several prompting strategies that differ in how explicitly language conversion is exposed: a two-stage translate-then-answer setup, a one-stage joint translation-and-answer prompt, and Translate-in-Thought (TinT)—a single-step strategy in which the model internally converts the input and outputs only the final answer. Across the native \rightarrow code-mixed \rightarrow English performance trajectory, we observe a consistent flip point—the transition from incorrect to correct prediction—between the native and code-mixed settings. Notably, this pattern holds both when the code-mixed representation is explicitly provided as input or when the model is prompted to convert internally using TinT.

paper.title: From Helpfulness to Toxic Proactivity: Diagnosing Behavioral Misalignment in LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: The enhanced capabilities of LLM-based agents bring an urgent need to address safety risks in planning and tool use. Due to the helpfulness–harmlessness trade-off in LLM alignment, agents typically also inherit the flaw of Over-Refusal, which is a passive failure mode. However, the proactive planning and action capabilities of agents introduce another emerging danger on the opposite side of this trade-off. We term this phenomenon **Toxic Proactivity**: an active failure mode in which an agent, driven by the optimization for Machiavellian helpfulness, prioritizes utility over ethics. Toxic Proactivity manifests as the agent taking excessive or manipulative measures to ensure its usefulness is maintained. Existing research pays little attention to identifying this behavior, as it often lacks the subtle context required for such strategies to unfold. To reveal this risk, we introduce a novel evaluation framework based on dilemma-driven interactions between dual models, enabling the simulation and analysis of agent behavior over multi-step behavioral trajectories. Through extensive experiments with multiple mainstream LLMs, we demonstrate that Toxic Proactivity is a widespread behavioral phenomenon and reveal two major tendencies: direct violation and strategic misalignment. We further present a systematic benchmark for evaluating Toxic Proactive behavior across contextual settings.

paper.title: THRD:A Training-Free Multi-Turn Defense Framework for Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a growing threat to LLMs by exploiting gradual escalation and cross-turn coordination. Many existing defenses either rely on costly retraining—often degrading utility—or analyze each turn independently, failing to capture risk accumulation across interactions. We observe that safety behavior in multi-turn interaction is trajectory-dependent: dialogue history reshapes the model’s conditioning context, making isolated turn-level evaluation insufficient. We present THRD, a training-free framework that explicitly models temporal risk accumulation for multi-turn jailbreak defense. THRD integrates four modules: a Turn-level Risk Assessor (TRA) for instantaneous risk estimation, a Historical Context Analyzer (HCA) for cross-turn intent escalation detection, a Response Evaluator (RE) for identifying facilitative outputs, and a Decision Module that combines these signals through a time-evolving scoring mechanism with attenuation-based modulation and trend-aware adjustment. Experiments against representative multi-turn attacks—including tree-search-based and multi-agent collaborative methods—across two target models show that THRD reduces ASR to 0.2–4.0% while preserving model utility within 1.5% degradation on MMLU and GSM8K. Ablation studies confirm non-redundant module contributions and consistent performance across both models. Over 70% of attacks require Turn 2 or later to detect, highlighting the importance of cross-turn information.

paper.title: Lost in Localization: Benchmarking Intralingual Cultural Adaptation in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Cultural adaptation, rewriting text for a different cultural audience, requires more than lexical substitution. A model must decide what to change, whether each replacement is locally valid, and whether it preserves the original item’s functional role. We formalize this as function-preserving cultural transfer and introduce a dataset, a taxonomy, and an evaluation framework constructed around that principle. CulturalAdapt-6K identifies 6,000 culturally rich texts in four discourse domains, while the Cultural Rewriting and Adaptation Failure Taxonomy (CRAFT) classifies errors into five categories. To mitigate the Anglocentric priors of current models, our proposed framework anchors each culturally significant item in a Wikidata-linked function frame, capturing its contextual role rather than surface denotation. Across 191,968 adaptations by eight instruction-tuned LLMs, we find that the models that substitute the most are not the ones that substitute best. High localization increases failure exposure, while conservative retention increases validity scores, yet both converge to the same overall functional quality. Current generative models can certainly dress text in a target culture’s vocabulary but ultimately cannot reliably preserve the contextual roles the vocabulary is meant to serve.

paper.title: Mining Legal Arguments in U.S. Corporate Case Law

author.affiliation: University of Maryland School of Law

paper.abstract: Legal argument mining supports passage classification, retrieval, and argument completion. This work introduces an expert-annotated dataset of 42 U.S. federal tax opinions on corporate reorganizations under I.R.C. §368. To our knowledge, it is the first expert-annotated, tree-structured argument corpus for this domain. Explicit spans receive one of five functional labels: *Rule*, *Analysis*, *Conclusion*, *Background Facts*, and *Procedural History*. Rule, Analysis, and Conclusion spans can be linked into directed support trees, while Background Facts and Procedural History serve a contextual function. The corpus provides span-based, sentence-based, flat, and tree-structured representations. Agreement analysis shows that functional node labels are more reliable than directed support edges and implicit intermediate conclusions. Directed-path agreement is stronger than direct-edge agreement, which indicates that broad reachability is more stable than exact local decomposition. Classification experiments show that functional labels are learnable under case-disjoint evaluation. Retrieval experiments show that supervised fine-tuning improves within-case retrieval. However, cross-case generalization remains weak. The dataset supports legal passage classification and provides a conservative benchmark for structured argument mining in U.S. federal tax case law.

paper.title: Patch the Distribution Mismatch: RL-Based Data Rewriting for Stable Downstream SFT
paper.abstract: Large language models are commonly adapted to downstream tasks through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but substantial distribution mismatch between downstream supervision and a model’s generation distribution can intensify catastrophic forgetting. Data rewriting offers a data-centric way to narrow this mismatch before SFT. Existing methods, however, typically sample rewrites from a prompt-induced conditional distribution, which need not align with the backbone’s natural question-answering generation distribution, and fixed templates can reduce output diversity. We formulate data rewriting as a policy-learning problem and train a lightweight LoRA rewriting policy with reinforcement learning. The policy optimizes question-answering-style distributional alignment and semantic diversity under a hard task-consistency gate, producing verified supervision for downstream SFT. Across three instruction-tuned backbones, the resulting models attain downstream gains broadly comparable to standard SFT while reducing degradation on non-downstream benchmarks in every evaluated setting. Additional experiments on logical reasoning and medical question answering provide preliminary evidence that a rewriting policy can be reused across domains for the same backbone.

paper.title: Conditional Accuracy Profiles: Diagnosing LLM Judges across Deployment Conditions

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Albany
State University of New York at Albany
State University of New York at Albany

paper.abstract: LLM-as-judge is now a standard tool for scalable evaluation, but judge performance is still often summarized by a single accuracy number. This aggregate view hides the deployment conditions under which a judge succeeds or fails. We introduce Conditional Accuracy Profiling(CAP), a post-hoc diagnostic framework that decomposes pairwise LLM-judge accuracy into eight conditions organized into content sensitivity, robustness, and rationale quality. CAP is benchmark-agnostic: it can be applied directly when a benchmark provides the required annotations, approximately through task-subset proxies, or through controlled augmentation when perturbation pairs can be generated. We instantiate CAP on seven LLM judges across six pairwise judging benchmarks, including judgerEva-Standard, a controlled testbed we created to support all eight conditions. CAP exposes profile differences hidden by aggregate accuracy: on judgerEva’s judge-independent Hard-Constructed subset, the two judges most sensitive to omitted qualifications rank in the bottom three of seven by overall accuracy, so omission sensitivity is not predicted by aggregate accuracy. Across benchmarks, Position Robustness shows the strongest rank stability (mean Spearman \bar{\rho}{=}0.87) but is itself fragile under JudgeBench-Pro adversarial stress, showing the largest mean accuracy drop among the shared conditions, though the dominant degradation channel varies by judge. Condition-level profiles provide a more actionable basis than aggregate accuracy for selecting LLM judges.

paper.title: Peak Information Flux: A Resource Rational Measure of Language Processing Difficulty
paper.abstract: A key goal in psycholinguistics is to quantify real-time language processing effort. A notable amount of literature links the processing effort to the amount of unexpected information carried by the new input. However, such theories fail to capture the dynamic evolution of comprehenders’ interpretation which may involve revision and operate under cognitive constraints. We propose peak information flux, a metric that better captures the cost of reanalysis through a resource rational framework. We characterize language comprehension as continuous belief updating under finite information processing capacity and that the maximal rate of belief change signals language processing effort. We validate the performance of peak information flux on Syntactic Ambiguity Processing and Natural Stories corpora featuring self-paced reading time and a variety of eye-tracking metrics representing different stages of lexical processing. Peak information flux predicts reading behavior across multiple measures and complements surprisal in measures associated with reinterpretation and recovery. Additional analyses reveal that garden-path constructions exhibit delayed and asymmetric information flux dynamics, supporting the hypothesis of a sustained probabilistic revision process. Our model provides an information-theoretic metric for language comprehension under resource constraints.

paper.title: KSAFE-MM: A Multimodal Safety Benchmark via Localized Contextualization for Korean Cultural Risks
