In long-form chatbot responses, factual errors can be subtle and embedded within mostly correct text.We develop a multi-perspective annotation study of medically relevant chatbot responses, combining first-pass annotation, LLM-as-a-Judge candidate discovery, and two forms of adjudication: domain-expert and evidence-based fact-checking. First-pass annotators frequently miss factual errors later validated by adjudicators. LLM-as-a-Judge improves candidate discovery, but is insufficient on its own: it misses factual errors that annotators catch. We also find disagreement among adjudicators, suggesting that adjudication over multiple candidate sources can improve benchmark completeness, but does not eliminate the need to apply judgment and expertise. Applied to an existing benchmark, this technique reveals a similar pattern of missed errors.Together, these results suggest that single-pass hallucination benchmarks achieve scale, but likely undercount errors. Multi-pass adjudication improves coverage, but benchmark results will still need to be interpreted in light of the judgment, expertise, and evidence used when deciding if an error is present.

paper.title: K-Humor: Dynamic Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Generation of Culturally Grounded Korean Jokes
paper.abstract: Humor generation is a challenging task in natural language generation that requires fluency, surprise, and cultural grounding. Although large language models (LLMs) show promise in English, little work addresses low-resource and culturally specific humor, such as in Korean. We propose **K-Humor**, a *dynamic multi-agent framework* for generating Korean jokes. Unlike static one-shot models, K-Humor integrates specialized agents for cultural awareness, audience simulation, editing, and punchline creation, which are coordinated through a dynamic iterative refinement loop. A human-data-grounded mechanism further guides the punchlines using authentic Korean jokes. Evaluation with automatic metrics, agent-internal diagnostics, LLM-as-a-judge, and human ratings shows that K-Humor consistently outperforms a single-prompt baseline and ablations in criteria such as fluency and cultural appropriateness. Although human-written jokes remain stronger overall, particularly on core creative dimensions, K-Humor demonstrates that dynamic, culturally grounded multi-agent systems can improve humor generation over standard LLM baselines in low-resource settings. Code is available at https://github.com/dxlabskku/k-humor.

paper.title: SWE-World: Building Software Engineering Agents in Docker-Free Environments
paper.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled software engineering agents to solve complex code modification tasks. However, most existing approaches rely on execution feedback from Docker-based environments, which require dependency-complete setup, program execution, and test validation, making agent training costly and difficult to scale. We propose SWE-World, a Docker-free framework that replaces containerized execution during downstream agent optimization with a learned surrogate environment. Trained on real agent-environment interaction traces, SWE-World predicts both step-level execution feedback and final test outcomes, preserving the standard agent-environment loop without repeatedly constructing or running Docker environments. This surrogate also enables test-time scaling (TTS) by scoring multiple candidate trajectories through simulated evaluation. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified show that SWE-World improves Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct from 6.2% to 52.0% with Docker-free SFT, 55.0% with Docker-free RL, and 68.2% with TTS. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SWE-World-2D1E.

paper.title: One-Token Rollout: Guiding Supervised Fine-Tuning of LLMs with Policy Gradient

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the predominant method for adapting large language models (LLMs), yet it often struggles with generalization compared to reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we posit that this performance disparity stems not just from the loss function, but from a more fundamental difference: SFT learns from a fixed, pre-collected dataset, whereas RL utilizes on-policy data sampled from the current policy. Building on this hypothesis, we introduce one-token rollout (OTR), a novel fine-tuning algorithm that guides SFT with the policy gradient method. OTR reframes the autoregressive learning process by treating each token generation as a single-step reinforcement learning trajectory. At each step, it performs a Monte Carlo ”rollout” by sampling multiple candidate tokens from the current policy’s distribution. The ground-truth token from the supervised data is then used to provide a reward signal to these samples. Guided by policy gradient, our algorithm repurposes static, off-policy supervised data into a dynamic, on-policy signal at the token level, capturing the generalization benefits of on-policy learning while bypassing the costly overhead of full sentence generation. Through extensive experiments on a diverse suite of challenging benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general domain reasoning, we demonstrate that OTR consistently outperforms standard SFT. Our findings establish OTR as a powerful and practical alternative for fine-tuning LLMs and provide compelling evidence that the on-policy nature of data is a critical driver of generalization, offering a promising new direction for fine-tuning LLMs.

paper.title: Towards Contextual Sensitive Data Detection
paper.abstract: The emergence of open data portals necessitates more attention to protecting sensitive data before datasets get published and used. To do so effectively, we observe the need to refine and broaden our definitions of sensitive data. We argue that the sensitivity of data depends on its context, and that this context should be considered in methods for assessing data sensitivity. To this end, we introduce a framework, termed ConSenser, for contextual sensitive data detection based on two aspects: 1) type contextualization, which considers the type of data values within the overall context of the dataset or document to assess their true sensitivity, and 2) domain contextualization, which assesses the sensitivity of data values informed by domain-specific information external to the dataset, such as geographic origin of a dataset. Experiments instrumented with language models confirm that type-contextualization significantly reduces the number of false positives for type-based sensitive data detection and reaches a recall of 94% compared to 63% with commonly used tools. Moreover, domain-contextualization through retrieval of sensitivity rules effectively grounds sensitive data detection in relevant context in non-standard data domains. A case study with humanitarian data experts also illustrates that context-grounded explanations provide useful guidance in manual data auditing processes. We open-source the code and annotated datasets at https://github.com/trl-lab/sensitive-data-detection.

paper.title: RING: Retrieval-Internalized Generation for Continual Large-Scale Knowledge Injection

author.affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality but adds latency and engineering overhead at serving time. We propose RING (Retrieval-Internalized Generation), a holistic paradigm spanning both architecture and training that injects large-scale external knowledge into a Mixture-of-Memory Experts and learns parametric search over this internal memory via reinforcement learning, removing the external retriever entirely. Training proceeds in three stages: continued pre-training injects new corpora into a Knowledge Expert via our novel Dual Causal Attention; supervised fine-tuning teaches a “search-then-answer” pattern; and reinforcement learning with hierarchical rewards optimizes the routing-and-search policy over the parametric memory. Unlike prior parametric injection methods that pair internal memory with a fixed or rule-based retriever, RING learns its retrieval policy directly from task signals. We further frame RING theoretically as a search-free approximation to the classical RAG objective. To evaluate large-scale injection of genuinely new knowledge without test-time leakage, we further construct News-2025, a benchmark built from news strictly post-dating the base LLM’s pretraining cutoff. RING matches or surpasses both search-based RAG and parametric injection baselines in accuracy and efficiency.

paper.title: Exemplar Choice Matters for Morphological Reasoning: Model Confidence Vs Exemplar Similarity
paper.abstract: LLMs have shown impressive linguistic competencies in a wide range of NLP tasks, yet morphological generalization remains challenging. Models can benefit from in-context learning, where the choice of few-shot examples significantly influences the outcome. We probe LLMs’ morphological capabilities by assessing how two targeted in-context exemplar selection strategies, Iterative Confidence-Based Exemplar Selection (i-CES) and Similarity-Based Exemplar Selection (SES), influence the model’s ability for inflectional and derivational modeling across multiple languages. Our experiments with LLaMA 3.3-70B-instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct models indicate that SES is more effective for accessing latent linguistic knowledge, showing a substantial performance advantage over i-CES in both derivational and inflectional tasks. In contrast, i-CES offers no clear advantage over random sampling.

paper.title: LLM generation novelty through the lens of semantic similarity

author.affiliation: Centre for Integrative Neuroscience, AG Bethge
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Parameter Lab

paper.abstract: Generation novelty is a key indicator of an LLM’s ability to generalize, yet measuring it against full pretraining corpora is computationally challenging. Existing evaluations often rely on lexical overlap, failing to detect paraphrased text, or do not consider the full pretraining corpus. We frame novelty as a semantic retrieval problem. This framing enables us to address novelty with modern embedding and indexing pipelines, allowing for efficient analysis at pre-training scale. Specifically, we propose a three-stage framework that retrieves semantically similar samples, reranks them at varying subsequence lengths, and calibrates scores using a human novelty reference for interpretability. We apply this framework to the SmolLM model family and report three key findings: (1) models draw on pretraining data across much longer sequences than previously reported; (2) some task domains systematically promote or suppress generation novelty; and (3) instruction tuning not only alters style but also increases novelty. These results highlight the value of semantic novelty analysis for studying generalization. To support reproducibility and further research, we release \sim 20 TB of corpus chunks and index artifacts upon acceptance.

paper.title: Transferring Math Reasoning Abilities from LLMs to MLLMs via Causal-Aware Model Merging

author.affiliation: Duke Kunshan University and Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University

paper.abstract: To build a math MLLM, current research efforts predominantly rely on elaborate training schemes or high-quality multi-modal math reasoning data. On the other hand, model merging has attracted much attention recently due to its low-cost and tune-free property, which has shown great potential for constructing math MLLM. However, most recent attempts either assume all parameters are task-relevant or adopt a less interpretable parameter selection strategy, thus merging parameters on a coarse granularity, leading to limited or even degrading performance. In this paper, we propose a causal-analysis–guided parameter merging framework, which identifies the math reasoning-related parameters in a finer granularity and interpretable manner, then merges the math LLMs with MLLM. Specifically, we first construct targeted arithmetic and logical tasks, generate reference and counterfactual samples, and then apply intervention-based causal attribution to localize parameters that are causally responsible for math reasoning. Once we identify the crucial reasoning parameters in the math LLM that exhibit higher causal effects, we can more precisely align and merge only the corresponding parameters from the math LLM into the base MLLM. The procedure is tuning-free and enhances both math reasoning and general reasoning abilities. Experimental results of three model families on four math reasoning benchmarks and two general reasoning benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paper.title: Sparse Long Memory and Transition Bottlenecks Shape Positional Recall in Mamba Language Models

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Mamba language models process sequences recurrently, but recurrent processing does not imply that all tokens are retained equally. We study this gap using structured recall tasks that expose primacy, recency, and lost-in-the-middle behavior. Our results suggest that Mamba uses two functional memory regimes: a short-lived state that supports recency, and a sparse long-lived channel subspace that preserves selected early inputs. Targeted interventions on this long-memory subspace selectively degrade early recall and transfer to long-context QA and summarization, indicating that the same channels support real long-context use. We then ask why middle items are forgotten despite being processed sequentially. We find that the central failure is a short-to-long memory transition bottleneck: middle items are no longer recent enough for short memory, but are often not promoted into the sparse long-lived subspace. Repeated input structure strengthens this bottleneck by changing the input-dependent discretization dynamics. These findings provide a mechanistic account of Mamba’s U-shaped recall curve as the interaction between long memory, short memory, and a fragile transition between them.

paper.title: TCHV: Type-Conditioned Hypothesis Verification for Multimodal Named Entity Recognition

author.affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences and School of Cyber Security, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) uses supplementary images to resolve ambiguity in entity mentions in noisy, short-form social-media text. Prevailing approaches typically fuse text with visually aligned features, but such cues often lack sufficient discriminative power and may support conflicting entity-type hypotheses. To address this issue, we propose TCHV, a lightweight framework grounded in a type-conditioned hypothesis-verification perspective. By formulating each span-type pair as a distinct hypothesis during inference, TCHV predicts the latent feature evidence expected under each hypothesis and validates it against observed multimodal representations through bidirectional text-image matching, using a visual relevance gate to suppress unin- formative images. Verification scores serve as surrogate evidence statistics; TCHV improves over established non-VLLM multimodal baselines on Twitter-2015/2017, and TCHV† leads the compared VLLM-based methods on Twitter-2017. Extensions demonstrate applicability to grounded and fine-grained settings. Code: https://github.com/ hanfeiyu703/ImaginE.git.

paper.title: Toward Cultural Alignment: Human-Centered Evaluation of Multimodal AI Stories Across Five African Communities
paper.abstract: In this paper, we examine how well AI-generated multimodal stories align with the lived practices, relationships, language, values, and visual expectations of the communities they represent. We conduct a community-grounded mixed-methods evaluation with 19 culture representatives across five African communities, combining quantitative annotations with qualitative focus group discussions. We find that cultural alignment depends not simply on recognizable cultural markers, but on how those markers fit social, linguistic, procedural, and visual context. From these evaluations, we develop a taxonomy of cultural alignment comprising five broader cultural marker categories and eight recurring mechanisms of misalignment. We additionally evaluate five multimodal LLM judges to examine whether automated evaluation can approximate community-grounded judgments at scale. Judge reliability and score calibration vary substantially across communities, with no single judge performing consistently across all five settings. These findings motivate community-calibrated evaluation pipelines in which automated judges are validated against community judgments to determine where they can be trusted and where human review remains necessary.

paper.title: Pivot Gradient Scaling: Reducing Dwell Time to Stabilize Extreme Low-Bit Quantization-aware Training

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Qualcomm Inc, QualComm

paper.abstract: Extreme low-bit quantization-aware training (QAT) is often unstable due to synchronized bin transitions, which can trigger catastrophic loss spikes. While prior works rely on scale-side controls to mitigate this fragility, we demonstrate that restricting pivot movement alone is insufficient. Instead, we identify a critical weight-side state governing low-bit QAT stability: pivot-proximal residence, where latent weights persistently linger near quantization pivots. We formalize this duration as dwell time and show that long dwell times accumulate a large, vulnerable population of weights prone to synchronized mass flips. To resolve this vulnerability, we propose Pivot Gradient Scaling (PGS) as a principled modification to the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) that leaves the forward pass intact and selectively amplifies latent-weight gradients within a localized pivot band. Crucially, we provide a mathematical guarantee proving that this sign-preserving amplification increases pivot-proximal mobility and systematically shortens expected dwell time under both SGD and Adam. Exhaustive empirical evaluations across Llama 3.2 and Qwen3 model families under full-training regimes up to 30 billion tokens demonstrate that PGS structurally stabilizes optimization, attenuates transition bursts, and delivers substantial downstream accuracy gains.

paper.title: The Emergence of Relevance Through Axiomatic Attention Patterns During LoRA Fine-Tuning

author.affiliation: Hokkaido University, Tokyo Institute of Technology and University of Massachusetts, Amherst

paper.abstract: LoRA fine-tuning is standard for adapting LLMs to reranking, but it remains unclear where in the network task-specific relevance behavior is learned and what attention-level changes accompany that learning. Through ablation and attention experiments, we identify where LoRA attention updates to RankLLaMA improve performance and whether those gains coincide with interpretable relevance-oriented attention patterns such as lexical matching, rarity sensitivity, and query-document interaction. We find that given LoRA fine-tuned MLPs throughout the network, restricting LoRA attention updates to a compact mid-network region is sufficient for recovering over half of the performance gained by applying LoRA to all attention layers, and that omitting attention fine-tuning in this region hurts performance more than elsewhere in the network. Additionally, we show that regions where applying LoRA affects performance the most overlap with regions where fine-tuning increased attention to axiomatic IR features. Rarity sensitivity, document-query interaction, and several compositional features are highly correlated with gains in ranking performance. Our results support an interpretable, correlational account of how relevance-oriented behavior emerges during LoRA fine-tuning and point toward improved strategies for adapting rerankers.

paper.title: Probe and Steer: Localizing and Mitigating Position Bias in Pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to costly human evaluation. However, LLM judges suffer from position bias in pairwise evaluation: the judge systematically favors the first or second candidate regardless of content, forcing practitioners to perform bidirectional evaluation at twice the inference cost. We propose Probe-and-Steer (PaS), a probe-localized, single-layer steering method for mitigating position bias. PaS localizes the bias-critical layer via a layer-wise logit-difference probe and trains a single residual-stream steering vector at that layer under a multi-objective loss, requiring minimal labeled data while keeping the LLM fully frozen. Through layer-wise probing across multiple model families, we uncover three qualitatively distinct bias-distribution patterns and delineate a clear applicability boundary for residual-stream steering. Experiments on an XSum-based dataset with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that PaS delivers the largest gains among all compared methods, improving consistency by 22.9 pp and accuracy by 16.4 pp while shrinking positional asymmetry by 33\times (from 0.471 to 0.014), adding the lowest inference overhead at 4%.

paper.title: PaveDSL: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Plan Specification and Verification for Multi-Agent Code Generation
paper.abstract: Recent multi-agent code generation frameworks often verify natural-language plans by simulating their behavior on test cases before code generation. However, such verification remains unreliable because model hallucination may cause flawed plans to be incorrectly accepted. Inspired by neuro-symbolic reasoning, we propose PaveDSL, which transforms natural-language plans into structured designs expressed in a domain-specific language. Based on this structured representation, PaveDSL combines symbolic checks with neural inference to examine plans before code generation. Specifically, PaveDSL applies two complementary verifiers in parallel. The deterministic symbolic verifier checks structural constraints without invoking an LLM, while the agent verifier performs graph-guided semantic reasoning over the structured design. If verification fails, a repair agent localizes errors and revises the design before code generation. Experiments on multiple benchmarks with different LLMs show that PaveDSL consistently improves the performance of baseline code generation methods.

paper.title: LLMTrace: A Corpus for Classification and Fine-Grained Localization of AI-Written Text
paper.abstract: The widespread use of human-like text from Large Language Models (LLMs) necessitates the development of robust detection systems. However, progress is limited by a critical lack of suitable training data; existing datasets are often generated with outdated models, are predominantly in English, and fail to address the increasingly common scenario of mixed human-AI authorship. Crucially, while some datasets address mixed authorship, none provide the character-level annotations required for the precise localization of AI-generated segments within a text. To address these gaps, we introduce LLMTrace, a new large-scale, bilingual (English and Russian) corpus for AI-generated text detection. Constructed using a diverse range of modern proprietary and open-source LLMs, our dataset is designed to support two key tasks: traditional full-text binary classification (human vs. AI) and AI-generated interval detection, facilitated by character-level annotations. We believe LLMTrace will serve as a vital resource for training and evaluating the next generation of more nuanced and practical AI detection models.

paper.title: GATE: General Arabic Text Embedding for Enhanced Semantic Textual Similarity with Matryoshka Representation Learning and Hybrid Loss Training
paper.abstract: Semantic textual similarity (STS) is central to retrieval, clustering, and semantic understanding, yet Arabic remains underserved by high-quality sentence-embedding models and evaluation resources. We introduce GATE, a compact family of Arabic sentence embedding models and a controlled study of Arabic-specific backbones, contrastive Matryoshka Representation Learning, dimensional truncation, and hybrid STS-NLI supervision. We evaluate the resulting models across Arabic semantic similarity, NLI, pair classification, sentence classification, clustering, retrieval, reranking, and dialectal semantic relatedness, against strong multilingual baselines including BGE-M3, Arctic-Embed-v2, and Qwen3-Embedding. Despite their 135M-parameter scale, GATE-family models are competitive with substantially larger multilingual encoders and achieve strong results on several native-Arabic semantic tasks. A three-annotator audit further finds high Arabic surface adequacy and 84.2% majority relation preservation for the translated supervision. The released checkpoints, data resources, and experimental artifacts support reproducible Arabic embedding research.

paper.title: Kwai Summary Attention
paper.abstract: Long-context capability has become increasingly critical for next-generation Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the quadratic time complexity of standard softmax attention introduces substantial computation and memory overhead as sequence length grows, limiting the scalability of LLMs in long-context scenarios. Beyond existing approaches such as linear recurrent architectures and KV-cache compression methods, we propose Kwai Summary Attention (KSA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces sequence modeling cost by compressing historical contexts into learnable summary tokens. Specifically, summary tokens are periodically inserted into the input sequence and interleaved with text tokens, partitioning the sequence into distinct chunks while enabling text tokens and summary tokens to operate under different attention scopes. This design preserves dense local expressiveness through full attention among neighboring text tokens, while modeling long-range dependencies efficiently via summary tokens. Empirical results demonstrate that hybrid-KSA consistently outperforms existing hybrid attention variants in long-context modeling. Moreover, KSA is fully orthogonal to GQA and MLA during inference, and combining KSA with these methods achieves up to 8x KV-cache compression while preserving model performance.

paper.title: SaToMe: Salience-Driven Token Merging for Omni-Capable Diffusion MLLMs
paper.abstract: Omni-capable Diffusion multimodal large language models (Diffusion MLLMs) unify text-to-image (T2I) generation and image-to-text (I2T) understanding within one backbone, but at substantial cost on both fronts: visual tokens far outnumber surrounding text, and for T2I this per-step cost compounds across many denoising steps. Token merging has been studied separately in adjacent fields, yet training-free acceleration spanning T2I+I2T in one omni-capable Diffusion MLLM remains limited. We present SaToMe, a training-free token-merging method built around a local-deviation operator that we interpret as measuring local representational uniqueness. The denoising trajectory exposes two natural inputs to this operator: the state h and the update direction Δh. Their spreads behave very differently along the trajectory: state-salience spread is dynamic and identifies the active merging window, while update-salience masks are window-stable and serve as a single-step protection signal for cell-level structural content. T2I uses both signals; I2T, with no temporal axis, instantiates the same uniqueness criterion on the state alone, producing a single-pass additive merge. The same I2T form transfers directly to a separate I2T-only Diffusion MLLM with a different visual representation, supporting its applicability across these visual representations. SaToMe attains +20.14% T2I wall-clock speedup on LLaDA-o at 68% visual-token retention while largely preserving reported generation quality, +35.5% I2T wall-clock speedup on LLaDA-o, and +27.5% I2T speedup on LaViDa.

paper.title: Skill Retrieval Augmentation for Agentic AI
paper.abstract: Agentic AI systems powered by large language models are increasingly expected to solve capability-intensive tasks by using reusable external skills, which package instructions, tool-use procedures, executable code, and auxiliary resources. However, mainstream skill-based systems typically assume that available skills can be directly placed in the prompt. As skill libraries grow, this assumption becomes impractical: large corpora cannot be fully exposed to the model, while excessive candidate exposure can distract the agent and degrade skill selection. Therefore, scalable skill augmentation requires retrieving a small set of task-relevant skills from a large corpus before incorporating them into the agent’s context. We formulate this paradigm as Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA), where agents dynamically retrieve, incorporate, and apply reusable skills from large external corpora on demand. To systematically study SRA, we introduce SRA-Bench, which enables decomposed evaluation across three stages: skill retrieval, skill incorporation, and skill application. SRA-Bench contains 5,400 capability-intensive instances from six domains, 636 manually constructed gold skills, and a corpus of 26,262 skills. Experiments across multiple LLM and skill-use strategies show that SRA can consistently improve agent performance, but current agents struggle to realize this promise in practical pipelines. Specifically, they remain sensitive to distractor skills, lack need-aware skill loading, and often fail to translate relevant skills into correct task execution. Together, these results establish SRA as a distinct research problem and provide a foundation for developing scalable skill-augmented agents.

paper.title: Beyond Ranking: Role-Specific Signals for Token-Budgeted SFT Data Selection

author.affiliation: Tohoku University, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a core stage in post-training general-purpose language models, but modern SFT training corpora are often large, heterogeneous mixtures, making data selection important under fixed token budgets. Simple ranking approaches can be informative yet insufficient: ranking alone does not determine how to allocate a fixed token budget across examples. We study the role-specific use of likelihood-derived signals for token-budgeted subset construction. An external instruction-tuned reference model computes response-side negative log-likelihood scores to rank training examples. We then combine this ranking with base model likelihood filtering to restrict the candidate region and response-side cosine filtering to reduce redundancy in the selected subset. In the OLMo fine-tuning setting studied here, ranking examples only by reference-model likelihood underperforms the random baseline, whereas the same ranking becomes more effective when combined with base model likelihood filtering and cosine-based redundancy control. Our results support viewing token-budgeted SFT data selection as a budget-allocation problem rather than only as an example-ranking problem.

paper.title: Influence Guided Sampling for Domain Adaptation of Text Retrievers
paper.abstract: General-purpose open-domain dense retrieval systems are usually trained with a large, eclectic mix of corpora and search tasks. How should these diverse corpora and tasks be sampled for training? Conventional approaches sample them uniformly, proportional to their instance population sizes, or depend on human-level expert supervision. It is well known that the training data sampling strategy can greatly impact model performance. However, how to find the optimal strategy has not been adequately studied in the context of embedding models. We propose **Inf-DDS**, a novel reinforcement learning–driven sampling framework that adaptively reweighs training datasets guided by influence-based reward signals and is much more lightweight w.r.t. GPU consumption. Our technique iteratively refines the sampling policy, prioritizing datasets that maximize model performance on a target development set. We evaluate the efficacy of our sampling strategy on a wide range of text retrieval tasks, demonstrating strong improvements in retrieval performance and better adaptation compared to existing gradient-based sampling methods, while also being 1.5\text{—}4\times cheaper in GPU compute. Our sampling strategy achieves a \mathbf{5.03} absolute NDCG@10 improvement while training the multilingual bge-m3 model and an absolute NDCG@10 improvement of \mathbf{0.94} while training all-MiniLM-L6-v2, even when starting from expert-assigned weights on a large pool of training datasets.

paper.title: Beyond the Explicit: A Bilingual Dataset for Dehumanization Detection in Social Media

author.affiliation: GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences
Fondazione Bruno Kessler and Universidad de Santiago de Compostela

paper.abstract: Digital dehumanization, although a critical issue, remains largely overlooked within the field of computational linguistics and Natural Language Processing (NLP). To our best knowledge, this work presents the most comprehensive annotated bi-lingual dataset on dehumanization, with almost 16.000 instances (44% dehumanizing) that exists today and can serve as both a training resource for machine learning models and a benchmark for evaluating future dehumanization detection techniques. Our comparison of 15 methods shows that traditional hate speech detection approaches perform poorly on dehumanization detection, particularly for implicit forms. By leveraging our dataset in few-shot and fine-tuning settings, LLMs achieve comparable performance on implicit and explicit dehumanization and substantially outperform zero-shot baselines, with average gains of 39% and 65%, respectively. However, detection accuracy remains slightly lower for mechanistic than for animalistic dehumanization, the latter being the dominant focus of prior work.

paper.title: Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning with On-Policy Intrinsic Knowledge Boundary Enhancement

author.affiliation: Chinese University of Hong Kong, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective for training LLM-based agents with external tool-use capabilities. However, we identify that agentic RL training induces increasing redundant tool calls and blurs the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary, where the model fails to distinguish when tools are needed versus when parametric knowledge suffices. Existing solutions based on reward shaping create coarse-grained optimization targets that tend to incentivize indiscriminate tool-call suppression, leading to reward hacking. In this paper, we propose **AKBE** (**A**gentic **K**nowledge **B**oundary **E**nhancement), an on-policy method that dynamically probes the model’s intrinsic knowledge boundary through dual-path (with-tool and no-tool) rollouts during training. We define the knowledge boundary as the per-instance determination of whether tools are required and the minimum tool calls necessary. By comparing correctness across paths, AKBE categorizes trajectories and constructs targeted supervisory signals that guide efficient tool-use patterns for each question. These signals are integrated seamlessly into the agentic RL training loop. Experiments on seven QA benchmarks demonstrate that AKBE improves task accuracy by on average +1.85 and reduces tool calls by 18% over standard agentic RL, yielding 25% higher tool productivity without any accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Further analysis suggests its plug-and-play compatibility across different RL algorithms and the mechanism of each signal category.

paper.title: Values Are Not Enough: Situational Modifiers Shape Moral Decisions in LLMs and Humans
paper.abstract: Personal values alone cannot fully explain moral decisions. They are often treated as the main driver of moral choice, yet situational pressures can still shift actions when values are fixed. To study this effect, we introduce VISDA (Value-Informed Scenario-Driven Actions), a dataset of 80 binary moral scenarios across various themes. Keeping value profiles constant, we evaluate three open-weight LLMs (Gemma 4 31B, Qwen 2.5 32B, LLaMA 3.1 8B), a utility-based mathematical baseline over 95 Schwartz profiles, and humans for their decisions under modifiers. Each scenario is augmented with eight situational modifier axes designed to capture contextual pressures on decision-making. LLMs reverse decisions (flips) less frequently (2.03%-8.92%), with larger models showing greater sensitivity. In LLMs, authority and self-preservation modifiers drive most flips and remain statistically significant. Humans showed a pooled shift (12.36%) in their decisions. Humans prioritized stakes and affective modifiers, while LLMs overweight personal-cost modifiers. This work reveals axis-level misalignment between human and LLM sensitivity to situational moral factors.

paper.title: DisasterLex: An Expert Concept-to-Schema Knowledge Graph for Geospatial Reasoning in Disaster Analytics
paper.abstract: Disasters are inevitable and increasingly costly, and effective response depends on querying structured tabular data: precise, information-dense records of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and lifeline infrastructure that underpin disaster management. Current text-to-SQL methods enable natural-language access to such tables but transfer poorly to the disaster domain, where queries span heterogeneous geospatial schemas and require reasoning over causal relations. We introduce DisasterLex, a knowledge-graph-mediated framework that inserts an Expert Knowledge Graph (EKG) of curated concepts and typed causal edges between the user query and the database, bridged to schema by concept-to-table links. The orchestration runs four stages (identifying query entities, routing to the operational domain, planning over causal edges, and grounding the SQL), restricting the schema passed to the model at each step. We instantiate it on a disaster-analytics database (36 geospatial tables, 150 columns) with an EKG of 107 concepts, 117 causal edges, and 52 concept-to-schema links, evaluated on a 75-query test set. On all seven base models spanning proprietary and open-weight families, DisasterLex beats four state-of-the-art baselines (LightRAG, HippoRAG 2, ReFoRCE, CHESS) by 1.4\times to 2.75\times, with absolute scores of 1.65 to 3.56 (of 5.0). Error analysis shows baseline failures cluster in routing and multi-table SQL composition, the operations our orchestration explicitly addresses. Code, data, and the EKG artifact are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DisasterLex-3D64.

paper.title: Mitigating New-Tail Collapse in Long-Tailed Class-Incremental Learning with CLIP
paper.abstract: Pre-trained vision–language models such as CLIP provide strong priors for class-incremental learning (CIL), yet they degrade sharply under long-tailed class streams. We show that this degradation is not merely a byproduct of forgetting: in frozen-CLIP long-tailed CIL, newly introduced tail classes are disproportionately absorbed into previously learned old classes, a boundary-level failure we call new-tail collapse. We diagnose this failure with an old-new margin and analyze it through a boundary-risk view, where CLIP semantic overlap, sparse tail supervision, and old-class expansion jointly increase old-dominant violations. Motivated by this view, we propose Smooth Boundary-Risk Loss (SBRL), which estimates effective old rivals from CLIP’s vision-language geometry and suppresses their smooth old-side pressure against new-tail samples. MC-SMERG further consolidates task-wise adapters into a single efficient model. Across ImageNetSubset-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and Food101-LT, our method consistently outperforms strong CLIP-based CIL baselines and substantially reduces boundary violations in high-similarity, low-shot regimes.

paper.title: Where Do Apparent LLM Clinical Triage Failures Arise? Localizing the Multiple-Choice Format Effect
paper.abstract: LLM evaluations using clinician-authored triage vignettes have reported substantial under-triage under constrained multiple-choice testing. Yet model performance on the same clinical cases can change when responses are generated in free text. We test whether this format effect appears while the case is processed or when clinical information is mapped to the final answer. Using sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features in Gemma 3 4B/12B IT and Qwen3-8B, we find that medical features fire on the shared clinical narrative under both formats but are inactive at the multiple-choice decision token. Emergency-tier information is linearly decodable from vignette representations with ROC-AUC 0.95–1.00 under both formats, with no significant format difference, but is attenuated at the decision token. Natural-language autoencoder verbalization and top-feature characterization associate that token with the multiple-choice scaffold. In a direct linear projection, the identified medical features contribute zero, whereas scaffold-peaking features account for over 91% of unsigned attribution in both Gemma models. Behaviorally, whether multiple choice improves or worsens performance depends on the model. Option-order shuffles rule out simple positional bias, and cases that differ between formats are usually one severity tier apart. Together, these findings place the strongest correlates of the format effect at answer selection while leaving open whether unmeasured clinical representations also differ.

paper.title: Beyond Binary: Turning Partial Success into Dense Verifiable Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Code Generation

author.affiliation: Institute of Artificial Intelligence (TeleAI), China Telecom
Insitute of Artificial Intelligence, China Telecom
China Telecom and Northwestern Polytechnical University

paper.abstract: Effective reward design is a central challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for code generation. Mainstream test-suite-level outcome rewards enforce functional correctness but induce sparsity, while external Reward Models (RMs) provide dense supervision at the cost of misalignment and additional overhead. Since code evaluation naturally yields multiple test-case-level outcomes, partial success—passing a subset of test cases—offers an intrinsic, verifiable source of dense supervision. In this paper, we propose VeRPO (Verifiable Dense Reward Policy Optimization), an RL framework that systematically turns verifiable partial success into reliable dense rewards. We analyze partial-success rewards using a weighted sum formulation, theoretically identifying a critical cardinality bias that causes policy updates to disproportionately favor gains from easy-test successes over progress on frontier tests. Based on this, VeRPO introduces a dynamic, density-calibrated local reward that explicitly corrects this bias and provides robust dense supervision from partial success. To enhance alignment with end-to-end functional correctness, VeRPO further integrates the local dense reward with global execution outcomes. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and settings demonstrate that VeRPO outperforms outcome-driven and RM-based baselines, achieving up to +8.83 pass@1 gain with negligible time cost (< 0.02%) and zero GPU memory overhead.

paper.title: Binned Relative Policy Optimization towards Efficient Thinking of VLMs

author.affiliation: OPPO Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Co., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Recent VLMs improve multimodal reasoning by generating explicit chains of thought, but often overthink with redundant reasoning. Although conventional length penalties mitigate this redundancy, they rely on coarse global rewards that fail to discern intermediate process quality or adapt to task complexity. To address this dilemma, we propose Binned Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO), a training-efficient framework that enables non-trivial process-level evaluation without introducing costly process reward models. Specifically, BRPO leverages high entropy lexical markers to segment reasoning trajectories into discrete intermediate prefixes, evaluating their problem-solving potential through forced answer completions. Building on this, we introduce Bin Normalization along with a length-aware adjustment to map prefixes into process bins, dynamically calibrating rewards and regulating length constraints based on reasoning stages and visual complexity. Experiments on six multimodal math benchmarks show that our method improves both accuracy and efficiency: on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it raises average accuracy from 47.8% to 53.6% while reducing the average response length by 39.0%.

paper.title: S2J: Bridging the Gap Between Solving and Judging Ability in Generative Reward Models
paper.abstract: With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), generative reward models (GRMs) have been widely adopted for reward modeling and evaluation. Previous studies have primarily focused on training specialized GRMs by optimizing them on preference datasets with the judgment correctness as supervision. While it’s widely accepted that GRMs with stronger problem-solving capabilities typically exhibit superior judgment abilities, we first identify a significant solve-to-judge gap when examining individual queries. Specifically, the solve-to-judge gap refers to the phenomenon where GRMs struggle to make correct judgments on some queries (14%-37%), despite being fully capable of solving them. In this paper, we propose the Solve-to-Judge (S2J) approach to address this problem. Specifically, S2J simultaneously leverages both the solving and judging capabilities on a single GRM’s output for supervision, explicitly linking the GRM’s problem-solving and evaluation abilities during model optimization, thereby narrowing the gap. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that S2J effectively reduces the solve-to-judge gap by 16.2%, thereby enhancing the model’s judgment performance by 5.8%. Notably, S2J achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among GRMs built on the same base model while utilizing a significantly smaller training dataset.

paper.title: Progressive Behavioral Drift through Compression Valleys in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: We show that attention sinks and compression valleys create a vulnerable region in decoder-only Transformers, where small activation perturbations can be amplified through the autoregressive trajectory. Based on this, we propose Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-space attack that anchors perturbations at the beginning-of-sequence token and adaptively reinforces them at sensitive layers and tokens. Instead of forcing an abrupt behavioral change, SSS induces a staged drift, making outputs gradually shift toward the target behavior while remaining fluent and benign-looking in early generations. Across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS achieves high attack success, preserves coherence, and causes negligible degradation to general capabilities. These results show that attention sinks and compression valleys are not merely mechanistic features; rather, they expose exploitable amplification mechanisms that can be treated as hidden-state weaknesses for activation-space attacks in white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

paper.title: Towards Faithful and Controllable Personalization via Critique-Post-Edit Reinforcement Learning

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning has driven the largest post-training gains on tasks with verifiable rewards, such as code and math. Extending this success to subjective tasks remains difficult: good responses must satisfy multiple soft criteria simultaneously, and no scalar reward can indicate which aspect of a response should improve. Personalization is a clear instance of this. A personalized response must balance helpfulness, user-specific relevance, and naturalness, yet standard verifiers cannot localize which specific dimension needs improvement. In this regime, supervised fine-tuning quickly saturates, and PPO with Bradley-Terry reward models is prone to reward hacking, especially via length bias, producing verbose or superficially personalized responses. We propose Critique-Post-Edit, an RL framework that combines (1) a personalized Generative Reward Model (GRM) producing multi-dimensional scores and natural-language critiques, and (2) a critique-guided editing step that turns feedback into nearby alternative responses for policy learning. The reward signal stays scalar; our contribution is to use personalized critiques to construct more informative local alternatives (responses close to the on-policy rollout in edit distance) during training. Under length-controlled evaluation, Critique-Post-Edit improves over PPO by 11.0 and 11.6 win-rate points on Qwen2.5-7B and 14B models, respectively. Notably, the 14B model matches or outperforms GPT-4.1 on the evaluated benchmarks. A static mechanism study further shows that critique-guided edits stay more local than extra rollouts and shift scores more favorably than generic rewrites. All of our experiments are on personalization; systematic evaluation on other subjective tasks is left to future work.

paper.title: TopoCurate: Modeling Interaction Topology for Tool-Use Agent Training
paper.abstract: Training tool-use agents typically relies on outcome-based filtering: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on successful trajectories and Reinforcement Learning (RL) on pass-rate-selected tasks. However, this paradigm ignores interaction dynamics—successful trajectories may lack error recovery or exhibit redundancy, while pass rates fail to distinguish structurally informative tasks from trivial ones. To bridge this gap, we propose TopoCurate, an interaction-aware framework that shifts the paradigm from linear outcome filtering to topological interaction modeling. By projecting multi-trial rollouts into a unified semantic quotient topology within the same task, we construct a structured manifold that explicitly captures the divergence between success and failure pathways across tool invocations and environmental responses. Leveraging this representation, we introduce a dual-selection mechanism: for SFT, we prioritize trajectories demonstrating reflective recovery, semantic efficiency, and strategic diversity to mitigate covariate shift and mode collapse; for RL, we select tasks with high error branch ratios and strategic heterogeneity, maximizing gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio to address vanishing signals in sparse-reward settings. Evaluations on BFCLv3 and Tau2 Bench show that TopoCurate achieves consistent gains of 4.2% (SFT) and 6.9% (RL) over state-of-the-art baselines.

paper.title: Selective Knowledge Edit Reversal via Gated Singular Vector Shrinkage

author.affiliation: Zhongguancun Laboratory, Beijing, P.R.China. and Beihang University
The Insititute of Advanced Computing Technology, Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Zhongguancun Laboratory and Beihang University

paper.abstract: Knowledge editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in large language models. However, malicious edits may introduce safety risks, making it necessary to reverse undesirable editing effects. Existing reversal methods for parameter-modifying edits mainly focus on global removal, which may also erase beneficial edits that should be preserved. In this paper, we study selective reversal of edited knowledge, where the goal is to reverse targeted edited facts while preserving the remaining edited facts. Based on the hypothesis that each edit is sparsely encoded within the dominant subspace of the edited matrix, we propose a spectral-based reversal framework that locates edit-sensitive components within the dominant singular subspace of edited weights. Experiments across multiple settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reversing selected edits while preserving unrelated edited facts. These results suggest that different edits are sparsely encoded within dominant singular components and can be separable when the number of edits is moderate, making selective spectral reversal a promising direction for locating edit-specific components and repairing edited language models.

paper.title: Text-to-SQL Benchmarks Toward Enterprise Realities: Under Massive Scopes, Complex Schemas and Scattered Knowledge
paper.abstract: Existing Text-to-SQL benchmarks remain idealized compared with enterprise scenarios, which require massive query scopes, complex schemas, and scattered external knowledge. We present BIRD-Ent and Spider-Ent, two enterprise-oriented benchmarks constructed via a refinement framework, together with Dual-Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (DRAG) Text-to-SQL, which formalizes table-schema and knowledge retrieval before SQL generation. The benchmarks feature over 4,000 columns per query and, for BIRD-Ent, documents totaling 1.5M tokens. Evaluation on state-of-the-art models shows sharp drops, with only 39.1% EX on BIRD-Ent and 60.5% EX on Spider-Ent. These results establish the Ent-series as a discriminative testbed for structurally robust and retrieval-aware Text-to-SQL.

paper.title: Full-Distribution Self-Distillation for Optimizing Soft Latent Reasoning

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Soft latent reasoning extends chain-of-thought reasoning beyond discrete token sequences by using continuous concept tokens. However, effectively training models in this space remains challenging: conventional reinforcement learning methods mainly optimize sampled rollout-action likelihoods and therefore underuse the full distributions produced during soft rollouts. We propose **Full-Distribution Self-Distillation (FDSD)**, an off-policy training framework that treats stochastic soft rollout distributions as dense pseudo-labels. FDSD aligns the current model distribution with advantage-weighted rollout targets via KL minimization and importance correction, enabling the model to learn from the full rollout distribution rather than only from sampled-action likelihoods. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH-500, OlympiadBench, and out-of-domain benchmarks show that FDSD achieves consistent average improvements in mathematical reasoning across model scales while preserving OOD generalization, with only modest computational overhead. These results suggest that full-distribution alignment is a promising training direction for soft latent reasoning.

paper.title: Anom3W: A Unified Benchmark for Video Anomaly Grounding and Understanding
paper.abstract: Understanding anomalies in real-world videos requires reasoning about when events occur, where they happen, and what actions unfold. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ignore one or more of these dimensions, making it difficult to evaluate whether multimodal large models (MLLMs) truly understand abnormal events beyond simple detection. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{Anom3W}, a benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs across \textbf{temporal, spatial, and semantic dimensions}. Our semi-automatic pipeline consolidates heterogeneous anomaly resources into verified spatio-temporal annotations, enabling rigorous, reasoning-oriented evaluation. By treating spatial boxes and tubes as evidence cues, Anom3W challenges models to reason about entities, locations, and behaviors, rather than merely flag anomalies. Experiments demonstrate that even state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle, highlighting the critical importance of spatial grounding and semantic understanding. Anom3W establishes a new standard for interpretable, context-aware video anomaly reasoning.

paper.title: Factorized Soft Prompts with Inference-Time Latent Control for LLM Personalization

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science

paper.abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires reflecting stable user preferences while adapting their expression to each target context. Soft-prompt personalization has become a practical route to this goal, but existing methods produce soft prompts in which stable preferences, target-induced content, and context-dependent expression are bundled into an entangled conditioning signal without separately addressable components, leaving inference with no principled space to intervene on individual aspects of personalization. We propose Factorized soft prompts with Latent Control (FaLCon), an LLM personalization framework built on two coupled stages. First, factorized soft prompts replace this entangled conditioning with a set of separately addressable preference factors, forming a structured control interface. Second, inference-time latent control treats the resulting factor weights as a continuous action space and adapts them per instance from teacher-forced likelihood feedback, keeping the LLM frozen and updating only a low-dimensional factor-weight posterior without back-propagating through the LLM. Experiments on multiple personalized generation tasks reveal that FaLCon consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating the individual necessity and joint effectiveness of the structured interface and the inference-time controller.

paper.title: Refinement Provenance Inference: Detecting LLM-Refined Training Prompts from Model Behavior
paper.abstract: Instruction tuning increasingly relies on LLM-based prompt refinement, where prompts in the training corpus are selectively rewritten by an external refiner to improve clarity and instruction alignment. This motivates an instance-level audit problem: for a fine-tuned model and a training prompt–response pair, can we infer whether the model was trained on the original prompt or its LLM-refined version within a mixed corpus? This matters for dataset governance and dispute resolution when training data are contested. However, it is non-trivial in practice: refined and raw instances are interleaved in the training corpus with unknown, source-dependent mixture ratios, making it harder to develop provenance methods that generalize across models and training setups. In this paper, we formalize this audit task as Refinement Provenance Inference (RPI) and show that prompt refinement yields stable, detectable shifts in teacher-forced token distributions, even when semantic differences are not obvious. Building on this phenomenon, we propose RePro, a logit-based provenance framework that fuses teacher-forced likelihood features with logit-ranking signals. During training, RePro learns a transferable representation via shadow fine-tuning, and uses a lightweight linear head to infer provenance on unseen victims without training-data access. Empirically, RePro consistently attains strong performance and transfers well across refiners, suggesting that it exploits refiner-agnostic distribution shifts rather than rewrite-style artifacts.

paper.title: Surveying Representation Collapse in Pretrained Models of American Sign Language

author.affiliation: University of Pittsburgh and Northeastern University

paper.abstract: The American Sign Language (ASL) lexicon contains heterogeneous sign types, including established signed words, neologisms, ad-hoc depictions of real-world phenomena, and fingerspelled words. Productions within each type exhibit unique phonotactics and substantial variability, potentially confounding models pretrained on downstream ASL tasks. To survey the capacity for representation collapse, we isolate and annotate 14 types of ASL productions as they appear in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) educational content. We then probe seven pretrained models’ latent representations of the annotated clips, reporting collapse metrics with respect to domain, sign type, and meaning. Our findings show that out-of-distribution signs are more frequent in STEM content, and that pretrained models lose information about their visual and semantic contents in varing ways. Among the tested models, those which encoded the phonological properties of signs generalized to STEM data more effectively, while English- and gesture-based models can exhibit more brittleness. Future work can design interventions to mitigate the kinds of collapse documented here or extend this survey by evaluating additional models and datasets.

paper.title: EYELIGNR: Aligning Gaze and Text via Contrastive Learning for Improved Reading Scanpath Prediction
paper.abstract: Modeling the interaction between gaze dynamics and linguistic structure remains a central challenge in scanpath prediction. Existing approaches either incorporate linguistic information in ways that do not fully respect the temporal progression of reading, or ignore linguistic structure altogether. Their effectiveness is further limited by the scarcity and heterogeneity of available eye-tracking data. To address these issues, we introduce EYELIGNR, a framework for spatiotemporal scanpath prediction that integrates linguistic information at the representation level. EYELIGNR conditions language representations on fixation order and aligns gaze and text within a shared embedding space through contrastive learning. Experiments on five reading corpora show that EYELIGNR generalizes effectively across reading conditions, improving over prior state of the art on multiple scanpath metrics (e.g., up to NLD ~57%, NLL ~27%, and FLA ~59%).

paper.title: HiDet: Hierarchical AI Text Detection via Coarse Filtering and Multi-Grained Contrastive Learning

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: Humanizing methods of AI-generated texts are emerging, which leads to severe performance degradation of current AI text detectors. Most existing detectors are struggling to ensure consistent performance in the huge span from detecting simple AI texts to detecting AI texts humanized in various ways. Targetedly, we propose HiDet, which contains coarse module and subdivision module to give AI texts a double check. We decouple the complete detection process into simple sample detection and difficult sample detection, the coarse module of HiDet filters out simple samples, while hard-to-detect samples like humanized AI texts will be carefully discriminated through the subdivision module which applies a multi-grained contrastive learning strategy. This hierarchical framework makes up for the loophole that humanized AI texts can successfully escape the traditional detector after a single detection, and shows excellent robustness in the task of detecting humanized AI texts. Meanwhile, our framework is flexiable, the subdivision module can be deployed separately on the existing detector as a plug-and-play patch to tremendously improve their performance when facing large-scale humanized AI texts. We hope our work can inspire new sparks in the field of AI-generated text detection.

paper.title: Mind the Motions: Benchmarking Theory-of-Mind in Everyday Body Language

author.affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul National University and Yonsei University

paper.abstract: Our ability to interpret others’ mental states through nonverbal cues (NVCs) is fundamental to our survival and social cohesion. While existing Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks have primarily focused on false-belief tasks and reasoning with asymmetric information, they overlook other mental states beyond belief and the rich tapestry of human nonverbal communication. We present Motion2Mind a framework for evaluating the ToM capabilities of machines in interpreting NVCs. Leveraging an expert-curated body-language reference as a knowledge base, we build Motion2Mind, a carefully curated video dataset with fine-grained nonverbal cue annotations paired with manually verified psychological interpretations. It encompasses 222 types of nonverbal cues and 397 mind states. Our evaluation reveals that current AI systems struggle significantly with NVC interpretation, exhibiting not only a substantial performance gap in Detection, as well as patterns of over-interpretation in Explanation compared to human annotators.

paper.title: FAIR-Eval: Reliable and Efficient Adaptive Benchmarking for Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Evaluating large language models typically requires thousands of benchmark items, making the process expensive and increasingly impractical. Existing protocols rely on average accuracy over fixed item sets, treating all items as equally informative—yet many items are too easy or too hard to distinguish between models, making evaluation both wasteful and imprecise. Item Response Theory (IRT) with Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) offers a principled alternative—separately estimating model ability and item difficulty, then adaptively selecting the most informative items. However, practical deployment is bottlenecked by costly item calibration, and standard greedy selection causes severe over-exposure of frequently picked items while leaving the rest of the bank under-utilized, which risks data contamination over time. We propose FAIR-Eval with two components: Feature-Driven Calibration (FDC), which jointly learns item parameters from text features and sparse responses, enabling low-cost bank expansion requiring only minimal model responses; and Maximum Fisher Information Plus (MFI+), which counteracts greedy selection by incorporating exposure control, while simultaneously enforcing difficulty coverage and domain diversity to systematically activate under-utilized items. On a 6,796-item bank (193 calibration models, 50 held-out), FAIR-Eval achieves Pearson r = 0.9882 and Spearman \rho = 0.9828 against full evaluation using around 3% of items. Crucially, it broadens difficulty coverage from 60.0% to 68.7%, achieving a more comprehensive and robust assessment of model capabilities with minimal test length.

paper.title: RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Rubric-Driven Review via Agentic Evidence Synthesis and Human-Aligned Generation
paper.abstract: Peer review at major venues is under unprecedented submission pressure, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers, however, face two structural limitations. First, they map manuscripts directly to reviews, leaving the underlying rubric implicit and entangling its derivation with the judgement. Second, the prevailing paradigms each capture only half of a good review: training-free agents gather broad evidence but produce undirected critiques, while training-based reviewers inherit human discriminative judgement together with its noise and uneven coverage. We introduce RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework that addresses both limitations. It makes rubric generation an explicit intermediate step, so that both review generation and the final assessment are conditioned on paper-adaptive rubrics. It further combines a training-free agent Scout that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model Aligner that consumes this evidence, fusing the strengths of both supervision sources. Experiments on real-world submissions show that RubricReviewer produces reviews that are markedly more comprehensive and more discriminative than prior systems, and exhibits the strongest robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of each component.

paper.title: PersuaRL: Reinforcement Learning-Driven Multi-Expert Selection for Persuasive Dialogue Generation in Insurance

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Patna, India

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing digital communication by powering conversational agents deployed across domains such as customer service, digital sales, and insurance. These agents, built on LLMs, can understand user input, retrieve relevant information, and generate coherent responses. However, while they excel at factual communication, they often lack the ability to engage in truly persuasive, context-sensitive dialogue, especially in domains like insurance, where trust and clarity are critical. Building on this need within the insurance domain, our work focuses on improving the persuasiveness of digital agents, aka LLMs. To support this, we introduce InsureDial, a Persuasive Insurance Dialogue dataset, designed to capture the nuances of persuasive communication specific to motor insurance interactions. We introduce PersuaRL, a reinforcement learning–based framework that equips LLM-driven dialogue agents with the ability to adaptively explore, select, and coordinate strategies across multiple expert modules, guided by the evolving dialogue context, to achieve more effective persuasion. We conduct extensive automatic human and qualitative evaluations on two benchmark persuasion dialogue datasets, including our InsureDial. Our evaluations consistently demonstrate that PersuaRL outperforms baseline, generating contextually appropriate and highly persuasive responses.

paper.title: Filter by Quality, Stop by Difficulty: Confidence-Aware Self-Consistency with Adaptive Early Stopping
paper.abstract: Self-consistency improves LLM reasoning by majority voting over multiple sampled solutions, but always exhausts the sampling budget and trusts every solution equally. Early-stopping methods cut token cost substantially via convergence monitoring. However, deciding when to stop cannot change what is voted on, so they save tokens without meaningfully improving accuracy. We introduce CASE (Confidence-Aware Self-consistency with Adaptive Early stopping), which improves both accuracy and efficiency by leveraging token-level confidence normalized at two scales: within-problem to filter low-quality solutions and weight survivors, and cross-problem to adapt the stopping threshold to problem difficulty. Across 5 models and 6 benchmarks, CASE simultaneously saves 85% of tokens and improves accuracy by +2.24pp over majority voting, outperforming every early-stopping baseline on both accuracy and efficiency. Component and role-swap analyses confirm that filtering and weighting are complementary and the two normalization scales are non-interchangeable.

paper.title: Routing Before Looking: Query-Adaptive Evidence Acquisition for Long-form Video Understanding

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences and University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Wuhan AI Research and Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Long-form video understanding remains challenging for video agents due to the mismatch between query demands and evidence acquisition strategies. Although recent planning-before-perception methods outperform query-agnostic pipelines, they often rely on a single dominant strategy, either generation-based strategy or retrieval-based strategy, limiting their ability to handle diverse query demands. We propose **Route2Look**, a lightweight and model-agnostic framework for query-adaptive evidence acquisition in long-form video understanding. Route2Look operates in a Route-Look-Memorize loop with three tools: Global Browse for holistic context, Temporal Ground for explicit temporal cues, and Semantic Retrieve for semantic search. The core component is a routing policy that dynamically selects evidence acquisition tools based on the query. To build this policy, Route2Look adopts a two-stage design: first distilling the routing skill from differential contrastive analysis between generation-based and retrieval-based trajectories, and then applying the distilled skill with hard routing rules and continue-or-stop criteria during inference. Experiments on challenging long-video benchmarks show that Route2Look achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining strong frame efficiency across datasets and query types. Oracle routing analysis further reveals the potential of query-adaptive evidence acquisition for future long-form video understanding.

paper.title: Skill-CDPO: Evolving Agent Tool-Use via Critical Step Preference Optimization
paper.abstract: Compact open-source language models lag behind their larger counterparts in agentic tool-use reliability, yet standard remedies face fundamental obstacles: supervised fine-tuning suffers from exposure bias, while reinforcement learning is hampered by sparse credit assignment over long tool-interaction trajectories. We introduce Skill-CDPO, a progressive framework that first acquires tool-use skills at inference time through static tool analysis and dynamic strategy refinement, then distills the resulting error-correction signals into parameter updates via Critical Step DPO (CDPO). CDPO identifies the specific trajectory steps where model capability is the bottleneck—through rollout divergence between a local policy and an expert model—and constructs distributional preference pairs from all cross-group rollouts at those steps, weighted by both step-level criticality and pair-level score gaps. This provides dense, fine-grained supervision without requiring a process reward model. We evaluate Skill-CDPO on three medical agent benchmarks—PubMed Search (a new PubMed-based deep research benchmark we contribute), CureBench, and MedBrowseComp—using an 8B-parameter deep research model. Skill-CDPO substantially outperforms SFT and trajectory-level DPO baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance compared to GPT-5.2 on retrieval-intensive tasks. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Skill-CDPO-BF51.

paper.title: Learning When to Think in Latent Visual Space: Reasoning Mode Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR) unfolds reasoning in a continuous visual embedding space, markedly improving Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on vision-intensive tasks. However, our experiments reveal a hidden cost: LVR inevitably undermines VLMs’ strong textual reasoning ability, causing substantial degradation on logic-intensive tasks. This motivates us to unify both reasoning modes within a single VLM that adaptively selects the appropriate one. We propose MoLaT (Mixture of Latent and Textual Reasoning), a novel method that trains VLMs via reinforcement learning (RL) to select LVR and text-only reasoning adaptively. MoLaT is trained in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning endows the VLM with a dual-mode capability using mixed CoT data. Then, MoLaT introduces two complementary designs: 1) The mode-adaptive advantage decouples the mode-selection signal from per-rollout correctness reward at the token level: mode-selection tokens receive dedicated cross-mode gradients, while content tokens retain the group-relative advantage. 2) The entropy-modulated advantage weight uses sequence-level entropy as a difficulty proxy, modulating signal strength to prevent premature mode commitment. Experiments confirm that MoLaT improves both vision-intensive and logic-intensive abilities, validating adaptive mode selection as key to general-purpose reasoning VLMs.

paper.title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware

author.affiliation: OPPO Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Co., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol — including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE — demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

paper.title: Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation
paper.abstract: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. We emphasize that the core contribution is this relational problem formulation itself, not the GNN architecture - CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. The per-edge signed deviation \delta_{ij} operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.

paper.title: Directional Drift in Arithmetic Reasoning: How Comparative Cues Steer LLM Predictions
paper.abstract: Arithmetic tasks are widely used to evaluate LLM reasoning because they provide objective truth.
