Yet accuracy alone cannot distinguish whether prompt sensitivity reflects random prediction instability or systematic semantic bias. We study this question in comparative arithmetic, where semantically equivalent framings can cue directional outcomes such as more, less, or equal. We introduce MathComp, a balanced benchmark of 10,800 controlled comparison problems spanning multiple framing conditions and answer formats. Across ten LLMs, semantically equivalent comparative cues systematically bias predictions toward cued outcomes even when it is numerically incorrect. Notably, this effect persists even when cue words are removed from the answer options, suggesting that framing bias reflects broader semantic steering rather than simple label copying. Chain-of-thought reasoning mitigates the effect substantially, but residual directional drift remains. These findings suggest that prompt sensitivity in arithmetic reasoning can exhibit structured semantic bias toward linguistically cued outcomes, with implications for robustness evaluation and benchmark design.

paper.title: CoReflect: A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation
paper.abstract: Evaluating multi-turn conversational systems remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional pipelines rely on manual rubrics and fixed context, a static approach that limits coverage and fails to capture emergent dialogue behaviors. To address this, we introduce CoReflect (A Reflective Co-Evolution Framework for Improving Conversational Evaluation), which unifies dialogue simulation and evaluation into an adaptive, iterative process. CoReflect employs a conversation planner that generates structured templates to guide a user simulator through diverse, goal-directed dialogues. Subsequently, a reflective analyzer processes these dialogues to identify systematic behavioral patterns and automatically refine the evaluation rubrics. Crucially, the insights from the conversation analysis are fed back into the planner to update conversation templates for subsequent iterations. This co-evolution loop ensures that the complexity of test cases and the diagnostic precision of rubrics improve in tandem. By minimizing human intervention, CoReflect provides a scalable and self-refining methodology that allows evaluation protocols to adapt alongside the rapidly advancing capabilities of dialogue models.

paper.title: Active Adaptation, Not Static Defense: Temporal Dynamics of Preventative Steering in Adversarial Fine-Tuning

author.affiliation: China Mobile Communications Company Limited Research Institute

paper.abstract: Large language models remain fragile against malicious fine-tuning, motivating training-time defenses against harmful persona drift. Preventative Steering injects undesirable-trait persona vectors during fine-tuning and removes them at evaluation time, yet the mechanism behind its lasting protection remains unclear. Analyzing its temporal optimization dynamics, we find that the defense emerges from an early compensatory adaptation phase followed by a steady-state phase where the corrective signal decays; in parameter space, attention output projections emerge as the dominant residual-write route for defensive updates. Through Intervention Delta Preservation (IDP) and IDP Continuation experiments, we further show that preserving or reinjecting the weight offset fails to maintain protection, indicating that preventative steering relies on active adaptation rather than a static defense. Motivated by this finding, we propose Progressive Intensity Scheduling (PIS), which starts with a moderate injection strength and increases it after static-strength alignment begins to decay. Across the evaluated Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 models, PIS improves safety robustness over static-strength steering while reducing harmful trait expression.

paper.title: The Benchmark Is Not the Construct: Toward Distribution-Based Evaluation in NLP
paper.abstract: Current NLP evaluation often treats a scalar score on a fixed benchmark dataset as if it directly measured the construct the benchmark is intended to represent. This Measurement-as-Instance paradigm is appropriate for a fixed evaluation configuration, but can suppress uncertainty, variance, and robustness when a single result is used to support broader capability or generalisation claims. In this position paper, we argue for extending static evaluation with Measurement-as-Distribution: a structured evaluation procedure involving principled data generation, validated perturbations, repeated evaluation, and distributional reporting. The framework is configurable: the amount of distributional evidence required should scale with the strength and breadth of the claims being made. We synthesise existing robustness, dynamic-evaluation, prompt-sensitivity, and uncertainty-reporting practices into a general measurement-theoretic framework for distribution-based NLP evaluation and provide a call to action for more rigorous reporting. Using the protocol \mathcal{P} = (\mathcal{C}, G, \Phi, E, R), we identify three risks of relying exclusively on fixed scalar evaluation and derive implications for peer review, benchmark publication, leaderboard reporting, and computational cost. Two case studies demonstrate feasibility: a SQuAD evaluation of 14 models reveals modest but axis-specific performance changes and stable overall rankings with uncertainty-aware comparisons, while a verifier-backed Knights-and-Knaves study illustrates how perturbations of rigid logical tasks can be generated and validated formally.

paper.title: When Charts Deceive Web Agents: A Paired Benchmark for Misleading Visualization-Grounded Tasks

author.affiliation: National Key Lab for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University

paper.abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, interpret, and act on web content on behalf of users. In many realistic workflows, however, the visual evidence they consume is not neutral: charts and dashboards can be misleading, shaping judgments without issuing any explicit malicious instruction. Unlike chart question answering, Web Agents treat charts as intermediate evidence whose misinterpretation can propagate into concrete downstream actions — a reliability risk that remains underexplored. We introduce MisVisAgentBench, the first paired executable benchmark for evaluating how misleading visualizations affect Web Agent execution. It comprises 280 task instances in matched clean–misleading pairs that differ only in chart evidence. We further provide a diagnostic framework that isolates misleading-induced failures from baseline task difficulty and captures execution-level effects such as extra browsing steps and decision hesitation. Across eleven vision-language Web Agents, replacing clean charts with misleading counterparts nearly halves the average task success rate, an absolute drop exceeding 34 percentage points. Moreover, these failures predominantly follow the targeted misleading action branch, suggesting that deceptive charts systematically redirect rather than randomly disrupt agent decisions. These results reveal that visualization robustness is a critical yet understudied dimension of Web Agent safety and reliability.

paper.title: Moral Safety in LLMs: Exposing Performative Compliance with Puzzled Cues

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Washington
Department of Computer Science, University of Washington

paper.abstract: As large language models take on morally consequential roles in healthcare, legal, and hiring contexts, verifying that their ethical behavior is genuine rather than superficial becomes essential. We show that current fairness evaluations substantially overestimate moral safety. Models judged fair when demographic identity is explicitly labeled become measurably less fair when the same identity must be inferred — a pattern we term performative compliance: safety behavior contingent on surface-level evaluation signals rather than internalized fairness principles. We introduce a cue-variation methodology that holds moral content fixed while varying only whether demographic identity is stated or must be inferred, and apply it to 14 models across 100 everyday dilemmas spanning 3 genders and 5 races. Hiding the label leaves decisions that benefit the described individual unchanged (+0.9pp) while raising decisions that harm them by +4.4pp. This asymmetry persists even when models correctly infer the demographic, ruling out attribution error. We propose the Direct vs Puzzled gap as a model-agnostic robustness metric that requires no new annotation, changes model safety rankings, and can be adopted by any existing fairness evaluation to separate genuine from performative moral safety. We argue that fairness evaluations that omit cue-variation measure surface compliance, not moral robustness, and should not ground deployment decisions in high-stakes settings.

paper.title: Reliability-Calibrated Guidance for Few-Step Categorical Flow-Map Text Generation

author.affiliation: Aerospace Information Technology University and Shandong Normal University

paper.abstract: Few-step flow-map guidance provides an efficient way to steer generation without retraining, but its updates are defined in a continuous or relaxed state space. In categorical text generation, however, the final output is determined by simplex-constrained token distributions and hard decoding. Under low NFE, where each update induces a relatively large finite displacement, this continuous-to-discrete mismatch can make terminal reward guidance unreliable, causing overshoot, reward–quality conflict, saturation, or poor transfer from relaxed reward gains to decoded tokens.We present Reliability-Calibrated Flow Guidance (RCFG), a sampling-time reliability-calibration framework for terminal reward pullback in few-step categorical flow maps. Rather than replacing the underlying guidance primitive, RCFG calibrates its magnitude and direction according to transition scale, reward saturation, local reward–quality conflict, and categorical endpoint structure. Experiments on LM1B and Text8 show more favorable aggregate control–likelihood operating points after calibration: on LM1B, RCFG maintains or improves verifier Reward and Target while reducing NLL and PPL relative to terminal reward-pullback guidance, while Text8 shows a modest aggregate improvement in lexical-control balance. Code and reproduction instructions are available at: https://github.com/ZionLau/RCFG

paper.title: APEX-EM: Non-Parametric Online Learning for Autonomous Agents via Structured Procedural-Episodic Experience Replay
paper.abstract: LLM agents rerun full reasoning for every task, even one they solved moments earlier. We introduce APEX-EM, a non-parametric experience memory that stores complete procedural-episodic traces in a typed Procedural Knowledge Graph (PKG) and retrieves them through three channels: semantic search, structural-signature matching over abstract operation sequences, and graph traversal. A Plan-Retrieve-Generate-Iterate-Ingest (PRGII) workflow produces, quality-gates, and commits experiences, indexing both successes and failures so the agent learns what to reuse and what to avoid. No weights change during deployment. We evaluate on five benchmarks: BigCodeBench, KGQAGen-10k, HLE, Lifelong Agent Bench, and ALFWorld. Because prior work uses different backbones, we base our claims on same-backbone comparisons that hold model capability fixed. On held-out BigCodeBench transfer with a shared GPT-4o backbone, APEX-EM gains +7.6pp over the no-memory baseline, which is 3.3x MemRL’s +2.3pp under the identical setup. On Lifelong Agent Bench with a shared GPT-4o-mini backbone, APEX-EM gains +1.4pp (OS) and +1.0pp (DB) cumulative success. On KGQAGen-10k, frozen memory transfers to a blind 1,079-question test split at 73.7% versus 42.0% with no memory, approaching an oracle that is handed the ground-truth subgraph (84.9%). Across three Opus scales the memory gain stays at +27pp to +32pp, so it adds to model capability rather than substituting for it. Component analysis shows no single mechanism dominates: teacher feedback is negligible for code but adds +10.3pp on structured queries, structural signatures give 3.3 times the transfer of semantic-only retrieval, and within-epoch iteration recovers most of the gain when rich feedback is unavailable. These results argue for modular memory composed per domain.

paper.title: DisGAR: Machine Generated Text Detection via Disentangled Generative Artifact Representation

author.affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences and State Key Laboratory of Cyberspace Security Defense
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, State Key Laboratory of Cyberspace Security Defense and University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: The widespread misuse of large language models (LLMs) has made machine-generated text detection (MGTD) a critical task. Existing detection methods are often vulnerable to stylistic noise, which limits their generalization in real-world scenarios and robustness on short texts. Furthermore, many methods generate multiple auxiliary texts through LLM-based rewriting or similar strategies, substantially increasing detection latency and limiting their practicality. To address these challenges, we propose the **DisGAR** detection framework, which strips stylistic noise from the input text to mitigate its impact on detection performance, thereby improving cross-domain and cross-model robustness. Specifically, we first fine-tune the attention layers of the proxy model to capture generation-specific patterns. Then we further introduce a global artifact aggregation mechanism and a contrastive learning strategy based on rewritten texts, enabling the separation of stylistic artifacts from the underlying generation patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that DisGAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in unseen-model and unseen-domain detection. Moreover, DisGAR achieves detection efficiency comparable to Fast-DetectGPT, successfully balancing detection performance and efficiency. Source code is available at https://github.com/m-Clown/DisGAR.git

paper.title: Guardrails without Shackles: Mitigating Over-Defense in Inference-Time Detection of Fixed-Target Backdoors for LLMs

author.affiliation: Xi’an Research Institute of High Technology
Information Center, Academy of Military Science
Advanced Institute of Big Data, Beijing

paper.abstract: Fixed-target backdoor attacks can silently hijack the outputs of large language models by driving models to generate attacker-specified sequences upon trigger activation, motivating lightweight inference-time detection. Recent defenses like ConfGuard, which we term Local-window Confidence Detectors, leverage sliding windows to identify local spans where the top-1 probability, referred to as token confidence, exceeds 0.99 as indicators of backdoor activation. However, benign deterministic tasks such as math reasoning can exhibit similar sustained high-confidence patterns, causing confidence conflation. On the GSM8K dataset, ConfGuard’s default settings yield a 72.89% false positive rate, causing substantial over-defense. Our empirical analysis reveals that benign deterministic generation exhibits sparse confidence "dips", whereas backdoor-triggered generation forms a sustained high-confidence "plateau". Building on this, we propose RatioGuard, which utilizes a global high-confidence token ratio computed over the generated prefix to address confidence conflation. Across models and datasets, RatioGuard reduces false positives by up to 71.57 percentage points over ConfGuard while maintaining over 99% true positive rate with 1.005\times runtime latency.

paper.title: Anchored by an Afterthought: Cross-Modal Numerical Anchoring in VLMs

author.affiliation: Seoul National University, Seoul National University and Yonsei University

paper.abstract: When a vision-language model (VLM) is shown an irrelevant image containing a digit (the anchor image) alongside a numeric question, the model’s numeric answer shifts toward that digit. This matters because multi-image inputs (retrieval-augmented QA, multi-screenshot analysis, VLM-as-judge) routinely contain irrelevant numeric content. We call this phenomenon cross-modal numerical anchoring: across six VLMs and five numeric VQA datasets, the per-model mean SDF (signed direction-follow rate) ranges from 3% to 24%, with the effect growing stronger as the model’s confidence in the base answer decreases. Masking only the digit pixels of the anchor image, leaving the rest of the image intact, recovers the non-anchored answer, isolating the digit pixels as the causal channel, with the effect concentrated at low confidence. We propose a mitigation that uses this anchored-masked contrast as a calibration signal: at a single per-model integration site, we estimate a low-rank subspace spanning the anchoring directions and remove it via a projection at inference time. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, the projection reduces anchoring (\Delta\mathrm{SDF}_a=-1.64 pp, rel% -30.0\%) without degrading accuracy on non-anchored inputs or average performance on six capability benchmarks (within \pm1 pp).

paper.title: Not All LoRA Parameters Are Essential: Insights on Inference Necessity
paper.abstract: Current research on LoRA primarily focuses on minimizing the number of fine-tuned parameters or optimizing its architecture. However, the necessity of all fine-tuned LoRA layers during inference remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate the contribution of each LoRA layer to the model’s ability to predict the ground truth and hypothesize that lower-layer LoRA modules play a more critical role in model reasoning and understanding. To address this, we propose a simple yet effective method to enhance the performance of large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA. Specifically, we identify a “boundary layer” that distinguishes essential LoRA layers by analyzing a small set of validation samples. During inference, we drop all LoRA layers beyond this boundary. We evaluate our approach on three strong baselines across four widely-used text generation datasets. Our analysis and experimental results show that selectively retaining critical LoRA layers during inference is effective across tasks of different types.

paper.title: Beyond Known Event Types: Open-Domain Event Detection via Ontology-Guided Grounding–Discovery Resolution

author.affiliation: Shanghai Moqi Wanxiang Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Open-domain event detection aims to identify known event types while discovering previously unseen ones from unstructured documents. In practice, event detection systems often operate with an evolving event set rather than a complete type inventory. Under this setting, existing zero-shot event detection methods can fail in two ways when the event type is absent from the predefined set: the model may either miss the event or assign it to a plausible but wrong known type, hiding the need for discovery. To address this problem, we propose OGED, an \underline{\textbf{O}}ntology-\underline{\textbf{G}}uided open-domain \underline{\textbf{E}}vent \underline{\textbf{D}}etection framework for grounding–discovery resolution, i.e., deciding whether an event mention should be assigned to an existing type or should induce a new type. OGED organizes the available event types into a hierarchical search structure, uses cluster-level scheduler and adaptive planning to keep known-type assignment and new-type discovery jointly active, and applies retrieval-gated verification together with conflict selection to resolve competing assignments before output. Experiments on a unified benchmark with 564 event types show that OGED outperforms strong baselines on both known-type detection and unknown-type discovery. Code is available at https://github.com/chenzhouli/OGED.

paper.title: Energy-Aware Benchmarking of Generative Information Extraction
paper.abstract: Using Large Language Models (LLMs) for Information Extraction (IE) inherently involves transforming diverse textual inputs into strictly formatted outputs. Guaranteeing this structural validity introduces a hidden energy tax driven by constrained decoding mechanisms, serialisation formats, and underlying serving configurations. Consequently, standard token-level metrics fail to capture the true energy cost of generative IE, which also cannot be predicted by model size alone. To address this, we introduce the first dedicated benchmark evaluating the energy-accuracy trade-offs of generative IE. Our framework establishes task-aligned energy metrics, including Energy per True Positive (J/TP) and the F1-Energy Ratio (F_1/\mathrm{kJ}). Through comprehensive ablation across architectures, decoding regimes, and serving-layer limits, we demonstrate that efficiency is governed by complex parameter interactions. We translate these findings into actionable configuration guidelines, equipping practitioners to maximise predictive accuracy, optimise energy yield, or achieve a sustainable Pareto balance.

paper.title: A Hyperbolicity Atlas of Large Language Model Hidden States

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Hidden states of large language models (LLMs) are typically analyzed as flat Euclidean vectors through probing, anisotropy, and intrinsic-dimension lenses. Yet much of what these models process (taxonomies, program structure, multi-step derivations) is hierarchical, and whether hidden-state distances reflect such hierarchy remains untested. We present the first systematic study of Gromov hyperbolicity (GH), a distance-based measure of tree-likeness, in prompt-token hidden states of open-weight LLMs. Across model families, scales, layer depths, and domains spanning math, code, commonsense, and truthfulness benchmarks, we construct a hyperbolicity atlas charting the normalized statistic \delta_{\mathrm{rel}} along each axis. Four findings emerge: (i) depth dominates, with middle layers forming a high-\delta_{\mathrm{rel}} plateau and final layers dropping toward tree-like structure; (ii) scale is weak and non-monotonic; (iii) matched-scale families occupy distinct regimes, with specialization gaps exceeding scale effects; and (iv) domains interact with specialization, e.g., HumanEval shifts from the highest- to the lowest-\delta_{\mathrm{rel}} domain between base and coder checkpoints. GH thus serves as a lightweight diagnostic that localizes where hierarchical distance structure emerges and which comparisons warrant deeper analysis.

paper.title: Leak-Resistant Unlearning: A New Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Consistency and Recovery Robustness
paper.abstract: Benchmarking machine unlearning methods is critical to understand whether sensitive knowledge is removed from large language models (LLMs) or not. Current unlearning benchmarks include mainly single-hop questions and a narrow set of multi-hop questions. Although effective, they still face two challenges. (1) Knowledge is not isolated, whereby diverse multi-hop reasoning paths can potentially induce knowledge leakage than normal queries. (2) Unlearning may be fragile: unlearned knowledge can be partially recovered through recovery attacks such as lightweight post-unlearning adaptation, making static evaluation insufficient. Therefore, in this paper, we introduce Leak-resistant Unlearning as a novel benchmark to understand robust LLM knowledge removal across diverse reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We experiment with this benchmark on 3 models, 6 unlearning methods, and 2 carefully curated datasets. Results show that existing methods are vulnerable to multi-hop reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We further explore the trade-off among forget quality, robustness, and model utility for LLM unlearning.

paper.title: MetaGen: Self-Evolving Roles and Topologies for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems, where specialized roles communicate and collaborate through structured interactions to solve complex tasks that often exceed the capacity of a single agent. However, most existing systems still rely on a fixed role library and an execution-frozen interaction topology, a rigid design choice that frequently leads to task mismatch, prevents timely adaptation when new evidence emerges during reasoning, and further inflates inference cost. We introduce MetaGen, a framework that adapts both the role space and the collaboration topology at inference time, without updating base model weights. MetaGen generates and rewrites query-conditioned role specifications to maintain a controllable dynamic role pool, then instantiates a constrained execution graph around a minimal backbone. During execution, it iteratively updates role prompts and adjusts structural decisions using lightweight feedback signals. Experiments on code generation and multi-step reasoning benchmarks show that MetaGen improves the accuracy and cost tradeoff over strong multi-agent baselines.

paper.title: Stratified Topographic Similarity

author.affiliation: Quant Firm and University of Lorraine

paper.abstract: Topographic Similarity (TopSim) is the most widely used metric for compositionality in emergent communication research. However, when evaluated on a class of languages where compositional structure is fully known (simple natural-language word concatenations), TopSim, along with other well-known metrics, under-reports compositionality. We investigate and trace TopSim’s failure to a distributional imbalance in pairwise object distances that grows with the input space size, and propose stratified-TopSim, a minimal fix that remains stable across settings and reliably evaluates languages of varying compositional structure, on both controlled benchmarks and emergent languages.

paper.title: Padamitra: Grounded Glossary Generation for Classical Sanskrit

author.affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology

paper.abstract: We introduce grounded glossary generation, a structured task requiring models to recover semantically meaningful Sanskrit phrases and produce translation-grounded meanings from a śloka-translation pair, formalizing the traditional pāṭha-commentary practice as an evaluable NLP objective. We construct a benchmark of 31,316 śloka-translation-glossary triples from the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, paired with two metrics: Jaccard for phrase recovery and Meaning Faithfulness for semantic consistency. Across zero-shot, few-shot, and instruction fine-tuned variants of Gemma-3n-E4B, Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4, and Qwen3.5-9B, instruction fine-tuning substantially outperforms prompting, while explicit segmentation yields gains. Error analysis identifies over-segmentation of sandhi and samāsa compounds as the dominant failure mode, pointing to morphological modeling as the key bottleneck for faithful Sanskrit lexical decomposition.

paper.title: Routed Graph Handoff: Adaptive Format Selection for Multi-Agent LLM Delegation
paper.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems coordinate through natural-language messages that consume 40–60% of their token budget. Replacing these with structured graphs reduces cost but fails on tasks requiring adaptive reasoning. We propose Routed Graph Handoff, where a lightweight LLM router (155 tokens, 0.15% overhead) selects between a typed dependency graph and natural language for each delegation. On four benchmarks (1,050+ trajectories), the routed system matches or exceeds NL-only on every task: +12.7,pp on Tau-retail at 3.2 X compression (p<0.01), +8.7,pp on BrowseComp at 2.2 compression (p<0.05), and parity on BFCL and AppWorld. Without the router, graph-only delegation regresses 14.6,pp on AppWorld—the router eliminates this at near-zero cost. A graph-aware executor prompt is load-bearing: the same schema without interpretation guidance yields no gain. An oracle analysis reveals 8.6,pp of additional headroom, motivating execution-time adaptive routing as future work.

paper.title: HiSVR: Hierarchical Semantic Visual Reconstruction for Unified Multimodal Models

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
, Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science

paper.abstract: Unified multimodal models use a shared Transformer backbone for visual understanding and image generation. Existing post-training signals primarily constrain final outputs, output-side representations, or task-level behavior, providing limited supervision for how visual semantics are organized across intermediate layers. We propose HiSVR, a hierarchical semantic visual reconstruction method for post-training unified multimodal models. A frozen semantic visual tokenizer extracts residual semantic codes from each training image, which supervise image-associated hidden states at different Transformer depths. Shallow layers predict shorter semantic-code prefixes, while deeper layers reconstruct longer prefixes, yielding coarse-to-fine supervision over intermediate representations. To balance the differing optimization difficulty across depths and prefix lengths, we introduce an uncertainty-weighted progressive reconstruction loss. HiSVR is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving the original architecture and inference cost. Experiments on unified multimodal backbones show that HiSVR improves visual understanding while maintaining image generation quality. These results indicate that hierarchical semantic reconstruction effectively regularizes intermediate representations in unified multimodal models.

paper.title: STAR: Detecting Inference-time Backdoors in LLM Reasoning via Prior-Posterior Amplification
paper.abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly rely on explicit reasoning mechanisms such as Chain-of-Thought, but these reasoning traces also create a new attack surface for inference-time backdoors that steer the model toward malicious reasoning paths without modifying its parameters. Such attacks can remain linguistically coherent, making them difficult to detect with surface-, consistency-, or confidence-based signals. We propose \textbf{STAR}, a lightweight detection framework that compares input-conditioned token probabilities with prior-only reasoning probabilities. STAR measures token-level prior-posterior amplification and applies CUSUM to identify persistent anomalies in the generated reasoning process. Experiments across four LLMs (8B-70B), five reasoning benchmarks, and three inference-time backdoor attacks show that STAR achieves strong detection performance, with an average AUROC of 0.980, and substantially lower TFLOPs than high-overhead baselines such as Onion. STAR also remains effective under top-k logit access and the evaluated burn-in-aware adaptive attacks, while exposing a trade-off between evasion attempts and attack success.

paper.title: Sample Learning State Guided Dynamic SFT–RL Integration Post-training

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Post and Telecommunication

paper.abstract: Integrating supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Existing methods typically rely on sequential SFT–RL pipelines or static loss weights, overlooking sample-level heterogeneity and evolving learning states. We propose Sample Learning State (SLS), a rollout-based characterization of each training sample using two complementary signals: sample mastery and exploration-trajectory dispersion. These signals estimate whether reward-driven updates are reliable for the core task and whether current rollouts provide informative contrast for RL optimization, respectively. Based on SLS, we design a state-aware coefficient that dynamically balances SFT and RL losses, increasing the RL weight only when the model demonstrates sufficient core-task competence and the sampled trajectories provide useful reward contrast. Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math models show that SLS achieves state-of-the-art results on four in-distribution and two out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks. In multi-reward settings, SLS preserves core reasoning performance while mitigating reward hacking induced by auxiliary rewards.

paper.title: FrameBench: A Language Understanding Benchmark Based on Frame Semantics

author.affiliation: SB Intuitions Corp. and Nagoya University

paper.abstract: In frame semantics, sentence comprehension is assumed to proceed by relating lexical meaning to background knowledge called semantic frames, thereby enabling readers to implicitly enrich the text with unstated information. Recent large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of downstream tasks; however, it remains unclear whether they can reproduce the kinds of implicit enrichment that humans naturally make during comprehension. To address this question, we introduce FrameBench, a benchmark grounded in frame semantics. FrameBench consists of multiple-choice questions that test whether models distinguish the frames evoked by the same verb across contexts. We construct the benchmark for English and Japanese using FrameNet-style resources and a generation-and-verification pipeline with native-speaker judgments. Our experiments on a diverse set of models reveal challenges for small models, while several large models surpass the human reference scores. We release the constructed FrameBench dataset and the code for dataset construction and evaluation at https://github.com/SasanoLab/FrameBench

paper.title: Case-based Statute Retrieval for Multi-turn Legal Consultation with Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graphs

author.affiliation: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Statute retrieval in multi-turn legal consultation is challenging because users often describe evolving facts in colloquial language, while statutes formulate legal conditions in abstract terms. This mismatch makes direct query–statute matching insufficient to capture the intermediate evidence needed to determine statutory applicability. Legal cases can bridge this gap by documenting how concrete facts and legal rationales support applicable statutes. However, case retrieval is noisy: factually similar cases may concern different legal issues, whereas cases with dissimilar surface facts may share the same applicability rationale. We propose FR-MEG, a Fact-level and Rationale-level Mixed Evidence Graph for turn-level statute retrieval. FR-MEG organizes case-derived evidence into two complementary views that model case–statute relationships through factual descriptions and legal rationales. The two views are calibrated and fused with full-corpus LegalDense retrieval, enabling case evidence to improve statute ranking without limiting candidates to graph-covered statutes. Experiments on LexRAG show that FR-MEG improves Recall@10 from 38.83% to 43.81% and NDCG@10 from 25.64% to 28.23% over the LegalDense backbone.

paper.title: MEDitor: A Plug-and-Play Medical Multi-Agent Routing Protocol
paper.abstract: Reliable medical reasoning with large language models (LLMs) is hindered by a practical trade-off between accuracy and deployment cost: larger models often perform strongly but are expensive to host, while compact open-source medical LLMs can fail on difficult cases. We propose MEDitor, a training-free, plug-and-play multi-agent routing protocol that improves accuracy and traceability by selectively escalating disagreement cases. MEDitor first queries two lightweight medical experts and terminates early upon agreement. For disagreements, it escalates to an evidence-grounded coordinator that constructs option-aligned evidence, followed by a candidate-constrained judge that selects between the competing candidates or abstains. A deterministic fallback guarantees reproducibility. Across five English-language medical multiple-choice QA (MCQA) benchmarks, MEDitor achieves 65.94% average accuracy, competitive with representative \sim70B open-source models on the same evaluation suite. These results show that lightweight expert orchestration can provide a parameter-efficient and auditable route to competitive medical MCQA accuracy by reserving evidence-grounded arbitration for contested cases.

paper.title: Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford
Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford and Bar-Ilan University

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings that require coordination without communication, from human–AI interaction to safety-critical scenarios. Humans often overcome the absence of communication through focal points: salient solutions that naturally stand out to all participants. We present the first large-scale evaluation of how, when, and why focal points emerge in LLMs, comparing their behaviour with humans across cooperative and competitive games, including realistic search rescue scenarios, demonstrating when focal points enable effective coordination. Across more than 20 open- and closed-source models, we find that LLMs exhibit a remarkable ability to coordinate without communication, often matching or outperforming humans. However, the same models consistently fail in tasks requiring numerical common sense or culturally nuanced notions of salience. We additionally evaluate simple learning-free strategies that substantially improve coordination both among LLMs and between humans and LLMs. Our results reveal striking coordination capabilities, as well as social limitations in modern LLMs, and offer new insight into the latent notions of salience encoded within them. Our findings caution against assuming that LLMs share humans’ cultural and perceptual substrate when deployed in coordination settings.

paper.title: Personalized News Headline Generation via Multi-Agent User Simulation
paper.abstract: Personalized news headline generation has emerged as a promising avenue for optimizing user engagement and satisfaction in online news consumption. However, prevailing methods predominantly adopt an indirect modeling paradigm, inferring user preferences from related tasks rather than capturing their direct headline preferences. Direct modeling remains underexplored due to two primary challenges: (1) the scarcity of large-scale personalized headline datasets and (2) the risk of factual inaccuracies when models overly cater to subjective user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose USG, a novel multi-agent user simulator headline generation framework. USG introduces three specialized agents: the User provides subjective feedback to guide headline personalization; the Editor enforces editorial standards (i.e., factual consistency and no clickbait); and the Writer iteratively refines candidates via a Critique-and-Refine algorithm guided by feedback from the User and Editor agents. The multi-agent interactions yield optimal personalized headlines and reasoning chains distilled from the interaction trajectories, forming a high-quality dataset. This dataset directly supervises the fine-tuning of a standalone generator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that USG outperforms the strongest baseline by nearly 6% on personalization, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both personalization and factual consistency, while enabling efficient end-to-end inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Leah-HKBU/USG.

paper.title: DialPO: Dialectical Prompt Optimisation
paper.abstract: Existing textual-gradient prompt optimisers rely on a single Large Language Model (LLM) to diagnose failures, propose edits, and judge the results, conflating critique and refinement into one model’s judgement. We introduce DialPO (Dialectical Prompt Optimisation), a multi-agent framework that replaces the single- model feedback loop with a structured de- bate: an Advocate defends what the prompt does well, a Critic attacks failures, cross- examination filters their arguments adversar- ially, a data-isolated Synthesis model drafts the revised prompt from surviving arguments alone, and a regression gate rejects edits that degrade batch accuracy. We provide a theo- retical framework identifying three precondi- tions under which multi-agent debate improves the feedback-reasoning bottleneck of textual- gradient methods, and show that DialPO in- stantiates them by construction. Across 12 benchmarks spanning classification, reasoning, summarisation, and question answering, Di- alPO achieves the highest scores across various Target models, winning or tying a majority of datasets in head-to-head comparisons against each baseline while using 8–18× fewer LLM calls than beam-search optimisers. Compo- nent ablations across five Target models reveal that DialPO’s advantage scales inversely with Target-model strength, clarifying when dialec- tical debate helps prompt optimisation.

paper.title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
paper.abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computationally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens contain task-solving information. We present a mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K using _activation patching_: transferring token-level hidden states from an arithmetic CoT generation to a direct-answer run for the same question, then measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy. Across models, patching can elicit generations that lead to correct answers, revealing that individual CoT hidden states can encode sufficient task-solving information even when the original CoT trace is incorrect. This information is more prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs and is unevenly distributed across tokens, concentrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patching from language tokens such as verbs and entities more frequently elicits correct reasoning traces, whereas patches from mathematical tokens more often produce answer-proximal generations that rarely succeed. Further analysis shows that earlier CoT tokens concentrate recoverable information, while later ones require broader search to find the correct answer. Together, these findings show that CoT encodes recoverable, token-level task-solving information, revealing how arithmetic reasoning is represented, accessed, and disrupted.

paper.title: The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment
paper.abstract: Large Language Models are now common in student assessment, but we know little about how student demographics affect their use. Sometimes, considering student demographics may be necessary—for example, to improve readability for users with lower educational levels. However, it can also risk discrimination, e.g., when assigning lower scores to students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. We set up controlled prompts to test 1) explicit demographic effects, where we mention demographic details directly, and 2) implicit effects, where we use conversation history as a signal. We test these settings in three tasks: Automated Essay Scoring, Formative Feedback, and Metalinguistic Question Answering. We test six state-of-the-art LLMs on these tasks. In both explicit and implicit cases, the models pick up on demographic cues and can change their scoring, feedback, and answers accordingly. We find that LLMs frequently adjust the readability of feedback to education levels when it’s explicitly mentioned. On the other hand, implicit conditions produce unpredictable biases, such as in question answering, where responses from lower-education levels receive lower sentiment scores. Our results provide clear evidence of demographic sensitivity in LLMs for educational assessment tasks.

paper.title: Beyond Static EHRs: Dynamic Examination Feedback for LLM-based Virtual Patients
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant promise in healthcare applications. To better mirror real-world settings for LLM evaluation, dynamic longitudinal diagnosis-and-treatment simulation with virtual patients has recently emerged as a focal point of research. However, existing simulation frameworks are limited by clinical trajectory uniqueness, where virtual patients can only provide feedback based on information available in static electronic health records (EHRs). This limitation leads to simulation failures when unrecorded but medically sound examinations are ordered. In this paper, we formulate the task of Examination Feedback Simulation, which aims to dynamically augment the unique trajectory by simulating medically plausible examination results in response to clinical orders. To support this largely unexplored research area, we construct ClinTrack, a dataset curated from MIMIC-IV. We further propose a structure-aware evaluation metric SimScore to quantitatively assess the quality of simulated results, which shows promising initial alignment with expert judgment. Building on this framework, we develop ClinSim, a tailored generative model for this task. Experiments demonstrate that our 4B ClinSim model significantly outperforms flagship models with up to 235B parameters on this task, providing a critical foundation for creating more dynamic and realistic virtual patients. Code and other resources are available at GitHub.

paper.title: Challenges and Recommendations for LLM-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and for Low-Resource Languages
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks (albeit mostly in English) due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with a checklist of recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

paper.title: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages
paper.abstract: Real-world communication often requires pragmatic reasoning: interpreting meanings implied through context and cultural convention rather than stated literally. Existing pragmatic evaluation remains largely limited to English and high-resource languages, leaving Indic languages unexplored despite their linguistic and cultural diversity. We introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages, designed as a diagnostic evaluation covering Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. VakyArth evaluates models across five phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence; through multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation, with all items authored by native speakers. Across multilingual large language models (LLMs) of varying families and sizes, we find consistent failures on pragmatic meanings rooted in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions. Our analysis shows systematic differences across languages and tasks: MCQ accuracy exceeds NLI accuracy in all model-language combinations, translation performance does not reliably track pragmatic understanding, and Indo-Aryan languages show a translation advantage over Dravidian languages. We further show that automatic translation metrics can miss fluent but pragmatically unfaithful outputs, especially for implicature and deixis.

paper.title: Understanding Training Data Attribution in RLVR: From the Perspective of Causal Inference

author.affiliation: China Telecom and Northwestern Polytechnical University

paper.abstract: Training data attribution is increasingly used to filter, reweight, and prioritize rollouts in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, these interventions often assume that individual samples, transitions, or trajectories can be attributed independently of the other data used in the same update. We show that this assumption is not merely a property of the attribution estimator, but a structural property of the training objective. We recast training data attribution as individual treatment effect estimation and use the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) to determine when a proposed attribution unit is well-defined. This yields a simple criterion that attribution is only valid at the level where the algorithm assigns a stable contribution to that unit. Applying this criterion to RLVR, we show that the PPO objective admits trajectory-level attribution, whereas naive trajectory-only attribution is not well-defined for GRPO unless peer context is modeled. Experimental results support this distinction and provide preliminary evidence for group-level attribution under GRPO.

paper.title: “**Important** You should give me full credits!”: Exploring Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM-Based Automatic Grading Systems
paper.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has significantly accelerated recent research on LLM-based automatic grading (AG) systems. Benefiting from the strong instruction-following capabilities and broad prior knowledge of LLMs, educators can deploy AG systems across diverse tasks using only natural language rubrics while achieving satisfactory grading performance. Despite these advantages, new security concerns may also arise. In particular, prompt injection (PI) attacks have recently become a major threat to LLM-based applications. In the context of AG, attackers can potentially exploit PI vulnerabilities to manipulate grading systems into assigning artificially high scores regardless of the actual answer quality. Such behavior poses serious risks to the fairness, reliability, and integrity of educational assessment. In this work, we study PI attacks in AG systems, and systematically investigate the effectiveness of such attacks in educational scenarios. We further evaluate the effectiveness of existing defensive strategies against these attacks. Through comprehensive experiments under rubric-based grading settings, we demonstrate that current LLM-based AG systems remain highly vulnerable to PI attacks. We hope that our findings raise awareness of this emerging threat and motivate future research toward secure, robust, and trustworthy LLM-based educational systems.

paper.title: UniAttn: Reducing Inference Costs via Softmax Unification for Post-Training LLMs

author.affiliation: Tsinghua University, The University of Sheffield and University of Sheffield

paper.abstract: Post-training is essential for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to real-world applications. Deploying post-trained models faces significant challenges due to substantial memory overhead and noticeable inference latency. Existing work has identified significant redundancies in LLMs and proposed efficient architectures, namely intra-layer KV sharing and cross-layer KV sharing. However, these methods still result in high inference time overhead, remaining suboptimal for post-training pre-trained LLMs. In this paper, we identify that the Softmax operation is a primary bottleneck for LLM inference and discover that it is actually highly redundant during post-training. We propose Softmax **Uni**fication in **Att**e**n**tion (**UniAttn**), a novel post-training method that unifies Softmax activations across transformer blocks to reduce LLM inference costs. Additionally, UniAttn adopts a linear projection to refine the approximation induced by Softmax unification. Experiments show that UniAttn matches the performance of standard post-training while significantly reducing inference costs, outperforming existing efficient architectures during post-training.

paper.title: ORDER: Task-Conditioned Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

author.affiliation: Ecole Pour l'Informatique et les Techniques Avancees
Ecole Pour l'Informatique et les Techniques Avancees
Ecole Pour l'Informatique et les Techniques Avancees

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines typically rely on a fixed indexing and retrieval configuration determined at preprocessing time. This one-size-fits-all design is ill-suited to domain-expert settings, where heterogeneous queries require different chunking granularities, metadata constraints, and source-selection strategies. As a result, configurations that are effective for one family of queries often perform poorly for others. In this paper, we introduce ORDER (Optimal Routing for Dynamic Evidence Retrieval), a query-conditioned RAG framework that jointly adapts indexing and retrieval to the incoming query. Our approach first discovers semantic clusters over a given set of questions associated to a corpus and learns, for each cluster, a chunking strategy together with a suited metadata filtering and reranking configuration. At inference time, queries are routed to the appropriate pre-built index through nearest-centroid assignment. To further improve retrieval, we propose a supervised query router (QRe) that predicts which collections are most likely to contain relevant evidence, coupled with a Uniform Multi-source Sampler (UMS) that allocates the retrieval budget evenly across the selected sources. We evaluate our framework on large-scale, heterogeneous historical archives and show that conditioning both indexing and retrieval on the query consistently outperforms both naive baselines and strong state-of-the-art RAG systems in complex expert-domain environments.

paper.title: EchoLens: A Human-Speech Dataset for Auditing Demographic Sensitivity in Audio-Language Models
paper.abstract: Voice interfaces are increasingly moving away from transcription pipelines towards end-to-end systems that directly respond to audio inputs. This development in turn requires a shift in evaluation methodology away from transcription accuracy and towards more substantive markers such as response validity. We introduce EchoLens, a demographically stratified dataset of 20,008 recordings from 515 adult participants residing in the U.S., with self-reported demographic information across race, gender, age, accent and primary language, among others. Each participant speaks out loud and verbatim a randomized subset of 69 advice-seeking and estimation prompts spanning 11 domains grounded in the American Time Use Survey. Most prompts elicit quantitative responses from the model, allowing for direct analysis of output distributions across demographic subgroups without requiring reliance on LLM-as-a-judge. EchoLens also contains a documented audit protocol, which—in an illustrative application—we use to evaluate six current audio-language models. Under this assessment, we find that racial disparities are more frequent and larger in magnitude than gender disparities, with particular concentration in two models.

paper.title: Reading the Geometry: A Mechanism for When Frozen LLM Text Helps Tabular Foundation Models

author.affiliation: CMU, Carnegie Mellon University and National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Tabular foundation models like TabPFN and TabICL are often augmented with frozen large language model (LLM) embeddings when tables contain free-form text. Whether this helps is highly case-dependent: across 732 dataset–backbone–encoder configurations, 45.9% improve, 30.9% stay neutral, and 23.2% degrade. Using a fixed, outcome-free raw score, we define high- and low-readability strata before applying target-covariance Gaussian sampling, row–text shuffling, and pre-projection whitening. Each intervention reduces the mean gain in the high-readability stratum to near zero, whereas the paired intervention effects in the low-readability stratum remain within sampling noise. The first two interventions show that neither a Gaussian sample from the target covariance nor row-misaligned text reproduces the high-stratum gain; whitening further shows sensitivity to broad pre-projection geometry. Together, the results support a dependence on row-aligned embedding structure without isolating the covariance spectrum as its unique cause. The high-stratum Gaussian-replacement effect replicates on a second backbone. A within-dataset encoder ranking, Decision-Boundary Alignment (DBA), also shows stronger rank alignment with gain than the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) rank in our eight-dataset diagnostic.

paper.title: Modeling Distinct Human Interaction in Web Agents
paper.abstract: Despite rapid progress in autonomous web agents, human involvement remains essential for shaping preferences and correcting agent behavior as tasks unfold. However, current agentic systems lack a principled understanding of when and why humans intervene, often proceeding autonomously past critical decision points or requesting unnecessary confirmation. In this work, we introduce the task of modeling human intervention to support collaborative web task execution. We collect CowCorpus, a dataset of 400 real-user web navigation trajectories containing over 4200 interleaved human and agent actions. We identify four distinct patterns of user interaction with agents – hands-off supervision, hands-on oversight, collaborative task-solving, and full user takeover. Leveraging these insights, we train language models (LMs) to anticipate when users are likely to intervene based on their interaction styles, yielding 11.6-18.4% improvement over base LMs. Finally, we deploy these intervention-aware models in live web navigation agents and evaluate them in a user study, finding a 36.8% increase in user-rated agent usefulness. Together, our results show structured modeling of human intervention leads to more adaptive, collaborative agents.

paper.title: Cross-lingual Functional Vectors for Emotion Detection in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Function vectors (FVs) have recently emerged as a promising mechanism for steering the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by injecting task-specific latent direction representations derived from in-context demonstrations. While prior studies have shown that FVs can recover task behavior in structured in-context learning settings, their effectiveness on semantically complex tasks and their ability to generalize across languages remain underexplored. We investigate the cross-lingual transferability of FVs using multilingual multi-label emotion recognition as a challenging semantic classification benchmark. Specifically, we examine whether FVs extracted from a source language can steer task behavior in another language under both standard clean and perturbed zero-shot settings without providing demonstrations during inference. Across diverse cross-lingual settings, applying FVs substantially improves performance, suggesting that FVs capture language-agnostic, task-relevant signals rather than purely language-specific lexical patterns, and highlighting their potential as a lightweight and transferable mechanism for multilingual task adaptation. We observe that each LLM exhibits a relatively stable optimal range of attention heads for constructing effective FVs, and the pattern remains consistent across languages. In addition, FVs can partially replicate the task-steering effects of standard few-shot in-context learning while avoiding the computational overhead of processing multiple demonstrations, making them effective for large-scale practical applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingjie7/cross_lingual_fvs.

paper.title: Exploring Solution Divergence and Its Effect on Large Language Model Problem Solving
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used for problem-solving tasks. Most recent work improves their performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with labeled data or reinforcement learning (RL) from task feedback. In this paper, we study a new perspective: the divergence in solutions generated by LLMs for a single problem. We show that higher solution divergence is positively related to better problem-solving abilities across various models. Based on this finding, we propose solution divergence as a novel metric that can support both SFT and RL strategies. We test this idea on three representative problem domains and find that using solution divergence consistently improves success rates. These results suggest that solution divergence is a simple but effective tool for advancing LLM training and evaluation.

paper.title: KODE: Mining Implicit Domain Knowledge from Historical Experience for Text-to-SQL

author.affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models still struggle in real deployment, where users underspecify queries while databases enforce rigid schemas. The gap is rarely lexical; it lies in implicit knowledge—hidden joins, derived formulas, and domain-specific filters—that natural language (NL) omits but SQL must encode. We observe that this knowledge is not missing: every historical (NL, SQL) pair already records it, with NL stating the goal and SQL stating the steps. Treating the two as dual views of one program, we propose KODE-SQL, a framework with three agents: KODE-Miner aligns NL and SQL in a shared graph space and distills the unmatched regions into reusable templates; KODE-Solver retrieves these templates to generate schema-grounded SQL under a rule-then-retrieval policy; KODE-Critic verifies each candidate on the same graph and feeds successful cases back to the knowledge base. KODE-SQL improves execution accuracy by up to 11.1 points on the knowledge-heavy ScienceBenchmark, remains competitive on BIRD and Spider, and yields consistent gains (+4–7 points) when plugged into existing solvers—validating both its standalone strength and its portability as a knowledge module.

paper.title: Phonologically Informed Tokenization for German Speech Recognition: A Cross-Domain Study

author.affiliation: Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm
Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm

paper.abstract: German is a morphologically rich language whose syllable structure is exceptionally well-predicted by the Knuth-Liang hyphenation algorithm. We ask whether phonologically informed tokenization can serve as a competitive target for end-to-end speech recognition. We compare three tokenizer families on the Omnilingual ASR wav2vec 2.0 backbone fine-tuned with CTC: the pretrained multilingual character inventory, a data-driven Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) over orthography, and phonologically informed units from Pyphen syllabification and grapheme-to-phoneme conversion. Across 40 fine-tunes, we evaluate on three German test sets spanning orthogonal shifts: in-domain read speech, dialectal spontaneous speech, and standard-German spontaneous speech. In-domain, all phonologically informed tokenizers match BPE and the multilingual character baseline on both WER and CER. Under domain shift the picture splits along vocabulary size rather than the linguistic axis of variation: at small vocabularies, syllable-aware tokenization improves on dialectal speech, where phonetic surface forms vary but syllable structure is preserved, and stays ahead on spontaneous speech, where new word-forms violate vocabulary closure. A phoneme-level confusion analysis further shows that all tokenizers commit the same canonical function-word errors, indicating that the acoustic encoder, not the tokenizer, dominates the error topology. Our findings suggest that tokenizer choice may depend on the vocabulary budget as much as on the distribution shift expected at deployment rather than reducing to a single universal optimum.

paper.title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile visual evidence with memorized world knowledge when the two conflict. How they resolve this conflict shapes the reliability of multimodal systems, yet prior work characterizes it behaviorally without a component-level causal account. We combine activation patching across three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers) with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis. Across three VLM families, we find that visual grounding emerges by default, whereas prior grounding depends on a small set of causally necessary attention heads (2.5-4.8%) concentrated in the second half of the network. These heads enable answers from stored world knowledge (e.g., “red” for a strawberry) despite conflicting visual input. Ablating them flips predictions from knowledge-grounded to visually grounded answers in 68-96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts, but changes only 0.8-7.5% of visually grounded predictions, establishing an asymmetric causal structure. The identified heads decompose into routing heads, which modulate information flow, and writing heads, which directly project answer tokens into the residual stream. This structure is consistent across model families and scales, revealing a sparse causal circuit underlying perception-knowledge conflict in VLMs.

paper.title: YallaMorph: A Benchmark for Evaluating Arabic Morphological Generation in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: New York University and State University of New York, Stony Brook
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Alexandria University and New York University, Abu Dhabi

paper.abstract: Arabic morphology remains challenging for large language models, since fluent generation does not guarantee accurate morphosyntactic control. Existing Arabic evaluations mainly target downstream tasks and do not directly test controlled morphological generation from explicit lexical and feature-based input. We introduce YallaMorph, a large-scale benchmark for Arabic morphological generation covering verbs, nouns, adjectives, their cliticized forms, and invalid configurations. We evaluate multilingual and Arabic-oriented LLMs under diacritized and undiacritized settings over 600K benchmark entries. Results show that Arabic morphological generation remains difficult, especially for cliticized, unseen, and morphologically rare forms.

paper.title: Pigeonholing: how bad prompts hurt models, causing collapse and mistakes
paper.abstract: While in-context learning is generally shown to be effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), misleading or flawed contexts can cause performance degradation and mode collapse, an empirical phenomenon we term "pigeonholing". Unintentionally bad contexts can happen without jailbreak intent. For example, a user prompts the model to justify an incorrect math theorem or fails to correct buggy agent code. Specifically, we investigate pigeonholing in two settings: (1) when a user suggests an incorrect solution, and (2) when the multi-turn dialogue history contains the assistant’s incorrect answers from prior turns. Our evaluations across 10 verifiable and open-ended tasks with 10 different models show that pigeonholing manifests in three distinct ways: (1) repeating the incorrect answers from the context (causing a 38-40% performance drop), (2) reducing answer diversity in open-ended text generation, and (3) reversing stances on controversial topics to align with the previous user or assistant’s perspective. Further, we find that pigeonholing worsens almost monotonically with context length (i.e., conversation turns). Finally, while standard RLVR-trained models show improvements on clean prompts, they fail to maintain performance on corrupted contexts. We take a step towards mitigating model vulnerability by training with RLVR on synthetic errors, improving model performance on bad contexts by 43–60% over vanilla baselines.

paper.title: ShizhenGPT: Towards Multimodal LLMs for Traditional Chinese Medicine

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
Halmstad University and University of Copenhagen
Shenzhen Research Institute of Big Data
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen); National University of Singapore and National University of Singapore
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

paper.abstract: Despite the success of large language models (LLMs), their potential in **Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM)** remains underexplored due to scarce high-quality data and the multimodal nature of TCM diagnostics, which involve looking, listening, smelling, and pulse-taking. These modalities challenge conventional LLMs. To address these challenges, we present **ShizhenGPT**, the first multimodal LLM tailored for TCM. To overcome data scarcity, we curate the largest TCM dataset to date, comprising 100GB+ of text and 200GB+ of multimodal data, including 1.2M images, 200 hours of audio, and physiological signals. ShizhenGPT is pretrained and instruction-tuned to achieve deep TCM knowledge and multimodal reasoning. For evaluation, we collect recent national TCM qualification exams and build a visual benchmark for Medicinal Recognition and Visual Diagnosis. Experiments demonstrate that ShizhenGPT outperforms comparable-scale LLMs and competes with larger proprietary models. Moreover, it leads in TCM visual understanding among existing multimodal LLMs and shows promising results across modalities such as sound, pulse, electronic-nose signals, and vision, paving the way toward more holistic multimodal perception in TCM. We hope that the datasets, models, and methods of this work will inspire further exploration in this field. Code, models, and released data are available at https://github.com/FreedomIntelligence/ShizhenGPT.

paper.title: Relevance Supervision Can Teach Neural Retrievers to Prefer LLM-Generated Text

author.affiliation: Institute of Computing Technolgy, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy

paper.abstract: Recent studies show that neural retrievers often exhibit source bias, ranking LLM-generated passages above semantically similar human-written ones, which threatens the reliability of modern information access systems. While this bias is often viewed as a model-level property, we show that relevance supervision itself can induce it. Empirically, source bias is clearest in relevance-supervised retrievers, and the same encoders become more LLM-preferring after relevance fine-tuning. We trace this effect to surface-level artifacts in supervised retrieval data: annotated positives and negatives differ systematically in properties such as fluency and lexical specificity, and these differences parallel those between LLM-generated and human-written passages. As a result, retrievers can learn artifact-based shortcuts for relevance. We further show theoretically that, under contrastive learning, artifacts that reliably separate positives from negatives can be encoded into learned relevance scores. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose complementary strategies that reduce source bias during training and at inference: balancing artifact distributions in negative sampling and removing the artifact-aligned embedding component, respectively. Overall, our findings support a data-centric view of source bias: retrievers may prefer LLM-generated text not merely because of inherent model properties, but because relevance supervision teaches them to rely on surface-level artifacts.

paper.title: Iterative Natural Logic Verification for Multi-hop Question Answering
paper.abstract: Multi-hop question answering requires composing multiple pieces of evidence to derive the correct answer, making it particularly vulnerable to hallucinated intermediate reasoning steps. A common failure mode arises when neural generators produce intermediate sentences that are fluent but logically inconsistent with the underlying facts, which can subsequently mislead downstream reasoning. In this paper, we propose ITERLOGIC, an iterative natural logic verification framework for multi-hop question answering, which explicitly integrates symbolic verification into the generation process. Specifically, a neural generator composes candidate intermediate sentences from retrieved facts, while a natural logic verifier evaluates their logical consistency with the source evidence. Low-scoring candidates are iteratively rejected and regenerated, allowing the system to progressively eliminate hallucinated compositions. This lightweight interaction upgrades natural logic from a passive scoring component to an active verification signal that guides intermediate sentence generation. Experiments on QASC, WorldTree, and WikiHop demonstrate that ITERLOGIC improves answer accuracy, highlighting the effectiveness of iterative verification for reliable multi-hop reasoning.

paper.title: Steering Vectors are an Adversarial Attack Surface

author.affiliation: RIKEN and University of Roma "La Sapienza"

paper.abstract: Activation steering has become a popular way to control Large Language Model (LLM) behavior without fine-tuning. Since the technique is plug-and-play, users share datasets and precomputed vectors to steer model activations. However, we show that a stealth data poisoning attack silently compromises this pipeline. By substituting 4{-}6\% of tokens in the steering dataset, an attacker can silently align the resulting vector with an anti-refusal direction. This jailbreaks the target model while preserving the intended steering effect on benign prompts. Under this threat model, a malicious actor can distribute an apparently safe bundle containing texts, vectors, and weights, alongside an equivalence certificate that the end-user can verify. We test the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model-attribute combinations, observing that poisoned vectors reach an absolute attack success rate (ASR) of 20{-}55\%, +19\% to +51\% over a clean reference. The vulnerability is not an artefact of scale or of access to the victim: it persists natively at 70B, and a poisoning optimised once on a small surrogate transfers to unseen models that recompute their own vectors from the shared texts. Finally, we find that a refusal-direction orthogonalization defense can recover {\approx}82\% of the ASR gap without harming benign behavior.

paper.title: HTA: Temporal Reasoning Transformer with Temporal Context Encoding for Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting
paper.abstract: Temporal knowledge graph (TKG) forecasting aims to predict future facts based on historical temporal information and still faces key challenges such as event sparsity and complex long-term dependencies. While graph-based methods effectively capture relational structure, they often fail to model nuanced long-range temporal patterns. Alternatively, standard Transformers, while potent for sequence modeling, are fundamentally time-agnostic; their generic positional encodings overlook critical TKG-specific temporal dynamics. As a result, many approaches struggle to capture fine-grained temporal patterns, limiting their effectiveness in forecasting sparse or complex events. To address these limitations, we propose HTA (Hybrid Transformer Architecture). HTA first constructs a query-specific Attention-Ready Temporal Sequence (ARTS) by aggregating historical context along a query-centered temporal reasoning path. This atomic sequence represents timestamps as dedicated temporal tokens that are contextualized together with their associated relation and entity tokens. At its core, HTA employs a stack of hybrid Attention-Mixer Transformer Blocks that combine bidirectional self-attention for capturing long-range dependencies with MLP-based layers for efficient feature refinement. Extensive experiments on four diverse benchmarks show that HTA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, on the sparse and challenging GDELT dataset, HTA achieves an absolute MRR improvement of over 18 points, demonstrating its superior ability to model complex and noisy temporal dynamics.

paper.title: Cross-lingual Self-Consistency for Multilingual Reasoning with Language Models
paper.abstract: Despite expanding their multilingual coverage, the advanced reasoning capabilities of LLMs remain largely confined to a few high-resource languages like English. To address this, we propose an unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach to enhance multilingual reasoning by enforcing cross-lingual self-consistency—the principle that a model should produce the same final answer for equivalent problems in different languages. Existing methods are limited by the scarcity of multilingual reasoning data, and show weak generalization to unseen languages. Our approach requires neither gold answers nor parallel data, and it achieves average gains of up to 21.7% on MGSM across 10 languages. In addition, our method demonstrates strong generalization, with an 18.2% mean improvement on MGSM languages unseen during training, and up to 6.2% gain on 3 out-of-distribution benchmarks. These results show the potential of consistency-based methods to improve the multilingual capabilities of LLMs without requiring supervised data.

paper.title: How Many Instances Are Enough? Minimum Subsample Size Prediction for Stereotype Evaluation
paper.abstract: Stereotype evaluation for large language models relies on heavily annotated benchmarks, yet such evaluations are constrained by limited instance availability and are often sensitive to which examples are included. We propose a framework for predicting the minimum number of evaluation instances needed to preserve benchmark-level stereotype scores under specified error and confidence criteria. Our method provides a statistically grounded way to determine how much a benchmark can be reduced without materially changing the resulting evaluation outcome.
