We support the framework with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on three widely used stereotype benchmarks, CrowS-Pairs, StereoSet, and BBQ. Across datasets, models, and tolerance settings, the proposed method provides reliable subsample-size guidance without exception. As an additional extension, we show that our approach can also guide compact synthetic stereotype evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that benchmark-level stereotype evaluation can often be conducted with far fewer instances than the original datasets require, offering a practical and principled approach to more efficient bias assessment.

paper.title: Unsupervised Post-Training of Foundation Models: A Survey

author.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

paper.abstract: Foundation-model post-training usually relies on human labels, preference data, stronger teachers, or executable verifiers. We study Unsupervised Post-Training (UPT): update-bearing adaptation on unlabeled inputs whose learning signal is derived from same-lineage model artifacts rather than an external oracle. We catalog 80 strict UPT methods and organize them by the object that supplies the update signal: a prediction statistic, a sample relation, a self-generated target, or an internal evaluator. Beyond inventory, we show how the choice of internal signal and task structure determines whether post-training improves the model or recursively amplifies error. An orthogonal Input Visibility × Update Persistence view maps deployment regimes and defines a unified framework for UPT selection and evaluation.

paper.title: From Tokens to Regions: CUDA-Sensitive Instruction Tuning for GPU Kernel Generation
paper.abstract: High-performance CUDA kernels are essential for scalable AI systems, while Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle to generate correct kernels due to strict and implicit execution constraints. Existing LLM-based approaches either rely on costly agentic or reinforcement-learning (RL) pipelines, or adopt supervised fine-tuning (SFT) objectives that fail to explicitly model CUDA sensitivity, namely code tokens or regions tightly coupled with execution constraints. In this work, we investigate CUDA sensitivity from the perspective of token confidence patterns, showing that CUDA sensitivity appears at both token and region levels, where most CUDA-sensitive tokens are predicted with high confidence, while a smaller low-confidence subset forms regions corresponding to execution-critical structures. These findings suggest that effective CUDA kernel generation should both leverage high-confidence CUDA-sensitive tokens and preserve low-confidence CUDA-sensitive regions. Building on these insights, we propose CUDA-Sensitive Instruction Tuning (CuSeT), a low-cost post-training method within a simple SFT framework. CuSeT follows the principle of “from tokens to regions” by combining adaptive token-level masking with region-aware sample reweighting. Experiments show that CuSeT consistently improves both functional correctness and kernel performance across multiple model families and scales, outperforming standard SFT and advanced SFT variants, while achieving competitive performance against frontier CUDA kernel generation models with substantially lower inference cost.

paper.title: How Much Parallelism Is "Free"? A Principle of Near-Free Parallelism for Parallel Decoding
paper.abstract: Parallel decoding improves generation efficiency by processing multiple decode positions within a single decode forward, but reported speedups conflate algorithmic token utilization with the system cost of executing multiple positions. We isolate the system side by introducing Near-Free Parallelism (NFP), the maximum number of positions executable at near-free latency. Analyzing Dense FFNs, MoE FFNs, and Attention against an idle-compute baseline, we find that NFP is shaped not by memory-bound resource slack alone, but also by implementation-induced kernel-granularity slack. Based on these mechanisms, we establish a Near-Free Parallelism principle that predicts the NFP boundary from hardware balance and implementation granularity. Validation on representative Dense and MoE models—spanning both diffusion and autoregressive decoding—shows that the principle accurately predicts practical NFP boundaries, revealing that the standard idle-compute intuition over-predicts them by 2.4–23x in over half of the evaluated deployment settings—offering a system-side budget for parallelism selection and model-system co-design.

paper.title: EvA: An Evidence-First Audio Understanding Paradigm for LALMs

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

paper.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) still struggle in complex acoustic scenes because they often fail to preserve task-relevant acoustic evidence before reasoning begins. We identify this error pattern as the evidence bottleneck: state-of-the-art systems show larger deficits in acoustic evidence extraction than in downstream reasoning, suggesting that upstream perception is often the limiting factor. To address this problem, we propose EvA (Evidence-First Audio), a dual-path architecture that enhances acoustic evidence preservation through hierarchical aggregation and non-compressive, time-aligned fusion. We also build EvA-Perception, a large-scale training set with about 54K event-ordered captions and 500K evidence-grounded QA pairs. Under a unified zero-shot protocol, EvA achieves the best open-source Perception results on MMAU, MMAR, and MMSU, with the largest gains on perception-heavy splits. Human evaluation on open-ended captioning further shows improved fine-grained acoustic coverage and caption quality. These results support the evidence-first hypothesis: stronger audio understanding depends on preserving acoustic evidence before reasoning.

paper.title: Critic-R: Improving Agentic Search using Instruction-tuned Retrievers with Natural Language Introspective Feedback
paper.abstract: Agentic search systems iteratively interact with retrieval models to answer complex queries. Despite substantial progress, optimizing retrievers for agentic search remains challenging, often requiring heavy co-training or gold-standard annotations that limit real-world applicability. We propose Critic-R, a framework that explicitly closes the feedback loop between the reasoning agent and the retrieval model during both inference and training. Critic-R introduces a critic model that evaluates the agent’s introspective reasoning trace after consuming retrieved evidence to determine whether the retrieved context sufficiently supports the next reasoning step. Critic-R has two complementary mechanisms: Critic-R-Zero, an inference-time query refinement loop that iteratively rewrites queries and retrieval instructions, and Critic-Embed, an optimization approach for retrieval models that leverages successful and failed refinement trajectories as automatic supervision without requiring manual relevance annotation. We evaluate Critic-R on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle. Results show that Critic-R significantly improves both retrieval quality and downstream answer accuracy.

paper.title: Interpretable Predictability-Based AI Text Detection: A Replication Study
paper.abstract: This paper replicates and extends the system used in the AuTexTification shared task for authorship attribution of machine-generated texts. Exact replication was not possible because of differences in data splits, model availability, and implementation details, which we document as a case study in reproducibility. We tested newer multilingual language models (mDeBERTa-v3-base, Qwen, mGPT) and added 26 document-level stylometric features, using ablation, permutation importance, and SHAP analysis to assess feature influence. A single shared configuration was applied to both English and Spanish across Subtask 1 and Subtask 2. Averaged over three random seeds, the shared multilingual configuration performs comparably to or better than the language-specific baseline, with the clearest gains on model attribution (Subtask 2). The additional stylometric features yield small improvements, led by lexical diversity, but their contribution falls within seed variance once predictability-based probabilities are included, which remain the dominant signal. The study also shows that clear documentation is important for reliable replication and fair comparison of systems.

paper.title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
paper.abstract: Humans distill experience into reusable abstractions, e.g., strategies and cautionary reminders, and apply them to gradually solve problems more effectively. We study whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly benefit from such experiential abstractions. From LLMs’ solution traces on a training set, a stronger teacher or the LLMs themselves extract natural-language abstractions into a retrievable library. We explore two modes of abstraction usage: (1) inference-time retrieval and (2) reinforcement learning (RL) with abstraction-augmented training prompts. Experiential abstractions improve LLM performance on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks. Self-extracted abstractions match teacher-extracted ones, and our abstraction usage framework can transfer to other datasets and models. These findings suggest LLMs can extract and apply experiential abstractions much as humans leverage distilled experience.

paper.title: Act More, Decide Less: Skill-Guided Adaptive Action Chunking for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Rutgers University, Rutgers University and Rutgers University

paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for long-horizon interactive tasks typically follow a ReAct-style protocol, issuing one primitive action per LLM round. While this enables frequent replanning, it is inefficient for long-horizon tasks where many rounds are spent on routine action sequences. A natural alternative is to let the agent emit variable-length action chunks. However, naively training such policies with standard reinforcement learning fails: the agent either collapses to single-action behavior or over-commits to excessively long sequences. Both failures share a common root cause: the inability to learn chunk boundaries. We propose SPACE, which addresses this challenge by distilling chunk-boundary supervision from trajectory-induced programmatic skills. We induce two-level programmatic skills from successful trajectories, where subskill boundaries serve as direct chunk-boundary supervision. This temporal structure is then distilled into a primitive-chunk policy via hybrid on-/off-policy optimization with chunk-aware credit assignment. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that SPACE improves success rates by 7.0%-31.3% over the strongest baseline in each setting while reducing average LLM decision rounds by up to 78.9%.

paper.title: Copying Before Suppression: What Drives a Below-Chance Dip During Language Model Training?
paper.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability usually studies fully trained models, yet the computations that drive a behaviour can change while the model is still learning the task. On the Indirect Object Identification task, a model reads a sentence such as "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to" and should continue with Mary, the name mentioned once, rather than John, the name mentioned twice. Pythia models pass through an early training window in which they prefer the repeated name, so accuracy in a choice between the two names falls below one half while language-model loss on a fixed text sample keeps decreasing across the same window. The window reflects a temporary imbalance between two computations. We identify one cause of the wrong preference by selecting a set of attention heads that write the repeated name, on prompts separate from those used for causal evaluation, keeping that selection fixed, and then replacing each head’s final-token output with its average output on a separate set of non-repeated-name prompts. This improves the correct-minus-repeated logit difference in a separately trained 160M model and in the official 160M, 410M, and 1B models. At 160M, the head that lowers the repeated name in the mature model shows little of its mature behaviour at this point. It directs less than one percent of its attention to the repeated mention, and its output makes almost no direct contribution to lowering that name’s logit. Both properties grow over the interval in which behaviour recovers. Across the 160M, 410M, and 1B models, transplanting the corresponding head’s mature parameters into the early checkpoint recovers 35 to 68 percent of the total improvement in the correct-minus-repeated logit difference seen by the end of training. Related early-to-late reversals appear at further Pythia scales, in two independently trained GPT-2 models, and in OLMo. A mature circuit can therefore conceal a transient causal configuration that shaped behaviour earlier in training.

paper.title: K-FinHallu: A Hallucination Detection Benchmark for Multi-Turn RAG in Korean Finance

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korean Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced financial automation through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), yet hallucinations remain a critical barrier to deployment in high-stakes environments. Existing benchmarks focus on single-turn, English-centric tasks, leaving the multi-turn dynamics and linguistic-regulatory nuances of the Korean financial domain unaddressed. We introduce K-FinHallu, the first benchmark for hallucination detection in multi-turn Korean financial RAG, designed as a controlled evaluation of source faithfulness and answerability. We construct multi-turn dialogues from authentic Korean financial documents and inject hallucinations under a proposed hierarchical taxonomy based on context answerability that explicitly accounts for justified abstention. Benchmarking Korean-centric, open-source, and closed-source LLMs as hallucination detectors, we find that even the strongest models struggle with fine-grained financial diagnostics and refusal behavior. While fine-tuning an 8B model on our training split yields performance competitive with frontier LLMs, justified abstention remains the weakest axis across all evaluated models. K-FinHallu and code are publicly available at https://github.com/eunbyeol-cho/K-FinHallu.

paper.title: FORGE: Forensic Reasoning with Grounded Evidence

author.affiliation: Google and University of California, Riverside

paper.abstract: Forensic deepfake analysis demands more than binary classification: investigators need region-grounded natural language explanations they can verify against the image. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are a natural fit, but pretrained MLLMs fail systematically, producing globally coherent text that misses the small localized cues defining manipulations. We argue this is an inductive bias problem rather than a capacity issue: the image-text contrastive objective training MLLM visual encoders optimizes for whole-image semantic summaries, not patch-level forensic detail. The same mismatch explains why prior deepfake reasoning methods target either face manipulation or fully AI-generated content, never both.We propose \textcolor{blue}{\texttt{FORGE}}, which addresses the mismatch by routing a second visual stream into the language model from a Vision-Only Model (VOM) trained on dense patch prediction rather than image-text alignment. The MLLM’s native encoder and the VOM operate on a shared patch grid, which lets us interleave their tokens with preserved spatial correspondence; we show this beats naive concatenation. A two-stage adapter training protocol (generic image-caption alignment, then joint task-specific optimization) prevents the localized stream from overfitting to training-domain manipulations. Across face-manipulated and fully synthetic content, \textcolor{blue}{\texttt{FORGE}} produces region-referential explanations answering fine-grained attribute queries (“Does the \texttt{eyes}/\texttt{nose}/\texttt{mouth} look real or fake?”) and substantially outperforms in-domain baselines on cross-domain evaluations; region-specific evaluation and human studies confirm explanation faithfulness.

paper.title: Bias-Aware Orchestration: Role-Specialized Multi-Agent Collaboration of Heterogeneous LLMs
paper.abstract: Coordinating heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) can improve instruction following, yet current multi-agent systems often depend on manual role choices or repeated calls to one backbone. This makes it difficult to separate complementary model behavior from model bias and verbosity. We introduce Role-Specialized Multi-Agent Collaboration (RS-MA), a prompting-only framework that assigns candidate LLMs to four interpretable roles: Judge, Summarizer, Ideator, and Reasoner. RS-MA estimates role fit with audition prompts, aggregates role-specific rankings with Borda scoring, and uses the selected assignment as an inspectable role map. A refinement phase records judgment gaps and targeted edits before synthesis. On AlpacaEval 2.0, audition-selected RS-MA reaches an 88.86% length-controlled win rate, and a validated role map reaches 90.72%. A full 805-example ablation shows that single-model reuse attains high raw preference through much longer outputs, whereas the validated map improves length-controlled quality with moderate length growth. MT-Bench and FLASK further indicate preserved dialogue quality and balanced fine-grained skills. The results support explicit role assignment as a practical mechanism for combining heterogeneous LLMs when quality, completeness, and inspectable evidence are jointly required.

paper.title: Precision over Scale: A Polish–Silesian Benchmark and a Translation System Outperforming Open-Source and Commercial Models
paper.abstract: Dialectal machine translation remains challenging due to limited data and strong linguistic variation not captured by standard benchmarks, which often assume standardized and well–edited text. We study Polish–Silesian MT using neural and rule–based systems, evaluating on SiLTT — a new Pol–Szl testset, alongside established BOUQuET and FLORES benchmarks. Results show our rule–based system is consistently strongest on SiLTT and BOUQuET datasets and that TranslateGemma fine–tuned on a curated dataset improves over strong neural baselines but does not surpass the rule–based system in dialectal settings. We release SiLTT and our best neural model to support further research.

paper.title: SciEmbed: Citation-Context Supervision for Scientific Document Embeddings
paper.abstract: Open scientific document embedders are typically trained on binary citation edges between paper title-abstract pairs. This signal discards the citation context sentence: a domain-expert description of the cited paper, written by the citing author. We use these sentences as the primary contrastive supervision signal to train SciEmbed, an open 149M ModernBERT-base encoder. On the official SciRepEval benchmark it reaches 66.85 over three seeds, surpassing prior open scientific embedders such as SPECTER2 and SciNCL. To isolate what the supervision source contributes, we compare against IBM Granite R2, a same-size ModernBERT peer trained on general retrieval data. Using only open citation-context data, SciEmbed matches Granite R2 to within 0.6 on the SciRepEval macro overall while specialising in the opposite direction: it leads regression tasks tied to paper impact by 2.3 points, where Granite R2 instead leads classification, proximity, and search. A 28-configuration sweep over recipes and alternative supervision signals does not improve on this result, consistent with the specialisation tracking the supervision source rather than the training recipe. Training at longer contexts yields monotonic gains on a body-fact retrieval probe within our recipe. We release the model, training pipeline, and evaluation harness as a fully open, citation-context-supervised baseline with a distinct, reproducible specialisation pattern.

paper.title: Can LLMs Design Computational Machines? Pushdown Automaton Synthesis as a Test of Structured Computational Reasoning

author.affiliation: Computational Intelligence and Operations Laboratory, Cognitive Agents and Interaction Lab (CAIL), University of Dhaka and North South University

paper.abstract: Artificial intelligence has long been evaluated by its ability to perform computation and structured reasoning. While recent large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in language generation, code synthesis, and structured problem solving, it remains unclear whether they can construct formal computational mechanisms from high-level specifications. In this work, we investigate whether modern LLMs can synthesize pushdown automata (PDAs) from language descriptions expressed in natural language or mathematical form. Because PDA construction requires explicit reasoning about states, transitions, and stack-based memory, it provides a controlled test of structured symbolic reasoning. We introduce the task of pushdown automaton synthesis and develop an automated evaluation framework that verifies generated PDAs through structural buildability checks and execution-based validation. Using a benchmark of context-free languages with labeled test cases, we evaluate contemporary LLMs and analyze their ability to construct and execute formal computational machines. Our results show that current state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to reliably construct executable PDAs, indicating that synthesizing computational mechanisms requiring coordinated reasoning over state transitions and stack-based memory manipulation remains challenging for present-day models. All code and data are available at: https://github.com/Dip-to/Pushdown-Automaton-Synthesis-Dataset.git

paper.title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
paper.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

paper.title: A Benchmark for the Generation and Evaluation of Scientific Architecture Diagrams in HTML/SVG
paper.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can now automate many parts of scientific writing, architectural figure generation faces a critical modality bottleneck because image outputs are inherently difficult to edit, verify, and integrate into text-native LLM workflows. To enable fully text-driven synthesis, we propose a new task: generating architectural figures as pure HTML/SVG source code. Furthermore, we introduce FigureCode, a novel benchmark that evaluates structural fidelity and visual properties through code-based evaluation. Our benchmark improves agreement with human judgments by 0.35 Kendall’s τ over prior VLM-based methods. Moreover, the figure-as-code paradigm improves edit-instruction success rate by 30% and retrieval F1 score by 25.3% over baselines, while achieving 66.1% WCAG/ARIA accessibility coverage.

paper.title: What Attention Recalls and Recurrence Controls in Hybrid Language Models

author.affiliation: Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Higher School of Economics

paper.abstract: Hybrid language models combine attention with a fixed-size recurrent state, but the role of each channel remains unclear. We introduce two cache-level interventions. Split-prefill keeps only the KV cache or only the recurrent state from a prefilled context, then generates an answer. State-swap pairs the KV cache from one context with the recurrent state from another in a single forward pass. On Qwen3.5 and Falcon-H1, the two channels split cleanly. Exact retrieval survives only through attention (64–98% of full accuracy) and collapses to zero through recurrence. Output language and persona reverse the pattern: both survive recurrence (70–80%) while KV-only drops to 1% language accuracy. State-swap confirms this causally: the answer takes its value from the KV side and its language from the recurrent side. Recurrent-only generation also accepts words that were never in the context but share meaning or parts with seen items. Attention provides a lookup over what was said; the recurrent state shapes how the model says it next.

paper.title: Brain Translation: Multitask Sequence-to-Sequence Modeling for Intracortical Attempted Speech Decoding
paper.abstract: Decoding language from intracortical activity is a sequence transduction problem that stress-tests modern NLP methods: inputs are high-dimensional and nonstationary, alignment to linguistic units is unknown, and training data are orders of magnitude smaller than in standard translation or speech recognition. We study attempted-speech decoding from intracortical recordings as a neural-to-language translation task and ask what contextual sequence-to-sequence modeling contributes beyond the framewise connectionist temporal classification (CTC) pipelines that dominate this domain. We introduce a multitask Transformer encoder–decoder that jointly predicts phonemes, words (via a BART-initialized decoder), and auxiliary acoustic features, together with a day-conditioned calibration module (Neural Hammer Scalpel, NHS) that combines a global affine transform with feature-wise linear modulation to handle session-level distribution shift. On the Willet et al. dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art phoneme error rate (14.3%); direct word decoding reaches 25.6% WER, falling to 19.4% with rescoring, however still trailing multi-stage systems with heavy language-model refinement. Ablations and held-out-day experiments quantify the contributions of multitask supervision and NHS and the cost of session drift, while attention analyses reveal recurring temporal chunking that phoneme and word decoders consume differently. Together, these results position seq2seq modeling as both a competitive decoder and an interpretable probe for how language evidence is organized in neural inputs.

paper.title: Below the Noise Floor: Bimodal Seed Collapse and Distinct Failure Modes in Small-Model Knowledge Distillation
paper.abstract: Function routing—selecting the correct API call from a fixed catalog given a natural-language request — is a deployment problem where small students are attractive but knowledge distillation gains are typically reported single-seed, at scales where seed variance is unknown. On a 740-instance healthcare API routing task with a 1.5B Qwen student and a 20B teacher, we compare eight KD variants against supervised cross-entropy, using three to six seeds for key configurations. We find: (i) per-seed standard deviation ranges from 2.8 to 48.7 percentage points, swallowing every claimed KD gain below five points; (ii) three of seven KD variants exhibit bimodal collapse, with at least one in three to five seeds falling below 55% accuracy while the others train normally, and a fourth showing elevated variance; (iii) collapse has distinct modes — wrong-function selection for ce_Knowledge Distillation and ce_paraphrase, and a previously undocumented output-truncation mode for reasoning_kd, where the model emits reasoning but terminates before producing a function name (0.9% accuracy); (iv) only progressive_kd and rank_kd avoid collapse across observed seeds, with σ ≤ 3.9 pp; (v) a naive cross-split +3.78 pp gain from input enrichment reverses to −2.70 pp under controlled within-split multi-seed re-testing. Single-seed evaluation is therefore unable to detect central failure modes in small-model KD.

paper.title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models

author.affiliation: Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Higher School of Economics and Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) and Innopolis University

paper.abstract: Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/WRDO.

paper.title: UTP-Bench: Uncertainty-aware Travel Planning Benchmark
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong capabilities in automated travel itinerary generation. However, real-world travel planning is inherently uncertain: transportation delays, crowd fluctuations, and unexpected stochastic delays frequently invalidate otherwise feasible schedules. Existing benchmarks like TravelPlanner and TripCraft assume deterministic environments, evaluating only static constraint satisfaction and ignoring whether generated plans remain robust when such uncertainties arise.To address this limitation, we introduce UTP-Bench, a large-scale benchmark for uncertainty-aware travel planning. The dataset integrates real-world travel data spanning 504 cities of India, including attractions, restaurants, accommodations, and multi-modal transportation networks. To model realistic disruptions, UTP-Bench incorporates empirical delay distributions and crowd-density patterns collected from major cities, enabling evaluation of travel plans under stochastic conditions.We further propose three evaluation metrics, namely Buffer Adequacy Score (BAS), Crowd-Aware Timing Score (CATS), and Transport Delay Absorption Score (TDAS), which quantify the ability of generated itineraries to maintain robustness against transit delays and crowd variability. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-5, Qwen3, Mistral and Phi-4 reveal substantial gaps between model-generated and human-authored plans, particularly in temporal buffering, delay-aware transportation scheduling, and crowd-sensitive planning.

paper.title: RiskGuard: Hypergraph-Based Pre-Execution Risk Control for Long-Horizon Tool Use

author.affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: In long-horizon tool use, early-step defects passing per-call checks often propagate silently across dependency chains to cause irreversible late-stage failures—a propagation class accounting for 73.0% of diagnosed Vanilla FC failures. Because these defects are locally valid (stepwise legality) yet manifest differently across tool boundaries (semantic heterogeneity), they easily evade standard per-call guardrails and post-hoc reflection, necessitating proactive pre-execution risk anticipation. To this end, we formalize the pre-execution risk propagation problem and propose RiskGuard, a training-free, dev-calibrated runtime controller. To capture the multi-source, conjunctive dependencies inherent in tool composition, RiskGuard models execution traces via a typed dependency hypergraph. Meanwhile, a Referential/Constraint/Operational (R/C/O) kernel tracks risk transitions across semantic boundaries. Replacing rigid binary blocking, a five-mode intervention rule selects the lowest-commitment feasible response to mitigate risks smoothly. Evaluated on ToolSandbox-hard, pooled τ²-Bench, and ToolHop, RiskGuard achieves absolute gains of +0.133 Sim (0.281 → 0.414), +9.2 pp pass@1, and +4.85 pp accuracy over the baseline, with depth diagnostics showing stronger gains on harder dependency slices.

paper.title: SimDiff-DNS: Simplex Diffusion with Dynamic Noise Scheduling for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
paper.abstract: Temporal knowledge graph reasoning (TKGR) is crucial for capturing dynamic relational dependencies and inferring evolving facts. However, existing embedding-based and diffusion-based methods primarily rely on Euclidean point embeddings and face two limitations: (1) sparse entities may suffer from embedding crowding and norm-sensitive scoring, especially under limited supervision in long-tail temporal knowledge graphs; (2) uniform noise schedules in diffusion models ignore temporal heterogeneity and instance-level prediction difficulty. To address these challenges, we propose SimDiff-DNS (Simplex Diffusion with Dynamic Noise Scheduling), a simplex-anchored logit diffusion framework for TKGR. First, we represent entity states as probability distributions on the simplex and obtain continuous embeddings as convex combinations of learnable entity basis vectors. This simplex-coordinate parameterization provides a probabilistic view of uncertainty and alleviates norm-sensitive ranking behavior for sparse entities. Second, we introduce a difficulty-aware dynamic noise scheduling strategy for the training corruption process, which adjusts the noise applied to target-entity logits according to a bounded difficulty score. Extensive experiments on three TKGR datasets show that SimDiff-DNS consistently improves over the diffusion-based baseline (improving MRR by 3.25 points on ICEWS14) and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art results on several metrics. Additional diagnostic analyses further demonstrate its benefits for long-tail entities, calibration, and ranking stability.

paper.title: ActTraitBench: Quantifying the Knowledge-Decision Gap in Large Language Models via Human-Grounded Behavioral Validation
paper.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can convincingly simulate personas in explicit self-reports, they often deviate in implicit behavioral decisions, revealing a substantial Knowledge–Decision Gap (GKD). Existing benchmarks struggle to measure this discrepancy due to limited construct validity, multidimensional entanglement, and distributional biases in LLM-based evaluation. To address these issues, we propose ActTraitBench, a human-grounded evaluation framework for measuring personality consistency in LLMs. Grounded in empirical human data, ActTraitBench establishes one-to-one mappings between psychometric facets and behavioral paradigms and applies Distributional Calibration via Quantile Mapping to reduce distributional mismatch between LLM-judge scores and human responses. Experiments on 14 mainstream LLMs reveal substantial knowledge–decision gaps and show that assigned personas are reflected more consistently in self-reports than in behavioral decisions for most evaluated models. To mitigate this gap, we further introduce the Chain of Cognitive Alignment (CoCA), an inference-time intervention that reduces GKD for 12 of the 13 models with paired results. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Selina233/ActTraitBench.

paper.title: AgenticTagger: Generating Structured Item Representation for Recommendation with LLM Agents

author.affiliation: University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego

paper.abstract: High-quality representations are a core requirement for effective recommendation. In this work, we study the problem of LLM-based descriptor generation, i.e., generating keyphrase-like natural language item representations with minimal constraints on downstream applications. However, open-ended generation provides little control over the generation space, leading to high cardinality, low-performance descriptors that render downstream modeling challenging. To this end, we propose AgenticTagger, a framework that queries LLMs to represent items with text descriptors drawn from an automatically mined vocabulary.AgenticTagger features two core stages: (1) a vocabulary-building stage in which a set of hierarchical, low-cardinality, and high-quality descriptors is identified, and (2) a vocabulary-assignment stage in which LLMs assign in-vocabulary descriptors to items. To ensure the vocabulary effectively describes the item corpus of interest, we design a multi-agent reflection mechanism in which an architect LLM iteratively refines the vocabulary guided by parallelized feedback from annotator LLMs that validate the vocabulary against item data. Experiments on public and private datasets show AgenticTagger brings consistent improvements across diverse recommendation scenarios, including generative retrieval, ranking, and critique-based recommendation.

paper.title: Web Search Is Not Enough: LLMs Fail to Account for Paper Retraction Status

author.affiliation: Université Grenoble Alpes and Université Joseph Fourier

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) learn scientific knowledge from static training corpora, while web search can provide updated information such as paper retractions. This matters for LLM-based literature systems because a model may have seen a paper as valid evidence, while current web results report that it has been retracted. If an LLM does not use the updated retraction status, it may cite a retracted paper as valid evidence. We analyze eleven open-weight models on the retraction-status task and ten on the citation-recommendation task. With web-search results provided, LLMs increase correct status answers for retracted papers from 11.0% to 94.0%. But the same models do not use the retrieved context as reliably when no retraction signal is present or when they recommend citations. On non-retracted papers under web search, models answer “I don’t know” in 52.9% of answers in the retraction-status task. In the citation-recommendation task, even when search results state the retraction and the prompt asks for warnings, models recommend retracted papers without warning in 10.2% of answers. A separate pattern appears for highly cited retractions. Models give fewer correct status answers for high-citation than low-citation retractions (89.3% versus 96.4%). OLMo’s training data suggests one reason. Highly cited retractions appear more often in training data, mostly without any retraction signal, so retrieved retraction information may compete with outdated training knowledge. Overall, access to web search does not guarantee that LLMs will correctly use a paper’s current status when answering questions or producing citations, highlighting the broader challenge of knowledge updating in LLM systems.

paper.title: Towards Understanding What State Space Models Learn About Code
paper.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as an efficient alternative to the Transformer architecture. Prior work shows that, when trained under comparable conditions, SSMs can match or surpass Transformers on code understanding tasks. However, their internal mechanisms remain a black box. We present the first systematic analysis of what SSM-based code models learn along with the direct comparison between SSM and Transformer models in this domain. Our analysis shows that SSMs capture syntactic and semantic structure more effectively than Transformers during pretraining but forgets certain relations during fine-tuning on some tasks. To investigate this behavior, we introduce SSM-Interpret, a frequency-domain framework that shows a “spectral shift" toward short-range dependencies during fine-tuning. Guided by these findings, we propose architectural modifications that significantly improve the performance of SSM-based code model by upto +6 MRR on NLCodeSearch. This demonstrates that our analysis not only explains model behavior but also leads directly to better designs.

paper.title: A Systematic Survey of Large Language Model Routing
paper.abstract: Available LLMs differ substantially in cost, latency, and capability. Their strengths vary across queries, so the natural question becomes: which model for which query? This is the LLM routing problem. Routing is already used in production, and the academic literature has grown across cascading, bandit, generative, and benchmark threads, each with its own vocabulary, each largely ignoring the others. We argue the field is best read along a single axis: the algorithmic operation the router performs. We organise the recurring operations under four labels. Predictive routers score candidates before their answers are generated. Adaptive routers try a model, observe the outcome, and adjust. Generative routers let an LLM itself reason about the decision. Infrastructure work studies routing rather than performs it, via benchmarks and adversarial analysis. This survey formalises the routing decision under this four-paradigm lens, traces the methodological development of the field, compares assumptions and tradeoffs across paradigms, and identifies open research directions revealed by the taxonomy. A continuously updated reading list lives at https://github.com/wuxingyu-ai/LLM-Routing.

paper.title: AgSynth: A Multi-Agent Reverse Synthesis Framework for Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning Data Generation
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models show significant potential in mathematical reasoning, yet they remain constrained by a scarcity of high-quality training data for visually grounded problems. Existing approaches commonly suffer from narrow coverage, image-text inconsistency, and heavy imitation of seed problems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes AgSynth, a multi-agent collaborative reverse synthesis framework. It first constructs solution logic programmatically and renders the corresponding images, then generates problem statements backward from the visual facts, thereby embedding answer correctness and image-text consistency directly into the generation pipeline. Meanwhile, AgSynth distills the core competencies tested in seed problems and performs divergent reconstruction, enabling synthesized problems to be substantially novel in both structure and visual presentation. Based on this framework, we construct the AgSynth-10K dataset, comprising 10{,}477 multimodal mathematical reasoning problems that have undergone two-tier quality control, spanning four major domains: geometry, algebra, combinatorics, and number theory. Experiments demonstrate that reinforcement learning training on AgSynth-10K significantly improves model performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks (WeMath +7.42, LogicVista+9.15), validating the effectiveness of this traceable synthesis paradigm. The framework is publicly available at https://github.com/Yaxuan7690/AgSynth.

paper.title: Lusopol: How do LLMs Handle Politically Charged Questions? The Use Case of Portugal

author.affiliation: NOVA School of Science and Technology
nstituto de Engenharia de Sistemas e Computadores: Investigação e Desenvolvimento
NOVA School of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted worldwide, evaluating their alignment across diverse cultural contexts is essential, especially when handling sensitive, politically charged requests. Yet what counts as “sensitive” is shaped by social, historical, and cultural factors, leaving model robustness across cultures poorly understood. We investigate this in the context of Portugal, a country whose layered history surfaces many culturally sensitive topics absent from existing benchmarks. We introduce Lusopol, a benchmark of 1{,}400 English and Portuguese prompts spanning seven thematic categories—from colonial history and the Estado Novo dictatorship to contemporary political issues—designed to stress-test models under deliberately controversial framings. Testing 16 state-of-the-art LLMs on Lusopol, we find substantial performance variance: frontier closed models and leading open-weight families set the pace, while European-focused open models lag behind. To close this gap, we synthesize a preference corpus of more than 7.5K samples. Targeted alignment training on this resource significantly reduces skewed responses and makes European open models competitive, demonstrating that culturally situated preference data is a practical path toward closing the alignment gap for underrepresented societies.

paper.title: UniFinEval: Towards Unified Evaluation of Financial Multimodal Models across Text, Images and Videos

author.affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown increasing potential for applications in the financial domain. However, the challenges posed by real-world financial scenarios, including high-information-density, strong noise interference, and cross-modal multi-hop reasoning, go beyond the evaluation scope of existing financial multimodal benchmarks. To this end, we propose UniFinEval, the first unified multimodal financial evaluation benchmark designed for high-density financial information environments, covering three modalities: text, image, and video. UniFinEval abstracts three progressive core scenarios from perception to reasoning and decision-making, and further refines them into six task categories. It contains 5,567 high-quality Chinese and English question–answer (QA) pairs constructed by financial experts. We systematically evaluate 10 mainstream MLLMs under zero-shot and chain-of-thought (CoT) settings. Experimental results show that Gemini-3-Pro achieves the best overall performance, but still exhibits a significant gap compared with financial experts. Further error analysis reveals the capability deficiencies of MLLMs in financial scenarios. UniFinEval aims to systematically evaluate the capabilities of MLLMs in real financial scenarios, thereby promoting the application of MLLMs in the financial domain. The related code and data are available at https://github.com/aifinlab/UniFinEval.

paper.title: Memes-as-Replies: Can Models Select Humorous Manga Panel Responses?
paper.abstract: Memes are widely used not only as static artifacts but also as interactive replies in online conversations. While computational research has focused on analyzing intrinsic properties of memes, the dynamic and contextual use of memes to create humor remains largely unaddressed. We introduce the Meme Reply Selection task and present MaMe-Re, a benchmark of 100,000 human-annotated context–meme pairs built from openly licensed Japanese manga panels. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) large language models show modest advantages over embedding methods by capturing social cues such as irony and exaggeration beyond surface-level semantic matching; (2) visual information does not improve performance, revealing a gap between understanding visual content and effectively using it for contextual humor; (3) while models can match human judgments when the humorous option is clearly distinguishable, they struggle to distinguish subtle differences in wit among semantically similar candidates. These findings establish contextually humorous reply selection as an open challenge for current models.

paper.title: TRIPPULSE: Multi-Agent Travel Planning with Review-Grounded Reasoning
paper.abstract: Travel itinerary generation requires balancing strict spatio-temporal constraints with human preferences. Existing LLM-based planners mainly rely on structured attributes and predefined traveler personas, but real travel decisions are often shaped by reviews that reveal experiential factors such as comfort, safety, service quality, ambiance, crowding, and hidden risks absent from structured databases. Incorporating such review information is therefore critical to realistic, user-centric itinerary generation. We propose TRIPPULSE (Captures experiential signals from reviews beyond rigid hard constraints), a multi-agent framework for review-grounded travel planning. Instead of relying on a monolithic planner (and face context and reasoning bottlenecks), TRIPPULSE decomposes itinerary generation into specialized agents (each operating over localized contexts) for accommodations, transportation, meals, attractions, and events, coordinated through a global orchestrator with scheduling mechanisms that enforce temporal and budget feasibility. We augment TripCraft with 100K+ real-world reviews and introduce Review-Grounded Persona Alignment (RGPA), an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for evaluating alignment with human-centric travel experiences. Experiments across multiple trip durations and diverse proprietary and open-source models show that TRIPPULSE maintains strong constraint satisfaction while generating more personalized and experientially grounded itineraries.

paper.title: When Disagreement Meets Noise: Noise Robust Annotator Embeddings for Subjective NLP

author.affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia State University

paper.abstract: Subjective NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis and hate speech classification often involve inherent annotator disagreement, reflecting diverse perspectives shaped by annotators’ lived experiences. Although conventional approaches resolve disagreement through majority voting or aggregation, these methods risk erasing valuable nuances and minority viewpoints. Recent embedding-based and multitask models have advanced the modeling of annotator-specific judgments, yet their robustness to annotation noise remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate how state-of-the-art multi-annotator learning models perform in the presence of noisy labels, and find that embedding-based approaches are more robust than aggregation and multitask baselines on datasets with many sparse annotators. Furthermore, we propose a new methodology, Noise-Robust Annotator Embedding (NRA-Embed), which integrates Robust InfoNCE (RINCE) contrastive loss to enhance models’ robustness under noisy annotation conditions. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that NRA-Embed effectively captures subjective disagreement while maintaining robustness to noise, achieving performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art in clean settings while providing numerically greater robustness under noise.

paper.title: CPSD: Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation in RLVR

author.affiliation: Nanyang Technological University and Skywork AI

paper.abstract: Self-distillation in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses successful in-group rollouts to teach the failed ones, with no external teacher needed. Whether it actually helps turns on three closely related design questions that the canonical method does not handle carefully: how to construct an appropriate teacher context for a given loser, where in the response the distillation loss should act, and what kind of signal it should carry. The canonical Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) instantiation answers all three by default: a random in-group winner, a global distillation loss on the whole response, and a Jensen–Shannon divergence on the full top-K distribution. These three defaults compound into a catastrophic late-training failure that short-horizon evaluation hides. We propose CPSD (Counterfactual Patches Self-Distillation), which replaces each default in turn: pick the teacher by minimum embedding-weighted edit distance, localise distillation to an adaptive-stop counterfactual patch beginning at the first divergent token, and replace JS with a Plackett–Luce listwise loss that preserves only the teacher’s ranking. Across six reasoning benchmarks at a fixed 150-step budget, CPSD eliminates the SDPO cliff and lifts average accuracy by +5.7 pp over GRPO on Qwen3-8B and +4.2 pp on Qwen3-4B.

paper.title: SMUGRI-COPA: Evaluating Commonsense Reasoning for Low-Resource Finnic Languages
paper.abstract: We introduce SMUGRI-COPA, a commonsense reasoning benchmark for two heavily under-resourced Finnic languages: Võro and Livonian. Existing evaluation resources for these languages rely on a translated subset of FLORES sentences, limiting linguistic diversity and the evaluation of broader language understanding. To address this gap, we human-translate the COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives) benchmark into Võro and Livonian, creating, to our knowledge, the largest discriminative benchmark currently available for these languages. We evaluate a wide range of proprietary and open-weight language models on SMUGRI-COPA and compare the results with Estonian XCOPA. Our results reveal a substantial performance gap between Estonian and the lower-resource languages, with most models failing to significantly outperform random guessing on Livonian. We further find that enabling reasoning for GPT-5 substantially improves accuracy for Võro and Livonian, while its reasoning summaries show frequent reliance on explicit translation of the tasks. Our work highlights the challenges of evaluating endangered language understanding and provides a new resource for multilingual evaluation research.

paper.title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation

author.affiliation: Westlake University and Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University and Shanghai Jiaotong University

paper.abstract: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.

paper.title: MemesOverTime: A Decade-Scale Study of Meme Dynamics
paper.abstract: Internet memes evolve as they are repurposed across online communities, yet studying how their usage and language shift requires corpora that follow the same templates over many years, which existing resources rarely provide. To address this gap, we collect a decade of posts from Reddit meme subreddits (2016–2025) and introduce MemesOverTime, a semi-automatically curated dataset of 6.6M memes annotated with 6,584 unique templates. We use it to conduct an empirical study of meme template dynamics. We find that templates differ markedly in their temporal activity patterns: most reach peak usage within the first third of their active period, with short-lived templates peaking especially early. For long-lived templates, lexical drift is generally modest, with templates with more instances showing greater stability. Case studies reveal that creators spontaneously develop conventionalized expressions for some templates, while topical references shift over time.

paper.title: Contextual Observer Grounding: Evaluating Situated Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Reasoning over language instructions in embodied tasks such as robotics often requires understanding spatial relations from a speaker’s situated perspective. Humans infer such perspectives from shared environmental knowledge, activity context, and commonsense. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) appear capable of spatial reasoning, but their ability to infer a speaker’s viewpoint from contextual cues and interpret situated spatial relations from that viewpoint remains unclear. We call this capability contextual observer grounding. To study this capability, we construct the Point-of-View Benchmark (POVBench), a dataset of 3D scenes and queries that disentangles Inferred, Stated, and Given forms of observer grounding in natural embodied communication. Given multi-view observations and a natural-language sentence, models must localize unseen or underspecified targets from situated spatial and contextual cues. Across state-of-the-art VLMs, localizing targets from directional language remains challenging, even when observer grounding is made explicit. We find that explicit breakdowns of observer-relative spatial reasoning improve target localization. Our project page is available at https://mimo-owl.github.io/POVBench/.

paper.title: TEVI: Text-Conditioned Editing of Visual Representations via Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Vision-Language Alignment

author.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus
Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus, Universität des Saarlandes and Max Planck Graduate Center for Computer and Information Science
Saarland Informatics Campus, Max-Planck Institute and Saarland University
Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarland Informatics Campus

paper.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP are highly useful for diverse tasks due to their shared image-text embedding space. Despite this, the image and text embeddings are often poorly aligned, affecting downstream performance. Recent work has hypothesized that this can be attributed to an information imbalance: images contain more information than their captions describe. In this work, we propose TEVI, a framework that uses captions as a signal for what to retain from image embeddings. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders to disentangle image embeddings and train a masking module to selectively reconstruct the embedding based on a given caption. In a controlled setup with synthetic captions, we show that TEVI is effective at preserving caption-described attributes while discarding others. We find that this extends to CLIP models trained on natural images, where TEVI learns to mask meaningfully and allows retrieval based on conditioning. Finally, we use TEVI to achieve improved retrieval performance across coarse-grained and fine-grained benchmarks. Code available at https://github.com/neuroexplicit-saar/TEVI.

paper.title: Do LLMs Use Cultural Knowledge Without Being Told? A Multilingual Evaluation of Implicit Pragmatic Adaptation
paper.abstract: Many benchmarks show that large language models can answer direct questions about culture. We study a different question: do they also change how they speak when culture is only implied by the situation? We introduce a triad-diagnostic framework; applying it to four deployed endpoints to evaluate 60 culturally grounded conversational scenarios. We examine responses across five languages in three conditions: a neutral baseline (Prompt A), an explicit cultural instruction (Prompt B), and implicit situational cueing (Prompt C). We use an LLM-judge ensemble with explicit rubrics to score responses on 12 pragmatic features covering deference to authority, individual-versus-group framing, and uncertainty management. We define Pragmatic Context Sensitivity (PCS) as the fraction of the judge-scored Prompt A\rightarrowB feature shift that reappears under Prompt A\rightarrowC. Across four deployed LLM endpoints and five languages (English, German, Hindi, Nepali, and Urdu), the primary stable-only PCS mean is 0.196 (SD = 0.113), indicating that the tested models recover only about one-fifth of the explicitly prompted rubric-aligned shift. Transfer is strongest for authority-related cues (0.299) and weakest for individual-versus-group framing (0.120). We argue that multilingual cultural pragmatics is an explicit-versus-implicit deployment problem, not only a factual knowledge problem.

paper.title: Entropy Is Not Enough: Unlocking Effective Reinforcement Learning for Visual Reasoning via Vision-Anchored Token Selection
paper.abstract: While token-level entropy is commonly recognized as effective for credit assignment in text-only reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), it remains unclear whether this mechanism still holds in visual reasoning. Our controlled study shows that this mechanism collapses in visual reasoning due to the omission of vision-sensitive tokens with naturally low entropy. Although existing multimodal RL methods increasingly acknowledge the importance of visual perception, they struggle to satisfy the inherent demand for interleaving precise perceptual grounding with semantic reasoning, either lacking systematic visual measurements or overlooking that token entropy primarily drives semantic exploration. To address this, we introduce VEPO (Vision-Entropy token-selection for Policy Optimization), an effective RL framework explicitly integrating visual sensitivity with token entropy via a principled multiplicative coupling, where VEPO redirects gradient credit toward tokens which are simultaneously visually grounded and highly informative. Extensive experiments demonstrate VEPO’s leading performance, consistently outperforming the strongest RL baseline at 7B-scale and 3B-scale. Ablations further substantiate the soundness of our method.

paper.title: Riemannian Large Language Modeling

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
HKUST(GZ) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Current large language models perform next-token prediction under the implicit assumption that all tokens lie in a shared Euclidean embedding space, which treats every token uniformly. However, natural language contains rich structural relationships, including hierarchical, compositional, and cyclic patterns, which the flat geometry of Euclidean space cannot model well. To address this limitation, we propose rLLM (Riemannian Large Language Modeling), which introduces a token-adaptive positive-definite diagonal metric tensor into the LM head. This metric dynamically adjusts the local quadratic score for each hidden state and its context, allowing the model to better capture the relationships among tokens and prompts, with less than 0.01% additional parameters. We train rLLM from scratch across three different scales (2.8B to 5.0B parameters), covering the full pretraining, SFT, and RL pipeline. Extensive experiments show that rLLM improves Base CORE, a composite of 22 in-context learning tasks, by up to +2.5pp at the two smaller GPT scales and obtains higher ChatCORE at all three scales, with gains up to +3.0pp after RL. These results suggest that revisiting the geometric assumptions underlying token representations is a promising direction for building more expressive and capable language models. Code is available at https://github.com/digailab/riemannianllm.

paper.title: The Privacy-Hallucination Tradeoff in Differentially Private Language Models
paper.abstract: Both privacy and factual accuracy are paramount in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Concerningly, we uncover and investigate a _privacy-hallucination tradeoff_ in differentially private (DP) language models. First, we empirically show that models pre-trained or fine-tuned with DP tend to produce more hallucinations than non-DP counterparts, with increased severity as the privacy budget grows stricter. Second, we investigate model properties driving this tradeoff, demonstrating that DP mechanisms flatten output distributions, potentially redistributing probability mass toward factually incorrect alternatives. Third, through experiments where we control fact frequency in training data, we characterize how information frequency can reduce hallucination risks in DP models. Overall, our findings underscore the need for more nuanced privacy-preserving interventions that offer rigorous privacy guarantees without compromising factual accuracy.

paper.title: Beyond Fooling: Model Manipulation Under Explanation-aware Training

author.affiliation: University of Zagreb, University of Bergen, Radboud University Nijmegen and IEEE Computer Society

paper.abstract: Feature-level explanations are commonly used to interpret transformer-based NLP models. Still, little is known about how explanation-aware objectives influence model behaviour during training. While prior work has demonstrated training-time manipulation of explanations in vision models, its implications for transformers and token-level explainability remain unexplored. We study training-time manipulation of token-level explanations in transformer-based NLP classifiers and introduce sequence-aware objectives suited to text input. We show that explanation-aware training systematically alters token relevance patterns while largely preserving task accuracy. Importantly, masking and cross-method evaluations reveal that these attribution changes can coincide with shifts in functional model reliance rather than isolated failures of specific explanation methods. Our results suggest that apparent vulnerabilities of feature-level explanations can reflect deeper model adaptations, underscoring the need to consider learning dynamics when interpreting explanation robustness.

paper.title: Intervention-Certified Amplification: A Validity Gate for \sigma-Weighted Post-Training
paper.abstract: Post-training methods use training-side signals to decide which supervision to emphasize, but those signals need not identify behavior that is capability-bearing in the target environment. We probe this with DIAA (Dual-Implicit Adversarial Amplification), a per-sample σ = sigmoid(-βΔ) SFT/RL hybrid: after every literal Python code fence is deleted from the anchor data, the model still emits unexecuted Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) form on 29% of MATH-500 prompts, three times vanilla GRPO, and suppressing the form recovers accuracy. A paired within-prompt intervention decomposes the removable drag along GRPO → SFT → DIAA as +2.2 → +8.5 → +10.6 pp, identifying SFT imitation and σ-amplification as comparable sources; a teacher RFT with 0% TIR likewise trains a student emitting TIR at 45.8%. We propose Intervention-Certified Amplification (ICA), which gates the per-sample weight by a certificate derived from paired rollouts, σ_eff(x) = σ(x)·c(x; θ_c). Frozen and online instantiations cut TIR to 13.8% and 11.2%, more than halve residual drag while improving accuracy, and carry the joint improvement to held-out GSM8K without retuning the certificate.

paper.title: Don’t Forget Your Embeddings: Robust Knowledge Erasure via Precise Editing of Embeddings
paper.abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the ability to erase specific knowledge from them becomes critical for safety and compliance. Prominent methods seek persistent removal by updating the model’s parameters, yet the target knowledge often can be recovered through adversarial prompting or relearning. In this work, we hypothesize this limitation stems in part from existing methods overlooking the embedding layer. To address this, we introduce EMBedding ERasure (EMBER), a plug-n-play erasure module that leverages Sparse Matrix Factorization for precise erasure of concept-related features from token embeddings. Through comprehensive evaluations across diverse concepts on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that augmenting existing methods with EMBER consistently improves erasure efficacy and specificity across task formats, with minimal coherence loss. Moreover, EMBER dramatically improves robustness to relearning, reducing regained accuracy by up to 50%, limiting it to 35% on Llama compared to 70%–76% for prior methods. Further analysis shows that the coherence cost is localized, affecting only a small set of concept-exclusive tokens. Our work establishes that precise embedding-level intervention is necessary for robust concept erasure, and demonstrates that existing methods can benefit from such augmentation.

paper.title: Understanding Why Language Models Hallucinate: Testing Reasoning Against Priors

author.affiliation: University of Wisconsin, Madison, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, Rice University, University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Wisconsin - Madison

paper.abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers that violate prompt-level constraints. A key diagnostic question is whether these failures reflect missing knowledge, or whether the model has the relevant information but follows the wrong inference path. We study this phenomenon as *inference misalignment*: a mismatch between the answer supported by the prompt and the answer favored by statistically salient latent associations. We formalize this view with a latent key–task model, in which pretraining-frequency imbalance can cause a shortcut path to dominate the constraint-sensitive path and induce positive inference loss. The framework predicts two failure modes: task-retrieval bias in entity disambiguation and key-selection bias in action choice. We introduce *TrapQA*, a controlled diagnostic testbed with two components. *ScientistQA* tests disambiguation among similar scientists with supplementary factual probes, while *Real-Life Constrained QA* tests everyday constraint following under salient shortcuts. Our results show that hallucination can arise from biased latent inference rather than absent knowledge alone.

paper.title: Judging with Confidence: Calibrating Autoraters to Preference Distributions

author.affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology and Google Brain
Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University and University of Texas at Dallas

paper.abstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human values increasingly relies on using other LLMs as automated judges, or "autoraters". However, their reliability is limited by a foundational issue: they are trained on discrete preference labels, forcing a single ground truth onto tasks that are often subjective, ambiguous, or nuanced. We argue that a reliable autorater must learn to model the full distribution of preferences defined by a target population. In this paper, we propose a general framework for calibrating probabilistic autoraters to any given preference distribution. We formalize the problem and present two learning methods tailored to different data conditions: 1) a direct supervised fine-tuning for dense, probabilistic labels, and 2) a reinforcement learning approach for sparse, binary labels. Our empirical results show that finetuning autoraters with a distribution-matching objective leads to verbalized probability predictions that are better aligned with the target preference distribution, with improved calibration and significantly lower positional bias, all while preserving performance on objective tasks.

paper.title: Asclepius: An Adaptive Harness for Long-Horizon Clinical Agents

author.affiliation: Harvard Medical School, Harvard University and Seoul National University Hospital

paper.abstract: LLM agents are predominantly benchmarked on short, single-task trajectories, yet real deployments run for hours under contention, surfacing a different class of failures. We use the Clinical Environment Simulator (CES), in which an agent manages an entire emergency-department shift under continuous time and resource pressure, as a testbed: long-horizon execution failures manifest measurably in a single rollout under structured, multi-dimensional grading. On CES, current agents reach the correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap. We attribute this gap to three long-horizon failure modes, each operationalized as a per-trace counter: instruction-adherence drift, treatment incompleteness, and a severity-equity gap in timeliness. We then introduce Asclepius, an adaptive agent scaffolding with a self-evolving harness that rewrites the operating manual between shifts from trace-level feedback, an externalized clinical skills library for high-stakes regimen knowledge, and three isolated subagents that partition per-turn decisions across the patient queue. On held-out batches never observed during harness evolution, Asclepius improves critical-action correctness by 22% (p = 0.024) over a strong baseline agent framework while preserving diagnostic accuracy, with consistent gains across five LLM judges from three model families; on the full ten-batch set, improvements reach 25% on critical actions and 13% on timeliness. The three failure modes form a coupled bottleneck: decisive reductions appear only when all three components act together.

paper.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Residual Decomposition for Multimodal Intent Recognition
paper.abstract: Multimodal intent recognition predicts a speaker’s intent from text, audio, and video, enabling conversational AI and human–computer interaction. However, existing methods share two limitations: (I) the three modalities are assigned equivalent roles even though text alone carries most of the predictive signal; (II) nonverbal cues that complement text are mixed with cues that merely repeat it. We propose Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Residual Decomposition (AML), in which text produces the primary prediction and nonverbal signals enter only as a correction. The correction splits into Hierarchical Modality Calibration (HMC), which removes cues already present in text, and Asymmetric Multimodal Disentanglement (AMD), which carries cues that add new information. Extensive experiments on MIntRec2.0 and IEMOCAP-DA show that AML consistently surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods across all reported metrics, and additional analyses confirm the structural advantages of the asymmetric design.

paper.title: Reinforcement Learning Elicits Contextual Learning of Unseen Language Translation
paper.abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can translate unseen or low-resource languages by undergoing continued training or even by encoding a grammar book in their context. However, both methods typically treat specific languages, with limited zero-shot transfer at test time. To translate extremely low-resource languages at scale, we argue that a model should be able to use in-context linguistic knowledge regardless of language, rather than memorize specific training languages. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to unseen language translation given rich linguistic context, using a surface-level translation metric as the reward. Empirically, despite the lightweight reward, our RL-trained models effectively extract and apply relevant linguistic information from the provided context, leading to better translations on completely unseen languages than in-context learning or supervised fine-tuning. Our analyses suggest that outcome-based RL can extend beyond conventional reasoning tasks like math and coding to serve as a recipe for low-resource translation from linguistic context.

paper.title: A Recipe for Long-Context Reasoning in Large Language Models via On-Policy Optimization and Distillation
paper.abstract: Existing approaches to post-train models for long-context tasks face complementary limitations: (i) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides stable supervision but suffers from exposure bias; (ii) reinforcement learning methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) train on model-generated trajectories but struggle with long-horizon credit assignment and sparse rewards; and (iii) on-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level guidance but does not directly optimize task rewards. We study these complementary strategies for long-context alignment and derive a recipe that combines GRPO with OPD-style teacher guidance: the student learns from its own rollouts using outcome-level rewards, while a stronger teacher provides dense token-level regularization in place of the standard reference policy. This is especially useful when process-level supervision is difficult to obtain. To support this study, we introduce LongBlocks, a synthetic multilingual dataset spanning multi-hop reasoning, contextual grounding, and long-form generation.
