This misaligns with real-world deployment, where tasks arrive sequentially and may have different distributions. We study recursive self-improvement as online learning over non-stationary task streams. In this setting, reliable execution and fallback are particularly difficult with limited evidence: different branches of self-improvement see different tasks, so raw rewards conflate capability with task difficulty, leading to overly conservative or optimistic reversion. We propose Online Anchor-calibrated Self-Improvement System (OASIS) that runs an adaptive reference agent on incoming tasks, converts raw rewards into paired comparisons, and uses confidence-calibrated rules for branch continuation and fallback without evaluating every agent on all tasks. Across SWE-Bench Pro and DeepResearch Bench, OASIS consistently improves over both the initial agent and prior RSI baseline SSA, raising the SWE-Bench Pro solve rate from 51.6% to 56.9% using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and DeepResearch Bench from 35.18 to 39.31 using Gemini 3 Flash. This enables OASIS to outperform larger open weights and proprietary systems, including Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Minimax 2.7, Qwen3.6-Plus, and GPT-5.3-Codex, with sustained deep self-improvements rather than shallow cycles.

paper.title: Language Modeling Across Script Variants: The Case of Japanese

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and The University of Melbourne

paper.abstract: We investigate the effect of script variants on language modeling in Japanese, which uniquely combines logographic (kanji) and phonetic (kana) writing systems. Motivated by educational curricula in which learners are gradually exposed to increasing numbers of logographic characters, we simulate this staged exposure during training to study its effect on model behavior. We construct multiple versions of a corpus with controlled script transformations, including fully transliterated kana text and intermediate variants corresponding to curriculum-based kanji levels, and train language models under different schedules that vary the timing and progression of script exposure during pre-training. In addition, we propose a cross-script evaluation framework using multiple versions of a minimal-pair benchmark with systematically varied kanji usage to assess the robustness of language models to script variation. Our results show that training on a mixture of two extreme script variants improves robustness across script conditions, whereas curriculum-based progression does not consistently improve performance.

paper.title: AMARIS: A Memory-Augmented Rubric Improvement System for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Rubric-based reward shaping provides interpretable and editable reward signals for fine-tuning LLMs via reinforcement learning (RL), but existing adaptive rubric methods typically update criteria from local evidence such as the current batch or instance-level comparisons. This local view discards diagnostic information produced during training, making it difficult to track recurring failures, evaluate previous rubric edits, or raise standards once earlier criteria become saturated. We introduce AMARIS, a Memory-Augmented Rubric Improvement System that grounds rubric updates in longitudinal training evidence. AMARIS stores rollout analyses, step-level summaries, and rubric update records in a persistent evaluation memory, then retrieves recent and semantically relevant history to revise rubrics. We evaluate AMARIS across science, medicine, instruction following, and creative writing under both global and instance-specific rubric settings, with policy models from the Qwen and Llama families trained by GRPO and PPO. AMARIS improves over static, local-adaptive, and memory-ablated baselines, such as +2.8 points on GPQA-Diamond and +2.2 points on IFBench over the strongest baselines, while analysis shows that memory reduces oscillatory rubric edits and supports a progression from early failure correction to later curriculum advancement. The final rubric set that AMARIS discovers is itself reusable, and the online trajectory contributes measurably beyond it. AMARIS runs asynchronously alongside the normal RL loop, reducing blocking latency relative to synchronous rubric updates. The source code is available at https://github.com/qualidea1217/AMARIS.

paper.title: Sense and Sensitivity: Benchmarking LLM Clinical Triage Recommendations with Physician Experts
paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, it is critical to evaluate their reliability under realistic variation in clinical text. We study this question in clinical triage, comparing LLMs to practicing physicians under text perturbations that preserve the underlying clinical setting. We introduce a benchmark of over 6{,}000 clinical scenarios, 7{,}000 physician annotations, and 225{,}000 model responses. Using this benchmark, we make two key observations. First, LLMs are more likely than physicians to recommend unnecessary care at baseline, and this tendency increases under perturbed inputs. Further, we find that LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations. Together, these results demonstrate that LLMs can vary under clinically irrelevant textual changes, highlighting the need for deployment-oriented evaluations grounded in expert physician behavior.

paper.title: Behavior Carries Over: An AI Sandbagging Detection Method Inspired by Honest Inertia

author.affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security

paper.abstract: Reliable capability assessment is essential for governing and securely deploying advanced AI systems. However, "AI Sandbagging," where models strategically suppress their true capabilities during evaluation, undermines existing assessment frameworks by making it difficult to distinguish genuine limitations from strategic concealment. To address this challenge, we propose a new black-box sandbag detection method inspired by "honesty inertia," a psychological phenomenon where humans struggle to maintain deception after answering simple questions truthfully. We hypothesize that large language models exhibit an analogous effect: inserting several simple, unrelated questions, which target models should answer correctly, before the target query induces honest inertia, causing sandbag models to involuntarily increase accuracy while standard models remain stable. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets with various model architectures, we confirm the validity of this hypothesis and establish this differential response as a reliable, model-independent sandbag detection signal. We further provide interpretability support for this phenomenon from two dimensions: theoretical derivation and hidden state analysis of models. This work offers a practical tool for enhancing AI audit and supervision.

paper.title: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
paper.abstract: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

paper.title: DP-IPI: A Hybrid Differential Privacy Text Rewriting Mechanism for Indirect Personal Identifiers in Clinical Texts
paper.abstract: Despite the strengths of modern anonymization and de-identification techniques, the risk of re-identification remains significant due to the indirect identifiers remaining in texts. To address this problem, recent works have applied text rewriting under Differential Privacy (DP) to prevent data linkage by perturbing texts via noise addition. Such methods privatize \textit{all} tokens in a text indiscriminately, diminishing text quality and usability in critical domains such as in clinical settings. Focusing on \textit{indirect personal identifiers} (IPIs), we introduce a utility-preserving DP text rewriting method that only privatizes spans containing IPIs. We show that our method effectively reduces re-identification risks in clinical texts while being producing more coherent and usable output texts, leading to higher privacy-utility trade-offs. In this, we demonstrate the effectiveness of \textit{hybrid} text privatization, which leverages the promise of DP in an efficient, usable manner.

paper.title: Training with Subword Variants Delays Overfitting in Repeated-Data Language Modeling

author.affiliation: SUPSI - University of Applied Sciences Southern Switzerland

paper.abstract: Subword tokenization introduces a computational layer in language models, where many distinct token sequences decode to the same surface form while preserving meaning, yet induce different internal computations. Despite this non-uniqueness, language models are typically trained using a single canonical deterministic tokenization. In this work, we use non-canonical subword variants as a strictly meaning-preserving form of data augmentation. We introduce a lightweight training architecture that conditions canonical next-token prediction on sampled subword variants via an auxiliary causal encoder and block-causal cross-attention, without modifying the training objective or token interface. In data-constrained pretraining, augmentations with subword variants consistently delay overfitting under repeated data exposure and reduce held-out next-token loss across evaluation datasets. In multilingual fine-tuning, we find that the effectiveness of training with auxiliary subwords depends on tokenizer quality: gains are strongest when canonical tokens are highly compressed and diminish when the tokenizer already over-fragments the input.

paper.title: Don’t “Overthink” Pointwise Reranking: Is Reasoning Truly Necessary?

author.affiliation: OpenAI and Massachusetts Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: With the success of reasoning models across complex natural language tasks, researchers in the information retrieval (IR) community have begun exploring how similar reasoning capabilities can be integrated into passage rerankers built on large language models (LLMs). These methods typically employ an LLM to produce an explicit, step-by-step reasoning process before arriving at a final relevance prediction. But does reasoning actually improve pointwise reranking? We investigate this question through controlled comparisons of Rank1, a pointwise reasoning reranker, with two non-reasoning counterparts. Across in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, we find that Rank1 generally underperforms Rank0, an otherwise equivalent non-reasoning pointwise reranker trained using the same backbone LLM and underlying training data as Rank1. To isolate the contribution of Rank1’s inference-time reasoning, we then replace its generated reasoning process with a fixed dummy sequence. Surprisingly, this variant, Rank1-NoReason, can also outperform Rank1. Analysis of Rank1’s score distributions provides a likely explanation: once Rank1 deems a passage relevant, it assigns nearly identical relevance scores, limiting its ability to distinguish degrees of relevance and ultimately harming its ranking accuracy. We release all code at https://github.com/nourj98/dont-overthink-reranking.

paper.title: Beyond Lexical and Syntactic: Better Text Simplicity Analysis Informed by Psycholinguistic Research
paper.abstract: Automatic text simplification measures correlate poorly with human judgments and are disconnected from psycholinguistic research on comprehension. We propose a multidimensional analysis framework grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and the Construction-Integration model, organizing over 400 linguistic features into six simplicity dimensions targeting distinct comprehension stages. Using this framework, we analyze four human-annotated and six aligned simplification datasets. We find that (1) our dimensions predict human simplicity judgments better than established measures on most datasets; (2) current datasets overwhelmingly target lexical and syntactic dimensions while under-targeting personalization the dimension psychological research identifies as most impactful for comprehension; and (3) existing measures overall do not capture any specific dimension. These findings provide actionable guidance for building measures and datasets better aligned with how readers actually process text.

paper.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
paper.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, demonstrating strong performance in terms of ranking correlation, calibration, and interval sharpness. BEiTScore++ not only produces accurate predictions, but also captures aleatoric uncertainty arising from ambiguous inputs, and epistemic uncertainty due to limited model knowledge, making it a reliable tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

paper.title: RFCLLM: Evaluating LLMs’ Reasoning Ability of Network Protocol State Machines
paper.abstract: Mapping textual specifications into formal representations is essential for ensuring the correctness of protocol designs and implementations. LLM-generated mappings, used for networking security or testing, are assumed to capture a perfect understanding of the specification, which may not hold in practice. The goal of this paper is to assess the extent to which LLMs can interpret the specification correctly. We examine the degree to which an LLM’s implicit representation of a finite-state transition system–defined via natural language descriptions–aligns with a manually generated ground-truth model.We designed 4 tasks and 1482 task queries for 16 protocols. We evaluated different judge biases, observed the inherent difficulty gaps between tasks, looked into the effect of 4 context types, and the influence of protocol characteristics. Our work contributes to a step toward verifying whether LLMs can really be trusted in FSM (Finite State Machine) reasoning of protocol specifications.

paper.title: Characterizing Opinion Evolution of Networked LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with one another in multi-agent systems, from simulations of human discourse to influence operations and fully LLM-driven social platforms. These interactions give rise to new regimes of opinion propagation that are not yet well understood. We investigate whether classical opinion dynamics models, which have long been used to explain how interactions shape collective beliefs in human societies, can capture the behavior of LLM networks. Specifically, we quantify the relative contributions of classical opinion-dynamics mechanisms, including neighbor influence, stubbornness, homophily, and bias, to the evolution of LLM opinions. Among the mechanisms considered, a bias term capturing regression toward a model- and topic-dependent opinion emerges as a significant explanatory component, with its inclusion reducing cumulative estimated mean opinion error by up to 88%. We additionally observe similar trends across the evaluated model families, discussion topics, and network structures.

paper.title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
paper.abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves .57 micro-F1 on a 20 class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

paper.title: Gnosis Deepsearch: Structured Search Space Navigation for Complex QA

author.affiliation: University of Edinburgh and Farama Foundation
University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh

paper.abstract: Complex, multi-step reasoning demands agents to be capable of dynamically exploring diverse research directions and adapting plans on the fly. We introduce Gnosis Deepsearch, a schema-guided framework for long-horizon planning in complex Question Answering, where variables, clues, and constraints are captured in a structured state representation maintained across trajectories. This state is cascaded into parallel search paths broadening exploration without relying on sequential execution, thereby mitigating both limited search space coverage and catastrophic forgetting. We couple Gnosis with a retriever that sidesteps challenges associated with retrieval and LLM reading when longer documents are involved. Our retrieval strategy ensures that the most relevant snippets from longer documents are considered, showcasing several benefits within both Gnosis and a more general ReAct framework on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark. Extensive experiments on several QA benchmarks of varying difficulty demonstrate the strong performance of Gnosis across different configurations.

paper.title: Mind the Phrase: Annotation and Identification of Multiword Expressions in Grammatical Error Correction
paper.abstract: Multiword Expressions (MWEs) are an important part of language competence which are both commonplace across languages and challenging for language learners to master. Since Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) systems tend to provide suggestions at the token level, they may fail to handle the semantic unity of MWEs. We present annotations of MWEs in learner English essays while identifying their intended spans. This not only allows us to analyse learner MWE errors in more detail for the first time, but also enables us to build GEC systems that provide more meaningful feedback to learners. We have annotated 1,850 essays that were previously tagged for grammatical errors with various types of MWEs. We extend an error annotation toolkit with an MWE error-type and present a method that leverages these annotations to make GEC evaluation more explainable, enabling fine-grained analysis of MWE errors. Experiments with current GEC systems show that an edit-based model fine-tuned on our dataset achieves higher F0.5 scores for the correction of common MWE error types, demonstrating its effectiveness for handling MWEs.

paper.title: CultureScore: Evaluating Cultural Faithfulness in Video Generation Models
paper.abstract: As video generation models like Veo 3.1 and LTX-2 advance, their ability to accurately represent diverse global cultures remains a critical yet understudied frontier. Current metrics, such as VideoScore, only measure visual quality but offer no mechanism for assessing cultural faithfulness. Consequently, a model that replaces a Namaste with a handshake receives the same score as one that generates the gesture correctly. We propose CultureScore, a compositional evaluation framework that decomposes cultural faithfulness into three granular dimensions: Identity (who is represented), Context (culturally localized background), and Behavior (normative gestures and interactions). We operationalize this framework through an evaluation suite spanning 10 countries, yielding 6,174 generated videos across three state-of-the-art models. Our evaluation reveals that no current model achieves culturally faithful video generation: the best-performing model reaches only 56.8% overall CultureScore, with Behavior the most challenging dimension; no model exceeds 52.1% on behavior. Furthermore, the highest-scoring model (LTX-2) on visual quality was ranked last by native annotators, while CultureScore’s Behavior dimension shows the strongest positive correlation with human cultural judgment among the automatic metrics we evaluate, underscoring that cultural faithfulness is an essential criterion for equitable video generation. Data and code are publicly available.[<https://huggingface.co/datasets/ankurani/CultureScore>]

paper.title: Gradient-Stable Attention Heads Signal LLM Correctness
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate plausible yet incorrect answers, posing risks in safety-critical settings such as medicine. Human evaluation is expensive, and LLM-as-judge approaches risk introducing hidden errors. Recent single-pass white-box methods detect contextual hallucinations using linear probes over model internals, but their generalization to out-of-domain, out-of-task, and training-free settings remains poorly understood. We introduce HeadEntropy, a method that predicts answer correctness by measuring how susceptible each attention head’s pattern is to modification under further gradient updates. The key insight is that the trace of the softmax Jacobian is a monotonic function of 2-Rényi entropy, linking attention spread to gradient stability during training, even without the reference annotation. With no training, HeadEntropy reaches 0.736 AUROC, outperforms every training-free baseline in paired comparison across 5 models and 5 datasets, and matches a hidden-state probe transferred across domains, at under 1% of inference cost. We evaluate broadly across 5 instruction-tuned LLMs and 5 datasets spanning general knowledge, multi-hop reasoning, mathematical reasoning, claim verification, and medicine. The code is available at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/HeadEntropy.

paper.title: UI-Oceanus: Scaling GUI Agents with Synthetic Environmental Dynamics

author.affiliation: Peking University and Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center

Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center, Fudan University Institute of Systems for Advanced Computing, Shanghai Institute of Systems for Open Computing and Key Lab of HCST (PKU), MOE; SCS, Peking University

paper.abstract: Scaling generalist GUI agents is hindered by the data scalability bottleneck of expensive human demonstrations and reliance on ungrounded synthetic teacher supervision. To transcend these limitations, we propose , a framework that shifts the learning focus from mimicking high-level trajectories to learning interaction dynamics from executed transitions. Through a systematic investigation of self-supervised objectives, we identify that forward dynamics, defined as the generative prediction of future interface states, acts as the primary driver for scalability and outperforms inverse and backward objectives. leverages this insight by converting low-cost autonomous exploration into high-density generative supervision to learn a semantic transition world model from executed transitions. Experimental evaluations across a series of models demonstrate consistent gains from our approach: models utilizing Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on synthetic dynamics outperform non-CPT baselines with an average success rate improvement of 7% on offline benchmarks, which amplifies to a 16.8% gain in real-world online navigation. Furthermore, we observe that navigation performance scales with synthetic data volume. These results suggest that grounding agents in forward predictive modeling offers a promising pathway to scalable GUI automation with cross-domain adaptability and compositional generalization.

paper.title: MCompassRAG: Topic Metadata as a Semantic Compass for Paragraph-Level Retrieval
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems depend critically on how documents are chunked and searched. Fine-grained chunks can improve retrieval precision but expand the search space, increasing latency and cost; larger chunks reduce the number of candidates but make dense similarity less reliable, as each representation mixes multiple topics and introduces more semantic noise. This trade-off becomes especially limiting in deep research tasks, where retrieval must be both fast and precise across large, heterogeneous corpora. We introduce MCompassRAG, a metadata-guided retrieval framework that uses topic-level signals as a semantic compass for selecting relevant evidence. Instead of relying only on cosine similarity between queries and noisy chunk embeddings, MCompassRAG enriches chunk representations with topic metadata defined in the same embedding space and trains a lightweight retriever through LLM-teacher distillation. At inference time, MCompassRAG performs topic-aware retrieval without additional LLM calls, improving both efficiency and evidence quality. Across six complex retrieval benchmarks, MCompassRAG improves information efficiency by 8.24% on average with over 5x lower latency than the strongest efficient RAG baselines.

paper.title: Spatial Reasoning via Modality Switching Between Language and Symbolic Representations
paper.abstract: Human reasoning is inherently multimodal: when problems become difficult, we rarely think in words alone. We often externalize our reasoning by sketching diagrams or drawing grids to understand the underlying conceptual structure and avoid mistakes. Building on this premise, our research investigates: (a) whether grounding multi-hop textual-spatial stories into geometry-aware modalities, such as layouts or grids, improves reasoning compared to natural language-based inference; and (b) whether a model can decide when to rely on natural language reasoning and when to switch to a structured modality. We address these questions by introducing a switching metric based on trustworthiness and complexity signals, which estimates when grounding a spatial story into a structure is likely to improve performance. This takes a first step toward principled modality selection in large language model (LLM) reasoning. Across our settings, switching from natural language-based reasoning to a grid-based representation improves LLM performance by up to 42%, highlighting the importance of modality choice in shaping reasoning outcomes.

paper.title: Humans’ ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration

author.affiliation: Northeastern University and University of Dublin, Trinity College
School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University

paper.abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as collaborative partners in human workflows. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning, partners’ intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today’s agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion rather than for maintaining the underlying mental models required for collaborative processes. Moreover, the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants’ self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans’ next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC’s utility in evaluating models’ ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models. The project page is available at https://human-agent-collab.hailab.io/almanac.

paper.title: Holmes-Graph: A Framework for Probing the Linguistic Competence of Graph-Based Text Embeddings

author.affiliation: Department of Informatics, University of Zurich, University of Zurich
Instituto de Investigaciones en Matemáticas Aplicadas y en Sistemas - UNAM

paper.abstract: We present Holmes-Graph, a framework to evaluate the linguistic competences of graph-based text embeddings generated by training graph neural networks (GNNs) on graph representations of text. The framework extends the Holmes benchmark, which previously covered only sparse, static, and transformer-based representations. The framework is flexible to be used with any graph representation and GNN architecture. Once weights are learned on a downstream task, frozen embeddings are probed across five linguistic competences. When applied to AI-generated text detection, Integrated Syntactic Graphs (ISG) combined with Graph Neural Networks (GNN) achieve an aggregate Holmes score of 0.662. This matches or exceeds DeBERTa-base on syntax, morphology, semantics, and reasoning, but not for discourse. The results confirm that graph-based text embeddings encode non-trivial linguistic knowledge and motivate their inclusion in future probing benchmarks.

paper.title: Debug or Regenerate? Test-Guided Selection for LLM Code Repair

author.affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Amazon and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as coding assistants, but the programs they generate often fail. Such failures can be addressed by debugging the existing implementation or regenerating a new solution from the problem specification, with existing repair workflows typically defaulting to debugging. We find that the effectiveness of debugging and regeneration depends strongly on initial program quality, suggesting that no single repair strategy is universally optimal. Motivated by this observation, we present PATSSEL (Program-Adaptive Test-guided Repair Strategy Selection), a test-guided repair selection framework that dynamically chooses between debugging and regeneration. Rather than committing to a single repair strategy, PATSSEL generates debugged and regenerated candidates for each buggy program, evaluates them using generated verifier tests, and selects the stronger candidate, leveraging the complementary strengths of debugging and regeneration. Experiments on LeetCodeDataset, LiveCodeBench, and HE+Fix show that PATSSEL achieves average absolute improvements of 2.7% with Qwen3-8B and 3.2% with Llama3-8B over the best single-strategy baselines under the same inference compute budget and routing using gold unit tests. The gains persist across repair models, routing models, and stronger debugger models. Further analysis shows that PATSSEL benefits from the complementary strengths of debugging and regeneration, highlighting the importance of adaptive strategy selection for reliable LLM-based code repair.

paper.title: EMBRACE: Emotion-Based Representation Across Cultures & Expressions
paper.abstract: Building speech emotion recognition (SER) models that generalize across languages remains challenging due to limited annotations, linguistic diversity and heterogeneous label spaces. Current multilingual SER approaches either rely on fully shared models or restrict training to a small set of overlapping emotions that restrict diversity in expressiveness. We propose EMBRACE, a multilingual speech representation for language-agnostic SER. Drawing inspiration from partial-label learning paradigms in computer vision, EMBRACE adapts a unified superset emotion modeling strategy. The approach enables training on mixtures of datasets with non-overlapping emotion categories by selectively masking absent categories during optimization. To balance this complex multi-domain training, the model leverages a knowledge distillation based progressive training procedure that stabilizes multilingual optimization and mitigates catastrophic forgetting. Experiments across seven languages show that EMBRACE improves cross-corpus performance by 31.8% and in-corpus by 15.2% over strong emotional speech representations, confirming its ability to learn discriminative and transferable affective representations.

paper.title: SproutRAG: Attention-Guided Tree Search with Progressive Embeddings for Long-Document RAG
paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems must balance retrieval granularity with contextual coherence, a challenge that existing methods address through LLM-guided chunking, single-level context expansion, or hierarchical summarization. These approaches variously depend on costly LLM calls during indexing or retrieval, limit context aggregation to a single granularity level, or introduce information loss through summarization. We present SproutRAG, an attention-guided hierarchical RAG framework that builds a binary tree over sentence-level chunks using learned inter-sentence attention from a sentence-level large language model (SLLM). To avoid proximity bias from uniform attention averaging, SproutRAG learns head- and layer-level aggregation weights that identify attention patterns most aligned with semantic document structure. At retrieval time, it uses hierarchical beam search over the tree to gather candidates at multiple granularities, capturing multi-sentence relevance beyond flat retrieval. The framework is trained end-to-end with a joint objective that improves both embeddings and tree structure, without requiring external LLM calls. Experiments across four benchmarks spanning scientific, legal, and open-domain settings demonstrate that SproutRAG improves information efficiency (IE) by 6.1% on average over the strongest baseline.

paper.title: How Calibration Content Shapes Attention-Based Reranking

author.affiliation: University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego

paper.abstract: Attention-based rerankers score documents by aggregating query-to-document attention and subtracting a null-query calibration pass to remove positional and structural bias. Although widely used, this calibration assumes that the null pass is independent of document relevance. We show that modern prompt content, e.g. constraints, instructions, personas, and demonstrations can violate this assumption when it enters the scoring readout, making the null pass relevance-aware rather than null. Through a three-pass decomposition, we find that calibration helps when the null-pass footprint is relevance-agnostic bias, but hurts when it is relevance-tracking signal: short shared constraints survive calibration, whereas long per-query instructions inject signal that subtraction destroys. We propose interpolated null calibration, a training-free modification that controls how much instruction content enters the null baseline. It recovers attention-based reranking on instruction-heavy tasks where standard calibration fails, while preserving calibration’s benefits when the null pass remains relevance-agnostic. On instruction heavy tasks, the recovered rankings surpass generative rerankers such as RankGPT. We also show that in-context demonstrations improve attention-based reranking with little calibration interference, since demonstrations act only through the query pass and leave the null pass unchanged.

paper.title: Do LLMs Choose Like Humans? Using Cognitive Theory to Evaluate LLM Decision-Making

author.affiliation: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, Technion

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a range of human-like decision-making behaviors, but whether these reflect similar underlying mechanisms or surface-level mimicry remains unclear. We evaluate whether LLM context sensitivity aligns with a cognitive economic theory that explains human behavior through problem categorization and attention allocation. Across 12 open-source and commercial LLMs on a novel 140,000-trial product choice benchmark, context induces human-like shifts in choice and problem categorization, but does not reliably reweight attention between features like price and quality. Neither scale nor chain-of-thought reasoning reliably attenuates context sensitivity or generates human-like behavior. These results suggest that LLM decision mechanisms are distinct from human ones.

paper.title: Latent Visual Sensitive Fingerprinting for Black-Box Vision–Language Model Tamper Detection

author.affiliation: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications

paper.abstract: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) may be silently fine-tuned, poisoned, compressed, or replaced after deployment, motivating black-box fingerprint verification. RESF tests response distributions but requires estimating the service temperature, making its reliability sensitive to estimation error. We propose Latent Visual Sensitive Fingerprinting (\mathtt{LVSF}), based on a local Pearson-sensitivity decomposition of the conditional top-k distribution of the first generated token. This decomposition separates observable output shifts from input-dependent exposure to parameter changes. Modeling tampering-induced relative top-k logit shifts as isotropic, we show that a uniform top-k anchor maximizes average sensitivity. Accordingly, \mathtt{LVSF} equalizes recorded top-k logits, maintains a margin from out-of-support tokens, and maximizes full-parameter Fisher sensitivity, yielding a reference distribution invariant to positive temperature scaling. These principles apply to both LLMs and VLMs. For VLMs, \mathtt{LVSF} fixes a natural-language query and optimizes an image in a pretrained VAE latent space to produce natural-looking fingerprints. Repeated API queries detect excess out-of-support first tokens or shifts in conditional in-support frequencies. Across four VLMs and multiple tampering types, \mathtt{LVSF} achieves consistently high detection rates with no observed false positives and substantially higher detection rates than evaluated baselines on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.

paper.title: A Dataset for Modeling Iterative Problem-Solving
paper.abstract: Solving problems through repeated attempts is a sequential modeling task: at each step, the solver receives feedback and decides how to revise their solutions. Predicting whether performance improves, plateaus, or regresses across attempts is central to understanding any iterative problem-solving process in both human learners and autonomous agents. Beyond outcomes, modeling what errors persist and how strategies shift across attempts provides deeper insight into the mechanics of sequential learning. Studying these dynamics requires observing many solvers as they attempt, receive feedback, and revise. Programming courses with automated grading provide this setting, as students iteratively submit code to test suites and receive feedback on every attempt. We therefore curate CodeInsight, a large-scale dataset of over 3 million submissions from 3,286 undergraduates across 2 introductory C++ courses in 2 academic years, with test-case-level outcomes, timestamps, and source code. On this dataset, we build a benchmark that evaluates models spanning parametric, sequential, and generative traditions under a shared calibration-and-scoring protocol, including a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) adapted to track solver characteristics through discrete latent variables and an LLM-based predictor that generates explicit solutions. The adapted RSSM achieves the strongest predictive accuracy on three of the four courses. The LLM predictor is less accurate but produces full submissions at each attempt, enabling direct analysis of failure modes. We find that the model’s coding proficiency is inversely related to predictive performance in this setting, with the LLM better understood as a generative solver conditioned on context rather than a faithful predictor of solver behavior. We publicly release our code and the dataset on request to facilitate future research.

paper.title: ReVision: Scaling Computer-Use Agents via Temporal Visual Redundancy Reduction
paper.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) rely on visual observations of graphical user interfaces, where each screenshot is encoded into a large number of visual tokens. As interaction trajectories grow, the token cost increases rapidly, limiting the amount of history that can be incorporated under fixed context and compute budgets. This has resulted in no or very limited improvement in the performance when using history unlike other domains. We address this inefficiency by introducing ReVision, which is used to train multimodal language models on trajectories where redundant visual patches are removed using a learned patch selector that compares patch representations across consecutive screenshots while preserving spatial structure required by the model. Across three benchmarks, OSWorld, WebTailBench, and AgentNetBench, when processing trajectories with 5 history screenshots using Qwen2.5-VL-7B, ReVision reduces token usage by 46% on average while improving success rate by 3% over the no drop baseline. This establishes a clear efficiency gain, enabling agents to process longer trajectories with fewer tokens. With this improved efficiency, we revisit the role of history in CUAs and find that performance continues to improve as more past observations are incorporated when redundancy is removed.

paper.title: PersonaForge: Realistic Multi-Turn User Simulation for Agentic Systems

author.affiliation: Department of Computer Science, The University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as agentic workflow executors, yet existing training data and benchmarks largely assume informationally complete, single-turn queries. Our analysis of 16K real-world sessions shows that 75.9% of interactions are multi-turn, revealing a substantial gap between how users interact with agents and how such systems are trained and evaluated. We introduce PersonaForge, a user simulation framework for synthesizing realistic multi-turn user–agent interactions. PersonaForge combines a four-dimensional persona space, SOUL-driven behavioral control calibrated to real-user statistics, and Reverse Deep Construction grounded in authentic seed queries. Using PersonaForge, we construct a 6.3K-record training dataset and PersonaForge-Bench, a manually annotated 138-task benchmark spanning over 20 professional domains with four-dimensional scoring. Experiments on Qwen3.5-27B show that PersonaForge training improves the composite score by +4.1%, with gains across all four dimensions and the largest improvements in Task Completion (+6.0%) and Response Quality (+6.8%). Further analyses show that PersonaForge-trained agents use fewer turns and tool calls, suggesting improved interaction efficiency, while ablations confirm the contribution of SOUL components and adaptive simulation. Together, PersonaForge and PersonaForge-Bench establish a foundation for training and evaluating agents under realistic multi-turn user interaction.

paper.title: EVA-Bench: A New End-to-end Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents
paper.abstract: Voice agents are increasingly deployed across enterprise applications. However, no existing benchmark jointly addresses realistic conversation simulation and comprehensive voice-specific evaluation. We present EVA-Bench, an end-to-end evaluation framework that addresses both. On the simulation side, EVA-Bench orchestrates dynamic bot-to-bot audio conversations with automatic simulation validation that detects user simulator error and appropriately regenerates conversations before scoring. On the measurement side, EVA-Bench introduces two composite metrics: EVA-A (Accuracy) and EVA-X (Experience). EVA-Bench includes 213 scenarios across three enterprise domains, a controlled perturbation suite for accent and noise robustness, and multi-trial measurements that distinguish peak from reliable capability. Across 12 systems spanning three architectures, we find: (1) no system simultaneously exceeds 0.5 on both EVA-A pass@1 and EVA-X pass@1; (2) peak and reliable performance diverge substantially (median pass@k - pass^k gap of 0.44 on EVA-A; and (3) accent and noise perturbations expose substantial robustness gaps, with effects varying across architectures, systems, and metrics (mean Δ up to 0.314). We release EVA-Bench under an open-source license.

paper.title: Prompt Optimization with Human Feedback

author.affiliation: Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performances in various tasks. However, the performances of LLMs heavily depend on the input prompt. This has given rise to a number of recent works on prompt optimization. However, the previous works often require the availability of a numeric score to assess the quality of every prompt. Unfortunately, when a human user interacts with a black-box LLM, it is often infeasible and unreliable to attain such a score. Instead, it is usually significantly easier and more reliable to obtain preference feedback from a human user, i.e., showing the user the responses generated from a pair of prompts and asking the user which one is preferred. Therefore, in this paper, we study the problem of prompt optimization with human feedback (POHF), in which we aim to optimize the prompt for a black-box LLM using only human preference feedback. By drawing inspirations from dueling bandits, we design a theoretically principled strategy to select a pair of prompts to query for preference feedback in every iteration, and hence introduce our algorithm named automated POHF (APOHF). We apply our APOHF algorithm to a variety of tasks, including optimizing user instructions, prompt optimization for text-to-image generative models, and response optimization with human feedback (i.e., further refining the response using a variant of our APOHF). The results demonstrate that our APOHF can efficiently find a good prompt using a small number of preference feedback instances.

paper.title: Reinforced Internal-External Knowledge Synergistic Reasoning for Efficient Adaptive Search Agent

author.affiliation: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a common strategy to reduce hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs). While reinforcement learning (RL) can enable LLMs to act as search agents by activating retrieval capabilities, existing ones often underutilize their internal knowledge. This might lead to redundant retrievals, potential harmful knowledge conflicts, and increased inference latency. To address these limitations, an efficient adaptive search agent capable of discerning optimal retrieval timing and synergistically integrating parametric (internal) and retrieved (external) knowledge is in urgent need. This paper introduces the Reinforced Internal-External Knowledge Synergistic REasoning Agent (IKEA), which could indentify its own knowledge boundary and prioritize the utilization of internal knowledge, resorting to external search only when internal knowledge is deemed insufficient. This is achieved using a novel knowledge-boundary aware reward function and a knowledge-boundary aware training dataset. These are designed for internal-external knowledge synergy oriented RL, incentivizing the model to deliver accurate answers, minimize unnecessary retrievals, and encourage appropriate retrievals only when its own knowledge is lacking. Evaluations across multiple knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks demonstrate that IKEA significantly outperforms baseline methods, reduces retrieval frequency significantly, and exhibits robust generalization capabilities.

paper.title: CAROB: A Benchmark for Cross-Artifact and Authority-aware Reasoning over Organizational Bundles
paper.abstract: Enterprise AI assistants suffer from two failure modes not captured by existing public-web QA benchmarks: authorized information leakage, where factually correct answers reach unintended readers, and aggregation failure, where evidence scattered across artifacts yields fluent but incomplete responses. Both stem from enterprise authority being per-item and partly body-embedded, a structure that existing benchmarks address along at most one axis. We argue that authority-aware evaluation must be conducted at the per-item level, and instantiate this principle through Cross-Artifact and Authority-aware Reasoning over Organizational Bundles (CAROB): a synthetic enterprise dataset in which every retrieval-and-citation item carries a time-indexed audience/approval/lifecycle annotation, paired with three tasks that decouple cross-artifact coherence, authority-aware retrieval, and role-conditioned answering. Evaluating five frontier and open-weight LLMs, we find that no single model dominates both axes of the benchmark: each task induces a distinct model ordering, and the model strongest on authority handling ranks last on answer coverage. Two structural patterns hold across the lineup: retrieval-side leakage amplifies substantially at the answer stage, and structural authority filtering eliminates the residual leak band that prompt-level mitigation leaves behind, with both patterns replicating on EnronQA and ACCESS DENIED INC. We release CAROB as an evaluation testbed for authority-aware enterprise system design, together with its per-item annotation, three-task structure, and label-first generation pipeline as reusable infrastructure.

paper.title: Do Backdoored LLMs Share Internal Trigger Representations? Evidence from Frozen SAE Feature Banks
paper.abstract: Backdoor evaluations ask whether hidden triggers elicit attacker-chosen responses. For generative LLMs, this behavioral test leaves unresolved which internal features contribute to triggered generation and whether those identified from source attacks remain actionable on held-out attacks. We study this question using pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) over residual stream states. We contrast triggered and matched clean source traces, retain coordinates with recurring activation increases at early answer positions, and freeze each bank before evaluation. For each evaluation, the tested attack family and its adapted checkpoint are excluded from bank construction. Attack Success Rate (ASR) is the behavioral readout. Across Gemma-3 1B/4B/12B LoRA models with Gemma Scope 2 SAEs, ablating the selected coordinates reduces complete-target generation from 1478/1500 to 1/1500. Repeating the protocol with separately constructed banks for checkpoints trained with full-parameter fine-tuning reduces complete-target generation from 1499/1500 to 0/1500. Matched random controls leave ASR near baseline. Average clean-task changes are small, although instruction following declines more on larger models. Whether the selected coordinates encode the trigger condition itself remains unresolved. The evidence supports these coordinates as transferable SAE-based intervention handles associated with triggered generation in the evaluated Gemma-3 setting.

paper.title: Conditioning Activation Interventions on Evolving Reasoning States in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Activation steering controls language model behavior at inference time by injecting behavior-relevant directions into internal representations. In the standard steering interface, a steering direction is estimated once before generation and then applied throughout decoding. However, during multi-step reasoning, the model’s internal state shifts continuously as reasoning progresses, while standard steering continues to apply the same fixed direction across these changing states. This creates a mismatch between the model’s evolving reasoning state and the static intervention applied to it. To address this mismatch, we introduce State-Conditioned Steering (SCS), which recomputes the additive update itself from the hidden states encountered during generation while keeping the same additive intervention interface. Rather than adapting when or how strongly to intervene, SCS re-estimates the update from intermediate reasoning states as generation proceeds. In a paired comparison setting, we compare fixed and state-conditioned updates and find that predefined directions often exhibit unstable effects, while SCS yields more consistent intervention behavior across decoding steps. Across reasoning benchmarks with explicit step structure and three instruction-tuned backbones, SCS achieves larger average gains than prompting-only decoding and baseline activation steering methods.

paper.title: Markovian Generation Chains in Large Language Models

author.affiliation: École Polytechnique and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) raises an important question: how do texts evolve when they are repeatedly processed by LLMs? In this paper, we define this iterative inference process as Markovian generation chains, where each step takes a specific prompt template and the previous output as input, without including any prior data. In iterative rephrasing and round-trip translation experiments, the output either converges to a small recurrent set or continues to produce novel sentences within a finite horizon. Through sentence-level Markov chain modeling and analysis of simulated data, we show that iterative process can either increase or reduce the diversity depending on factors such as the temperature parameter and the initial input sentence. These results offer valuable insights into the dynamics of iterative LLM inference and their implications for multi-agent LLM systems.

paper.title: Not Safe for All: Auditing the Dialect Penalty in Text-to-Image Safety Pipelines
paper.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety guardrails fail to generalize equitably to non-standard dialects. Evaluating 23,080 paired prompts across five English dialects, we formalize this failure as the dialect penalty, where filters trigger based on linguistic surface features rather than semantic intent. Text-level filters fail in opposing directions: NSFW-T over-flags benign dialect prompts and LatentGuard over-flags toxic ones (bias gaps up to +28.29 pp), while the OpenAI Moderation API under-detects them. A controlled typo ablation confirms this penalty originates from flagging dialectal features, not generic out-of-distribution sensitivity. The pixel-level generator is largely dialect-agnostic; the penalty enters at text processing and cascades unevenly to post-hoc guardrails. We show this bias tracks training data imbalance and is mitigable via group-balanced retraining, with an ablation attributing the gain to balanced exposure rather than to the worst-group objective of GroupDRO (group distributionally robust optimization). Current pipelines systematically fail dialect speakers, an equity failure masked by mean accuracy benchmarks. Our official code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/minguinho26/dialect-penalty-t2i.Content Warning: This paper contains offensive, toxic, or disturbing text prompts and generated images.

paper.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
paper.abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a K{\times}K feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

paper.title: Entropy Meets Importance: A Unified Head Importance–Entropy Score for Stable and Efficient Transformer Pruning
paper.abstract: Transformer-based models have achieved remarkable performance. However, their structural characteristics—multiple layers and attention heads—introduce efficiency challenges in inference and deployment. To address these challenges, various pruning methods have recently been proposed. Notably, gradient-based methods using Head Importance Scores (HIS) have gained traction for interpretability, efficiency, and ability to identify redundant heads. However, HIS alone has limitations as it captures only the gradient-driven contribution, overlooking the diversity of attention patterns. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel pruning criterion, HIES (Head Importance-Entropy Score), which integrates head importance scores with attention entropy, providing complementary evidence on per-head contribution. Empirically, HIES-based pruning yields a 1.13% improvement in model quality and 3.52% improvement in stability over the HIS-only method on average, substantially reducing the accuracy and stability cost of aggressive compression. Code will be released upon publication.

paper.title: Do We Require Large Language Models To Be HHH Aligned For Reasoning, Safety, Value, and Pluralistic?
paper.abstract: Alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) studies whether model responses satisfy the Helpful, Harmless, and Honest (HHH) objectives. Imbalances across these objectives may produce divergent behavior across Reasoning, Safety, Value, and Pluralistic dimensions. Existing benchmarks including CR-LLM, SAFETUNEBENCH, VALUEBENCH, and PERSONA study these dimensions separately and capture partial aspects of HHH behavior. To study HHH behavior across overlapping dimensions, we introduce RSVP-HHH, a framework for HHH evaluation across all four dimensions. We construct RSVP-X, an English-HHH dataset containing 9,228 prompt-response pairs spanning 106 domains through Step 1 Latent Behavioral Projection, Step 2 Behavioral Region Overlap, Step 3 Density-Aware Downsampling, Step 4 Behavioral Compatibility Evaluation, and Step 5 Latent Refinement. Experimental results on RSVP-X show that TrinityX (46.6%) outperforms AlignX (45.0%), SAGE (49.1%) outperforms VAL-BENCH (48.2%) and R-Zero (47.6%), DeepSeek (45.0%) outperforms Qwen (43.7%), and Gemini (49.6%) outperforms Claude (47.7%) in Avg across HHH objectives.

paper.title: C-QUERI: Congressional Questions, Exchanges, and Responses in Institutions Dataset

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Binghamton
State University of New York at Binghamton
State University of New York at Binghamton

paper.abstract: We introduce C-QUERI, a dataset of question-answer exchanges from U.S. congressional committee hearings spanning the 108th–117th Congresses, with the pipeline used to construct it. C-QUERI transforms congressional hearing records into structured question-answer exchanges, enabling researchers to study political questioning and witness responses systematically and at scale. Congressional hearings provide a particularly valuable setting for such research: interactions are structured by formal rules, members of different parties are guaranteed opportunities to question witnesses, and witnesses are expected to respond. As an initial application demonstrating the resource’s utility, we examine whether questioner party affiliation can be predicted from question text alone. Question text contains a modest aggregate partisan signal, with substantially greater distinguishability in some committees, hearing types, and configurations of partisan control than others. C-QUERI provides new infrastructure for studying congressional politics and a general framework for analyzing question-answer interactions in other interview-like settings.

paper.title: Benchmarking Speech-to-Speech Translation Models

author.affiliation: The University of Tokyo and Sony Group Corporation

paper.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) has advanced rapidly, but offline evaluation lacks a unified protocol: studies report non-overlapping metric subsets, preventing direct comparisons. While prior toolkits target subsets of metrics or simultaneous and text-only translation (e.g., stopes-eval, SimulEval, IWSLT), we introduce COMPASS, the first offline S2ST benchmarking framework to unify 46 metrics across eight dimensions with domain-aware validation, and deploy it on 1,248 model-language configurations from FLEURS and CVSS, spanning cascaded and end-to-end architectures over ten language pairs. Architectures exhibit complementary strengths: best-vs-worst gaps exceed 30% on naturalness and speaker preservation but remain within a few points on translation quality, so single-metric rankings systematically misrepresent system quality. Correlation filtering reduces 46 metrics to 10 per direction, with three axes requiring different metrics across X\toEN and EN\toX (e.g., TER/UTMOS vs. ChrF++/NISQA-MOS); these subsets preserve rankings (Spearman’s \rho>0.80) while cutting evaluation time by \approx 2.5\times. Human validation across dubbing, podcasts, and medical domains shows standalone MOS predictors fail to predict listener preference, while top domain-specific metrics correlate with human judgment (\rho \geq 0.90). We release COMPASS as a foundation for domain-aware S2ST evaluation.

paper.title: VisualThink-VLA: Visual Intermediate Reasoning for Effective and Low-Latency Vision-Language-Action Policies
paper.abstract: Recent work has begun to equip vision-language-action (VLA) policies with explicit intermediate reasoning. In embodied control, however, textual chain-of-thought is a poor fit: irrelevant or weakly textual information can interfere with action prediction, while autoregressive text decoding adds too much latency for real-time closed-loop execution. We present \textbf{VISUALTHINK-VLA}, a visual intermediate-reasoning framework for accurate, low-latency VLA policies. We define visual intermediate reasoning operationally as constructing typed visual evidence, selecting a task-dependent budgeted route, and composing the selected channels into compact states before action decoding. Our bootstrapping philosophy is to \textit{guide action with effective visual thinking}: VISUALTHINK-VLA bootstraps action prediction through a compact visual-evidence interface that preserves spatial precision and supports low-overhead decoding. Besides, to further improve performance and efficiency, VISUALTHINK-VLA adopts a tailored selective routing mechanism to learn the visual evidence tokens, enabling low-latency inference while preserving high-capacity specialization. We also introduce \textbf{VisualEvidence-Kit}, a supervision-and-audit resource centered on a \textbf{VisualEvidence-Agent} that constructs 754.7k VLA instructions in the \textbf{VisualEvidence-Set} for route supervision and counterfactual faithfulness tests. Across multiple benchmarks and real-robot evaluation, VISUALTHINK-VLA achieves the highest success rate on most benchmarks while reducing the \textbf{multi-second} latency of reasoning-augmented baselines to the \textbf{sub-second} regime. On BridgeData V2, policy-side latency falls from 8.377,s with ECoT to 0.367,s, achieving a \textbf{22.8$\times$ speedup}.

paper.title: MRMAD: A Multi-Round Multi-Audio Benchmark for Evaluating Acoustic Degradation Perception in Large Audio-Language Models

author.affiliation: State University of New York at Stony Brook
University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and State University of New York at Stony Brook
Bose Corporation, Bose Corporation and Bose Corporation

paper.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have shown promising progress in understanding speech, music, and general sound events, yet their ability to reason about how audio signals are degraded remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate semantic understanding, event recognition, or high-level audio reasoning, leaving a basic question unanswered: Do LALMs understand the differences in audio quality? We introduce MRMAD, a Multi-Round Multi-Audio Degradation benchmark for evaluating audio degradation perception and understanding in LALMs. MRMAD spans speech, music, and sound, and frames evaluation as multi-turn dialogues across multiple audio inputs, requiring models to identify types of degradation, compare severity, and perceive corruption changes across turns. Unlike current single-turn audio-language benchmarks, MRMAD evaluates whether LALMs can maintain consistent degradation hypotheses with new evidence and comprehend low-level acoustic phenomena over multi-turn dialogues. Through a systematic evaluation of 18 representative LALMs from non-thinking to reasoning and Omni models, we find that current models often recognize coarse content while failing to diagnose, compare, or reason about degradations reliably. Human evaluations further reveal a significant perception gap between LALMs and human listeners. MRMAD thus exposes a critical yet overlooked aspect of audio-language understanding and provides a diagnostic foundation for building future LALMs that are robust to real-world acoustic conditions.

paper.title: 3D Visual Prompting: Empowering 3D-Aware Visual Generation via In-Context Self-Refinement
paper.abstract: Recent advances in image and video generation have highlighted the need for intuitive, high-precision manipulation. However, traditional text-based prompts or 2D Visual Prompts (e.g., dragging, 2D trajectories) often suffer from unintuitive prompt engineering or depth ambiguity. To address these limitations, we introduce 3D Visual Prompting, a novel paradigm that significantly improves input intuitiveness for visual manipulation tasks. We develop a framework that integrates intuitive 3D constraints into 2D generative processes. Our approach projects 3D Visual Prompts onto 2D visual planes and leverages Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to verbalize intent, allowing plug-and-play use of existing 2D models. Furthermore, we incorporate In-Context Self-Refinement (ICSR) to summarize insights from self-correction into a meta-strategy. This enables high-precision 3D control in single-pass inference, eliminating the need for iterative computation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional 2D Visual Prompting for object translation and rotation. By utilizing pre-trained models without additional parameter tuning, our framework remains highly adaptable to future developments in generative models.

paper.title: Control-Data Flow Separation: Stable Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent LLMs
paper.abstract: Prompt optimization can improve multi-agent LLM systems, but the prompts being optimized often serve two entangled roles: generating task-relevant content and specifying execution-critical protocols, such as message routing, output formatting, and termination signals, on which the underlying code relies. As a result, a prompt edit intended to improve content generation can inadvertently corrupt the protocol and cause the entire agent pipeline to fail. Our key observation is that these two roles have different representations: execution protocols are typically structured, while task-relevant content is usually expressed in unstructured language. Based on this, we propose control-data flow separation, where execution-critical control is represented as typed, validated program objects, while task-relevant language remains the optimizable data flow for agent communication. This design allows optimizers to improve multi-agent behavior without exposing the routing or formatting interface to prompt drift. Across synthetic reasoning, collaborative review generation, and insurance rating workflows, our framework empirically achieves 100% eventual protocol validity while consistently improving task performance.

paper.title: Can Omni-models Imagine the Future? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal World Modeling
paper.abstract: Recent progress in Omni-models has yielded strong performance on benchmarks focused on static observations. However, their ability to maintain spatiotemporal continuity when predicting coherent future states from previous context remains underexplored. We address this by formulating Next Scene Prediction (NSP) as a diagnostic task for assessing multimodal near-future state prediction, requiring models to anticipate the immediate future from a given context. We introduce OmniNSP, a benchmark evaluating causal and cross-modal coherence across physical, logical, and social dynamics. Unlike prior tasks that often rely on textual or discriminative proxies, OmniNSP asks models to express predicted future states through text-mediated visual and speech synthesis. Our analysis shows that current Omni-models can produce plausible textual forecasts while still failing to preserve future-state consistency in generated outputs. A frozen-generator control substantially narrows cross-model visual-consistency gaps, attributing much of the original system-level difference to model-specific realization stacks rather than textual foresight alone. A modality-input ablation further shows that audio provides complementary predictive cues beyond vision, with the largest gains for logical transitions and contexts with informative speech. These results position OmniNSP as a diagnostic of both near-future prediction and the preservation of predicted state through multimodal realization.

paper.title: Toward Autonomous Long-Horizon Engineering for ML Research
paper.abstract: Agentic systems increasingly automate pieces of AI research. Yet turning underspecified research objectives into runnable, experimentally validated ML systems remains a central bottleneck. We study this operational setting as long-horizon ML research engineering: converting a research specification into a runnable ML system through repeated implementation, experimentation, and refinement. The central challenge is to sustain cumulative project progress across heterogeneous stages under delayed, confounded feedback. We introduce AiScientist, a multi-agent system built around thin control over thick state: a lightweight hierarchical research team coordinates through a File-as-Bus workspace that preserves decision-relevant artifacts across roles and invocations. On PaperBench, AiScientist improves over the strongest matched baselines by 9.92 and 11.15 points with Gemini-3-Flash and GLM-5, respectively. On MLE-Bench Lite, it reaches 81.82 Any Medal% under both backbones, improving over the strongest matched baselines by 4.55 and 16.67 points, and exceeding a Codex/GPT-5.5 xhigh frontier harness reference by 13.64 Any Medal points. Ablations and process analyses show that durable project state is central to later-round refinement: removing File-as-Bus lowers PaperBench score by 6.41 points and MLE-Bench Lite Any Medal% by 31.82 points. These results suggest that long-horizon AI research is not only a problem of stronger local reasoning, but a systems problem of maintaining cumulative, inspectable project progress.

paper.title: OPERA-MoE: Output-aware Routing Perturbation Alignment via Observable Discrepancy for MoE Quantization
paper.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have become a dominant paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs), but their large memory footprint still makes post-training quantization (PTQ) essential for practical deployment. Unlike dense LLMs, quantized MoE models exhibit routing perturbations, where quantization alters expert routing behavior. Existing router alignment methods mitigate this issue by uniformly minimizing routing discrepancies across all tokens. However, we observe that routing perturbations exhibit highly heterogeneous relationships with observable output discrepancy: many tokens preserve nearly identical output distributions despite substantial routing changes. Motivated by this observation, we propose OPERA, an output-aware router alignment strategy for quantized MoE models that selectively prioritizes tokens exhibiting observable output discrepancy after quantization. We further analyze output-preserving routing perturbations and show that they frequently occur on highly predictable tokens, where substantial routing perturbations and hidden-state deviations may not strongly affect projected output distributions. Experiments across multiple MoE LLMs demonstrate that OPERA generally improves over conventional router alignment, with particularly noticeable gains under aggressive low-bit quantization settings.

paper.title: AutoLexSteer: Automatic Contrast Construction for Lexical Activation Steering

author.affiliation: University of Melbourne and Carnegie Mellon University

paper.abstract: Steering vectors have rapidly emerged as a popular and effective method for guiding the output of LLMs in very specific ways. But constructing accurate steering vectors is a difficult manual process due to the opacity of embeddings. We introduce Hangman, a novel type of steering vector that operates using word senses, as well as AutoLexSteer, the first fully automated process for building steering vectors. AutoLexSteer employs families of closely-related words extracted from WordNet to specify both the steering source to be avoided and the desired steering target. The steering vectors are quite precise, can be used to steer at the level of words and sets of word senses (meanings), and are able to steer certain LLM behaviors like sycophancy. The dataset and code can be found at https://github.com/ShuheWang1998/autolexsteer.

paper.title: Knowledge Acquisition During Pre-training? Large Language Models Learn Better With Auxiliary Views

author.affiliation: University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania and University of Pennsylvania

paper.abstract: Gaps remain in our understanding of how large language models (LLMs) acquire knowledge during pre-training. We posit that auxiliary views, reformulations of knowledge across different contexts, are causally helpful for learning. We design controlled experiments to isolate this effect. First, we confirm that repetition is necessary for acquisition and clarify that paraphrasing helps only at smaller batch sizes. Second, holding the token budget fixed, reallocating tokens from document repetition to auxiliary views improves learning, even for factual recall, which is counterintuitive. Third, the effectiveness of auxiliary views is not contingent on the strength of the teacher model that generates them. Fourth, we identify forms of knowledge, contextual and foundational, that aid learning in the presence of prior knowledge gaps. Finally, we examine how these effects manifest mechanistically via layer-wise biases and compression. Together, our findings suggest that auxiliary representations of knowledge, which arise naturally in large pre-training corpora, are a key factor in the success of pre-training and offer a plausible explanation for why data diversity matters.

paper.title: Discovery, Articulation and Analysis of Communication Framings
paper.abstract: In social media discourse, the framing of a topic dictates the way opinions are formed. This paper presents two multi-agent frameworks: one for discovering what issues are framed in a topic, and another articulating interpretations of these issues. This enables an analysis of a topic’s discourse that reveals what frame issues are dominant while also providing insights about which issues have more possible interpretations. Experiments across four different topics show promising results for discovering and analyzing framings, allowing new comprehension of controversial topics.

paper.title: OpenSeal: Good, Fast, and Cheap Construction of an Open-Source Southeast Asian LLM via Parallel Data
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have proven to be effective tools for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications. Although many LLMs are multilingual, most remain English-centric and perform poorly on low-resource languages. Recently, several Southeast Asia–focused LLMs have been developed, but none are truly open source, as they do not publicly disclose their training data. Truly open-source models are important for transparency and for enabling a deeper and more precise understanding of LLM internals and development, including biases, generalization, and multilinguality. Motivated by recent advances demonstrating the effectiveness of parallel data in improving multilingual performance, we conduct controlled and comprehensive experiments to study the effectiveness of parallel data in continual pretraining of LLMs. Our findings show that using only parallel data is the most effective way to extend an LLM to new languages.
