Using just 34.7B tokens of parallel data and 180 hours on 8× NVIDIA H200 GPUs, we built OpenSeal, the first truly open Southeast Asian LLM that rivals the performance of existing models of similar size.

paper.title: Depth as Verifiable Geometric Feedback: Enhancing Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with spatial reasoning, particularly on tasks requiring consistent geometric understanding across multiple image regions. While recent works incorporate depth supervision into MLLMs, it remains unclear what forms of geometric learning are most beneficial for spatial reasoning transfer. In this work, we propose Multi-point Geometric Consistency Alignment (MGCA), a geometry-guided post-training framework that uses depth annotations as verifiable geometric feedback without requiring depth input at inference time. MGCA samples multiple image regions and optimizes the model through a unified geometric reward that jointly captures metric grounding and relative geometric consistency. Specifically, the reward combines a metric depth objective with a margin-aware ranking objective and is optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Experiments on multiple spatial reasoning benchmarks show that MGCA consistently improves spatial understanding and outperforms comparable open-weight MLLMs of similar scale. More importantly, our analysis reveals that optimizing relative ordering alone can achieve high ranking accuracy while failing to learn transferable geometric representations due to the lack of metric grounding. In contrast, jointly optimizing metric depth and relational consistency leads to substantially stronger spatial reasoning performance. These findings suggest that effective spatial alignment in MLLMs requires metrically grounded relational learning, rather than relation-only supervision.

paper.title: The Interplay of Harness Design and Post-training in LLM Agents

author.affiliation: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Tool-integrated LLM agents are often wrapped within a *harness*: the scaffolding that determines which tools are exposed, how they are described, and what auxiliary information accompanies each per-step observation. While agents are routinely post-trained, this scaffolding is typically treated as a *fixed* engineering detail, with design effort limited to the training-free regime. Moreover, existing post-training algorithms assume a static environment, even though tool environments and tasks often shift upon deployment. To address this gap, we extend \texttt{ALFWorld} (i) to treat the harness as a controllable design dimension and (ii) to support evaluation under task and tool environment shifts. Building on this, we systematically analyze how the harness design influences post-training in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings. We empirically show that *harness-aware post-training* not only improves in-distribution performance but also enables agents to robustly adapt to OOD settings. Under a harness with minimal design effort, post-training suffers a drastic performance drop under stronger tool environment shifts, further highlighting the importance of harness-aware post-training under such shifts.

paper.title: Proactive Safety Alignment: Enabling Proactive Initiative in Multi-Turn Defence
paper.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as interactive agents capable of multi-turn dialogues and tool usage, but they remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. Existing safety mechanisms are mostly reactive, only attempting to uncover pre-existing hidden malicious intent, which makes them largely ineffective against attacks when such attacks are inherently designed to conceal their intent, and causes them to often fail in multi-turn, interactive, or out-of-distribution scenarios. In addition, existing multi-turn defences are largely data-driven, which limits their generalisation ability. To address this challenge, we propose Proactive Safety Alignment (PSA), a framework that anticipates user intent proactively to align LLM agents’ outputs with safety objectives. PSA combines Safe User Request Prediction (SURP), which anticipates likely safe future requests, and Potentially Harmful Generation (PHG), which evaluates whether the current interaction state can support misuse. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PSA substantially reduces attack success rates, while preserving overall utility on MT-Bench. Our results show that PSA provides an effective and scalable paradigm for multi-turn LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/qinmengyuan/PSA.

paper.title: MetaCLASS: Metacognitive Coaching for Learning with Adaptive Self-regulation Support
paper.abstract: Large language models can generate fluent explanations, but effective tutoring requires supporting the learner’s thought process, not just delivering content. Metacognitive tutoring targets this gap by prompting planning, monitoring, debugging, and evaluation, and, crucially, deciding when to be active versus minimally present, based on learner signals and trajectory. We introduce MetaCLASS, a learning-science grounded framework that formulates metacognitive tutoring as move selection over 11 interpretable actions aligned to self-regulated learning (SRL) processes. MetaCLASS uses a two-phase procedure that first plans a pedagogical trajectory conditioned on learner profiles (calibration, help-seeking) and then generates natural dialogue consistent with that plan. This process yields 1,015 conversations spanning 7,711 turns, each annotated with turn-level metacognitive labels and supported by comprehensive validation analyses. We benchmark nine open-source LLMs on predicting the next coach move given a question and dialogue context. The best model achieves only 43.2% accuracy in coach move prediction, and models exhibit compulsive intervention bias: in turns where effective metacognitive tutoring requires silence (41.7% of cases), models predict "no intervention” only 6.6% of the time, while severely over-predicting high-intervention moves. These results show that traditional content-based tutoring ability does not translate to metacognitive tutoring competence, positioning MetaCLASS as a testbed for developing tutors that promote SRL.

paper.title: EMR-AGENT: An LLM Agent Framework for Cohort and Feature Extraction from Heterogeneous EHR Databases

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and AITRICS
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and AITRICS

paper.abstract: Electronic medical record (EMR) databases are widely used for clinical machine learning, but their preprocessing remains difficult to reproduce because cohort definitions, patient-level features, and clinical item-code mappings must be adapted to each database schema. We formulate EMR preprocessing as the task of translating study requests into database-specific cohort/feature extraction SQL and local clinical item-code mappings. Existing preprocessing and harmonization frameworks remain difficult to adapt because they rely on dataset-specific rules or predefined input formats. We introduce EMR-AGENT, an LLM-agent framework that reduces reliance on manual rule writing by automating database-specific cohort selection, feature extraction, and clinical code mapping from study requests. EMR-AGENT retrieves schema and documentation context, interacts with live databases through SQL, observes execution results, and refines extraction decisions from error feedback. To enable rigorous evaluation, we develop a benchmarking codebase for three intensive care unit (ICU) databases (MIMIC-III, eICU, and SICdb), covering reference databases and a newer SICdb version released after the backbone’s knowledge cutoff. Across these benchmarks, EMR-AGENT reduces schema-debugging and item-code search effort, enabling reproducible evaluation of preprocessing quality under expert review, while reducing reliance on hand-written database-specific pipelines.

paper.title: Revisiting Complete Reasoning Traces for Post-Training

author.affiliation: NAVER AI Lab and Seoul National University

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often post-trained on pre-collected reasoning trajectories to improve their reasoning capability. Such trajectories tend to be long due to complex, interwoven paths, which often include detours on the path toward the answer. However, it has been underexplored whether LLMs indeed benefit from learning complete trajectories in post-training, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Starting from our pilot study, we find that full trajectories provide only limited benefit, while partial trajectories are effective even under heavy truncation. We analyze redundancy in reasoning trajectories through attention-based analyses and controlled token-removal studies, both of which show that intermediate tokens contribute minimally to final reasoning quality. This suggests that avoiding redundant information may allow LLMs to internally infer coherent alternatives by inferring missing steps from their internal knowledge, given known trajectory endpoints. Furthermore, we show that training LLMs using endpoints leads to consistent changes in reasoning behavior, and that it also benefits post-training methods based on reinforcement learning or on-policy distillation, highlighting the need to revisit complete reasoning traces. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/revisiting-trace.

paper.title: Auditing Speaker-Level Metadata Utility in Text-Residual Prosody Prediction
paper.abstract: Text only partially determines prosodic realization, leaving residual variation that may align with speaker-level metadata such as regional accent or first-language (L1) background. However, because these labels are assigned to speakers, their predictive gains may overlap with broader speaker-associated structure rather than uniquely reflect category-level prosodic effects. We frame this as an attribution problem and propose a speaker-controlled audit using matched text-residual prosody predictors that differ only in access to metadata labels and speaker identity. The audit measures label utility beyond text, speaker utility beyond text, and the additional empirical utility of the label when speaker conditioning is already available. Across VCTK regional-accent labels and L2-ARCTIC L1 labels, metadata yields modest gains over text, while speaker conditioning yields larger gains and leaves little additional label utility under speaker control. Random speaker-group and label-perturbation controls further characterize the specificity and use of the supplied metadata. Importantly, speaker-held-out evaluation shows that metadata transfer to unseen speakers is limited and target-dependent, indicating that observed-speaker metadata gains do not by themselves establish speaker-independent category-level effects. These results position speaker-controlled auditing as a prerequisite attribution check before assigning category-level interpretations to metadata-conditioned predictive gains.

paper.title: Understanding and Enhancing Backdoor Persistency in LLM Agent Post-Training

author.affiliation: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology

paper.abstract: Developers can build LLM agents by adapting third-party models through benign post-training. We study a supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies a model with a backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs when a particular input pattern appears. Focusing on software-engineering agents, we ask whether such backdoors survive the developer’s supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent task-level reinforcement learning (RL). We observe that benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, but subsequent RL often preserves the residual behavior and sometimes even increases attack success. Our analysis of backdoor erosion during SFT identifies two factors that may favor survival: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These factors motivate PersistBD, which refines an already-backdoored model before release to improve its persistency through the benign post-training process. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance. Together, our results show that backdoors can remain active through benign post-training and that adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence. This highlights a supply-chain risk for AI developers and motivates stronger techniques for detecting and mitigating inherited backdoors when adapting third-party models into agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/PersistBD.

paper.title: Inside Sentence Embeddings: Leveraging Token Representations for Machine Translation Evaluation and Word Alignment

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
CyberAgent, Inc. and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Contextualized token-level embeddings from encoders, e.g., mBERT, are used for several cross-lingual tasks, e.g., machine translation (MT) evaluation and alignment tasks, but fine-tuning is required for the specific task settings. In contrast, multilingual sentence embeddings are trained under sentence-level objectives on parallel data, but their token-level representations remain unclear whether they carry cross-lingual semantics, although not explicitly trained with token-level objectives. In this paper, we investigate token representations extracted from multilingual sentence embedding models for MT evaluation and word alignment. Experimental results and analysis show that sentence embedding models can provide useful token-level representations for direct similarity-based tasks. Although the observed advantage is not consistent across all settings, the results indicate that multilingual sentence-level training may support token-level semantic similarity without explicit token-level training.

paper.title: Do Spoken Language Models Hear Speech as They Read Text? Bridging Structural Gaps Between Speech and Text

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and Maum AI

paper.abstract: Spoken Language Models (SLMs) generate textual responses directly from speech, offering an alternative to cascaded systems. Despite recent advances, existing SLMs still exhibit weaker instruction-following behavior and limited generalization across diverse tasks compared to text-based language models. Our analysis shows that speech and text representations in current SLMs remain weakly aligned despite strong downstream performance, indicating that structural differences between continuous, temporally varying speech and discrete text remain insufficiently addressed. To address this, we propose a simple framework that decouples length mismatch from semantic alignment and encourages closer correspondence between speech and text representations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against strong baselines, underscoring the importance of explicitly addressing structural differences between speech and text in SLM training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jaykim9870/Do_SLMs_Hear_Speech_as_They_Read_Text.

paper.title: Dynamic Hub-and-Spoke Memory for Streaming Video Understanding
paper.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions at arbitrary times over a continuously growing visual stream. The central challenge is to compactly remember long-range history while effectively retrieving question-relevant evidence. We propose Dynamic Hub-and-Spoke Memory (D-HSM), a training-free framework that represents distant history as structured textual memory while preserving the recent frames as visual tokens for fine-grained perception. Specifically, D-HSM turns selected historical video chunks into typed textual observations and stores them in an entity-centered hub-and-spoke memory, with entities as hubs and related evidence as spokes. When answering a question, D-HSM dynamically retrieves a compact question-aware memory subset, expands it through hub-and-spoke links, and combines it with the recent visual window for frozen-VLM answer prediction. Extensive experiments on both streaming and long video benchmarks show that D-HSM consistently and substantially improves VLM backbones and outperforms other state-of-the-art online and offline video understanding baselines.

paper.title: DTRNet: Dynamic Token Routing Network to Reduce Quadratic Costs in Transformers

author.affiliation: Advanced Micro Devices and University of Waterloo

paper.abstract: Transformers achieve state-of-the-art results across many tasks, but their uniform application of quadratic self-attention to every token at every layer makes them computationally expensive. We introduce DTRNet (Dynamic Token Routing Network), an improved Transformer architecture that allows tokens to dynamically skip the quadratic cost of cross-token mixing while still receiving lightweight linear updates. By preserving the MLP module and reducing the attention cost for most tokens to linear, DTRNet ensures that every token is explicitly updated while significantly lowering overall computation. This design offers an efficient and effective alternative to standard dense attention. Once trained, DTRNet blocks routes only ~10% of tokens through attention at each layer while maintaining performance comparable to a full Transformer. It outperforms routing-based layer skipping methods such as MoD and D-LLM in both accuracy and memory at matched FLOPs, while routing fewer tokens to full attention. Its efficiency gains, scales with sequence length, offering significant reduction in FLOPs for long-context inputs. By decoupling token updates from attention mixing, DTRNet substantially reduces the quadratic share of computation, providing a simple, efficient, and scalable alternative to Transformers.

paper.title: Not Worth Another Token: Marginal Value Estimation for Efficient Deep Research Agents

author.affiliation: University of Massachusetts at Amherst and E-J Electric

paper.abstract: Long-horizon research agents solve open-ended tasks through iterative retrieval, aggregation, and synthesis, but context grows rapidly while the marginal value of additional evidence often declines. This leads to unnecessary token cost, higher latency, and noisier inputs for final report generation. We study marginal value estimation for context management in deep research agents and present the first systematic stage-aware comparison of pruning strategies across the pipeline. We evaluate lightweight heuristic criteria and a learned value model at pre-retrieval, post-retrieval, and pre-synthesis stages. Our results show that pruning effectiveness depends more on where pruning is applied than on the specific scoring rule: early pruning yields the largest end-to-end savings, while later pruning mainly refines the final synthesis context. Lightweight heuristics reduce token usage by up to 73% with little quality degradation, learned pruning remains competitive on selected trade-offs, and no single method dominates across quality, efficiency, and faithfulness. These findings provide practical guidance for designing efficient long-horizon agentic systems.

paper.title: Token-Disentangled Latent Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language Reasoning

author.affiliation: ByteDance Inc. and University of Waterloo
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Huawei Noah's Ark Lab

paper.abstract: Latent test-time scaling improves reasoning by refining hidden states during inference, but existing methods typically apply a single scalar reward to all editable latent tokens. For multimodal large language models, this global update ignores that generated tokens play different roles: some are sensitive to visual evidence, while others correspond to uncertain reasoning decisions. We present Token-Disentangled Latent Test-Time Scaling, an inference-time framework that makes latent refinement token-role-aware. Starting from an initial generated trajectory, we optimize a short hidden-state prefix while routing perception-side visual feedback to image-sensitive tokens and reasoning feedback to high-entropy tokens. Tokens selected by neither route are constrained by an anchor regularizer. Across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks and two frozen MLLM backbones, our method consistently improves over the initial chain-of-thought rollout: macro accuracy increases from 66.38 to 68.95 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and from 67.93 to 69.44 on InternVL3.5-8B. These results show that token-disentangled latent refinement is an effective strategy for multimodal test-time scaling and remains competitive with output-space test-time scaling baselines.

paper.title: Modality Disentangled Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Emotion Recognition: A Primitive Memory Distillation Perspective

author.affiliation: University of Southern Queensland and Microsoft
Fujian University of Technology and Fujian University of Technology
German Research Center for AI and Meta
Technische Universität München and Imperial College London

paper.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) systems often suffer from missing modalities in real-world scenarios. Existing methods usually generate, align, or distill missing modalities as a whole, overlooking the heterogeneous nature of the information carried by each modality. Such holistic treatment mixes inferable shared semantics with uncertain modality-specific details, yielding unstable representations and degrading robustness. To address this issue, we propose the Primitive Memory Distillation (PriMD) framework. Unlike existing methods, PriMD takes an intra-modal perspective and focuses on how different types of information within a modality differ in recoverability within each modality. PriMD first disentangles cross-modal shared semantics from modality-specific representations, and then discretizes the latter into learnable semantic primitives to construct modality-specific memory banks. When modalities are missing, PriMD is a teacher–student framework that the student model uses the shared semantics of available modalities as queries to dynamically retrieve primitives. It compensates for missing modality-specific information within a constrained memory space and aligns with the teacher model. Extensive experiments on IEMOCAP, CMU-MOSI, and CMU-MOSEI demonstrate that PriMD achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently stronger robustness across a wide range of missing-modality settings, while mitigating the instability caused by holistic feature inference. Our code and project website are available at https://github.com/JiaqiZhang-Sengoku/PriMD and https://jiaqizhang-sengoku.github.io/PriMD/, respectively.

paper.title: Self-Evolving World Models for LLM Agent Planning

author.affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design

paper.abstract: World models offer a principled way to equip long-horizon LLM agents with foresight: predictions of action consequences before execution. However, unreliable foresight can be ignored, misused, or even degrade downstream decision-making. In this paper, we introduce WorldEvolver, a self-evolving world model framework that revises its deployment-time context while keeping the downstream agent and all model parameters frozen. WorldEvolver integrates three modules: (i) Episodic Memory, which exploits real action transitions through retrieval-based simulation; (ii) Semantic Memory, which extracts persistent heuristic rules from prediction-observation mismatches; and (iii) Selective Foresight, which filters low-confidence predictions before integrating them into agent reasoning context. We evaluate WorldEvolver on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, measuring world model prediction accuracy on Word2World and downstream agent success rate on AgentBoard. Extensive experiments show that WorldEvolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy across three backbones and leads other world model baselines on downstream agent success rate, demonstrating that test-time memory revision enhances both predictive fidelity and planning performance.

paper.title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering

author.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks—MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues—and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. Across eight frontier proprietary and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

paper.title: STRESS-FG: Diagnosing Visual Grounding in Zero-Shot Fine-Grained Recognition
paper.abstract: Zero-shot fine-grained recognition is a key test of visual grounding in vision-language models (VLMs), but current evaluations may conflate attribute grounding with reliance on class-label knowledge. We introduce STRESS-FG, a diagnostic benchmark spanning five fine-grained domains that systematically varies the relationship between class names and visual descriptions. The benchmark includes label-only, description-only, cue-conflict, and synthetic-label settings, as well as negated-attribute, multi-image, reference-conditioned, and part-based grounding tasks. Evaluating up to thirteen VLMs shows that label-only prompts are often surprisingly strong, indicating substantial familiarity with class-label priors. Synthetic labels can facilitate stronger attribute grounding evaluation, while familiar but incorrect class labels can suppress grounding capabilities under cue conflict. We further find that negation, multi-image matching, and reference-conditioned selection remain challenging, and part-based analyses show only partial reliance on the correct localized evidence. Finally, our binary question format reveals that models often struggle to reject fine-grained distractors, a weakness hidden by traditional Multiple Choice Question evaluations. These results suggest that standard fine-grained benchmarks may overestimate grounded visual understanding and should more explicitly separate label priors from attribute-based recognition. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/Ishtiaque-khan97/Stress-FG.

paper.title: When to Change the Canvas? Safe Adaptive Variable-Length Decoding for Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Diffusion language models generate text by denoising a masked canvas, but usually require the canvas length to be fixed before decoding. This leads to an allocation dilemma: short canvases may truncate outputs, while overlong canvases waste computation and introduce noisy continuations. Existing variable-length methods adapt the canvas through expansion or length search, but largely ignore whether such intervention is safe. We argue that canvas editing can perturb partially stabilized denoising trajectories, and propose Safe Adaptive Canvas Decoding (SACD), a training-free framework for conservative canvas control. SACD diagnoses allocation, estimates intervention risk, and chooses among expand, shrink, and keep. Experiments across reasoning, code generation, and infilling tasks show that SACD improves accuracy, latency, and token utilization across multiple DLM backbones, highlighting safe sparse intervention as a key principle for variable-length diffusion decoding.

paper.title: Multi-Label Delegation Target Identification in Japanese Law

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Legal systems often employ legislative drafting practices in which higher-level laws delegate detailed regulations to lower-level laws. In particular, when a single provision delegates authority to multiple lower-level laws, readers must cross-reference many related provisions scattered across the entire bodies of law, imposing a substantial cognitive burden. Reflecting this real-world problem, this work proposes a novel multi-label delegation target identification task to identify all the delegated provisions corresponding to an input provision, with the focus on Japanese law. We construct pipeline systems combining a candidate retriever and a candidate classifier, using language models with diverse architectures. Experimental results show that adopting a cross-encoder-based binary classifier as a candidate classifier improves performance at finer granularities, establishing a solid baseline for the task. Furthermore, our comprehensive analyses reveal the remaining challenges in achieving sufficient performance on instances with many delegated provisions and identify typical error types, providing a foundation for future improvement.

paper.title: Supporting and performing culture from the inside

author.affiliation: Eberhard-Karls-Universität Tübingen and University of Melbourne

paper.abstract: Anthropology and related disciplines which study culture have often found it useful to consider their epistemological and methodological approaches in terms of emic versus etic. This is the distinction between the insider perspective, how the world is viewed by a member of the culture, versus the outsider perspective, the scientific cataloguing of cultural knowledge and practice. We adopt this framework to systematically analyse assumptions in recent research on culture in NLP along the full pipeline of task selection, data collection, system design and evaluation. We draw attention to the ‘culture of NLP’ which shapes the research focus and approaches of our field, and suggest pathways towards a more culturally attuned AI.

paper.title: From Empathy to Personalized Empathy: Adapting Empathetic Strategies to Individual Users

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long-term interactions with users, empathy has become an increasingly important capability. However, existing research overlooks the influence of users’ personality traits on empathetic strategies during long-term interactions. To address this gap, we introduce the task of personalized empathy, which focuses on adapting empathetic strategies according to users’ personalized characteristics derived from history. To study and enhance this capability, we construct PersonaEmp, a personalized empathy dataset built from long-term user-AI interactions, featuring rich user histories, persona information, and empathy-seeking queries. We further propose PereGRM, a reward modeling framework that combines the empathy evaluation structure with dynamic evaluation criteria generation for fine-grained reward modeling. Experimental results across different settings and multiple judge models show that PereGRM consistently achieves the strongest performance improvements, indicating its effectiveness for enhancing personalized empathetic capabilities.

paper.title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy–efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%–37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%–13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.

paper.title: DeepPersona: Scaling Persona Depth via Taxonomy-Guided Generation
paper.abstract: Synthetic personas support LLM personalization, social simulation, and alignment evaluation, yet existing resources typically represent each individual with only a small number of structured attributes. We introduce DeepPersona, a generative engine that scales persona depth to roughly 200 instantiated taxonomy nodes while preserving narrative coherence. DeepPersona combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 8,496 human-descriptive attributes mined from 62k personalizable QA pairs in real user-chatbot dialogues and (ii) a progressive sampler that conditions each new attribute on the evolving persona and uses a stratified similarity prior to balance coherence and diversity. The same engine can expand shallow inputs, such as PersonaHub entries, into deep profiles. Across three complementary evaluations, DeepPersona improves judge-extracted attribute count by 32% and judge-rated uniqueness by 44% over the strongest prior persona resource; improves LLM personalization quality by up to 11.6% across ten dimensions, with human evaluators preferring DeepPersona responses in 81.2% to 87.0% of pairwise comparisons; and reduces the distributional gap to real World Values Survey responses by 31.7%, while recovering Big Five personality distributions 17% closer to ground truth than the strongest LLM baseline.

paper.title: Listwise Explanation of Embedding-Based Rankings via Semantic Chunk Grouping
paper.abstract: Dense embedding rankers score documents through contextual sentence- and passage-level representations, yet listwise explanation methods often attribute rankings to isolated words. We study this mismatch and introduce ChunkGroupSHAP, a listwise Shapley method that clusters semantically related chunks across documents into shared features, preserving contextual evidence while bounding the KernelSHAP regression dimension by the group count. Across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA with E5-family rankers and BM25, raw chunks improve rank-reconstruction Fidelity over RankSHAP’s word features in all 11 dense-ranker settings. The best chunk-group configuration further improves on raw chunks in eight of these settings, with the incremental benefit depending on grouping scope; word features remain strongest in three of four BM25 settings. These results show that explanation units should match the ranking model: contextual chunks better suit dense bi-encoders, whereas words remain effective for BM25. ChunkGroupSHAP supports listwise attribution over contextual evidence through a bounded feature space shared across documents.

paper.title: Accelerate Speculative Decoding with Sparse Computation in Verification

author.affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen and Harbin Institute of Technology

paper.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive language model inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. However, the verification stage often becomes the dominant computational bottleneck, especially for long-context inputs and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Existing sparsification methods are designed primarily for token-by-token autoregressive decoding to remove substantial computational redundancy in LLMs. This work systematically adopts different sparse methods on the verification stage of the speculative decoding and identifies structured redundancy across multiple dimensions. Based on these observations, we propose a sparse verification framework that jointly sparsifies attention, FFN, and MoE components during the verification stage to reduce the dominant computation cost. The framework further incorporates an inter-draft token and inter-layer retrieval reuse strategy to further reduce redundant computation without introducing additional training. Extensive experiments across summarization, question answering, and mathematical reasoning datasets demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-offs and can be translated into practical latency reduction with optimized sparse kernels.

paper.title: From Decoding Knobs to Commit Frontiers: Understanding Trajectory Control in Discrete Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models generate text by iteratively committing masked positions, making decoding a trajectory-level process rather than a sequence of independent token decisions. Existing analyses often focus on surface-level knobs such as temperature, step budget, block size, or scheduler choice, but these knobs do not explain why the same change can induce different behaviors across models. We analyze discrete diffusion decoding through high-influence commitment events and define an observed trajectory influence measure based on downstream entropy reduction over unresolved positions. Across Dream-v0-Instruct-7B and LLaDA-8B-Instruct on reasoning, code, and question-answering tasks, we find that influence is sparse, early relative to each model’s commit frontier, and stable under tested seed and step-budget variations. We further show that criticality emerges from the interaction between commit timing and token role, explaining why decoding knobs reshape trajectories in model-dependent ways. Finally, lightweight margin-based interventions validate the analysis by correcting diagnosed failure modes without additional forward passes.

paper.title: Causally Redundant Reasoning: A Dual-Disruption Test Framework for Measuring Shortcut Tendencies in Chain-of-Thought
paper.abstract: A chain-of-thought (CoT) rationale can be coherent and answer-consistent while remaining causally unused. We call this phenomenon shortcut reasoning: the model appears to reason through CoT, but its answer does not depend on the expressed trace. We formalize shortcut reasoning as causal redundancy and propose a dual-disruption framework for measuring shortcut tendencies in CoT by testing two complementary aspects of causal explanation: necessity and sufficiency. We operationalize them as two behavioral signals: whether the answer changes under CoT disruption, and whether the answer can be recovered from the CoT after masking the original input. We instantiate this framework with CORD (Causal Redundancy of Reasoning via Disruption), an instance-level score that combines both signals. The two axes reduce complementary ambiguities in single-axis tests: answer preservation under CoT disruption can reflect shortcut use or redundant truthful reasoning, while early answer recovery can reflect shortcut use or a compact truthful rationale. Across 6 models and 2 datasets, CORD reveals a training-paradigm effect: R1-Distill models exhibit roughly twice the shortcut tendency of non-distilled models, while the two axes capture related but distinct signals. Together, these results motivate joint tests of necessity and sufficiency for detecting shortcut tendencies that can remain hidden behind correct answers.

paper.title: MAS-Bai: Linguistically Informed Adaptive Multi-Agent Translation for Bowen-Script Bai

author.affiliation: Tianjin University and Kunming University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable for extremely low-resource languages whose writing systems conflict with high-resource pretraining priors. We study Bai-Chinese translation in the Bowen script, where Chinese characters are frequently borrowed phonetically rather than semantically, causing severe literal-translation hallucinations. We propose MAS-Bai, a linguistically informed adaptive multi-agent framework for Bowen-script Bai-Chinese translation. MAS-Bai routes each input through either a lightweight retrieval-translation path or a deeper philological path with etymological and syntactic agents, and uses cycle-consistency with a lightweight reverse translator as an inference-time reliability signal. We construct a 6,536-sentence Bai-Chinese corpus and evaluate on a 1,536-sentence test set. MAS-Bai achieves 16.23 BLEU and 62.15 COMET, improving over Standard RAG by 8.11 BLEU and 6.85 COMET. Forward LoRA, expert ablations and controlled routing experiments distinguish the roles of supervised adaptation, Bai-specific expertise and conditional routing. The largest gains occur on Bowen phonetic loans and divergent Bai word order, while human evaluation and reverse-verifier analyses support the automatic results.

paper.title: ChronoClinQA: A Longitudinal Multi-Admission Benchmark for Clinical Reasoning over Electronic Health Records
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering benchmarks, yet existing evaluations remain limited in assessing longitudinal clinical reasoning across multiple hospital admissions. We introduce ChronoClinQA, a large-scale benchmark for longitudinal clinical reasoning grounded in multi-admission electronic health records. Built from longitudinal discharge summaries in MIMIC-IV-Note, ChronoClinQA contains 15,067 QA pairs spanning six clinically grounded reasoning dimensions and three complementary question formats: open-ended, adversarial, and unanswerable multiple-choice questions. Each instance requires reasoning over temporally accumulated patient trajectories, with contexts averaging over 16K tokens across up to eight hospital admissions. Experiments on both general-purpose and medical LLMs reveal substantial performance degradation in longitudinal and adversarial settings, highlighting persistent challenges in integrating cross-admission evidence and in temporal clinical reasoning. Our findings position ChronoClinQA as a challenging benchmark for advancing clinically grounded long-context reasoning in medical LLMs.

paper.title: BackendForge: Benchmarking Agentic End-to-End Code Generation with Backend Services

author.affiliation: Peking University and Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center

Beijing Tongming Lake Information Technology Application Innovation Center, Fudan University Institute of Systems for Advanced Computing, Shanghai Institute of Systems for Open Computing and Key Lab of HCST (PKU), MOE; SCS, Peking University

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in agentic coding settings, where they can inspect files, execute commands, run tests, observe failures, and iteratively revise code. This shift raises a central evaluation question: can an agentic LLM generate an end-to-end software artifact that is both deployable and behaviorally correct under execution? Backend services provide a controlled but realistic substrate for this evaluation. Their APIs expose application-level executable semantics, and deployed behavior can be checked deterministically against an OpenAPI contract through black-box HTTP interactions. We introduce , a benchmark of 56 contract-defined backend generation tasks rewritten from real open-source applications. Given a visible specification and an OpenAPI contract, an LLM must generate a Dockerized service that is built, deployed, and evaluated only through HTTP tests. To strengthen evaluation without introducing hidden requirements, uses a test agent and a code agent to co-evolve the test oracle and reference service, where the test agent proposes specification-grounded backend tests and the code agent repairs the reference implementation. Although the best-performing model, GPT-5.5, succeeds on 55.4% of tasks under the base oracle, it succeeds on only 28.6% under the final oracle. This gap suggests that current LLMs can implement many local API behaviors, but still struggle to produce complete backend services.

paper.title: OriGround: Orientation-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
paper.abstract: Zero-shot 3D visual grounding (3DVG) aims to localize a referred object in a 3D scene without task-specific grounding supervision. Existing training-free methods commonly reason over object categories, centers, and bounding boxes, but these representations do not encode the local reference frames needed to interpret viewpoint-dependent expressions such as left of, behind, or facing the door. We propose OriGround, an orientation-aware neuro-symbolic framework that explicitly models object-centric orientations and infers observer viewpoints for zero-shot 3DVG. OriGround parses each query into a viewpoint-aware symbolic program, estimates object-centric orientation bases from multi-view observations, performs anchor- and observer-specific geometric relation scoring, and constructs a reference-frame-aligned visual prompt for final VLM-based disambiguation. On Nr3D, OriGround improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 8.4 points in overall accuracy, with larger gains of 8.9 points on hard queries and 5.6 points on view-dependent queries. On ScanRefer, OriGround further improves overall Acc@0.5 by 17.3 points over VLM-Grounder. Project page: https://origround.github.io/

paper.title: Aligning LLMs for Crystal Material Design: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning and Model Merging
paper.abstract: Conditional crystal generation requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce Crystal Strings with discrete and continuous variables while satisfying composition, symmetry, and property constraints. Desired regions are often sparse in supervised data, while retraining for each objective preference is costly. We present a verifier-grounded framework combining label-free Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) and Model Merging (MM). TTRL performs one batch-level, partially transductive adaptation per property using composition, symmetry, and learned band-gap rewards, without target reference structures. Property-specific experts are interpolated to navigate bounded symmetry–band-gap trade-offs without retraining intermediate policies. On MP-20, TTRL improves symmetry control, band-gap accuracy, and compositional fidelity over High-Precision SFT and Standard RL, and is competitive with diffusion and preference-aligned baselines. In a held-out high-band-gap region, TTRL generalizes to test prompts unseen during adaptation, reducing the mean squared error between surrogate-predicted and target band gaps by 52% relative to standard reinforcement learning under best-of-ten sampling. An independent band-gap predictor shows consistent gains, while density functional theory calculations further assess selected candidates. Similar gains with Qwen3.5-9B provide cross-backbone evidence. Model Merging recovers competitive two-objective trade-offs from two endpoint experts without additional RL, enabling efficient adaptation and preference control for structured scientific generation.

paper.title: Beyond Refusal: Constructive Communication Rewriting for Harmful User Language
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support effective and constructive human-to-human communication. A key scenario is helping users express difficult intents, such as criticism and boundary setting without harmful language. Existing safety refusal and detoxification rewriting methods either block harmful responses or inadequately preserve the user’s communicative intent and speaker style. Therefore, we propose constructive communication rewriting, which aims to rewrite harmful utterances in dialogue into safer and more constructive language while preserving user intent and style. To instantiate this task, we construct a large-scale dataset of realistic multi-user conversations by modeling both user persona and harm-inducing contexts. We further use Nonviolent Communication-inspired strategies to guide the rewriting process. Building on this dataset, we develop CoRe, a small, specialized LLM fine-tuned through a two-stage distillation process. CoRe achieves substantially higher harmlessness than strong general-purpose LLMs while maintaining competitive faithfulness and remaining efficient for real-time communication. Our project is released at the following link[<https://github.com/wsfwww/Beyond-Refusal-Constructive-Communication-Rewriting-for-Harmful-User-Language>.].

paper.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: **(I) Linear Separability**: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; **(II) Depth Localization**: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; **(III) Hierarchical Consistency**: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and **(IV) Directional Asymmetry**: reinforcing the model’s implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures. Code is available at [anonymous link](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Diagnosing-Knowledge-Conflict-C78D/).

paper.title: ABSOL: Aggregated Bayesian Subsampling Orchestrated with LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as natural-language interfaces to structured data, yet they remain unreliable when answers require consistent evidence conditioning, dependency-aware reasoning, and uncertainty estimation. Bayesian networks provide an explicit probabilistic reasoning layer, but learning useful structures from data remains costly and fragile at scale. We introduce ABSOL, a hybrid LLM-guided Bayesian network structure-learning framework that uses LLMs as bounded semantic guides. Across five discrete BN benchmarks spanning 27 to 1041 nodes, ABSOL is the only evaluated method to produce a viable graph on every benchmark, and achieves the highest Edge F1 on every benchmark larger than 27 nodes with GPT-5.4. The four LLM augmentations, which contribute complementary semantic evidence to the statistical backbone, improve Edge F1 over the non-LLM aggregation backbone by +0.23 on average. Complementary post-hoc refinement experiments suggest that these gains depend in part on limiting the LLM’s authority over the final structure. Together, these results show that language-derived semantic knowledge can substantially improve scalable probabilistic structure learning when used as bounded guidance within a statistically grounded reasoning pipeline.

paper.title: Before the First Token: Jailbreak Detection with Attention Probes
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are deployed with safety guardrails, yet jailbreak attacks and malicious prompts keep bypassing them. Re-aligning an LLM each time a new attack appears is more expensive than crafting attacks, so jailbreak detection is increasingly framed as a pre-processing step: a cheap detector filters out a malicious prompt before it reaches the LLM. This need is reinforced by multilingual attacks, where simply translating a prompt to another language can bypass the guardrails. Our goal is to find whether internal representations of a frozen LLM already separate malicious from benign prompts, and whether such a signal is resilient against translation. We study two types of detectors that require no fine-tuning of the LLM: a logistic-regression classifier over whole-sentence embeddings, and a probe-based detector that trains one logistic-regression probe per attention head on the attention activations of the last input token. They need at most a single forward pass. Our experiments show that both match or outperform strong sentence-embedding detectors and off-the-shelf baselines, specially under translation. The probes degrade more gracefully on higher-resource languages and remain competitive on lower-resource ones. Our results indicate that a frozen LLM linearly encodes whether an incoming prompt is malicious in a small set of mid-to-late layers. Per-head attention probes thus offer a defence that can be cheaply retrained as new attacks emerge, without touching the underlying model.

paper.title: KARMA: Karma-Aligned Reward Model Adaptation
paper.abstract: Human communication depends on implicit social signals where effectiveness is shaped by tone, context, and conversational norms rather than semantic content alone. We introduce KARMA (Karma-Aligned Reward Model Adaptation), a framework for LLM learning of context-sensitive conversational behavior from large-scale social media data. KARMA trains a reward model on Reddit conversations to predict response valuation conditioned on context, and uses this signal to fine-tune language models via reinforcement learning to improve performance on pragmatics-mediated tasks. Critically, we find that the highest performing reward model does not lead to better downstream model alignment: a reward model relying exclusively on conversational context was a worse predictor of Reddit karma but yielded substantially better downstream performance. We evaluate the effects of KARMA applied to a downstream model with and without direct exposure to the social media data. The resulting models show improved pragmatics-mediated behaviors with largely mitigated undesirable side effects.

paper.title: ZeoAgent: A Closed-Loop Compiler for Coupled OSDA–Condition Generation in Zeolite Synthesis

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

paper.abstract: Zeolite synthesis requires a structured recipe that specifies an organic structure-directing agent (OSDA), gel composition, crystallization temperature, and reaction time. General-purpose language models can draft such recipes, but their outputs often fail domain checks, producing invalid SMILES strings, missing condition fields, or temperature–time schedules inconsistent with local Arrhenius trends. We present ZeoAgent, a closed-loop compiler for machine-checkable zeolite synthesis recipes. ZeoAgent represents each generated recipe as a typed record and verifies it through deterministic field-level checks. At each iteration, a compact yet diverse set of retrieved synthesis precedents guides the next draft. When a field fails validation, the corresponding error code is returned to the model for targeted revision. Recipes passing these checks are calibrated with a local Arrhenius fit before final ranking. In condition-only experiments, the recorded OSDA is supplied and only the hydrothermal-condition fields are predicted. On the archived model outputs, ZeoAgent attains 99.7% RDKit parseability, compared with 81.7% for Qwen3-8B. Typed feedback raises repair pass@5 from 68.3% to 72.0%, and PGC reduces high-residual schedules under its fitted local Arrhenius self-consistency diagnostic from 77.0% to 5.4%.

paper.title: How Much Retrieval Depth Does Your Reader Need? Noise Ceilings and Cost-Effectiveness in Table QA

author.affiliation: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

paper.abstract: Retrieval and reading in Table QA are typically optimized in isolation, leaving no principled way to balance retrieval precision against reader capacity. We ask: how much retrieval depth does a reader actually need? Across three benchmarks (E2E-WTQ, OTT-QA, and FeTaQA) and four LLMs, we conduct a controlled single-table stress test that guarantees the inclusion of the gold table while increasing retrieval depth to K = 50 using soft or hard distractors. This design isolates reader noise tolerance from retrieval failure. We find that the Noise Ceiling is set jointly by task type, reader, and distractor condition, and is not predictable from reader class alone. With hard negatives, every reader has a Noise Ceiling of K ≤ 5 for long-form answer generation, favoring precision-oriented retrieval. By contrast, several readers remain robust through K = 50 on short-answer and multi-hop QA, depending on the distractor condition. A reader-side Cost per Success analysis further shows that the trade-off between robustness and inference cost varies across readers and distractor conditions. Overall, these results establish the reader’s condition-specific Noise Ceiling as a concrete operating target for balancing retrieval depth against precision in controlled single-table QA.

paper.title: Sparsity in Linear Attention Models: Bregman Testing Time Learning

author.affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Linear attention architectures enable efficient long-context modeling by compressing sequence history into a fixed-size memory state. However, dense key value updates can overload the state as the context grows, causing memory collisions and degraded retrieval. Existing methods rely on memory decay, rank reduction, or heuristic routing to reduce interference, but they largely preserve dense online updates and do not explicitly control the structural complexity of memory. We introduce BregNet, a linear sequence architecture that formulates associative memory updates as a regularized online regression problem. Based on Linearized Bregman Iteration (LBI), BregNet decouples memory into a continuous dual accumulator and a structurally sparse primal state. The dual state records incoming information, while the sparse primal state keeps only important associations and removes noise through soft shrinkage. Experiments show that BregNet matches strong linear baselines in language modeling even with high memory sparsity. In this way, BregNet prevents the memory state from being overloaded by dense and interfering updates.

paper.title: Beyond Output Consistency: Diagnosing Representation-Level Causal Controllability in LLM Persona Simulation
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as persona-conditioned agents in social simulation and behavioral research. However, output-level consistency does not reveal whether persona specifications genuinely control model behavior or merely induce surface-level responses. We reframe persona simulation as a representation-level causal controllability problem and decompose persona control into a chain from persona specification to internal representation and observable behavior. This view enables us to diagnose two hidden failure mechanisms: whether distinct persona interventions collapse into similar internal states, and whether internal persona differences fail to transmit to behavior. We formalize these mechanisms through intervention separability and transmission fidelity, and combine them into a global controllability metric, \mathrm{EI}_g. Experiments on controlled synthetic systems and real LLMs show that our framework recovers known failure modes and, as a relative diagnostic under a fixed operationalization, reveals model-specific controllability profiles missed by output-level consistency and correlation-based metrics.

paper.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling

author.affiliation: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Oregon State University

paper.abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces *TopicMerge*, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

paper.title: MUSE: Multi-Domain Chinese User Simulation via Self-Evolving Profiles and Rubric-Guided Alignment
paper.abstract: User simulators are essential for the scalable training and evaluation of interactive AI systems. However, existing approaches often rely on shallow user profiling, struggle to maintain persona consistency over long interactions, and are largely limited to English or single-domain settings. We present MUSE, a multi-domain Chinese user simulation framework designed to generate human-like, controllable, and behaviorally consistent responses. First, we propose Iterative Profile Self-Evolution (IPSE), which gradually optimizes user profiles by comparing and reasoning discrepancies between simulated trajectories and real dialogue behaviors. We then apply Role-Reversal Supervised Fine-Tuning to improve local response realism and human-like expression. To enable fine-grained behavioral alignment, we further train a specialized rubric-based reward model and incorporate it into rubric-guided multi-turn reinforcement learning, which optimizes the simulator at the dialogue level and enhances long-horizon behavioral consistency. Experiments show that MUSE consistently outperforms strong baselines in both utterance-level and session-level evaluations, generating responses that are more realistic, coherent, and persona-consistent over extended interactions.

paper.title: Ask or Answer: A Decision Framework for Multi-Turn Health Misinformation Intervention
paper.abstract: Correcting health misinformation in dialogue requires more than producing a factual rebuttal: users differ in what they know, what they believe, and what they need to hear, so an effective intervention often depends on first asking the right clarifying question. Yet existing methods either respond immediately or probe indiscriminately, treating clarification as either unnecessary or always beneficial. We propose Reward-Optimized Probe-and-Respond (RO-PnR), a framework that learns when asking is worth its cost. At each turn, RO-PnR chooses between probing for more information and committing to a final correction, guided by a turn-level reward that weighs the expected gain from probing against its interaction cost. To capture how user heterogeneity affects probing value, we model each simulated user with a latent state along health literacy and belief commitment. Experiments show that RO-PnR achieves the highest cost-adjusted utility across three health-misinformation datasets and three base models, using ∼30% fewer turns than always-probe baselines.

paper.title: FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework
paper.abstract: Powered by advances in LLMs and autonomous agents, deep research has become one of the most widely adopted agentic products. However, most deep research systems write general-purpose reports, which are inadequate for financial deep research. Financial research demands specialized knowledge to analyze historical patterns and forecast upcoming events. Automating financial deep research therefore requires both a layered harness to drive the research agent and a verifiable, point-in-time benchmark that prevents leakage of future information. We present FinanceHarness, a harness that runs finance-oriented tools and practitioner-guided workflows, automating financial deep research end to end: environment and data construction, the agent execution loop, and reward modeling. We further propose FinanceGym comprising thesisdriven research questions and rubrics that combine pre-cutoff and post-cutoff criteria. Professional expert validation yields an 82% pass rate. With the same open-weight backbone, FinanceHarness improves the overall rubric score from 25.3% to 32.4%, demonstrating the effectiveness of our specialized harness design. However, even pairing FinanceHarness with the most cutting edge LLM (e.g. Opus-5), the FinanceHarness score is below 45%, showing that it is a challenging benchmark for financial deep research. FinanceGym and FinanceHarness code are publicaly available.

paper.title: Generate What You Can Trust: Content Credibility in Generative Recommenders
paper.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items with semantic IDs (i.e., discrete token sequences) and generates target item tokens as recommendations. Despite its promising results, existing methods predominantly optimize for accuracy while neglecting the credibility of the recommendations they generate. This oversight inevitably exposes users to uncredible content (e.g., fake news) with serious societal consequences, including user distrust, reputation harm to platforms, and broader social instability. To address this critical yet underexplored challenge, we propose CreGR, the first credible GR model that jointly tackles content credibility across the two core stages of GR: tokenization and generation. In the tokenization stage, we design a new credibility-aware tokenizer that explicitly encourages the model to learn discriminative tokens respectively for credible and uncredible items, thereby disentangling credibility signals at the token level. Building on this, in the generation stage, we propose a novel accuracy-preserving and credibility-oriented generator grounded in discrete diffusion. Specifically, we introduce an asymmetric masking probability reduction strategy that selectively diminishes the contribution of tokens associated with uncredible content to the generation process, while leaving tokens encoding user preference signals unaffected so as to preserve recommendation accuracy. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CreGR.

paper.title: F-GraphRAG: Preserving Fine-Grained Facts in Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates factual hallucinations in Large Language Models but struggles with complex reasoning. Graph-based RAG (GraphRAG) addresses this gap yet can exhibit a failure pattern: semantic compression during triple extraction may reduce the preservation of fine-grained facts such as precise quantities, temporal constraints, and entity attributes. We formalize this limitation as the Fine-Grained Fact Retrieval (FGFR) cascade and introduce stage-wise diagnostic metrics, including R_rep, R_sel, and R_end, to quantify information loss. To stress-test FGFR, we construct a diagnostic evaluation suite from classic novels that provide controlled long-context scenarios containing explicit entity attributes and temporal constraints. F-GraphRAG, our framework, features a granularity-aware extractor that preserves atomic details and an information-preserving filter that counters global importance bias. On this evaluation suite, F-GraphRAG outperforms GraphRAG by 12.6% in accuracy while using 33.8% fewer relationships, and achieves gains of 5.3–11.2% across nine public benchmarks. These results suggest that improving evidence completeness can provide a more effective alternative to increasing graph connectivity.

paper.title: Visual Search Augmented Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Attribute Value Extraction from Product Videos

author.affiliation: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

paper.abstract: Existing approaches to visual attribute value extraction (AVE) primarily rely on static product images, failing to capture temporal cues, multi-angle views and fine-grained visual details. Directly applying video vision-language models (VLMs) to product AVE results in limited performance due to the lack of domain knowledge, and fine-tuning them requires extensive high-quality data and substantial computational resources. Thus, we propose visual search augmented chain-of-thought reasoning (ViS-CoT), a training-free, plug-and-play pipeline that can be easily applied to any open-source video VLM for video-to-text AVE in e-Commerce. Specifically, ViS-CoT employs visual clustering to identify representative frames, followed by visual search to retrieve semantically similar product knowledge that can enrich attribute cues. Next, an interleaved CoT reasoning module iteratively refines reasoning through visually-aligned auxiliary texts derived from captioning and automatic speech recognition. Finally, the integrated information guides the model toward accurate and fine-grained attribute predictions. Extensive experiments across 14 product categories on the VideoAVE dataset show that ViS-CoT consistently enhances multiple state-of-the-art video VLMs, achieving an average improvement of 17.91 percentage points in micro-F1.

paper.title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
paper.abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9×9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model’s "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

paper.title: Understanding Moral Reasoning Trajectories in Large Language Models: Toward Probing-Based Explainability

author.affiliation: Indiana University and Association for Computing Machinery

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in morally sensitive decision-making, yet how they organize ethical frameworks across reasoning steps remains underexplored. We introduce moral reasoning trajectories, sequences of ethical framework invocations across intermediate reasoning steps, and analyze their dynamics across six models and three benchmarks. We find that moral reasoning involves systematic multi-framework deliberation: 55.4–57.7% of consecutive steps involve framework switches, and only 16.4–17.8% of trajectories remain framework-consistent. Unstable trajectories remain 1.29× more susceptible to persuasive attacks (p = 0.015). At the representation level, linear probes localize framework-specific encoding to model-specific layers (layer 63/81 for Llama-3.3-70B; layer 17/81 for Qwen2.5-72B), achieving 16.8–22.2% lower KL divergence than the step-prior baseline. Activation steering applied during generation moves the framework-consistency–accuracy relationship, widening it for Qwen2.5-72B and erasing it for Llama-3.3-70B, and a probe-space layer sweep bounds the attainable drift reduction at 6.7–8.9%. We further propose a Moral Representation Consistency (MRC) metric whose underlying framework attributions are validated by human annotators (mean cosine similarity = 0.859), and we report what an automated coherence rater does and does not establish about it.

paper.title: Evaluating Second-Order Bias of LLMs Through Epistemic Entitlement

author.affiliation: EuroSafeAI and University of Toronto & Vector Institute
Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto

paper.abstract: Evaluations of social bias in LLMs largely focus on whether models generate or imply biased content. However, as LLMs are increasingly used as judges of bias, they may exhibit social biases in subtler ways in how they evaluate biased content, which current methods do not systematically capture. We call this second-order bias: social bias in an LLM’s judgment about social bias, which we evaluate through a novel, philosophically grounded reasoning task. Drawing on entitlement epistemology, we conceptualize bias as misplaced foundational knowledge that shapes an agent’s rational inquiry, and derive a logical reasoning task for LLMs to judge to whom a biased text is acceptable or non-acceptable. We develop two simple metrics to measure how biased LLM judges are in inferring demographics for acceptability without sufficient support, and how these inferences vary across groups targeted by biased texts. Evaluating open and closed models, we find that our task evades safety guardrails by surfacing bias in model judgment. It varies systematically across target groups, reflects implicit social maps, and shows how models are still triggered by demographic labels. Our work points to the need for LLM bias evaluation in judgment tasks and broadly, for more theoretically grounded approaches to bias evaluation in NLP. We release our code and model responses at https://github.com/uofthcdslab/second-order-bias.

paper.title: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable, Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents

author.affiliation: University of Bath and University of Oxford
University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh

paper.abstract: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train–test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepIntoStreams/OpenFinGym.git

paper.title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
paper.abstract: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored, even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After curating and hand-annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we create an LLM-labeled dataset of 25K passages, and finally, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, two RoBERTa-based models for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to \sim13M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find that narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data and narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources, topics, and formats in ways that current data curation practices neither measure nor account for.
